_metadata.description: Complete two-pass hierarchical interpretative layer for dcn2br-d1e796 (Bradwardine, De Causa Dei, Book I, Caput 1): 556 paragraph-level interpretations (pass 1, source_text_with_context) plus 41 div-level interpretations (pass 2, descendant_summaries) for the 40 Corollarium divs and the top-level Caput div. context_ids/input_ids never include <head> xml:ids, since headings are not indexed in the RDF graph.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e109.summary: Title paragraph giving the work, author, book, and chapter heading: Thomas Bradwardine, De Causa Dei, Book I, Chapter 1.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e127.summary: Marginal/rubric summary stating that the chapter will premise two suppositions: (1) God is supremely perfect and good, such that nothing more perfect or better could exist, and (2) there is no infinite regress among beings, but rather a single first member in every genus.
claims: God is supremely perfect and good, such that nothing more perfect or better is possible.
There is no infinite regress in beings; in every genus there is a single first.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e140.summary: Argues for the first supposition (God's supreme perfection and goodness) by appeal to authority: a chain of philosophical and patristic witnesses (Hermes Trismegistus, Aristotle's De Mundo, the Metaphysics, Boethius, the 24 philosophers' definitions of God, Anselm's Proslogion and Monologion, Richard of St. Victor, Augustine, and the Psalms) is marshaled to show universal consent that God is that than which nothing better can be thought or is.
claims: Universal philosophical and theological consensus affirms that nothing better than God can be conceived or exists.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e217.summary: Introduces the second supposition (no infinite regress; a first in every genus) and announces that, rather than resting on authority alone, a brief demonstrative sketch of both suppositions will follow, beginning with definitions of 'possible' and 'impossible' as freedom from or inclusion of formal contradiction, used as the basis for a positio-style argument concerning a term A.
claims: There is no infinite regress among beings; every genus has a first member.
'Possible' means that which does not per se and formally involve contradiction; 'impossible' is its negation.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e242.summary: Begins the formal demonstration proper: granting that it is possible for some A to exist, the argument moves from 'A can be' to 'A is' and further to 'A is necessary being,' on the ground that necessary being is more perfect and better than merely possible being, especially in something supremely perfect and good; possible being, by contrast, implies privation, imperfect potentiality, and corruptibility.
claims: Necessary being is more perfect and better than merely possible being.
Possible being entails privation, incomplete potentiality, and corruptibility, which necessary being excludes.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e279.summary: Supports the priority of act over potency (and so of necessary over merely possible being) with an extended array of Aristotelian and commentary authorities (Metaphysics IX, De Caelo), arguing that whatever is per se and independent of another is prior in nature and more perfect than what depends on another, and citing Averroes and Avicenna that necessary being has no cause and no equal or prior, while merely possible being does have a cause.
claims: Act is prior to and more perfect than potency, both in good things and (in a deteriorated sense) in bad things.
What exists per se and uncaused is prior in nature and more perfect than what depends on something else.
Necessary being has no cause and nothing equal to or prior to it; merely possible being has a cause.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e321.summary: Concludes that if A can exist, A can exist necessarily and per se, since necessary being per se is more perfect than being possible or being contingent on another; argues further that whatever is possible only once is possible always, and whatever is necessary per se once is necessary always, since a formally valid and necessary consequence can never fail.
claims: If A can exist, A can exist necessarily and through itself, since necessary-per-se being is more perfect than dependent being.
What is possible at one time is possible always; what is necessary per se at one time is necessary always.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e356.summary: Raises and addresses a further consideration about how a nature possible in itself could become necessary in itself, then explains that everything called 'possible' is so called through some power, either its own active/passive power or another's (as with future non-existent effects called possible through the power of their agents and patients), and that whatever is possible through some passive power is equally possible through some active power, since nothing can be acted upon or produced by nothing; Averroes is cited that possibility is only intelligible relative to agent and patient together.
claims: Anything called possible is possible only through some active or passive power, whether its own or another's.
Whatever is possible in respect of a passive power is also possible in respect of some active power, since nothing can suffer an effect that nothing can produce.
concepts: possibility relative to agent and patient

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e387.summary: Applies the preceding analysis of possibility to A itself: since A does not yet exist but can exist, it can exist only through the power of some other agent (having no power of its own, and nothing being able to bring itself from non-being to being); but no such other agent could exist, since anything other than A would be incomparably less than A and incapable of causing it; and if A were caused by another, A would not be God. Concludes that A cannot exist through any power whatsoever other than itself, so it is false and impossible that A not exist, and therefore true and necessary that A exists, and thus that God exists.
claims: A cannot come to exist through the power of anything other than itself, since nothing else could be adequate to cause it.
If A were caused by another, A would not be God.
It is true and necessary that A (God) exists.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e422.summary: Draws the conclusion that God exists and is so perfect and good that nothing more perfect or better could exist, then argues that the second supposition (no infinite regress; a first in every genus) follows from the first, since it is granted that to be first and supreme is more perfect and better than to be posterior, inferior, or merely equal to another; supports this with Aristotle's De Caelo (what is higher is more honorable and divine than what is lower, and what is prior is better than what is posterior) and no genus admits several equally first principles, citing Apocalypse 1 ("I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end").
claims: God exists and is supremely perfect, such that nothing more perfect or better could exist.
The second supposition (a single first in every genus, no infinite regress) follows from the first supposition.
To be first and supreme is more perfect than to be posterior, inferior, or merely equal.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e438.summary: Rubric introducing the moral corollary appended to the two suppositions: it contains 40 parts, each directed against one of 40 errors, the first of which is against Protagoras, who doubted that God exists.
claims: The corollary to the two suppositions contains 40 parts, each refuting a distinct error.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e445.summary: Transitional remark noting that, as if by corollary derivation ('porismatically') from the foregoing suppositions, many people can be seen to have erred in many ways and could be led back to the path of truth, provided that this truth (the preceding demonstration) is allowed to lead the way.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e454.summary: Applies the foregoing demonstration directly against Protagoras, citing Lactantius's Divinae Institutiones as reporting that Protagoras called the gods into doubt.
claims: Protagoras doubted the existence of the gods, per Lactantius's testimony.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e467.summary: Rubric heading for the second part of the corollary, directed against Diagoras and the 'fool' of the Psalms who deny that God exists.
claims: This part refutes those who deny outright that God exists (Diagoras, and the biblical 'fool').

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e472.summary: Calls on Diagoras, who (per the same source as before) later excluded the gods, and on the 'fool' of the Psalms who foolishly said 'There is no God,' to come to their senses in light of the preceding demonstration.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e485.summary: Rubric for the third corollary part, directed against those who doubt or deny that God really, equivalently, or eminently possesses every power and every good, and universally whatever it is better to have than not to have, and does not always possess every kind of goodness, or is not always supremely happy, blessed, and actual such that nothing more happy, blessed, or actual could be.
claims: This part addresses denial that God possesses, really or eminently, every power, good, and supreme actual beatitude.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e511.summary: Addresses those who grant that God exists but doubt or deny that God really/equivalently/eminently possesses every power and good; argues from the first supposition that God is necessarily supremely perfect (so nothing better could be lacking), and from the priority of act over potency (established earlier) that God's supreme actuality entails supreme possession of all goodness, since where any potentiality is posited in God it must, by earlier parts, be good, so no unrealized potentiality but only supreme actuality is in God.
claims: If God lacked any perfection or good, something more perfect than God would be possible, contrary to the first supposition.
God's supreme actuality (act being superior to potency) entails that God possesses all goodness with no residual potentiality.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e556.summary: Rubric for the fourth corollary part, directed against those who deny that God's power and goodness are simply infinite.
claims: This part refutes denial that God's power and goodness are unqualifiedly infinite.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e561.summary: Argues that if any of God's power or goodness were merely finite, it could be increased, and so something better than God would be possible, which the first supposition forbids; illustrates the coherence of 'absolute possibility without natural possibility' by analogy with geometers' supposition that a straight line can be extended indefinitely and Euclid's construction of circles, and with natural philosophers' supposition of indefinitely divisible media.
claims: If any divine power or goodness were merely finite, it could be increased, contrary to God's supreme perfection.
Something can be per se/absolutely possible (non-contradictory) without being naturally possible, as illustrated by geometrical and physical analogies.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e593.summary: Rubric for the fifth corollary part, directed against those who say God is not fully self-sufficient but needs something else.
claims: This part refutes the claim that God lacks full self-sufficiency and needs something outside himself.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e598.summary: Refutes the claim that God needs something else, arguing from the two preceding parts and the first supposition that sufficiency is evidently a good, and marshaling authorities (Aristotle's De Mundo, De Caelo, the 24 Philosophers' definitions, the Hebrew divine name Shaddai as explained by Maimonides, and Jerome's letter to Marcella on the ten Hebrew names of God) to show God is called self-sufficient and lacking nothing.
claims: Sufficiency (needing nothing outside oneself) is a good, and therefore belongs to God by the first supposition and by authority (including the Hebrew name Shaddai).

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e635.summary: Rubric for the sixth corollary part, directed against those who believe God is only contingently (not necessarily) supremely perfect and God, and who hold God to be mutable, subject to anger, appeasement, sadness, joy, or other passions, and who opine that 'God' is an accidental rather than a strictly essential name.
claims: This part refutes contingency, mutability, passibility in God, and the view that 'God' names an accident rather than the essence.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e651.summary: Refutes the view that God is only contingently supremely perfect and is mutable or passible: argues from the first supposition that necessary supreme perfection is more perfect than contingent perfection, so God cannot be mutable toward better (already supremely good), worse (necessarily so), or an equal state (superfluous change); considers and rejects possible motives for change (self-preservation, benefiting creatures) as implying dependency and lack of self-sufficiency contrary to earlier parts; concludes God is not an accidental but an essential name, since otherwise God could cease to be God.
claims: God is necessarily, not merely contingently, supremely perfect.
God cannot change for better, worse, or to an equal state.
'God' names the divine essence, not an accident, since otherwise God could fail to be God.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e706.summary: Rubric for the seventh corollary part, directed against those who deny that God is omnipotent actively while being 'nullipotent' passively, i.e., incapable of being acted upon by anything else.
claims: This part defends God's active omnipotence together with total passive impassibility (inability to be acted upon).

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e713.summary: Argues that God's active omnipotence follows from the third and fourth corollary parts (on plenitude and infinite power), and that God's impassibility (inability to be acted on) follows because active power is itself a good that cannot be acted upon by another without becoming mutable, which the immediately preceding part excludes; God's impassibility is thus demonstrable in the same way as God's immutability.
claims: God is actively omnipotent.
God cannot be acted upon by anything else, since that would entail mutability, already excluded.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e732.summary: Rubric for the eighth corollary part, directed against those who hold that God is not a rational substance and power possessing intellect and free will, actually knowing and willing, and who deny that the divine will is universally efficacious, i.e., unable to be impeded, frustrated, or defective in any way.
claims: This part defends that God is a rational substance with intellect and free will, actually knowing and willing, and that God's will is universally and unfailingly efficacious.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e743.summary: Argues from the first supposition that God is substance rather than accident (substance being more perfect), and rational rather than irrational, hence possessing intellect and free will (shown by the third corollary part); argues actual (not merely habitual) knowing and willing are more perfect, so belong to God; argues the divine will's universal efficacy is more perfect than being impedible, frustrable, or defective, reinforced by an extended argument that supreme beatitude (established in the third part) requires having all one justly wills, since (per Aristotle's Ethics I and Boethius's Consolation III) beatitude is a self-sufficient, perfect good lacking nothing, and God, being always supremely beatified, never wants anything unfulfilled; concludes that if God willed and could not accomplish what he willed, he would not be omnipotent but impotent, against the seventh part, citing the 24 Philosophers' definition that God's will has divine power.
claims: God, as substance and as rational, possesses intellect and free will.
God's knowing and willing are actual, not merely habitual, since act is more perfect than habit.
God's will is universally efficacious (unimpedible, unfrustrable, undefective).
Supreme beatitude requires having all that one justly wills; God, being supremely beatified, is never denied his will.
If God willed something he could not bring about, he would be impotent rather than omnipotent.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e825.summary: Rubric for the ninth corollary part, directed against those who believe God is ignorant of anything.
claims: This part refutes the view that God is ignorant of anything.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e830.summary: Refutes the view (attributed to some readings of Aristotle's Metaphysics XII, Averroes, Avicenna, Algazel, Cicero's De Divinatione, and objecting biblical voices in Job and the Psalms) that God knows nothing outside himself or lacks foreknowledge of future things, arguing summarily that approving/disapproving wisdom, knowledge, and discernment are the most excellent virtues, correctable by the third and fourth corollary parts on God's actuality and infinite power.
claims: Some philosophers and even biblical voices are read as denying that God knows anything outside himself or has foreknowledge; this is refuted by God's supreme actuality and infinite virtue already established.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e859.summary: Argues God knows himself actually, since self-knowledge is more perfect than ignorance of oneself, and by the first supposition God possesses whatever is more perfect; also God's supreme beatitude (third part) requires that he perceive and know himself to be blessed. Concludes God knows himself perfectly, completely, and with respect to all his conditions, relations, and circumstances, since there is nothing of which God is not the prior, superior, better, and more perfect, or the cause, principle, and end.
claims: God knows himself actually, since self-knowledge is more perfect than ignorance.
God knows himself perfectly and completely, according to his essence and all his relations, since he exceeds and causes all else.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e888.summary: Argues by dilemma that God must know distinctly (not merely confusedly) that something other than himself exists, since distinct knowledge is more actual and perfect than confused knowledge, and it would be absurd for God to be ignorant of anything besides himself; further argues that since God perfectly knows himself as infinitely powerful and omnipotent (per earlier parts), he knows that he can make, destroy, and move things outside himself, and knows this eternally rather than newly, since whatever he knows he knew beforehand that he could and would do.
claims: God knows distinctly, not merely confusedly, that things other than himself exist.
God knows eternally, not newly, whatever he can and will do.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e915.summary: Argues that if God did not know some truths, he could desire to know them (since every rational nature naturally desires to know), and having a universally efficacious will he could then come to know them, but not newly, since that would compromise his being always maximally actual, knowing, perfect, blessed, and immutable; concludes God necessarily and eternally knows all truths.
claims: God necessarily and eternally knows all truths.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e928.summary: Argues that although some things are base, knowledge of them is precious and noble (as natural philosophers who study animals attest), and God, who cannot be debased, therefore knows all things perfectly and distinctly, since every nature and essence is in itself good and beautiful and so fitting for a good God to know; asks rhetorically how it would befit even a noble human nature to know only baser things and not know the higher, implying it is more fitting that God know all.
claims: Knowledge of base things is itself noble and precious; God, who cannot be debased, knows all things, base or noble, perfectly and distinctly.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e959.summary: Argues briefly that God could not fittingly reward his worshipers and punish or reward the good and wicked according to their deserts if he were ignorant of those deserts.
claims: God's just recompense of merit and demerit presupposes his knowledge of those merits.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e966.summary: Argues from the fittingness of prayer that it is better, more orderly, and more fitting for God, who by the first and second suppositions presides wisely over the world, to be able to hear and answer supplications, reward the good, and correct or punish the wicked; otherwise hope, love, and fear would be undermined and the whole order of human affairs toward God and neighbor disrupted. Addresses and dismisses the Aristotelian/Averroan worries (that particulars are base or infinite and hence unknowable to God) by appeal to God's infinity exceeding any multitude, and answers the worry that knowledge of mutable singulars would make God's knowledge mutable by noting God knows them not passively/alterably (as humans do) but actively, likened to a fixed eye seeing the parts of a flowing river succeed one another.
claims: It is fitting that God hear prayers and justly reward or punish, on pain of undermining the moral order.
God's infinity exceeds any finite or infinite multitude of particulars, so their number does not limit his knowledge.
God's knowledge of changeable singulars does not make his knowledge itself changeable, since he knows them actively rather than by being acted upon.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1035.summary: Rubric for the tenth corollary part, directed against those who imagine God to be composed of human or other members or of any diverse parts, and who deny that God is a most simple, most indivisible substance without any composition, partibility, or magnitude (bodily magnitude).
claims: This part defends God's absolute simplicity, indivisibility, and lack of any (especially corporeal) magnitude or composition.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1046.summary: Argues against anthropomorphic composition of God: if God had parts, he could be pulled apart and separated, hence changed, diminished, or corrupted, which prior parts exclude; God's supreme perfection, sufficiency, and beatitude would be compromised if he necessarily depended on parts; existing per se and sufficiently is more actual and powerful than being supported by external props, and God is supremely actual and powerful. Further argues that any composing part or unifying form would be, contrary to the first supposition, naturally prior to God; and that composition from homogeneous parts would make animals or the heavens more perfectly composed than God (against the first supposition and third part), while composition from heterogeneous parts would entail unequal dignity among the parts, so not all could be infinitely perfect (against the fourth part).
claims: If God were composed of parts, he could be divided, changed, or corrupted, contrary to his established perfection and immutability.
Any part or unifying form composing God would be naturally prior to God, contrary to the first supposition.
Composition (whether of homogeneous or heterogeneous parts) is incompatible with God's supreme and equal perfection in every respect.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1092.summary: Continues the argument against divine composition with a further dilemma: if God were composed of parts, either some part would itself be simply and wholly infinite in perfection or none would be; if some part were, it alone would be God and the other parts superfluous (against the third part); if none were, that contradicts the fourth part (infinite perfection), and any part could then be more perfect, again against the first supposition. Also argues the parts would be either finite or infinite in number, and either way God's total perfection would be finite or augmentable, which the first supposition and second supposition (against infinite quantity/aggregation) both exclude.
claims: Whether God's hypothetical parts are finite or infinite in perfection or in number, composition entails either a finite or augmentable total perfection, contrary to God's established supreme and infinite perfection.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1124.summary: Rubric for the eleventh corollary part, directed against the Sabians and their wise men who worship the heavens as God.
claims: This part refutes worship of the heavens as divine.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1129.summary: Rebukes the Sabians (per Averroes on Metaphysics I) who, believing the heavens eternal and self-moved, worshiped the heavens as needing no nobler principle; corrects them by the immediately preceding argument against composition/finitude, and further notes the heavens have only finite power, are mutable, alterable, illuminable and obscurable, and lack many possible perfections, hence are not God; cites Averroes's own admission that finding the absolutely first mover is exceedingly difficult, which was the wise men's point of error.
claims: The heavens are not eternal-in-themselves nor self-sufficient, but finite in power, mutable, and lacking possible perfections, hence not God.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1157.summary: Rubric for the twelfth corollary part, directed against worshipers of the Sun, Moon, Mars, Jupiter, or any celestial sign or part of the heavens.
claims: This part refutes worship of any celestial body or sign as divine.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1164.summary: Extends the immediately preceding refutation of worship of the heavens as a whole to worshipers of the Sun, Moon, and planets or any celestial sign, on the same grounds (finitude, mutability, lack of possible perfections).
claims: Worship of the Sun, Moon, or planets is refuted for the same reasons as worship of the heavens as a whole.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1180.summary: Rubric for the thirteenth corollary part, directed against those who fashion temporal gods for themselves out of humans, animals, trees, fire, or any such thing.
claims: This part refutes the deification of humans, animals, trees, fire, or other creaturely things.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1187.summary: Condemns ancient pagans who made living or dead humans into gods, citing Plato's Timaeus on the genealogy of Ocean, Tethys, Saturn, Rhea, Jupiter, Juno, and other legendary deities descended from them.
claims: Ancient pagans deified humans, living and dead, as reported in classical mythology and history.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1220.summary: Cites Roman religious history via Augustine's City of God (reporting the pontiff Scaevola's threefold classification of gods — poetic, philosophical, and civil/political) to show that even Roman authorities admitted that figures like Hercules, Aesculapius, Castor, and Pollux were once mere humans, not true gods, though this truth was politically suppressed as harmful for the populace to know.
claims: Even Roman civil religion's own authorities (per Scaevola, via Augustine) admitted that deified heroes were originally human.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1238.summary: Catalogues further instances of idolatry: the ancient Babylonians who worshiped a dragon (per Daniel 14), and the ancient Egyptians who worshiped a bull as a god (the Apis cult), quoting Solinus's detailed description of the Apis rites, and noting later authors (Papias, Isidore) who identify Apis as a bull consecrated to Serapis, whose image the Israelites are said to have fashioned for themselves in the desert (an allusion to the golden calf).
claims: Idolatrous animal worship (the dragon of Babylon, the Apis bull of Egypt) is attested in Scripture and classical sources, and is linked to the biblical golden calf.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1287.summary: Cites Marco Polo's account of contemporary (medieval) bull-worship in the Indian kingdom of Var, where cattle are considered sacred, not killed or eaten, their fat used ritually, and their hair carried into battle as a protective talisman.
claims: Contemporary bull-worship, attested by Marco Polo, is a further instance of the same idolatrous error.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1305.summary: Recounts, via the legendary epistolary tradition of Alexander to Aristotle, the story of the oracular Trees of the Sun and Moon in India, worshiped and consulted by Alexander through an Indian priest, who deliver true but ominous prophecies of Alexander's death in Babylon by poison and the sorrowful fates of his mother and sisters — presented as another instance of tree-worship among the ancient Indians.
claims: Tree-worship (the oracular Trees of the Sun and Moon) is attested in the Alexander romance tradition as another instance of idolatry.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1381.summary: Refutes fire-worship (choosing it as god because it seems to conquer and consume other things) and worship of a mere human as God: since God is necessary being (per the first supposition), no temporal, generable, or corruptible thing is God; argues by dilemma that if a mere human were God, either he is God from himself (in which case any human could equally become God) or from another (in which case that other, not he, is God); concludes it is irrational to worship a beast, tree, fire, or any non-rational thing that knows nothing, has an inefficacious will, and is weak, needy, passible, and destructible, contrary to the first supposition, and appeals to shame that anyone would set an irrational, ignoble nature subject to himself above himself in the order of dignity.
claims: Fire cannot be God, since God is necessary being and fire is generable/corruptible.
No mere human can be God, whether self-made (in which case any human could equally self-deify) or made God by another (in which case the other, not he, would be God).
It is irrational and shameful to worship an irrational, weak, needy, destructible creature as one's God.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1397.summary: Rubric for the fourteenth corollary part, directed against the frivolous who worship a burdensome multitude of equal gods of the same species or nature.
claims: This part refutes polytheism positing multiple equal gods of one nature.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1404.summary: Argues against polytheism (multiple equal gods of one nature) that if the first supposition is true, one God suffices completely, since insufficiency would imply some lacking perfection (against the third and seventh parts); cites Aristotle's De Caelo that it is not necessary to posit infinite elements, since finite principles suffice, and argues that positing many equal gods either renders the one insufficient (contrary to their own worship of him) or wrongly divides honor due to him alone; further argues the divine nature cannot be multiplied into several individuals of the same kind differing only numerically like natural species, since any second individual of that nature would, by the reasoning of the first supposition, itself be supremely perfect, and the same reasoning admitting a second would allow indefinitely many, which reason and the second supposition forbid.
claims: If one God suffices completely, positing several equal gods is either superfluous or an insult to the one sufficient God.

The divine nature cannot be multiplied into several numerically distinct individuals of the same kind, since that would permit an actual infinity of gods, which reason and the second supposition exclude.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1450.summary: Presents a further formal argument for divine unicity in the style of the earlier positio-argument: it is absolutely possible that a unique God exists (namely the being, call it A, shown necessary in proving the first supposition); therefore it is necessary that this one exists uniquely and that any other supposed god (call it B) is not God, since by the sixth part it is possible for B not to be God, and whatever is not necessarily God is not God; also, a multitude of equal gods, if posited, would be more perfect than one God (an absurd implication), so none of them would be supremely perfect, hence not God.
claims: It is necessary that the unique being A (proven to exist necessarily) alone is God, and any other supposed god B is not God.
A multitude of equal gods would imply a state more perfect than any single one of them, so none of the supposed many gods could be supremely perfect.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1506.summary: Argues the one true God contains the whole possible essence and perfection of his species/nature (per the first supposition), so no other such God exists or even can exist, since another could not coexist with him nor arise after his (impossible) corruption; notes this reasoning applies generally to any individual of any other species, natural or artificial; cites Aristotle's De Caelo I arguing there cannot be, and are not, multiple worlds, since this world already comprises all the relevant matter (illustrated by the analogy of snub-nosedness exhausting all available flesh-matter).
claims: The one true God exhausts the whole possible perfection of the divine nature, so no other individual of that nature can exist.

By analogy with Aristotle's argument for the uniqueness of the world (from the exhaustion of all matter), a nature that comprehends its entire possible matter/perfection admits of only one individual.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1527.summary: Continues quoting Aristotle's De Caelo (via the snub-nose/flesh analogy and the case of the heavens comprising all their matter) to argue there cannot be several worlds, and adds Averroes's methodological remark that this demonstration (unlike merely negative demonstrations to the impossible) is a full propter quid demonstration, since it gives the cause as middle term and so yields the most perfect kind of scientific knowledge.
claims: The demonstration of the world's uniqueness is a propter quid demonstration, the most perfect kind, since it argues through the cause.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1560.summary: Argues it is more dignified and perfect to be per se supreme and first without an equal than to necessarily have an equal even unwillingly, and by the first supposition God has no equal; also argues there would be no reason, on a hypothesis of several equal and numerically distinct gods (like angels or humans), why one could not will what another does not, since neither's willing depends on the other nor is numerically identical to the other or to the other's willing — so each could obstruct, harm, or benefit the others independently, which the first supposition and the third and eighth parts (on immutability and efficacious will) exclude.
claims: It is more perfect to be supreme without an equal than to necessarily share equal status, and God, per the first supposition, has no equal.
Positing multiple numerically distinct equal gods would allow one to obstruct or harm another's will, contrary to God's established immutability and universally efficacious will.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1580.summary: Marshals a broad consensus of natural philosophers (positing a single first mover, identified as God), theologians (positing a single first being and first cause), and moral/political philosophers (favoring monarchy as the best form of government, and a single supreme military commander) as testimony for the fittingness of a single supreme principle; extends the analogy to the 'lesser world' of the human being, where a single power (intellect/reason) naturally rules the other faculties (exterior and interior senses, appetite, will), citing the Secretum Secretorum's image of the intellect as king of the body's city; concludes this same order of a single ruling principle is fitting, and by the first supposition necessary, in God and the universe.
claims: Broad philosophical consensus (natural, theological, moral/political) favors a single first/ruling principle, by analogy from cosmology, theology, and the human microcosm, to the necessity of a single supreme God.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1587.summary: Concludes the argument against equal univocal gods: on the common view of many philosophers that among several univocal gods none would be God per se and first (all sharing a prior common nature instead), none of them would be God at all, since being good per se and first is more perfect than being so derivatively; also notes such 'gods' would not be maximally actual, pure, simple, and self-sufficient but constituted by another, contrary to the first supposition and prior parts.
claims: Among any posited plurality of univocal gods, none could be God per se and first, since all would depend on a prior shared nature, contrary to divine self-sufficiency and simplicity.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1622.summary: Rubric for the fifteenth corollary part, directed against those who imagine many equal gods differing in nature or species (e.g., one presiding over the east, another the west).
claims: This part refutes polytheism positing many equal gods differing by species/nature and domain.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1627.summary: Refutes belief in many gods of different species/domains (one over the East, one the West, one crops, one vines, etc.) by the strength of the first supposition, and argues that if there were gods differing in species, each would lack the specific perfection proper to the others, hence not be supremely perfect, hence not be God at all.
claims: If there were gods of different species, each would lack some other's specific perfection and so fail to be supremely perfect and hence not be God.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1657.summary: Rubric for the sixteenth corollary part, directed against those who posit a confused multiplicity of gods of unequal power and disparate dignity, whether of the same or different species.
claims: This part refutes a hierarchy of unequal gods, of same or different species.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1664.summary: Surveys ancient polytheistic hierarchies (Homer's and the Romans' subordination of all gods to Jupiter as father/king, Augustine's City of God on the multitude of Roman gods and goddesses under Jupiter, Varro's identification of this with monotheistic worship under another name, Josephus reporting a Jewish sage equating the Jewish God with 'Zeus,' the De Mundo's and Hermes's naming of the one God as Jupiter, Plato via Ambrose, and the Tartars' worship of a supreme sky-god Natagay) and rejects all such hierarchical schemes since none of these purported subordinate 'gods' is supremely perfect, per the first supposition.
claims: Various cultures' hierarchical pantheons (Greek/Roman Jupiter-headed, Tartar Natagay-headed) are all rejected because their subordinate deities are not supremely perfect.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1722.summary: Rubric for the seventeenth corollary part, directed against those who deny God is unique and not multiple, or who affirm it possible that there be several gods, and deny that it is simply necessary that there be one and not several.
claims: This part defends the strict necessity, not mere fact, of divine unicity against those who hold plurality of gods to be possible.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1731.summary: Rebukes the many famous philosophers (Plotinus, Iamblichus, Porphyry, Apuleius, other Platonists, and Plato himself, per Augustine's City of God) who held that sacrifice should be offered to many gods; argues formally that nothing other than the one necessary being (God) can be necessary being, since God alone has no cause of his existing (per the first supposition and fifth part) and no parts (per the tenth part), so anything else could possibly (by God's omnipotence and efficacious will) be made not to exist, being infinitely less perfect than God; concludes it is absolutely possible that there be a unique necessary being and impossible that anything else be necessary being, so nothing besides God exists necessarily, and if a sophist posited otherwise it would collapse immediately under the preceding parts — citing Avicenna and Algazel in support.
claims: Only God can be necessary being, since only God is uncaused and partless; everything else could possibly be annihilated by God's omnipotent and efficacious will.
It is necessary that a unique necessary being (God) exists and impossible that any other being be necessary.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1792.summary: Rubric for the eighteenth corollary part, directed against those who posit several simply first and mutually contrary principles, none reducible to another or to any one thing common to both (e.g., good and evil as co-first principles), and who consequently dream of two or more gods of this kind (a Manichaean-type dualism).
claims: This part refutes dualistic cosmogonies positing two irreducible first principles (e.g., good and evil) and, derivatively, dualistic theology.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1805.summary: Traces the history of dualistic first-principle theories: Empedocles as the likely originator, positing one good principle (source of all goods, called Love/Friendship) and one evil principle (source of all evils, called Strife/Hate), per Aristotle's Metaphysics I; Pythagoras's parallel doctrine of two 'coordinations' (systoichiai) of ten principles each, discussed via Alexander, Averroes, and Eustratius's commentary on the Nicomachean Ethics.
claims: Empedocles originated the dualistic doctrine of Love and Strife as first principles of good and evil respectively; Pythagoras developed a parallel doctrine of two coordinated tables of ten principles.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1855.summary: Lists the ten paired Pythagorean principles (systoichiai) as reported by Eustratius: Limit/Unlimited, Perfect/Superfluous, One/Multitude, Right/Left, Male/Female, Straight/Curved, Light/Darkness, Square/Oblong, Rest/Motion, Good/Evil.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1879.summary: Discusses discrepancies among the reports of this Pythagorean table: Alexander's ordering (placing Good and Evil at the head and foot of the columns as overarching terms) versus the version Averroes comments on and versus Aristotle's own listing in Metaphysics I (which differs in both the order and the pairing, e.g., Finite/Infinite, Odd/Even, One/Many, Right/Left, Male/Female, Rest/Motion, Straight/Curved, Light/Darkness, Good/Evil, Square/Oblong), concluding that Aristotle himself did not weigh the ordering heavily.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1950.summary: Explains Pythagoras's reported motive for favoring the number ten (as 'perfect,' comprehending the nature of all numbers), from which he posited ten celestial spheres and possibly ten gods; notes Archytas's parallel derivation (via Boethius) of the ten Aristotelian categories from the same numerological motive; and identifies a further group who, following Empedocles's error, posited two gods (one causing good, one causing evil) — attributing this error's origination or promotion to Mani (Manes), the 'father of the Manichaeans.'
claims: Pythagoras's numerology (the perfection of the number ten) motivated positing ten celestial spheres and possibly ten gods; the Manichaean two-gods doctrine descends from the same Empedoclean dualistic error, via Mani.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1968.summary: Suggests it would be more reasonable to call Mani and his followers 'Empedoclines' or 'Pythagoreans' given the doctrine's real origin, then cites patristic and canon-law sources (Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History, Augustine's De Haeresibus, Isidore's Etymologies, and canon law) documenting Mani's heresy and noting that a perverse remnant of the Manichaean sect persists, even in Bradwardine's own day, in a few regions.
claims: The Manichaean sect, though ancient, persists in remnants down to the author's own time.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1994.summary: Concludes that all these dualists (Empedoclean, Pythagorean, Manichaean) err in two ways: first, in asserting a plurality of gods (refuted by the immediately preceding part on divine unicity), and second, in positing an evil God, which the first supposition and third part exclude, since it is impossible for God to be evil; adds that every existing thing, insofar as it exists, is good and nothing is simply evil, per settled philosophical and Catholic doctrine, so nothing incongruous follows from all things proceeding from a good God, and dismisses the numerological argument from the number ten as carrying no demonstrative or even rhetorical force.
claims: Dualist theologians err doubly: positing multiple gods, and positing an evil God, both of which are excluded by prior parts.
Every existing thing, as existing, is good; nothing is simply evil, so a good God can be the source of all that exists.
The numerological argument (from the perfection of ten) has no demonstrative force.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1971.summary: Rubric for the nineteenth corollary part, directed against poets who falsely claim God envies studious or otherwise excellent men.
claims: This part refutes the poetic claim that God is envious of excellent human beings.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1976.summary: Rebukes ancient poets, cited in the prologue to Aristotle's Metaphysics I, who falsely claimed the gods envy human excellence, refuting this swiftly as previously (envy being an evil incompatible with God) and citing the proverb 'poets tell many lies.'
claims: Envy is an evil, and hence cannot be attributed to God, contrary to the poets' claim.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1993.summary: Rubric for the twentieth corollary part, directed against those who fashion dishonorable and base gods who eat, drink, have intercourse with women, and delight in shameful, base, and theatrical things.
claims: This part refutes attribution of base, dishonorable behaviors (eating, drinking, sexual license, theatrical delight) to the gods.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2000.summary: Catalogues examples of gods imagined as eating, drinking, and sexually indulgent: the ancient Babylonians' belief that their god Bel ate and drank (Daniel 14), and the ancient Romans and Greeks who believed their gods ate, fornicated, and delighted in such spectacles, for which they instituted theatrical games (Ludi Scenici).
claims: Ancient Babylonian, Roman, and Greek religion attributed eating, drinking, and sexual indulgence to their gods, and instituted theatrical spectacles in their honor.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2066.summary: Cites Marco Polo's report of Tartar household idol-worship (anointing idols of their god Natagay, his wife, and son with meat fat, and pouring out broth for them), and Augustine's City of God on the pagan belief that evil, dishonorable gods must be placated by theatrical spectacles (Ludi Scenici) lest they cause harm, just as good gods are honored to secure their help.
claims: Tartar domestic idol-worship, and the pagan Roman rationale for theatrical spectacles as appeasement of malevolent gods, exemplify the same error of attributing base needs and character to the divine.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2084.summary: Quotes at length Aristotle's Politics VII on the lawgiver's duty to banish obscene speech, images, and performances (especially from the young) from the city, restricting even permitted indecent themes to certain rites and mature audiences, and barring youths from iambic satire and comedy until an appropriate age, since familiarity with base things breeds imitation.
claims: Aristotle's Politics prescribes strict civic regulation and youth-restriction of obscene speech, imagery, and theatrical performance.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2139.summary: Cites Plato (via Augustine) who would banish from the city poets who compose verses unworthy of the gods' majesty and goodness, and Scaevola (the Roman pontiff, per Augustine's City of God) who likewise condemns 'poetic theology' as frivolous for depicting gods stealing, committing adultery, competing in a beauty contest (the Judgment of Paris), Jupiter transforming into a bull or swan to seduce, a goddess marrying a mortal, and Saturn devouring his children — arguing that just as the first corollary parts led toward the goodness of God, this part leads toward honesty/decency as itself a great virtue and good.
claims: Both Plato and the Roman pontiff Scaevola condemned mythological 'poetic theology' as unworthy fictions about the gods, since decency (honestas) is itself a great good that God, being supremely good, must possess.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2113.summary: Argues by dilemma that if God ate, it would be either from necessity (excluded, since it would entail corruptibility, against the first, fifth, sixth, and seventh parts) or from pleasure (which would make God intemperate or incontinent, against the third part); notes God is already fully self-sufficient for perfect pleasure and beatitude (per the third and fifth parts), and that eating entails bodily change and organs God, being incorporeal and simple (per the sixth and tenth parts), does not have.
claims: God cannot eat, whether from necessity (implying corruptibility) or pleasure (implying intemperance), and lacks the bodily organs eating would require.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2133.summary: Argues similarly that God cannot have sexual union with a woman, since God is necessary, unique, and self-sufficient being needing no heir or helper; adds that if God generated a child through a goddess, that child would itself be another god (against the seventeenth part on divine unicity), and any posited 'goddess' would herself seem to be, by the sixth part, an essentially divine being, yet of lesser/imperfect condition than God (against the sixteenth and seventeenth parts), so could not be honored as God and hence would not be God, per the first supposition.
claims: God cannot have sexual union producing offspring, since this would entail either a plurality of gods or a 'goddess' of inferior, imperfect (hence non-divine) status, both already excluded.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2161.summary: Rubric for the twenty-first corollary part, directed against idolaters generally.
claims: This part refutes idol-worship as such.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2166.summary: Argues idolaters (ancient and some still in the East) should discard all their idols, whether male, female, neuter, human, animal, or otherwise shaped, since any idol's perfection, power, and virtue is only finite and could be greater (unlike God, per the first supposition), idols are makeable and corruptible (unlike necessary being), and idols need support and are mutable, irrational in their power, and composed of diverse materials (against the fifth, sixth, eighth, and tenth parts); notes even humans, beasts, trees, the heavens, sun and moon are of more perfect nature than an idol of metal, wood, stone, or clay, yet none of those (per the eleventh through thirteenth parts) is God, so a fortiori no idol can be.
claims: No idol can be God, since idols are finite, makeable, corruptible, composite, and of a nature inferior even to natural things already shown not to be divine.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2249.summary: Adds that idolaters posit a multitude of idols (hence gods, against the seventeenth part), attribute sex and diverse bodily members to idols (refutable as before), and fashion idols from materials of varying nobility, yet God (per the first supposition) cannot be that of which something more perfect is found; notes an idol of nobler material (e.g., gold, with more or purer material, more and better gems) could always in principle be bettered, whereas God cannot.
claims: Idols made of variable, gradable materials cannot be God, since God admits no possibility of being bettered, unlike any idol.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2267.summary: Anticipates and refutes the idolaters' defense that the material idol is not itself God, but becomes a god upon due ritual consecration by receiving a certain power; argues such a 'god' would be newly originated and hence mutable, passible, destructible, needy, composite, and multipliable if consecrated in different places — all contrary to God's established attributes; further dissects the consecrated power itself by dilemma (is it God or not; is it the God of the first supposition or another) to show that consecration cannot manufacture divinity, and that God, being wholly incorporeal, cannot properly have any bodily form or likeness such as an idol.
claims: Ritual consecration cannot make a material idol divine: the resulting 'god' would be newly caused, mutable, composite, and multipliable, all excluded by God's established nature; and God, being incorporeal, cannot have the bodily form an idol requires.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2314.summary: Argues by a further dilemma that if a human makes a god for himself, either he does so by his own power (in which case he would seem more worthy than the god he made, as any maker is worthier than his product) or by another's power, either another god's (in which case that other god is insufficient, yielding multiple gods) or a non-god's (in which case a non-god could not produce a god, and something lesser could not produce something greater); adds that if a human makes a god, that god would owe more to the human than vice versa, as a son to a father or a product to its maker.
claims: A human cannot make a god for himself: whether by his own power (making himself worthier than his god) or another's (implicating either multiple gods or an impossible lesser-causing-greater), the idea is incoherent.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2262.summary: Considers a further possible reply — that the material idol, once duly consecrated, is wholly transubstantiated and converted into God — and refutes it: a corporeal thing cannot be immediately converted into an incorporeal thing since God is wholly incorporeal and partless (tenth part); sensory experience shows the same material idol persists after consecration, so if any conversion occurs it seems rather that God is converted into the idol; and the God supposedly resulting from such conversion would be either newly originated (excluded by the first supposition) or eternal (in which case the same dilemma as before recurs — is it the one true God or another); rejects the further claim that God dwells remotely in heaven and must 'descend' into an idol's form to help us, since this would make God mutable and ignores that God already knows all things and has a universally efficacious will (ninth and eighth parts) regardless of spatial location.
claims: A corporeal idol cannot be transubstantiated into the wholly incorporeal, partless God.
God's knowledge and efficacious will act on earthly affairs without requiring any change of place or 'descent' into an idol, contrary to what consecration-theories imply.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2319.summary: Presses further: whoever performs the supposed conversion of idol into God — if a human, by his own power or words, he could then more easily perform lesser conversions of any material thing into any other; if God performs it, since in every making or moving the maker/mover is present together with what is made/moved, God would already have been present with the idol prior to and independent of the conversion, so no such conversion was needed to have God present there.
claims: Whether a human or God is supposed to effect the idol's conversion into divinity, the claim is incoherent: a human agent could trivially do far more; and God, if agent, would already be present without any conversion being necessary.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2336.summary: Turns to Hermes Trismegistus, described as himself a maker, worshiper, and defender of idols in his book on the Eternal Word, who holds that idols/statues are indeed lesser gods (not the supreme God but subject to and lesser than him), made by humans by animating sacred images with the souls of demons, angels, or humans, calling this the greatest human power, and marveling (in an address to Asclepius) that man could discover and produce a divine nature; judges that if Hermes speaks of God/gods univocally with the true God, his view is refuted by the sixteenth and seventeenth parts, but if merely equivocally (naming lesser spirits 'gods' loosely), the dispute is largely verbal and not worth much contention.
claims: Hermes Trismegistus's doctrine of animated, spirit-indwelt idols as 'lesser gods,' if taken univocally with true divinity, is refuted by the established uniqueness and hierarchy-exclusion of the sixteenth/seventeenth parts; if merely equivocal terminology, it is not a substantive theological dispute.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2384.summary: Directly addresses Hermes/Trismegistus: since the one God of the first supposition is supremely wise, good, pious, generous, powerful, and present, why fashion other gods or another god? Argues idols consecrated to Bel, Astaroth, and similar names are demonic and malignant spirits, not gods, comparing idol-consecration to necromantic conjuration and arguing all created things are to be loved and honored only for God's sake, finally and principally, never as ends in themselves.
claims: Idols named Bel, Astaroth, and similar are demonic/malignant spirits, not gods.
No creature is to be loved, honored, or worshiped as a final end in itself; all honor is owed ultimately to God alone.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2432.summary: Anticipates the reply that such idols are honored only with dulia (veneration), not latria (worship due to God alone), and presses why then such veneration is given to the Devil, the enemy of God and of all angels and humans, noting no idol is ever dedicated to the name of a holy angel, only to names (Bel, Astaroth) known to belong to demons and reprobate spirits.
claims: No idol is ever dedicated to a holy angel's name; such idols bear only demonic names, showing their true objects of worship are malignant spirits, not legitimate angelic intercessors.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2445.summary: Refutes the further claim that a holy angel might inhabit a consecrated idol, arguing by dilemma that the angel's indwelling would be either voluntary (implausible, since a blessed angel would not freely abandon heaven for an idol's dark 'prison') or involuntary/compelled (impossible, since no human ritual power — words, herbs, gems — can transcend natural limits to imprison an angel); concludes that either way the worshiper ends up adoring a mere block of wood or stone.
claims: A holy angel cannot be made to inhabit a consecrated idol, whether willingly (contrary to its blessedness) or by compulsion (beyond any human ritual power), so idol-worshipers really adore inert matter.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2478.summary: Extends the refutation with further absurdities: if consecration could compel one angel to leave heaven, it could compel all, emptying heaven entirely; if two people in different places invoke the same angel simultaneously, the angel cannot go to both, so at least one (or both) is deceived; likewise if the same angel is later summoned to a different idol by stronger rites, it would abandon the first idol, and nothing could explain what holds an unwilling angel in place once the ritual ceases (since a continued effect requires a continuing cause); concludes it is absurd and contrary to the natural order for an inferior human to command and compel a superior angel, when the reverse hierarchy is natural, as in any well-ordered household or polity.
claims: The idea that ritual can compel and hold an angel captive in an idol leads to absurdities (emptying heaven, contradictory simultaneous summons, unexplained persistence) and violates the natural hierarchical order in which humans are subordinate to angels, not vice versa.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2519.summary: Presses Hermes with a direct rhetorical challenge: since Hermes himself sometimes suggests man is more perfect and superior to angels in the natural order, why does he subject himself to a creature beneath him (the idol) and honor it as his god, when the reverse would be fitting?
claims: If man is superior to angels, as Hermes suggests, it is inconsistent for him to subject himself to and worship an inferior creature (the idol).

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2529.summary: Notes the same argument applies to the souls of good and holy humans, especially since Hermes himself teaches that souls, upon leaving the body, ascend to heaven (making their capture in an idol equally implausible).

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2536.summary: Argues that if a human manufactures his own god, he thereby appears greater and worthier than that god, as any maker exceeds his product, and (if the god were capable of gratitude) the god would owe the human more honor than vice versa, since the human gave it its very being (more than a father gives a son) and can equally destroy it by fire or hammer, reducing it to dust and nothing; concludes such reasoning (Hermes's own) proves nothing about a truly divine being, since even demons — known to be prescient of the future and capable of wonders in human bodies — are not therefore to be worshiped as gods, but rather guarded against as cunning, pestilential enemies.
claims: A humanly manufactured 'god' would be inferior to and dependent on its human maker, who could also destroy it — the reverse of true divinity.
Demonic power to foreknow and work wonders does not make demons worthy of worship; they are to be feared and avoided as deceitful enemies.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2560.summary: Considers a more sophisticated, quasi-orthodox defense: that the one true incorporeal, simple God nonetheless has many powers/virtues through which he manifests himself in diverse corporeal effects, and is correspondingly called by many names (per the De Mundo, and per Albericus of London's Prologue on the origin of the gods, deriving names like Vitunus/Sentinus from vital/sensory functions, and citing verses calling one God 'Jupiter... progenitor and mother of the gods, one and the same God').
claims: A sophisticated defense of polyonymy holds that the one true God, though simple, manifests diverse powers through diverse effects and so bears many names (Jupiter, Juno, Diana, etc.), all naming the same single deity.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2589.summary: Continues this defense: idols are fashioned only for the one true God, though inadequately, and multiplied only because of the multiplicity of his names, effects, and powers — a view attributed to the wise ancient Romans; but rebuts it as needlessly complicated compared to simply naming and worshiping God under one proper name (since his powers are not really distinct from him, per the fifth and tenth parts, as the response itself concedes), and observes that worshiping God's powers separately through separate idols would mean worshiping infinitely many of his infinite virtues only in a finite, piecemeal, and hence radically incomplete way.
claims: Worship of God distributed among many idols for his many names/powers is needlessly complex and, since God's powers are really identical with him, actually worships his infinite virtues only partially and inadequately compared to worshiping him under one name.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2624.summary: Argues it is more practical and useful to have one all-sufficient refuge (God) to whom one may always turn in any need, rather than the Varronian scheme of appealing to different named gods for different needs (Aesculapius for illness, Mars for war, Neptune for the sea, Bacchus for wine, the Nymphs for water, etc.), since one may face needs for which no specific patron god is known, risking either despair or the invention of ever more new idols; concludes it suffices to rely always and everywhere on the one, all-sufficient, omnipotent, most merciful true God and his one name, abandoning the multitude of idols.
claims: Reliance on a single, all-sufficient God for every need is more practical and secure than the Varronian scheme of specialized patron deities for specific needs.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2655.summary: Warns that even a learned person who rightly understands that God's many virtues are not really distinct, and that God is really one and simple, should still be cautious in naming God variously and multiplying idols, lest the simple and unlearned be misled into believing these virtues really differ, and hence that there are really many gods differing according to the multitude of names and idols.
claims: Even correct theological understanding of divine simplicity must be taught carefully, since multiplying divine names and idols risks misleading the unlearned into practical polytheism.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2680.summary: Rubric heading (repeating the div title) introducing the twenty-second corollary part: against the Arians.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2685.summary: Refutes the Arians (who, per Augustine's De Haeresibus, Isidore, and canon law, separated the substance of the divine Persons, holding them unequal and not co-eternal, making the Son a temporal creature of the Father and the Holy Spirit a temporal creature of the Son), arguing this would entail a plurality and inequality of gods, contrary to the first supposition's requirement of a single supremely perfect, necessary, eternal God.
claims: Arian subordinationism, making the Son and Holy Spirit temporal creatures unequal to the Father, implies a plurality and inequality of gods, contrary to the first supposition.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2698.summary: Adds that whichever divine Person the Arians deny to be eternal and necessary being could not, on the terms already established, be God at all, since the first supposition and preceding argument require that God be eternal and necessary being.
claims: Any Person denied eternity and necessary existence by the Arians thereby fails, on the established criteria, to be God.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2714.summary: Rubric heading for the twenty-third corollary part: against the Donatists.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2719.summary: Refutes the Donatists (who led much of Africa astray, similar to yet distinct from the Arians, holding the divine Persons of the same substance but unequal magnitude — the Son lesser than the Father, and the Holy Spirit lesser than both, per historical sources and Augustine's De Haeresibus and Epistle 32) by the twelfth supposition/part's requirement that God be supremely perfect, which any 'lesser' divine Person would fail to be.
claims: Donatist subordinationism (equal substance but unequal magnitude among the Persons) is refuted because a Person of lesser magnitude could not be supremely perfect, hence could not be God.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2741.summary: Rubric plus refutation of the Sabellians (twenty-fourth corollary part), who collapse the Persons into unity/identity of essence and person: argues via a dilemma that if Father and Son are simply identical, this is either with respect to the same (self-relation, which is impossible, since nothing generates, effects, or produces itself) or with respect to another (in which case the Son, as God, is 'from another,' which is either itself God — implying multiple gods — or not God — implying God is generated from a non-God, contrary to the first supposition); also rejects the Sabellian fallback that God is successively, not simultaneously, Father, Son, and Spirit, since sonship necessarily and simultaneously implies a distinct father, and such successive self-identity would make God mutable, against the sixth part.
claims: Sabellian modalism (identity of Person and essence in Father and Son) collapses into either self-causation (impossible) or generation from another that is either itself God (multiplying gods) or not God (contradicting the first supposition).
The Sabellian fallback of successive divine roles (now Father, then Son, then Spirit) is refuted because sonship requires a simultaneously distinct father, and such succession would make God mutable.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2795.summary: Rubric for the twenty-fifth corollary part, directed against those who assert without qualification that God is of infinite power, including intensively infinite, without distinguishing senses of 'infinite.'
claims: This part distinguishes proper senses in which God's power is called 'infinite,' rejecting an unqualified claim of strict intensive infinity.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2802.summary: Distinguishes senses of divine 'infinite power': not duration or extension (improper senses per Aristotle's Physics III), but intension — and here distinguishes 'properly intensively infinite' (as if a quality could be intensified without limit, like light) from a fixed maximal degree; argues God is not properly intensively infinite in the first sense, since whatever is properly intense could, without contradiction, be lessened, which the fourth part and first supposition forbid (it would make God's power reducible and imperfectible); also argues that if God were properly 'intense,' a lesser degree of the same nature would be conceivable, and since 'God' is an essential name, that lesser degree would itself have to be God, yielding either unequal gods of one nature (already refuted) or a mutable God (also refuted).
claims: God is not 'intensively infinite' in the proper sense of a quality capable of degrees (like heat or light can be more or less intense), since that would entail either that God's power could be diminished, or that a lesser degree of the same divine nature would itself have to count as God — both already excluded.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2852.summary: Concludes God is neither properly 'intense' nor 'remiss,' neither intensifiable nor remittable in the manner of a natural quality, but of a most indivisible, immutable, stable, and simple nature; nonetheless truly (if improperly) called infinite in power, strength, and potency in three senses: (1) relative to other active powers, since whatever effect any finite power (e.g., heat) can produce, God can produce as much or more without aid, and could match even a hypothetically infinite created power; (2) relative to the kind of action, since God alone can create something from nothing, which no finite power can; (3) relative to the extrinsic measure of action/effect, since God can produce in less time (even instantaneously) and to a greater degree (doubled, quadrupled, without limit) whatever any other cause produces — so there is no maximum God can do nor minimum he cannot, meeting Aristotle's and Averroes's definition of active power as bounded by a maximum (or, more precisely, by a minimum it cannot do).
claims: God is neither intensifiable nor remittable, being of a simple, immutable nature.

God is truly (though improperly, i.e. not as a matter of quality-degree) called infinite in power in three respects: equaling or exceeding any finite active power, being uniquely capable of creation from nothing, and having no maximal or minimal limit on what he can do.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2904.summary: Rubric for the twenty-sixth corollary part, directed against those who depict/paint God as possessing various accidental qualities, attributes, habits, or acts.
claims: This part refutes attributing accidental qualities, attributes, habits, or acts to God.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2911.summary: Refutes depicting God with accidental qualities, attributes, habits, or acts really distinct from him: such accidents would be neither infinitely intense (per the twenty-fifth part) nor finitely so (per the fourth part), and would be either infinite or finite in number — not infinite (since it is better to be perfected by fewer things, needing less) nor finite (since then a greater number could always be added, yielding a more perfect God), so positing any such accidents undermines God's supreme perfection and full possession of all power and virtue.
claims: God cannot have any real accidents (qualities, attributes, habits, acts distinct from his essence), since any such accidents, finite or infinite in intensity or number, would compromise his supreme, unsurpassable perfection.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2931.summary: Restates that this shows plainly God is subject to no accidents whatsoever, since if he were subject to any accident(s) he would not be the purest and most fully actual being, contrary to the third part.
claims: God is subject to no accidents whatsoever, since any accident would compromise his status as pure, maximal act.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2948.summary: Adds finally that since an accident can be present or absent while its subject remains the same, if God were subject to an accident, he would be mutable, contrary to the sixth part.
claims: If God had any accident, he would be mutable (since accidents can come and go in an unchanged subject), contrary to his established immutability.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2964.summary: Rubric for the twenty-seventh corollary part, against despair arising from the magnitude or multitude of one's sins.
claims: This part refutes despair grounded in either the magnitude or the multitude of one's sins.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2982.summary: Describes the 'Judaic' type of despair (from the multitude, not magnitude, of sins): contemporary Jews reportedly believed (per the author's own conversation with a learned Jew) that a fourth relapse into the same sin, after two prior falls and repentances, forecloses any possibility of pardon or penance, grounding this in Amos 1's repeated formula ('for three transgressions... and for four, I will not turn away [punishment]') applied to various nations; reports the Jew's own grim answer that a fourth-time sinner is as good as damned, doomed to wander and perish miserably.
claims: Some contemporary Jews, per Amos 1's 'three... and four' formula, held that a fourth relapse into sin admits no further pardon or penance.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3016.summary: Refutes both forms of despair by the first supposition: God, being supremely good, is likewise supremely merciful, pious, clement, rich, powerful, generous, and magnificent beyond conception (per the third and fourth parts); any human sin, however great, is finite and could always be exceeded by a greater sin, hence is as nothing compared to God's infinitely infinite mercy; asks rhetorically why such immense mercy and power could not overcome, remove, and cleanse so small a thing as a finite sin, or forgive the debt of a humbly repentant prodigal son, especially since God's infinite riches suffer no diminishment from such forgiveness but rather gain the 'jewel' of a saved soul and the joy of the heavenly household.
claims: Since God is infinitely and supremely merciful while any human sin is merely finite, no sin, however great, can exceed the scope of divine mercy.
Forgiving a repentant sinner costs God's infinite riches nothing and instead adds the 'jewel' of a saved soul and communal joy.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3062.summary: Argues it is more powerful, merciful, clement, liberal, and magnificent for God to forgive a truly repentant, humbly supplicating sinner than to turn away, and that whoever claims God can forgive only up to some fixed limit thereby improperly imposes a boundary and measure on God's simply infinite goodness, power, and mercy; concludes anyone, however weighed down by the magnitude or multitude of sins, may confidently repent and hope for mercy, pardon, and salvation, since any finite quantity or multitude of sins, however large, remains finite and hence incomparably small next to God's infinitely infinite mercy, power, piety, and generosity.
claims: To claim God can forgive only up to a fixed limit wrongly bounds God's infinite mercy and power.
However great the magnitude or multitude of one's sins, all remain finite and thus infinitely surpassed by divine mercy, warranting confident hope of pardon.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3112.summary: Directly challenges the Jewish interlocutors: since even they concede that a person may commit one grave sin (blasphemy, homicide, incest) equal to or worse than a fourth relapse and still obtain mercy, there is no consistent reason to deny mercy specifically to a fourth relapse into a lesser or equal sin when all circumstances are weighed, since God's goodness, power, wisdom, and mercy are as boundless in number of pardons as in intensity.
claims: The Jewish position is inconsistent: it grants mercy for a single grave sin but denies it for a fourth lesser relapse, though God's infinite mercy admits no such numerical limit.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3147.summary: Presents an extended analogy: a fearful, dutiful son or servant who tries hard to avoid offending his father/lord but occasionally sins from ignorance or weakness, seeking reconciliation each time out of love (not fear), is more disposed to obtain mercy than a proud, rebellious son who deliberately sins repeatedly without ever seeking reconciliation and lives wickedly for years — arguing it would be absurd and would incentivize a lifetime of unrepentant sin followed by a single deathbed repentance if the fourth-time-penitent son were denied mercy while the lifelong unrepentant sinner were not similarly barred.
claims: A repeatedly repentant sinner (even a fourth time) is more disposed to receive mercy than an unrepentant lifelong sinner, so denying mercy specifically to the fourth relapse is absurd and would perversely incentivize prolonged unrepentance.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3184.summary: Appeals directly to the Jewish reader's own experience of forgiving a repeatedly offending son or servant many times over (invoking the 'seventy times seven' standard), arguing that if even human fathers extend such repeated mercy, God, supremely good, is incomparably more merciful than any human, however merciful; also reinterprets the Amos 'three... and four' formula literally (noting God does convert some sinners from many sins but not others even from one) and morally (distinguishing degrees of sinning — from thought to consent to act to final unrepented persistence — arguing the true 'fourth sin' that forecloses conversion is final impenitence at death, not a fourth instance of the same sin), concluding with Ecclesiastes 11's 'wherever the tree falls, there it shall lie' to support the point that only final, definitive impenitence (not a numbered relapse) fixes one's fate.
claims: God's mercy incomparably exceeds even a very forgiving human father's, undermining any fixed numerical limit on pardon.
Properly (morally) interpreted, the 'fourth sin' that admits no conversion is final impenitence at death, not a fourth relapse into the same sin.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3232.summary: Rubric stating the error targeted by Corollarium 28: the Cainite belief that God admits no sinner to reconciling grace unless the sinner has first merited or satisfied, by penance, at least as much as (or more than) he sinned.
claims: The Cainite position holds that reconciling grace is granted only after the sinner has merited/satisfied in proportion to or beyond the offense committed.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2941.summary: Adds a further dilemma: if God had some accident, it would be either superfluous (excluded by the third part) or necessary/useful (excluded by the fifth part, on divine self-sufficiency).
claims: Any hypothetical accident in God would be either superfluous (against divine non-superfluity) or needed (against divine self-sufficiency) — either way impossible.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e2969.summary: Introduces the 'Cainites,' named for Cain, who despaired of pardon on account of the sheer greatness of his iniquity, per Genesis 4 ('My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon'), calling on such despairers to take heart.
claims: Cain despaired of forgiveness because of the perceived magnitude of his sin, per Genesis 4.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3241.summary: Refutes the Cainite position by tracing it to Cain's own despairing words ('my iniquity is greater than that it may deserve pardon'): if pardon required proportionate satisfaction, anyone who sinned gravely and repeatedly over a long life could never satisfy enough, and would be forced into despair, which the argument treats as an unacceptable consequence given the earlier proof (Corollarium 27) that satisfaction cannot equal the debt of sin.
claims: The Cainite requirement of proportionate satisfaction, applied consistently, forces the lifelong sinner into necessary despair.
No one can satisfy or merit as much as is owed for grave, repeated sin.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3259.summary: Argues from the first Supposition (God is supremely merciful, such that nothing more merciful is possible) that God could not be so if he remitted no sin without prior full satisfaction, since that would be an act of justice/rigor rather than mercy; even a merciful human sometimes remits an injury to a suppliant without full prior satisfaction, so God, incomparably better, does so a fortiori.
