claims: Requiring full satisfaction before any remission is an act of justice, not mercy, and so is incompatible with God's supreme mercy.
A fortiori argument from human mercy to divine mercy supports gratuitous remission.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3289.summary: Rubric stating the error targeted by Corollarium 29: the Pelagian/Cainite claim that God gives no benefit gratuitously (gratis) but always in return for preceding merit.
claims: The Pelagian position holds that divine benefits are given only in proportion to preceding merit, never gratuitously.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3296.summary: Attacks the Pelagian position by tracing it to Cain (implicit) and making it explicit in the Pelagians, then argues from the very meaning of the term: if grace (gratia) is not given gratis (gratis/free), the etymological and conceptual link between the words collapses ('if grace is not given freely, what is given freely?'). Marshals classical testimony for the gratuitousness proper to gratia/the Graces: the poetic image of the three unbound, freely-clothed Graces (Hesiod, Homer, Chrysippus and other Greek poets), Seneca's De Beneficiis on benefits owing nothing in return, and Aristotle's Rhetoric II definition of gratia as helping the needy not for one's own advantage.
claims: The concept of gratia (grace/favor) is definitionally gratuitous; a 'grace' given only for merit is not truly grace.
Classical authorities (poets, Seneca, Aristotle) confirm that true benefit/favor expects nothing in return.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3329.summary: Further argues from the first Supposition (God supremely good and supremely liberal) that giving is more liberal than selling/exchanging for merit, and that a liberal human gives many things gratis; therefore God, infinitely more liberal, must give gratuitously all the more.
claims: Giving is a higher act of liberality than exchange for merit.
God's infinite liberality entails gratuitous giving, by analogy with human liberality.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3350.summary: Rubric for Corollarium 30, against those unlearned in 'the art of loving' who deny that God is to be loved for his own sake (with all else loved for God's sake and referred finally to him), and who hold that a person able to avoid some great good or evil without sin may nonetheless knowingly commit even the smallest sin against God's precept or conscience.
claims: The targeted error denies that God alone is to be loved for himself and holds that minor, knowing sin may be excused for the sake of avoiding evil or securing good.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3372.summary: A short verse couplet, styled as an invitation ('if anyone among this people does not know the art of loving, let him read this and, having read the poem, learn to love'), echoing Ovid's Ars Amatoria as a rhetorical frame introducing the corollarium's teaching on the true 'art of loving' (God).

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3379.summary: States the thesis to be defended: every person should know that God is to be loved for his own sake, all else for God's sake, all human acts finally ordered to him, and God loved above all; consequently no one should ever knowingly sin even minimally against God for the sake of gaining any good or avoiding any evil. Grounds this in the natural order whereby the less perfect is ordered to the more perfect, and everything short of God is less perfect and good than he, per the first Supposition.
claims: God alone is to be loved for his own sake; all else is to be loved for God's sake and ordered to him.
No temporal good or evil justifies knowingly sinning against God, even minimally.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3411.summary: Adds that it is more worthy, perfect, and better to be loved for oneself than for another (as already established); since God is to be loved, he is loved for himself, per the first Supposition and the corollarium's third part.
claims: Being loved for oneself is a higher mode of being loved than being loved for another.
God, being lovable, is therefore loved for himself.
concepts: being loved for oneself vs. for another

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3424.summary: Argues that if God were loved only for the sake of something else, that other thing would, by the correct order of loving, be loved more (since the end is loved more than what is for the end, and what is loved for itself more than what is loved only for another) — citing Aristotle, Posterior Analytics I.2 ('that on account of which each thing is, is that thing more'). But nothing can be more lovable than God, the supreme good, so this is impossible.
claims: If X is loved only for the sake of Y, then Y is loved more than X.
Nothing can be more lovable than God; therefore God cannot be loved merely for the sake of something else.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3440.summary: Argues from the second Supposition (no infinite regress among beings) applied to objects of love: among lovable things ordered by rank, one thing is loved on account of another, and that on account of a further one, and so on, but this series cannot regress infinitely; therefore there is something loved finally for its own sake, with other things loved for its sake — and nothing is more worthy of that position than God.
claims: The chain of things loved 'for the sake of' another cannot regress infinitely.
There must be a final, self-terminating object of love, and God best fits that role.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3451.summary: Argues that there is some natural end of all beings, and by the natural order this end is more perfect, worthier, and better than the things ordered to it (as already established and as the Philosophers attest); but nothing among natural beings is more perfect, worthy, or good than God, so God is the natural end of all things, to be loved for himself, with all else loved for his sake — the second and third points following from the first, and the fourth and fifth from the preceding.
claims: There exists a single natural end of all beings.
God, being the most perfect being, must be that natural end and thus the ultimate object of love.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3477.summary: Argues that offense against a good and great person is to be avoided, and more so against a better and greater person; since no person could be better or greater than the divine person (per the first Supposition), offending God must never be knowingly committed, whatever the reason.
claims: The gravity of avoiding offense scales with the dignity of the person offended.
Since God is the greatest possible person, offending him may never be knowingly risked for any end.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3486.summary: Challenges an opponent ('falsigraphus', a 'false writer') to state the contrary position — that someone may, to gain some good or avoid some evil, knowingly offend God by an act A that could be avoided without sin — and works through a dilemma: considering all factors, A is either wholly rightly done, sinful, or indifferent. If rightly done, it cannot offend the perfectly just and rational God; the question becomes how such an act could offend him at all, since contemning the very rightness God himself would dictate would itself be the real offense.
claims: If an act is, all things considered, rightly done, it cannot truly offend a perfectly just and rational God.
The dilemma's first horn (A is rightly done) cannot coherently be classified as an 'offense against God'.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3518.summary: Continues the dilemma against the falsigraphus: if A is rightly done it is meritorious and so should be rewarded, not punished, since God rewards even those who act imperfectly — so how could he fail to reward, or even punish, one who acts rightly? Also, if God is justly offended by A, then A is unjust (contradiction, since A was posited as rightly done); if unjustly offended, God is unjust (contradicting the first Supposition). If instead A is classified as sin, it should simply not be done — sin being a deviation from right practical reason — and if the agent truly acts according to right reason (as God himself would counsel), no sin occurs; citing Aristotle, Topics III, that necessary goods are to be chosen over non-necessary ones even if the latter are individually better, and avoiding sin against God is necessary for every rational creature by natural synderesis. Concludes that classifying A as an indifferent/neutral act also fails, since it would not then offend a mild God at all.
claims: A rightly-done act cannot coherently be punished nor treated as an unjust divine offense.
Avoiding (even minimal) sin against God is a necessity of natural reason (synderesis), overriding merely contingent goods.
None of the three horns of the dilemma (right, sinful, indifferent) supports the falsigraphus's claim that minimal sin may licitly be committed for a good end.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3571.summary: Rubric for Corollarium 31, against the 'unrestrained' (effraenes) who claim good and evil befall the good and the wicked equally, that some evil goes unpunished or some good unrewarded, and who falsely allege that God either punishes some abundantly beyond or exactly to condign measure while rewarding sparingly (short of condign), or else that divine mercy requires that every offense always be mercifully left unpunished.
claims: The targeted error denies proportionate divine reward and punishment, either alleging disproportionate severity or alleging that mercy requires all sin go unpunished.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3591.summary: Restates and refutes the effraenes' position, calling them crude for weighing only visible, worldly goods and evils: by the doctrine of the previous corollarium, every knowing sinner immediately and inseparably incurs so great an evil (sin itself) that it should never be risked for any temporal gain, while every obedient soul immediately incurs so precious a merit that failing to act rightly to avoid some temporal loss is never justified — showing that reward and punishment are inseparable from the acts themselves, contrary to the claim that good and evil befall all equally.
claims: Sin itself is an immediate, inseparable evil consequence of sinning, regardless of external outcomes.
Right action itself is an immediate, inseparable good/merit, regardless of external outcomes.
The 'unrestrained' err by attending only to visible/worldly goods and evils, missing this moral/spiritual dimension.
concepts: inseparability of sin and its evil
inseparability of merit and its good

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3637.summary: Argues that no just, discerning, and powerful human ruler permits good and bad subjects to be treated equally, but provides better things to the better according to differences of merit; God, infinitely more just, discerning, and powerful (per the first Supposition and following parts), therefore evidently leaves no evil unpunished, as already shown regarding the immediate consequence of sin.
claims: A just ruler differentiates treatment of subjects according to merit.
God, being infinitely more just and powerful than any human ruler, must a fortiori differentiate, leaving no evil unpunished.
concepts: analogy from human rulers to God

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3656.summary: Argues that every sinner, by the very act of sinning, becomes worse and more culpable, loses prior liberty, innocence, and immunity, and becomes more unlike and more distant from God — and this itself is a punishment, and a great one, deriving from the first justice, the primary retributor, who is God. By the same reasoning, God permits no good to go unrewarded, since it would be cruel and impious for God to be more prone to punish sinners than to reward the meritorious, contrary to his supreme goodness, piety, and mercy (per the first Supposition and third and fourth parts).
claims: Sinning itself constitutes an immediate punishment: loss of innocence and increased unlikeness to God.
It would contradict God's goodness for him to be more disposed to punish than to reward.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3678.summary: Parallels the prior argument for the reward side: whoever acts well, meritoriously, and laudably is thereby better and more praiseworthy than if he had not merited at all — this inseparable reward, this 'beautiful wage' of merit, comes from the first justice and primary retributor, God.
claims: Meritorious action carries its own immediate, inseparable reward: increased goodness and praiseworthiness of the agent.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3694.summary: Argues it would be unfitting for the supremely just, liberal, powerful, and abundant God — lover of inexhaustible treasures — to leave his own servants (per the doctrine of Corollarium 30) unrewarded and equal to those who neither love nor serve him at all.
claims: It would be unfitting for God to leave his faithful servants no better off than those indifferent or hostile to him.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3705.summary: Argues God does not punish anyone abundantly beyond condign measure (that would be unjust, impious, merciless, and cruel — and by the corollarium's third part God is none of these), nor even exactly to condign measure (that would savor of severity and lack of mercy, whereas the opposite virtues are fully present in God per the third and fourth parts).
claims: God does not punish beyond condign measure (that would be unjust and cruel).
God does not even punish exactly to condign measure (that would lack mercy); he remits mercifully below it.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3716.summary: Argues that for any offense committed knowingly against God, however small, he could justly inflict any degree of punishment, even the annihilation of the offender (per Corollarium 30, since no punishment should be avoided by committing such an offense); yet God inflicts only finite and small punishments on his offenders, showing he could justly inflict far graver ones and so mercifully remits incomparably more than he inflicts. Likewise God does not reward sparingly, short of condign measure: that would stem from impotence or from injustice/illiberality/stinginess/avarice, none of which pertain to God (per the third, fourth, and seventh parts); presented also as a dilemma — either God wills to reward to condign measure and cannot (impotence, against the seventh part) or can but does not will to (injustice, against the third part).
claims: God could justly inflict extreme punishment for any knowing offense but inflicts only small, finite punishment, hence remits mercifully.
God does not reward short of condign measure: the alternatives (impotence or injustice) are both excluded from God.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3749.summary: Argues it is also unfitting for God to reward only exactly to condign measure and no further, since rewarding to condign measure alone belongs to justice and necessity, not to grace or liberality; but God is supremely generous and superabundantly liberal (per the first Supposition and third and fourth parts), and his abundance cannot be diminished by any magnificent giving (per the seventh and eighth parts).
claims: Rewarding only to condign measure pertains to justice, not liberality.
God's superabundant liberality entails rewarding beyond mere condign measure, without depleting his inexhaustible resources.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3766.summary: Argues a fortiori: God, per the preceding point, grants great undeserved benefits even to his enemies and offenders, mercifully punishing them well below condign measure; how much more, then, does it befit him not to withhold all grace, gift, and liberality from his own lovers and servants, reducing them to bare payment of simple debt (against the position refuted in Corollarium 30).
claims: If God is generous even to undeserving enemies (via reduced punishment), he must be even more generous to his faithful servants.
concepts: generosity to enemies vs. to servants

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3782.summary: Argues that a liberal and powerful human sometimes rewards his workers beyond condign measure, and God is infinitely more liberal and powerful (per the third and fourth parts); nor does punishing sinners conflict with infinite divine piety and mercy, since God punishes not from hatred or desire for vengeance (which would be unfitting to his supreme goodness) but from a zeal for correction, chastisement, amendment of the one punished, or (through him) of others, always intending the good, beauty, and order of the universe — being so good and pure of evil and baseness that he can finally intend only what is good and beautiful, per the first Supposition and third part.
claims: Divine punishment is medicinal/corrective in intent, not vindictive, and always ordered to the good of the universe.
This reconciles God's punishing sinners with his supreme mercy and goodness.
concepts: order and beauty of the universe

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3804.summary: Argues that God is shown as just and wise (per the first Supposition and third and fourth parts) in the same measure that he is merciful and pious; but it would not befit a supremely wise and just being to treat sinners the same as non-sinners, or non-sinners the same as sinners in every respect — implying differentiated treatment is required by wisdom and justice themselves.
claims: Supreme wisdom and justice require differentiated treatment of sinners and non-sinners.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3813.summary: Argues it is already clear from the foregoing that every sinner is, immediately and inseparably, by the necessity of indispensable justice, justly punished; and this justice must derive from the first just disposer of all things, the first justice, the primary truth — that is, from God necessarily, as the Suppositions show.
claims: The necessary, immediate justice attaching to sin must originate from God as first justice.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3824.summary: Draws a political analogy: every well-ordered polity requires two things to restrain citizens from vice and advance them toward virtue — fear of punishment for wrongdoers and love of reward for the meritorious. It therefore befits God, as founder and ruler of the great polity of the world, to establish similar means for all his subjects for similar reasons; observation confirms this need, since many, scorning the fear of punishment, run unrestrained toward vice, and would do so far more without any threatened penalty, many being restrained from sin solely by fear of punishment.
claims: Good governance requires both punitive deterrents and rewards to secure virtuous behavior.
God, as ruler of the cosmic polity, must institute analogous mechanisms of punishment and reward for the same reason human polities do.
concepts: fear and love as governing mechanisms

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3852.summary: Rubric for Corollarium 32: against philosophers who presume they can fully know God and any of his actions, and who therefore mock Christians for believing certain wondrous things about God and about creaturely actions performed by divine power that cannot be demonstrated by human reason.
claims: The targeted error is philosophical overconfidence in fully comprehending God and his works, leading to derision of Christian belief in things beyond natural demonstration.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3863.summary: Argues that since the human soul is small and finite while God is infinite in extent (numerically/extensively, per the third part) and in intensity (per the fourth part), no finite mind can grasp, examine, or know God fully; God, being of infinite entity, truth, and knowability, is fully known only by himself, unless he should lend a human his own infinite cognitive power.
claims: No finite created mind can fully know an infinite God through its own finite power.
Full knowledge of God would require God's own infinite cognitive power, not a merely human one.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3905.summary: Presses the philosopher further: he cannot even fully know the smallest creature (an atom in sunlight, a grain of dust, a drop of water), since every tiny body contains infinitely many geometrical and arithmetical truths ordered so that later ones depend on prior ones, of which any philosopher or all philosophers together could know only finitely many; concludes that everyone, individually and collectively, knows far less than he does not know even about the smallest body, so a fortiori cannot fully know God, the greatest object.
claims: No philosopher, nor all philosophers together, can exhaust the infinite mathematical truths contained in even the smallest physical body.
If the smallest creature cannot be fully known, God (the greatest) cannot be fully known a fortiori.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e3952.summary: Argues from the second Supposition and Aristotelian doctrine that in a graded series of increasing difficulty of knowledge there must be a supremely difficult term, which can only be God; since every infinite series of such graded truths (as in creatures) is inexhaustible by any philosopher, God — infinitely more difficult to know than any or all of them, while himself knowing all of them perfectly and infinitely more besides (per the ninth part) — cannot be fully known.
claims: Among graded objects of knowledge there must be a supremely difficult one, namely God.
God cannot be fully known since even the lesser members of the graded series already exceed philosophical knowledge.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4046.summary: Concludes that any sober philosopher should recognize, as the highest philosophy, that nothing short of God can fully know God except perhaps through God himself, invoking authorities: the 24 philosophers' definitions of God (unsignifiable by words, unintelligible by intellect, known only through ignorance), Hermes on divine truth having no shadow-trace in the world, and Plato's Timaeus on the maker of the universe being as hard to find as impossible to worthily describe once found.
claims: Classical philosophical authorities themselves affirm the fundamental unknowability/ineffability of God.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4068.summary: Extends the argument from God's being to God's acting: if the philosopher, being finite in intellect, cannot fully know God's incomprehensible being, he cannot fully know God's action either, since action is proportioned to the agent; since God (per the first Supposition, third, fourth, and ninth parts) is of simply infinite power, he can easily conceive and perform wondrous deeds and modes of acting beyond any finite ingenuity's full comprehension.
claims: Full knowledge of an agent's action requires proportion to the agent's power; God's infinite power outstrips finite comprehension of his possible actions.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4101.summary: Illustrates the incomprehensibility of even natural operations: a tiny spark of fire produces infinitely many luminous circles, intersecting spheres, luminous and visual pyramids, and rays with infinitely many optical properties (an infinity of geometric/arithmetic and perspectival conclusions), which no one can fully know.
claims: Even a minimal natural action (light from a spark) generates effects too numerous and complex for any mind to fully comprehend.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4047.summary: Asks rhetorically whether the philosopher fully knows the action of the magnet on iron, or many similar hidden natural properties and modes of action — implying he does not.
claims: Even ordinary natural phenomena like magnetism remain incompletely understood by philosophers.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4053.summary: Argues that philosophers do not even certainly and perfectly know any single natural thing or action, since rival philosophers (and even one's own later self) contradict a given opinion, and the passage of time regularly overturns confidently-held views, showing the instability and non-certainty of natural philosophical claims.
claims: The history of philosophical disagreement and self-revision shows that natural-philosophical claims lack the certainty philosophers ascribe to them.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4075.summary: Notes that one's confidence in an opinion diminishes as more rival authorities dissent, so much that if all philosophers and common people uniformly held the contrary, the philosopher himself would abandon his view; concludes that such 'natural philosophy' is really just faith grounded in the momentary absence of a stronger contrary argument or a larger body of dissenting witnesses, not genuine scientific certainty — a position the Academic skeptics candidly embraced, denying that anything can be known where probable contradiction exists.
claims: Confidence in philosophical opinions tracks social consensus, not demonstrative certainty, making such 'knowledge' effectively a kind of faith.
The Academic skeptics rightly recognized that nothing is known with certainty in matters admitting probable contradiction.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4099.summary: Observes that philosophers hold many positions merely from childhood habituation and sectarian allegiance (Academic, Peripatetic, Stoic, etc.) without rational necessity, as shown by the fact that each sect can maintain, without evident contradiction, a view another sect rejects, in probable/disputed matters.
claims: Much of philosophical doctrine is sect-conditioned habituation rather than demonstrated truth.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4117.summary: Cites Aristotle (Categories, on relatives) admitting the difficulty of confident assertion in such matters without long study, and 'doubting is not useless'; and Plato (Timaeus) that giving account of the divine powers exceeds human capacity, so we should rely on credulity — concluding that if philosophy itself rests on such credence-based method (citing Hermes on humans seeing celestial things dimly, 'as through a mist'), Christians may likewise be permitted articles of faith reached similarly.
claims: Philosophy's own greatest authorities (Aristotle, Plato, Hermes) concede that ultimate matters are approached through credence/faith rather than demonstration, licensing an analogous epistemic status for Christian articles of faith.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4142.summary: Piles up further Aristotelian testimony (Metaphysics II on truth being both easy and hard, likened to bats' eyes before daylight; Ethics VI on trusting experienced/prudent people's unproven assertions as much as demonstrations; Posterior Analytics/Elenchi on the learner needing to believe; De Caelo on 'human' credal certainty sufficing) to show that philosophers themselves profess faith within natural philosophy — so if philosophers permit this in natural matters, Christians should be allowed the same in moral/religious matters, where even less persuasion and certainty is required.
claims: Aristotle repeatedly licenses belief/trust as an epistemic mode even in philosophy, undercutting the objection that Christian faith is illegitimately non-demonstrative.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4175.summary: Turns to a further overreach of the philosopher: presuming he can demonstratively prove every divine operation. Counters that since God is a rational power of free will (per the eighth part), no demonstrative reason naturally precedes and compels his will to act or not act — God can freely do or omit many things as reasonable, just as humans do; nor does the claim that 'God must always do the best possible' hold, since God cannot 'do better' in the sense of doing the single optimum, for any candidate optimum A would either be God himself (absurd — multiplying gods, against the first Supposition and 17th part) or, being less perfect than God, could always be surpassed by God's infinite power (per the fourth and seventh parts) doing better and better without end.
claims: God's will is free and not determined by an antecedent demonstrative necessity to always produce the objectively 'best possible' thing.
There is no single 'best possible' creature, since God's infinite power can always exceed any candidate.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4212.summary: Reinforces that God can always make things better, unimpeded by lack of knowledge or power (per the first Supposition and fourth, third, seventh, eighth parts); denying this would make God's power non-free/non-rational (contra the eighth part), and would entail, since all things flow from divine providence and will, that everything happens by absolute necessity (contra the first Supposition and third part) — which philosophers themselves deny, since a more perfect mode of acting (freely) is possible. Notes the philosopher is caught in his own words: saying God 'necessarily does the best' implies both that alternative possibles exist and that God could do otherwise.
claims: Denying God can always improve on his works would collapse divine action into absolute necessity, which even philosophers reject.
The claim 'God necessarily does the optimum' is self-undermining.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4238.summary: Applies the point concretely: if God always does what is better, and it is better that a good and true law be divinely given to humans than not given, then God did give humans such a law — and what law could this be but the most holy Christian law?
claims: Given that a divinely-given true law is better than none, and God (per the prior argument) provides such goods, the Christian law is identified as that law.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4247.summary: Since God cannot be fully known by natural human inquiry, and is necessarily far more unknown than known (with his multifarious operations proportionately unknown), there is no reason God could not, if he willed, reveal some of his secrets and operations, whenever, to whomever, and however he willed — through angels, prophets, or himself — just as a person can reveal the secrets of their own heart and deeds to others who cannot otherwise discover them. Philosophers should therefore stop scorning Christians for believing divinely revealed truths about God that cannot be demonstrated, provided Christians can defend them against contrary demonstrations; it should suffice for any Christian, indeed any person, that 'God says it' as proof, since God (per the first Supposition and third part) cannot err or lie — and such are the articles of the Christian faith.
claims: Divine revelation is a coherent and legitimate source of knowledge unavailable to unaided natural reason.
God's own testimony ('God says it') is sufficient warrant for the articles of faith, since God cannot lie or err.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4273.summary: Asserts confidently that every article of the Christian faith, however great or small, was revealed long before its inauguration through solemn prophets, as the authentic books of Old and New Testament show, and that no article of Christian faith fails to find efficacious grounding in the Old Testament and ancient prophecies for an unbiased, non-sophistical, sober judge — illustrated at length by the legendary account of Emperor Constantine's conversion and the disputation before Pope Sylvester, in which twelve learned Jewish masters and two pagan philosophers debate Christian doctors, with Sylvester refuting the Jewish masters from their own Scriptures and overcoming a rival's magic with a true miracle, converting the Queen, judges, and other unbelievers present.
claims: Every Christian doctrine is grounded in Old Testament prophecy antedating Christianity.
The Constantine/Sylvester disputation narrative is offered as historical confirmation of Christian truth over both Jewish and pagan objection.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4331.summary: Rebuts the objection that Christians fabricated the Old Testament and prophetic books after the fact to make them appear to predict Christianity, citing the testimony of pagan histories predating Christianity (Ptolemy II Philadelphus's commissioning of the Septuagint translation, attested by Josephus) as independent evidence that the Old Testament long predates Christ.
claims: Independent pre-Christian pagan historical testimony (the Septuagint's commissioning) refutes the charge that the Old Testament was retroactively fabricated by Christians.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4351.summary: Adds that the Jews themselves — sworn enemies of the Christian faith, in continuous existence since Abraham and Moses — possess and attest, in their own Hebrew tongue, the entire Old Testament and its prophetic books as ancient compositions of their forefathers and prophets, providing hostile-witness corroboration of the texts' antiquity and content.
claims: Jewish preservation and attestation of the Old Testament, as a hostile witness to Christianity, corroborates the text's antiquity and authenticity.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4364.summary: Anticipates the objection 'if so, why do Jews not universally believe in Christ,' answering that many Jews who understood the Law and Prophets best did believe, adhered to Christ, wrote the Gospels and Epistles, founded the New Testament on the Old, and were martyred for their faith — invoking the Jewish historian Josephus (still a practicing Jew) and his famous (if disputed) Testimonium Flavianum passage describing Jesus as a wise man, wonder-worker, teacher, crucified under Pilate, who appeared alive on the third day as the prophets foretold, and from whom the Christians take their name.
claims: Many learned Jews (the apostles and evangelists) did convert and found Christianity on Jewish scripture.
Josephus's testimony (even as a non-Christian Jew) corroborates the basic Gospel narrative.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4403.summary: Notes that many Jews continue to convert, while others refuse from pride and malice (sometimes converting only on their deathbed) or are deterred by the punitive custom, in some regions, of confiscating a converted Jew's goods to their lord.
claims: Continued Jewish non-conversion is attributed to pride, malice, or fear of material/social punishment (confiscation), not to lack of evidence.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4416.summary: Adds ignorance of the Law and Prophets and lack of sound doctrine as further causes of Jewish non-belief, compounded by hostile, non-traditional interpretive habits instilled from childhood in opposition to Christian doctrine — noting philosophers themselves know how powerful early childhood habituation is.
claims: Ignorance and inherited interpretive bias, not lack of evidence, explain much Jewish non-belief.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4432.summary: Invokes prophetic texts (Moses's curses for disobedience — blindness, madness, groping at noon; Isaiah's 'hear and do not understand... make the heart of this people fat') to explain the Jews' collective blindness as a divinely foretold punishment for sin, deferred until the general conversion of Gentiles and Jews at the world's end.
claims: Jewish non-belief is itself prophesied as a temporary, providentially ordained blindness, to be lifted before the end of the world.
concepts: eschatological conversion of Israel and Gentiles

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4475.summary: Continues citing prophecy of hardened unbelief and eventual future understanding: the angel's words to Daniel about a sealed book to be opened only at the appointed time, and Isaiah's oracle of a sealed book/vision that the wise cannot read, God having 'closed their eyes' because the people honor him with lips but not heart — imagery of the incomprehension and eventual future clarification of these mysteries.
claims: The Daniel and Isaiah sealed-book prophecies are read as foretelling both present incomprehension of scripture by unbelievers and future disclosure.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4519.summary: Cites further prophecies (Moses, David, Jeremiah, Hosea) of Israel's eventual return to God 'in the latter days,' identifying the promised Davidic king as the Messiah, since the promise to David that his seed would reign forever is why the Messiah is often figured under David's name in the prophetic books.
claims: Old Testament prophecy foretells a future national return of Israel to God and the coming of a Davidic Messiah.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4552.summary: Notes it was prophesied that, on account of the sin to be committed against Christ, Jerusalem and its Temple would be destroyed and the Jews irrecoverably dispersed among foreign lands — fulfilled shortly after Christianity's founding and still ongoing roughly 1200-1300 years later, as the Jews themselves concede — suggesting this judgment serves so that the Jews and their own books, beyond suspicion of bias, provide unwitting testimony for Christianity against themselves.
claims: The destruction of Jerusalem and the ongoing Jewish diaspora, as fulfilled prophecy, functions as unwitting hostile-witness confirmation of Christian claims.
concepts: destruction of Jerusalem as fulfilled prophecy

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4572.summary: Argues it is incredible that the prophets, who so consistently condemned vice, taught virtue publicly and privately even unto martyrdom, and whose God-worked miracles are attested, could have been frauds; and equally incredible that they should be truthful about everything else they foretold concerning their own and other nations (Babylonians, Egyptians, Persians, Medes, Cyrus, Greeks, Romans — all verified by events and reputable chronicles) yet fabricate only the matters pertaining to Christians — especially since, if fabricating, they would hardly have invented such calamities for their own descendants and such benefits for us, who were not yet born.
claims: The prophets' proven reliability regarding verifiable historical predictions supports trusting their Christ-related predictions too.
It is implausible that fabricators would invent prophecies harmful to their own people and beneficial to outsiders.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4622.summary: Claims that all the great philosophers whose writings he has consulted concede the reality of prophecy and true prophets, listing Aristotle (Secret of Secrets), Averroes (on Sleep and Waking, citing Socrates), Avicenna, Algazel, Ptolemy, Albumazar, Haly, and other astrologers as affirming prophets and prophecy.
claims: Major philosophical and astrological authorities across traditions concede the reality of prophecy.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4640.summary: Argues further that anyone who concedes true dreams as genuine indicators of future/past/present events must also concede the truth of prophets and prophecy, since all philosophers and common people concede true dreams; supports this with Aristotle's De Somno et Vigilia and Averroes's commentary distinguishing divinations and prophecies as species of the same class of veridical dream-based comprehension, treating denial of these as tantamount to denying the plain evidence of the senses.
claims: Universal acceptance of veridical dreams logically commits one to accepting prophecy as a related phenomenon.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4674.summary: Continues with Averroes's account of dream interpretation (citing Aristotle on the interpreter's disposition) and Algazel and Avicenna on true predictive dreams, then reports that the philosophers, seeking the cause of prophecy and true dreams, agree it is God, who illuminates and inspires prophets waking or sleeping out of divine solicitude for humans — citing Aristotle's Secret of Secrets at length on prophets' purified intellect arising from detachment from bodily desires, and on the 'fiery power' (identified with the agent intellect) as the source of this illumination, tracing the origin of philosophy itself (Indians, Persians, Greeks, Latins) back to revelations given to prophets, and citing Enoch's secret knowledge as an example.
claims: Philosophers themselves trace the cause of prophecy and true dreams to God's illuminating providence.
The very origins of philosophical learning are traced back to prophetic/revelatory sources, per Aristotle's Secret of Secrets.
concepts: agent intellect as source of prophetic illumination

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4736.summary: Cites Avicenna and Algazel similarly affirming that the prophet is sent by God through divine inspiration and illumination as part of God's providence and governance, and Avicenna's claim (Metaphysics X.3) that the prophet's mission and content originate necessarily from God's wisdom.
claims: Avicenna and Algazel affirm prophetic mission as divinely necessitated by God's providential wisdom.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4756.summary: Cites Ptolemy's Centiloquium and Haly's commentary distinguishing two ways of knowing future things — astrological observation of the stars, versus knowledge gained through divine grace and inspiration, called by philosophers 'divine' when pure — with Ptolemy noting some diviners under the lunar sphere gain this art by teaching, others by divine inspiration, and Socrates (via Averroes) disclaiming that his own knowledge, though not divine science, was 'human science.'
claims: Ptolemy and Haly distinguish a purely astrological mode of prediction from a divinely-inspired mode, both attested by philosophical authority.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4792.summary: Argues syllogistically that whoever concedes true dreams are from God must concede prophecies are too, since the cited philosophers all concede true dreams are from God; supports this with Averroes's extended account (De Somno et Vigilia) that the same agent intellect that furnishes first principles to waking cognition furnishes knowledge in dreams — a nobler mode of giving attributed to the divine will — and that this is why prophecy, sharing this mode, is attributed to God and to angels, illustrated by Pharaoh's dream interpreted by Joseph.
claims: The agent intellect's role in veridical dreaming is philosophically analogous to, and continuous with, prophetic revelation, both traced to God.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4836.summary: Concludes that true prophets should be believed as fearlessly, securely, constantly, and firmly as God himself, since they prophesy to humans nothing but what they had first seen and learned from God, and it is God who speaks through them.
claims: Because true prophets speak only what God has shown them, believing the prophets is equivalent to believing God.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4847.summary: Notes that disciples routinely trust teachers, and lesser or later philosophers trust greater or earlier ones, even absent demonstrative argument, simply on their bare assertion — as Plato himself does regarding the lesser gods/daemons in the Timaeus, arguing that since giving an account of such invisible divine powers exceeds human capacity, 'credulity' toward the ancients (sons and grandsons of the gods, by their own claim) suffices, since they speak of their own domestic affairs; Calcidius's commentary similarly reports Pythagoras's dictum 'he himself said it' as ending inquiry without further proof for those imbued with ancient divine wisdom.
claims: Philosophical tradition itself sanctions deferring to ancient authorities' bare testimony without demonstrative proof, especially regarding divine matters — a precedent for accepting prophetic testimony similarly.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e4890.summary: Adds Aristotle's own statements (Sophistical Refutations, De Caelo) that the learner must believe, and that one ought to trust the accounts of the ancients, especially one's forebears, as true; concludes that if such non-demonstrating ancient authorities are to be believed in philosophical matters, far more should the famous prophets, divinely inspired and taught, be believed — introducing the pagan Sibyl as a further prophetic witness, recounting her interpretation of a Roman senatorial dream-vision of nine suns representing nine future generations, leading into her prophecy of the fourth sun/generation.
claims: If Aristotle sanctions trusting ancient non-demonstrating authorities, a fortiori the divinely-inspired prophets (including the pagan Sibyl) deserve belief.
Introduces the Sibylline oracle as independent pagan prophetic testimony to be examined.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5005.summary: Quotes the Sibyl's prophecy of the 'fourth sun/generation': a virgin of Hebrew stock named Mary, betrothed to Joseph, will conceive without union of man by the Holy Spirit a son named Jesus, true God and true man as all the prophets foretold, fulfilling and joining the Hebrew law with his own, his kingdom lasting forever, attended by angelic hosts singing 'Glory to God in the highest' and a heavenly voice calling him 'beloved son.'
claims: The pagan Sibylline oracle is presented as a virgin-birth/Incarnation prophecy matching the Gospel Nativity accounts almost verbatim.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5025.summary: Continues quoting the Sibylline oracle: Hebrew priests protest her words as terrible, she insists it must happen though they will not believe (they cite God's covenant with the fathers as reason for their disbelief), then foretells a single true God creator of heaven and earth, the eternal life and paradise of those who honor him, and a catalogue of coming miracles (resurrection of the dead, the lame walking, the deaf hearing, the blind seeing, the multiplication of loaves and fishes, calming storms, walking on water, healing, raising the dead).
claims: Continued Sibylline text purportedly foretells specific Gospel miracles in detail.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5065.summary: Continues the Sibylline prophecy into the Passion narrative: the Law will be dissolved and fall into the hands of the impious, the priests will conspire against Jesus for his signs, seize him, strike, spit on, scourge, and crown him with thorns, give him gall and vinegar, hang him on a tree and kill him, the Temple veil will tear, darkness will fall at midday for three hours, he will descend to the dead and rise on the third day, appear to his disciples, and ascend to heaven with an unending kingdom — the Sibyl anticipating she will be called mad and a liar until these things happen, after which she will be remembered as 'God's magician' rather than insane.
claims: The Sibylline text purportedly details the Passion, Crucifixion, Resurrection, and Ascension in remarkably specific terms.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5103.summary: Introduces a second pagan Gentile Sibylline prophetess (the Chronicles attest ten Sibyls in all): at the time of the coming of Christ, under Augustus, during the twelve peaceful years another Sibyl had foretold, when this Sibyl was asked whether she should allow herself to be worshipped as a god as the Romans proposed, she responded, after a three-day fast, by an act of prophecy in accordance with the earlier Sibyl's prediction: heaven opened at once, great splendor poured over her, and she saw in heaven a most beautiful Virgin standing on an altar holding a child in her arms, and heard a voice saying, 'This is the altar of the Son of God.' Greatly amazed, she prostrated herself in adoration and reported the vision to the Senators, who likewise marveled greatly; in worthy memory of this vision a church of St. Mary, called Ara Coeli, was built in Rome at the place where it appeared to the emperor.
claims: A second pagan Sibyl, consulted about accepting worship as a god, instead received a vision of the Virgin and Child and was told the altar belonged to the Son of God, occasioning the founding of the Roman church of Ara Coeli.
concepts: vision of the Virgin and Child

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5132.summary: Asks rhetorically whether all these things do not bear witness to Christ, and adds two further pagan/foreign witnesses: Balaam, a foreigner, who likewise gave testimony to Christ; and a long-dead and buried man whose tomb, discovered in Constantinople in the first year of the Emperor Constantine and his mother Irene, contained a golden tablet inscribed 'Christ will be born of the Virgin Mary, and I believe in him; under Constantine and Irene, O sun, you will see me again' — arguing that since the outcome proved the second part of this inscription true, the first part (about Christ's birth) should likewise be believed, since it was evidently added to confirm the first.
claims: Balaam's oracle and a Constantinopolitan tomb inscription naming Constantine and Irene together constitute further pagan/foreign testimony to Christ, and the inscription's fulfilled second half authenticates its Christological first half.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5154.summary: Recounts a further wondrous testimony: in the time of King Ferdinand of Castile, a Jew breaking open a rock near Toledo to expand a vineyard found within it, in an uncracked cavity, a book of leaf-like wooden pages written in three languages (Hebrew, Greek, and Latin), the size of a Psalter, describing a threefold division of the world from Adam to Christ and the character of the men of each age, and placing the start of the third age in Christ with the words 'In the third world the Son of God will be born of the Virgin Mary, and will suffer for the salvation of men'; the same book stated it would be found in King Ferdinand's time, which duly happened, confirming its truth. Moves from witnesses foretelling Christ's coming to witnesses of his presence: John the Baptist in the womb and in adulthood, the just and aged Simeon, the aged Anna, all filled with the spirit of prophecy, and the three Magi from the East, instructed by Balaam's teaching, who followed a miraculous guiding star and brought gifts to the newborn Christ — asking what Christian could have corrupted or coached so many witnesses when the very name 'Christian' was not yet known. Suggests this guiding star may have been the comet seen by the Romans and Octavian Augustus (under whom Christ was born), citing Pliny's Natural History on the comet popularly taken as a sign of Julius Caesar's soul received among the gods, and Calcidius's account of a rarer, holier star tradition in which Chaldean sages, seeing such a star, sought and worshipped the newly born God rather than reading it as a portent of disease and death.
claims: A miraculously discovered ancient trilingual book at Toledo foretold Christ's virgin birth and suffering and validated itself by a fulfilled prediction of its own discovery.
John the Baptist, Simeon, Anna, and the Magi constitute witnesses of Christ's actual presence, complementing the earlier prophetic witnesses to his coming.
The star that guided the Magi may be identified with the historically attested comet of Augustus's reign, which pagan authors themselves associated with a divine or numinous significance.
concepts: pagan and Jewish testimony to Christ
the Magi and the guiding star

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5233.summary: Passes over (deliberately) further alleged Christ-testimonies in Ovid's De Vetula and Albumasar, then cites other classical signs said to attest Christ: the legendary prophecy that the Temple of Peace and the statue of Romulus in Rome would not fall until a virgin gave birth (fulfilled at Christ's Nativity), the fall of all Egypt's idols at the Holy Family's entry into Egypt, and the angelic annunciation of Christ's birth to the shepherds ('Glory to God in the highest').
claims: Various classical Roman legends (Temple of Peace, statue of Romulus, fall of Egyptian idols) are marshaled as pagan corroboration of Christ's Nativity.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5253.summary: Cites the theophany at Christ's baptism (Epiphany) and the darkening of the sun during the Crucifixion (from the sixth to the ninth hour, near full moon) as further attesting signs; anticipates and rejects the objection that the darkness was merely a chance thick cloud, arguing it is implausible that Matthew, Mark, and Luke would independently and concordantly record such an event in their foundational texts if it were merely an ordinary cloud, especially given the astronomical impossibility (explained via solar/terrestrial geometry) of any single cloud covering the whole visible sun given the sun's size relative to the earth.
claims: The Gospel accounts' agreement, combined with astronomical reasoning about cloud/sun geometry, rules out a naturalistic 'passing cloud' explanation for the Crucifixion darkness.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5312.summary: Concludes the darkness was a preternatural, supernatural eclipse signifying something about the Author of nature, citing the pagan philosopher Dionysius the Areopagite's famous exclamation ('either the God of nature suffers, or the fabric of the world is being dissolved') and his subsequent altar 'To the Unknown God,' later recognized by him as Christ when Paul preached in Athens; also gives Dionysius's detailed eyewitness account (in an epistle to Polycarp against the sophist Apollophanes) of an astronomically anomalous eclipse witnessed at Heliopolis — the moon crossing the sun outside a conjunction and reversing its usual direction — as a supernatural sign proper to Christ alone.
claims: Dionysius the Areopagite's altar 'To the Unknown God' and his eyewitness account of an astronomically impossible eclipse are presented as pagan philosophical corroboration of the Crucifixion darkness as a genuine miracle.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5362.summary: Analyzes the physical impossibilities in the reported eclipse (moon moving too fast between oppositions, eclipse occurring mid-lunar-month, unusual duration and direction of motion) as things no one trained in astronomy could regard as natural, comparing it to the biblical miracles of the sun standing still for Joshua and reversing for Hezekiah (attested also, per Dionysius, by the Babylonians' astonishment); concludes by urging the sophist Apollophanes (and, by extension, the reader) to trust Christian/Gospel histories, since consistent refusal to credit any nation's histories (including one's own, much of which one has not personally witnessed) would destroy the basis of all human trust and social bonds.
claims: The described eclipse's physical anomalies parallel other biblical solar miracles (Joshua, Hezekiah), reinforcing its supernatural character.
Consistent skepticism toward all historical testimony (including of one's own nation) is self-defeating and socially destructive.
concepts: argument from the necessity of historical testimony

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5434.summary: Cites Amos's prophecy ('the sun will set at noon... I will darken the earth in daylight') as literally referring to the final destruction of the Jews (fulfilled shortly after Christ's death, under Titus and Vespasian, and persisting to the present), among other similar ancient prophecies, while rejecting any reading of it as a mere natural eclipse, since it would be incredible for so many prophets to foretell an ordinary, predictable natural eclipse as a great prophetic sign.
claims: Amos's prophecy of darkness is read as referring to the destruction of Jerusalem, not a natural eclipse, since prophets would not present a predictable natural event as a portentous sign.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5458.summary: Turns to directly refute the sophist Apollophanes's skepticism as logically and materially defective: logically, because it commits the fallacy of arguing from an author's silence to falsity ('no Greek or Barbarian wrote of this, therefore it did not happen'), especially since such observers, never having witnessed or heard of anything similar occurring mid-lunar-month (and knowing it impossible by nature), would not have carefully noted it, presuming instead — if they noticed unusual darkness at all — that it was due to a dense cloud, as commonly happens.
claims: Apollophanes's skeptical argument from silence is a logical fallacy (argumentum ad ignorantiam), compounded by observers' natural tendency to misattribute an unusual event to an ordinary cause.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5479.summary: Anticipates a similar skeptical cavil against other celestial signs mentioned earlier, but corrects it by noting (per mathematical/astronomical theorems, not sophistry) that a solar eclipse, unlike a lunar eclipse, is not visible everywhere at once due to parallax of viewing angle — so the eclipse could have occurred and been visible in Judea even if unseen in Greece on a clear day there.
claims: The geographic non-universality of solar eclipse visibility (due to parallax) explains why Greek observers might not have seen an eclipse visible in Judea.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5495.summary: Further faults Apollophanes's argument on the facts, since (as already shown) it is false that no Greek observed or mentioned the eclipse; adds further corroborating Christian evidence — the Resurrection witnessed and attested by angels, the Ascension witnessed by many with angelic attestation, and the sending of the Holy Spirit as shown by the sudden, powerful transformation of the unlearned lay disciples (speaking in tongues, understanding Scripture) — as further testimony to Christ.
claims: Apollophanes's factual premise (that no Greek recorded the eclipse) is false.
The Resurrection, Ascension, and Pentecost transformation of the disciples provide further corroborating testimony to Christ.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5511.summary: Argues that Christ's other miracles, vastly exceeding the powers of nature, as attested by authentic and famous histories, produce firm faith, since philosophers customarily reason from known sensible effects to unknown causes; begins a catalogue of miraculous effects persisting among Christians in Christ's name up to the present day.
claims: The scale and persistence of miracles attributed to Christ (and continuing among Christians) argue, by the standard philosophical method of inferring cause from effect, to a genuinely supernatural cause.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5542.summary: Lists Gospel miracles (water into wine, feeding the five thousand with twelve baskets left over, instantaneous cleansing of lepers, sight to the blind, healing of paralytics, cure of all manner of sickness, and true raising of the dead) as attested concordantly by authentic histories and foretold by ancient prophets and Sibyls, even conceded by the hostile Jews and Josephus; challenges the philosopher to name the cause of such effects, arguing that since the effects exceed the power of all created nature, so must their cause.
claims: The catalogue of Gospel miracles, exceeding natural power, requires a cause likewise exceeding created nature.
concepts: argument from effect exceeding natural causes

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5560.summary: Notes that irreligious sophists respond in various ways to such arguments; some simply deny all miracles outright, but are refuted as Apollophanes was, since it is uncivil and inhuman to simply deny all Christian and even Jewish histories; anyone denying miracles altogether must also deny any possibility of miracles occurring, which presumes one can fully know all divine operations — contrary to the corollarium's opening argument and the seventh/eighth parts (of an earlier corollarium on divine power).
claims: Blanket denial of all miracles requires the (already refuted) presumption of fully knowing all possible divine operations.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5593.summary: Challenges deniers of miracles to witness contemporary ones firsthand: reports the English king's (the 'royal touch') healing of scrofula ('the king's evil') by prayer, laying on of hands, and the sign of the cross, said to be performed continually and successfully by the kings of England and France, attested by crowds, chronicles, and common report (whence the disease's name); also cites the miracle to be experienced at St. Patrick's Purgatory in Ireland.
claims: The English/French royal touch for scrofula and the phenomena of St. Patrick's Purgatory are offered as contemporary, verifiable miracles.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5649.summary: Offers pagan-attested miracles as further corroboration for skeptics unwilling to credit Christian histories: Aristotle's account (De Mundo) of a great earthquake/fire near Etna that miraculously spared pious young men carrying their aged parents (also told by Solinus, with the site named 'Field of the Pious'), and Solinus's account of the Vulcanian Hill in Sicily where sacrificial wood spontaneously ignites for the pious, and flame plays harmlessly among diners after sacrifice.
claims: Pagan historians (Aristotle, Solinus) themselves record miraculous, providence-attesting events unconnected to Christianity, undercutting selective skepticism.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5662.summary: Adds Pliny's account of the Hirpi family near Rome who walk barefoot over burning coals in an annual sacrifice to Apollo without being burned (and are exempted from military and civic duties for it); Aristotle's Secret of Secrets recounting a miracle worked through a praying magus, and his testimony (citing Hermogenes) that the sole worker of miracles is God, from whom every wonder descends.
claims: Further pagan-attested wonders (the Hirpi fire-walkers) and philosophical testimony (Aristotle/Hermogenes) that God alone works miracles.
concepts: Hermogenes on God as sole miracle-worker

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5682.summary: Cites further philosophical concessions of miracles (Avicenna, though erring on their causes; Algazel; Albumasar on prophetic miracles) and Josephus's argument (regarding the Israelites' crossing of the Red Sea) that no one should disbelieve such an ancient miracle, given that even Alexander the Great's army reportedly experienced a parallel parting of the Pamphylian Sea, as all his historians concede.
claims: Josephus argues for the plausibility of the biblical Red Sea miracle by analogy to an attested parallel wonder in Alexander's campaign.
concepts: Alexander and the Pamphylian Sea parallel

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5713.summary: Recounts further wonder-tales: the legend (via the Historia Scholastica and Josephus) of Alexander enclosing the Ten Lost Tribes behind the Caspian mountains by prayer; Valerius Maximus's account of the Vestal Virgin who proved her chastity by carrying a sieve full of water from the Tiber without spilling; and introduces Ovid's account (Fasti) of the goddess Cybele's miraculous ship stuck in the Tiber's mud, freed only by the falsely-accused Vestal Claudia Quinta's prayer and light pull on a rope.
claims: A series of pagan wonder-legends (Alexander/Ten Tribes, the Vestal's sieve, Claudia Quinta's ship) is compiled as further evidence that pagan sources themselves attest miracles.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5750.summary: Quotes at length Ovid's verses (Fasti) narrating the Claudia Quinta episode: the ship stuck fast in the mud despite the combined efforts of the Roman populace, until the falsely-accused Vestal Claudia prays to the goddess for vindication and draws the ship free with ease, to the crowd's astonishment.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5837.summary: Anticipates the objection that these tales rest only on suspect poets, and corroborates them with historians: Livy (on the Second Punic War) and Solinus attest the Claudia Quinta story, and Augustine (City of God) concedes it along with related matters; adds Solinus's account of Hercules's shrine in the Forum Boarium, mysteriously avoided by flies and dogs due to the smell of a club Hercules is said to have left there.
claims: The Claudia Quinta legend is corroborated by historians (Livy, Solinus, Augustine), not merely poets.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5864.summary: Recounts, from Hayton's history of the Tartars, the legend of Chinggis Khan ('Chamguiscam') receiving a dream-vision of a white knight commanding him, in the name of the immortal God, to cross the Belian mountains westward to conquer new lands after worshipping toward the east with nine genuflections — which he obeyed, whereupon the sea miraculously receded nine feet from the mountain, opening a path for his people.
claims: The legend of Chinggis Khan's providential dream and the miraculous parting of the sea is presented as further cross-cultural attestation of divine intervention.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5916.summary: Concludes only a hard-hearted denier of all such witnesses would reject them, and if one credits these (pagan/Tartar) histories, one should far more credit the more famous Hebrew and Christian ones; turns to address those who concede Christian miracles but dispute their true cause, beginning with physicians who attribute Christ's healings to an optimally balanced bodily 'complexion' (humoral temperament).
claims: Consistency requires that if pagan wonder-histories are credited, the more attested Hebrew/Christian ones should be credited more.
Introduces and sets up refutation of the naturalistic 'good bodily complexion' explanation of Christ's healing miracles.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5964.summary: Refutes the 'good complexion' theory: it might explain a few healings by touch, but not those Christ performed without touching or even entering the house of the sick, at a distance, merely by consenting to a request — whereas philosophers and physicians agree (citing Aristotle) that in any real or spiritual action, mover and moved must be together (proximate), which a merely bodily 'complexion' cannot satisfy at a distance.
claims: The 'complexion' theory cannot explain Christ's distance-healings, since bodily causation (per Aristotle) requires proximity between mover and moved.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5977.summary: Further argues a merely finite 'complexion,' being of finite virtue, would require time and a gradual alteration proportioned to the resistance of the illness (with worse illness requiring more time, per ordinary medical understanding, producing a 'convalescence' stage) — whereas Christ healed instantly and perfectly whomever he willed, showing the cause was not a natural complexion.
claims: A finite natural cause (complexion) requires proportional time and gradual convalescence to heal, unlike Christ's instantaneous, perfect cures — proving the cause was supernatural.
concepts: instantaneous healing as evidence against natural cause

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6014.summary: Notes further that even granting a complexion could achieve such feats, some illness could still in principle be so severe as to exceed its curative power — yet scripture records Christ curing even the gravest, most chronic diseases without exception, and even raising the dead, which no bodily complexion (however potent) could ever accomplish.
claims: Christ's power to raise the dead exceeds what any bodily complexion, however powerful, could in principle achieve.
concepts: raising of the dead as decisive counterexample

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6032.summary: Argues that if a mere 'complexion' sufficed for Christ's miracles, lesser complexions should proportionally work lesser miracles — yet no complexion could raise a four-days-dead, decaying corpse by word alone, turn water to wine, multiply loaves and fish, walk on water, move the earth and open tombs at the Crucifixion, eclipse the sun, rise from death, ascend to heaven, or send the Holy Spirit to inspire the apostles so effectively; nor could a single 'complexion' account for miracles worked through many different Christians (men, women, old, young, living, dead), nor through Moses and the ancient prophets (drying seas, moving mountains, stopping and reversing the sun).
claims: The full range and diversity of biblical/Christian miracles (across many different agents, and exceeding any conceivable degree of bodily 'complexion') cannot be explained by the complexion theory.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6042.summary: Adds that 'complexion,' being an irrational natural power, acts necessarily toward only one effect (like fire heating) and not freely/electively toward either of two opposites as miracles require — yet Christ's complexion, if the cause, would then have acted necessarily and continuously whenever a suitable patient was present, whereas scripture records Christ and others performing miracles voluntarily and by free choice.
claims: A natural, irrational power like 'complexion' acts of necessity, not by free choice — contradicting the voluntary, selective character of Christ's recorded miracles.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6094.summary: Asks why God would need to be prayed to for miraculous effects if a natural complexion sufficed on its own — yet the saints through whom miracles occur do pray to God, which would be wholly superfluous unless God himself were working the miracles.
claims: The practice of praying for miracles is otherwise inexplicable/superfluous unless God, not a natural cause, is the true agent.
concepts: prayer as evidence of true divine causation

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6120.summary: Argues that if any creature can work miracles, so can God (per the first Supposition), and it befits God all the more to do so when humbly petitioned; cites Hermogenes (that God alone works miracles, seconded by Aristotle) and Aristotle's Secret of Secrets on the practical value of foreknowledge of the future for prompting prayerful petition to avert threatened evils — quoting Avicenna that since the 'First Truth' knows all this, prayers, sacrifices, and litanies (e.g., for rain) genuinely avail, since certainty of this fact should move one to shun evil and pursue good, and this certainty rests on the evidence of miracles; Avicenna also denies natural causation for the providential design of animal/plant anatomy, attributing it instead to divine care — a fortiori applicable to miracles — noting the common people intuitively grasp this truth better than would-be philosophers who deny it out of ignorance of its true causes.
claims: If any creature can work wonders, God (of infinite power) can do so a fortiori and is fittingly moved by prayer.
Avicenna's denial of purely natural causation for providential biological design supports, a fortiori, a non-natural cause for miracles.
The common people's intuitive acceptance of divine causation is epistemically sounder than the skeptical 'philosopher's' denial.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6133.summary: Turns to refute an alternative naturalistic theory (astrologers like Albumasar) that attributes miracles to conjunctions and celestial influences; counters that any celestial body or conjunction, unable to act immediately on earth, would require an intermediate medium (not merely fire or air, but some great, specially-conceived/born/marked person) — but such a person would then be working miracles by virtue of his own 'complexion,' collapsing this theory back into the already-refuted complexion theory.
claims: The astrological-conjunction theory of miracles, when analyzed, reduces to the already-refuted complexion theory, since it still requires a bodily intermediary.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6196.summary: Further asks how a celestial conjunction/virtue could break its own regular celestial influence (stopping/reversing the sun, or a mid-lunar-month solar eclipse), then recounts (via the traveler Hayton) the legend of a mysterious impenetrable darkness enveloping a whole province (Hanissen) in Georgia, said to have arisen miraculously to shelter fleeing Christians from a persecuting pagan emperor, sparing them while their pursuers remain trapped in that darkness to this day.
claims: The astrological theory cannot explain celestial phenomena that contradict celestial regularity itself (stopped/reversed sun, anomalous eclipse).
The Georgian 'darkness province' legend is presented as a further inexplicable-by-nature miracle protecting persecuted Christians.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6251.summary: Continues with further celestial-influence-defying wonders and legends: (from Marco Polo's account of oriental regions) a church built in Samarkand whose great dome rests on a single marble column whose base-stone, seized back by resentful Muslims after the Christian patron's death, caused the column to be miraculously suspended unsupported in mid-air (by three palms' height) rather than let the church collapse, a state persisting to the present day.
claims: Marco Polo's account of the Samarkand church's miraculously suspended column is presented as a further wonder unexplainable by celestial influence.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6283.summary: Asks further how celestial influence could annually, for a set number of days, dry the sea to preserve a young child left in its midst, unharmed a year later — recounting the legend of St. Clement, thrown into the sea with an anchor by a persecuting prince, whose disciples' prayers cause the sea to recede three miles for seven days, revealing a marble shrine housing his body, an event later repeated annually.
claims: The St. Clement sea-recession legend is offered as a further example defying naturalistic (celestial) explanation.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6299.summary: Adds the detail that during the St. Clement miracle a mother's small child, left behind by mistake when the sea returned, was found unharmed and merely asleep a year later, concluding that innumerable such glorious miracles fill the histories, none of which can be plausibly attributed to the mere power of celestial bodies.
claims: The child-preserved-in-the-sea detail reinforces that celestial/natural causation cannot account for the full range of recorded miracles.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6343.summary: Challenges the astrologer to specify, from celestial data alone, exactly which miracle will occur, of what kind, when and where, how it will begin and how long it will last — insisting he not evade with vague, unfalsifiable answers (e.g., 'in Gades after 100 years') — arguing that since it is really God's free will (per the eighth and fourth parts) that determines what, when, and where a miracle occurs (and equally, negatively, when and where none will occur), no antecedent necessary celestial cause can be assigned; confirms this since miracles occur in response to prayer, which would be superfluous if mere celestial influence, not God, were the cause.
claims: The astrologer cannot in practice specify miracles predictively from celestial data, because miracles depend on God's free will, not a determinable antecedent celestial cause.
Miracles' correlation with prayer confirms divine, not celestial, causation.
concepts: divine free will vs. celestial determinism

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6395.summary: Turns to a third naturalistic theory: that the human rational soul itself, when sufficiently dominant over the body (citing Aristotle's Secret of Secrets on the prophetic soul, and Avicenna's De Anima IV.4 on a noble/commanding soul obeying its own will to affect even external bodies and matter, e.g. healing, causing rain, drought — comparable to the 'evil eye' — a view also endorsed by Algazel), works miracles through the power of imagination/will alone; responds that this 'imaginative' theory collapses just as readily as the prior ones, since (per the same philosophers and physicians) nothing acts on a distant object except by acting through the intervening medium, so if such a soul willed to heal many equally-afflicted patients placed in that medium, all would be healed equally — a further reductio to be developed.
claims: The 'powerful soul/imagination' theory of miracles is introduced and about to be refuted on the same grounds (action requires acting through an intervening medium) as the complexion theory.
concepts: medium requirement for action at a distance

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5029.summary: Gives, in Latin, the acrostic Sibylline verses on the Last Judgment themselves: the earth will sweat blood in the judgment season, the King will come from heaven through the ages, present in the flesh to judge the world; unbeliever and faithful alike will see God, exalted with the saints at the world's end; souls will stand with their flesh, to be judged; the rough earth will lie amid thick brambles, men will cast away their idols and all their gold; fire will burn the lands, sea, and sky; it will seek out and break the gates of grim Avernus; free light will then be given to the flesh of all the saints, while the guilty are handed over to eternal flame; hidden deeds will be revealed and every man will speak his secrets, which God will lay open; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth; the sun's light will fail, the stars will fall, heaven will be rolled up, the moon's brightness will vanish; hills will be cast down and valleys raised, mountains made level with the plains and the sea's blue depths; all things will cease, the shattered earth will perish, rivers and springs alike will be scorched by fire, and the trumpet will send out its mournful sound; the earth, gaping open, will show forth wretched Tartarean chaos and its manifold woes; kings will stand together before the Lord; and a river of sulfurous fire will fall from heaven.
claims: The Sibylline verses predict a cosmic Last Judgment in which the dead rise with their flesh to be judged, the natural order collapses, and the impious are sent to eternal fire while the saints receive light.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e5090.summary: Notes that any mismatch between the poem's initial letters and the acrostic they are meant to spell could easily be corrected if one wished, and reports what follows in the Sibylline text after these verses: that God will then judge each according to his own deeds, the impious will go into everlasting fire while the just receive the reward of eternal life, and there will be a new heaven and a new earth and a new sea, with the Lord reigning together with the Saints for ever and ever.
claims: The Sibylline prophecy concludes with a final judgment according to works, everlasting punishment for the impious, eternal reward for the just, and a renewed heaven, earth, and sea under God's eternal reign.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6430.summary: Presses the imagination-theory further with a cascade of counterexamples: if the soul's imagination alone could work miracles, any soul's proportionally strong imagination should work proportional miracles, and could raise the dead, recall souls from heaven or hell, or make bodies immortal — none of which anyone claims. Asks whose imagination sustained the darkness at Christ's death (not the Christians', who expected flight, nor the persecutors', who expected to keep pursuing), and whose imagination held up a church column after its base was removed, or (citing Marco Polo) moved a mountain in answer to a Christian's prayer when Saracens threatened Christians with death unless they proved their faith by moving it. Challenges Avicenna directly to move so much as a clod of earth by imagination for a reward, and asks whose imagination converted Saul the persecutor into Paul the apostle.
claims: If imagination alone caused miracles, its effects should scale with the strength of imagination and occur wherever anyone strongly imagines, which manifestly does not happen.
Specific attested miracles (the darkness at the Crucifixion, the moved mountain, the conversion of Paul) cannot be assigned to any human imagination consistent with the imagination theory.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6511.summary: Extends the challenge to miracles worked at the tombs of dead Christian saints (citing St. Clement and, per Marco Polo, the tomb of St. Thomas the Apostle in India, revered even by Saracens who call him a holy man): since a corpse has no imagination, such miracles must be worked by the souls of the saints, which are therefore powerful, holy, and blessed — and if the imagination of the living venerators were the true cause, there would be no reason for them to pray to the saints rather than simply imagining the effect themselves.
claims: Miracles at the tombs of dead saints cannot be explained by the dead body's imagination, and are more plausibly worked through the saints' still-living, powerful souls.
The practice of praying to saints for their intercession is incoherent if imagination alone (rather than the saints' or God's real causal power) produces such effects.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6545.summary: Cites a miracle of St. Thomas Becket (Archbishop of Canterbury) in which a woman who prayed at his tomb out of vanity, wishing for more beautiful eyes, was instead struck blind — arguing her own imagination was aimed at the opposite outcome, so imagination cannot have caused this and other such heavenly miracles.
claims: A miracle that runs contrary to the petitioner's own expectation or desire (as with the woman blinded rather than beautified at Becket's tomb) cannot be explained by the imagination theory of miracles.
