dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6556.summary: Argues that if a human soul could work miracles (as the objection supposes), God — who is shown by the first Supposition and preceding parts to be supremely powerful, merciful, kind, and generous — can work them still more; it is more fitting that God miraculously aid his devoted lovers in their great needs than that he mercilessly reject them, especially since Hermogenes, Aristotle, and Avicenna themselves earlier affirmed God to be the worker of miracles. Notes that even granting some fascinating power to the evil eye of a diseased complexion (as Avicenna allows), this does not extend to true miracle-working, since miracles do not follow the properties of bodily complexion or operate only at short range as ocular fascination does.
claims: God's supreme power and goodness make it more fitting that he work miracles for his devoted followers than withhold aid.
Even the philosophers' own doctrine (Hermogenes, Aristotle, Avicenna) affirms God as the true worker of miracles, undermining their alternative explanations.
The natural phenomenon of ocular 'fascination' from a diseased bodily complexion is disanalogous to true miracles and cannot explain them.
concepts: divine goodness as ground for miracles

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6637.summary: Turns the philosophers' own principle against them: if only a soul 'similar to' the higher principles (God and the angels, per Avicenna) can work miracles, and Christ and holy Christians have in fact worked miracles, it follows their souls are similar to those principles — whereas Muhammad, by his own admission in the Qur'an (responding to those who asked him for miracles, 'I am not sent with this'), could not work miracles, nor can his most ascetic followers, since a disciple is not above his master. Concludes the Saracens and Tartars must therefore have souls unlike the divine principles, and asks rhetorically why they do not become Christians to be made more like them.
claims: By Avicenna's own criterion, Christ's and the saints' miracle-working proves their souls are like the divine principles, while Muhammad's admitted inability to work miracles proves the opposite for him and his followers.
concepts: argument from the interlocutors' own principles

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6666.summary: Anticipates a reply from Aristotle and Avicenna that they do not deny God or some souls work certain miracles, and presses them to distinguish rationally between greater and lesser miracles, since the greatest and most glorious miracles are most fittingly attributed to God. Argues that the miracles surrounding Christ's forerunners (the ancient prophets) and Christ himself are the greatest and most glorious attested, so God is the one who works these glorious Christian miracles in witness to the Christian faith — while Jewish opponents claim Christ's miracles were false, performed by magic or evil spirits (some even alleging he used magical formulas from a book called the Cow of Plato), a claim turned back on the Jews by comparing it to the Manichaean charge that Moses' own miracles came from an evil god.
claims: The greatest, most glorious miracles (those of the prophets and of Christ) are most fittingly attributed to God, establishing God as the source of the Christian miracles.
The Jewish charge that Christ's miracles were magical trickery is self-undermining, since an analogous (Manichaean) charge could equally be leveled against Moses' miracles.
concepts: Manichaean rejection of the Old Testament

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6707.summary: Responds to an anticipated Jewish appeal to the authenticity of their own Scripture attesting Moses' miracles by claiming Christian Scripture is even more authentic: Moses alone wrote of his own miracles, unattested beforehand by other prophets, whereas Christ did not write of his own miracles at all — four principal evangelists and many lesser writers, not conspiring together in one place or time but writing independently in Judea, Italy, Achaia, and Asia, in different languages and manners, agreed in testifying to Christ's teaching, deeds, and miracles, with the Apostles as eyewitnesses who were themselves Jews.
claims: The Gospel testimony to Christ's miracles is more credible than Moses' self-attested miracles because it comes from multiple independent, geographically and linguistically dispersed eyewitnesses rather than a single author writing of himself.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6736.summary: Notes that Christ's miracles, like Moses', were prophetically foretold beforehand (by prophets and the Sibyl alike), so the same reasoning validating Moses' miracles from his conduct applies to Christ; challenges the objector to find any life more innocent, holy, and honest than Christ's, attested even by Gentile sources, and asks whether Christ's manner of life did not match exactly what the Jews' own prophets and the Sibyl had foretold of the coming Messiah.
claims: Christ's miracles were, like Moses', prophetically foretold, and his life's moral perfection (attested by Jewish, Gentile, and Sibylline sources alike) matches the very portrait Jewish prophecy gave of the Messiah.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6759.summary: Answers the objection that Christ sought to overturn the Jewish Law by replying he did not pervert it but expounded and fulfilled it, as had been divinely prophesied; turns the same objection back on the Jews' own future hope, since their own expected Messiah (per their prophet Hosea), who will come riding an ass, will likewise have to prove himself through miracles that could be similarly impugned — so the Jews must defend their future Messiah's miracles by the same standard the author uses to defend Christ's.
claims: The charge that Christ subverted the Law is false, since he fulfilled rather than perverted it as prophesied.

The Jews' own expectation of a future Messiah working miracles is vulnerable to the identical skeptical objection they raise against Christ, so consistency requires them to accept the same standard of proof for both.
concepts: fulfillment versus subversion of the Law

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6775.summary: Argues it is implausible that Christ, if he had been a deceiver working only false, diabolical miracles, would have been so solemnly and consistently foretold by prophets beforehand and attested in person, and confirmed by the Jews' own historian Josephus, as recounted earlier — since true prophecy would not approve a false prophet wholesale rather than condemning him. Adds that Jewish Law itself required a false prophet and law-subverter to be put to death, so if Christ truly were such, his execution would have been meritorious rather than blameworthy — yet the Jews were afterward severely punished (through the Roman destruction of their cities and Temple, captivity, dispersion, and humiliation, as attested by their own historian Josephus) far beyond anything in their prior history, which a good, just, and merciful God (per Suppositions 1 and 3) would not have inflicted except for some singularly grave sin exceeding all their prior sins.
claims: It is inconsistent that true prophecy would wholeheartedly foretell and approve a false prophet, so the prophetic attestation of Christ counts against the charge that he was a deceiver.

If executing Christ as a false prophet had truly been lawful and meritorious, it would not explain the unprecedented severity of Israel's subsequent punishment under Rome, which a just God would reserve for an exceptionally grave sin.

The scale of Jewish national catastrophe after Christ's death is itself evidence that his condemnation and execution constituted a uniquely grave sin, rather than a justified act against a false prophet.
concepts: the Jewish War and destruction of the Temple as divine punishment

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6909.summary: Presses the rhetorical question of what sin other than the killing of Christ could explain the magnitude of Israel's punishment, since their prior sins — adulteries, killing the prophets, forsaking the Lord, and idolatry — had already occurred without incurring punishment of comparable severity.
claims: No sin in Israel's earlier history besides the rejection and killing of Christ is severe enough to account for the unprecedented scale of their subsequent national punishment.
concepts: rejection of Christ as Israel's culminating sin

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6862.summary: Anticipates the objection that the calamity befell the Jews for the unjust killing of John the Baptist or James the brother of Christ (both venerated by Jews as holy), and answers point by point: both were in fact truest witnesses to Christ (John pointing him out directly, James preaching Christ's faith to martyrdom), so this only confirms Christian faith; moreover it was Herod Agrippa, not the Jews collectively, who killed John, and only a rogue high priest Ananus (not communal Jewish consent) who had James stoned — an act that moderate Jews themselves condemned and reported to the king, resulting in Ananus's deposition. Notes that the Jews' earlier killing of prophets did not bring comparable punishment, and even a hypothetical collective guilt for John's and James's deaths, unrepented by later generations, would not by itself explain punishment of this unprecedented severity given God's sworn promise of the land.
claims: The deaths of John the Baptist and James cannot explain Israel's catastrophic punishment, since both were in fact witnesses to Christ, their deaths were not carried out by communal Jewish consent, and the Jews' earlier killing of prophets brought no comparable retribution.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6998.summary: Appeals to the Jews' own Law and history for the pattern of proportionate divine punishment: when the fathers murmured against Moses and despaired of entering the promised land, God kept the guilty generation wandering forty years until they died and only then let their innocent children enter; likewise the Babylonian exile for idolatry lasted only seventy years before the innocent children returned and rebuilt city and Temple; and Moses himself, invoking heaven and earth as witnesses, warned that after such judgment the people would remain scattered among the nations, yet if they sought the Lord with their whole heart and returned to him in repentance, he would restore them.
claims: The precedent of the wilderness generation and the seventy-year Babylonian exile shows that God's punishments for Israel's sins have historically been finite and proportionate, followed by restoration once the guilty generation passed or repentance occurred — setting up a contrast with the present, seemingly unending calamity.
concepts: Mosaic warning of dispersion and restoration

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7048.summary: Draws the contrast explicit: since the present calamity vastly exceeds all previous ones in scale and duration, it must answer to a vastly graver, longer-lasting sin — namely the killing, approval of the killing, and continued denial of Jesus Christ. Appeals to Daniel (via Josephus) as the prophet who alone specified not merely that these things would happen but precisely when, through the prophecy of the seventy weeks: the coming of the 'Holy of Holies' (Christ), the cutting off of the Anointed leader, the people's denial of him, the destruction of the city and sanctuary by an invading people with their prince, and a permanent, non-transitory desolation — all of which, the author insists, has been plainly fulfilled in the coming of Christ and Rome's destruction of Jerusalem.
claims: The unprecedented severity and permanence of Israel's punishment corresponds to an unprecedented sin — the rejection and killing of Christ.

Daniel's prophecy of seventy weeks precisely predicted the coming of the Anointed One, his being cut off, and the definitive, non-temporary destruction of Jerusalem and its Temple, and this prophecy has been fulfilled exactly in the events surrounding Christ and the Roman destruction of the city.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e6997.summary: Rebuts an anticipated Jewish sophistical objection that minor adjustments to the regnal chronology could show Daniel's seventy weeks were not fulfilled at the time claimed, by pointing out that no honest manipulation of the dates could stretch the interval all the way to the present (some 1,300 years later); challenges any learned Jew, if the weeks were not yet fulfilled at Christ's time, to say when they will be fulfilled and to produce the 'Holy of Holies' the prophecy names, or else to trust the author's (and Josephus's) demonstration from Law, Prophets, and true histories that the prophecy was in fact completely fulfilled at the time claimed.
claims: No plausible manipulation of regnal chronology can extend the fulfillment of Daniel's seventy weeks to the present day, so the prophecy must already have been fulfilled at the time of Christ.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7028.summary: Presses further that Daniel truly predicted the destruction of the city and sanctuary, the cessation of sacrifice, and the enduring desolation, as the present Jewish calamity and the relocation of worship away from the original Temple site attest; argues that since Daniel accurately predicted these events he also predicted their timing (the seventy weeks), so if any Prophet foretold this uniquely great calamity it must have been Daniel, since it is implausible that prophets who diligently recorded lesser calamities would have been silent about by far the greatest. Notes that if Daniel did not predict this calamity, his prophecy of restoration remains unfulfilled and the Jews should still expect one further such disaster after any future restoration — which, per the prophetic voice, ought never to occur again — and adds that Jewish teachers themselves hold the Temple is not to be rebuilt a third time, interpreting prophecies of a rebuilt Jerusalem/Temple as referring to a heavenly, not earthly, city. Concludes that sober Jews, reasoning honestly, should recognize that their people's desolation stems from the rejection and killing of the Messiah, and that they and their descendants continue to bear its penalty precisely by continuing to approve, love, and imitate that ancestral crime through ongoing denial and blasphemy — such that no one reflecting on this could reasonably call Christ a deceiver or his miracles fake.
claims: Daniel's prophecy, correctly read, accounts for both the fact and the permanence of Jerusalem's destruction, and Jewish tradition's own interpretation of a heavenly (not earthly) restored Temple corroborates that no further earthly rebuilding is expected.
The Jews' persistent approval and imitation of their ancestors' rejection of Christ perpetuates their guilt and thus their ongoing punishment.
Taken together, these considerations make it unreasonable to regard Christ as a deceiver or his miracles as fraudulent.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7104.summary: Turns to address the Jews directly on their own future hope: argues that even their still-awaited true Messiah, when he comes and works true miracles, will — on the pattern the objectors themselves apply to Christ — be unrecognized, rejected, and put to death by them, bringing about the same predicted destruction and dispersion foretold by Isaiah, Daniel, and other prophets; anticipates the Jews would then invent the same false charge (that he is a deceiver working fake miracles) rather than admit true miracles, citing their own prophet speaking in their voice about the Messiah: 'When you work miracles, we will not endure it.' Urges them, given how long they have already erred, to repent and acknowledge Christ's miracles and their wondrous author.
claims: The same skeptical pattern the Jews apply to Christ would, by their own prophetic tradition, lead them to reject their own true Messiah when he comes, exposing the pattern itself as unreliable rather than Christ specifically as false.
concepts: argument from parity applied to future Messiah

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7131.summary: Cites Rabbi Moses ben Maimon (Maimonides), called the greatest of Jewish philosophers, as writing in his work on judges that Jesus of Nazareth appeared to be the Messiah and was executed by the court, and that he was the cause (or merited the cause) of Israel's destruction by the sword and the dispersion and degradation of its remnant; adds a personal anecdote of asking a prominent Jew whether Maimonides' writings were considered authoritative, who struck his own cheek in emphasis and affirmed that whatever Moses [Maimonides] said was as authoritative among them as if it had come from the mouth of God, and that none greater than he had arisen among the Jews between the first Moses and himself.
claims: Maimonides, the most authoritative Jewish philosopher by the Jews' own testimony, himself linked Jesus's execution to the destruction of Israel — corroborating the author's argument from an unimpeachably Jewish source.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7151.summary: Argues that if Christ had truly been an evil deceiver, he would have mocked rather than wept over the coming destruction of Jerusalem that he foresaw and foretold — especially since he also foreknew his own crucifixion at Jewish hands and their rejection of his teaching — yet the histories attest he wept over the city out of compassion; similarly, a false prophet would not knowingly and willingly endure such a death for the salvation of others and the fulfillment of prophecy, nor would he, while dying, pray for his own executioners — both of which Christ did, as the authentic histories clearly show.
claims: Christ's compassionate weeping over Jerusalem's foreseen destruction and his willing, redemptive death with prayer for his executioners are incompatible with his being a malicious deceiver.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7265.summary: Marshals a dense cluster of Old Testament prophetic testimony to Christ's foreseen Passion: Isaiah's Suffering Servant ('he was offered because he himself willed it... he was reckoned among the wicked, and he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors'), David's Psalm 21 [22] describing the manner and circumstances of the Passion in detail (supplemented by Psalm 68 [69]), and notes that Christ himself, dying, began reciting Psalm 21 in Hebrew ('Eli, Eli, lamma sabachthani'), signaling its fulfillment in himself, and said 'It is finished' after receiving vinegar for his thirst, as the histories attest. Adds the Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs as further (if debatable) testimony, and argues that if the pagan Sibyl — wholly outside the Jewish prophetic lineage — could give clear testimony to Christ, there is no reason the sons of Jacob, themselves prophets testifying in their father's manner, could not also have done so, as Jacob himself did in Genesis 49 ('The scepter shall not depart from Judah... until Shiloh come'), a prophecy whose Aramaic Targum and Jewish glosses the author reads as pointing to the Messiah and as fulfilled completely in Christ.
claims: Isaiah's Suffering Servant oracle and David's Psalms 21 and 68 predict, in precise detail, the manner and circumstances of Christ's Passion, and Christ's own words on the cross signal his conscious fulfillment of these texts.
Jacob's prophecy in Genesis 49 that the scepter would not depart from Judah until 'Shiloh' comes — read by Jewish tradition itself as messianic — is fulfilled completely in Christ.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7318.summary: Reinforces the Shiloh/scepter argument historically: Jewish histories attest that from the time of Moses there were always seventy-one ordinary judges or scribes holding ordinary and royal jurisdiction, even including capital cases, and that this authority persisted (in a diminished, non-royal form) after the Babylonian exile removed the crown and scepter from Judah, continuing right up to Herod and Christ, after which it was entirely destroyed — meaning the 'scepter' departing from Judah aligns with Christ's own time, so that if this prophecy was not fulfilled in Christ, the Jews must locate another Messiah who came before the scepter and judicial authority finally and completely departed from Judah. Adds that even if the Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs cannot presently be found among the Jews, this does not prove it fabricated, since Jewish books were plausibly lost, burned, or carried off (some even translated into Greek and then Latin) amid the great Roman destruction.
claims: Jewish judicial and royal authority persisted in diminished form until Herod and Christ and was then permanently extinguished, matching the timing required by the Shiloh/scepter prophecy for Christ to be the Messiah.

The unavailability of the Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs among present-day Jews does not establish it as fabricated, given the plausible loss or destruction of Jewish texts during the Roman conquest.
concepts: loss of texts in the Roman destruction

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7260.summary: Argues that if Christ were a deceiver it is implausible everything prophesied of the Messiah would have been fulfilled in him so precisely (including the very timing given by Jacob and Daniel), and that the Jews cannot invent an alternative account of these fulfillments; further argues that had Christ been a malicious sorcerer working miracles through demonic aid, he would (like other necromancers) have needed fumigations, rings, instruments, characters, incantations, and appropriate time to prepare his effects, whereas he in fact worked diverse miracles instantly by word or command alone, sometimes praying to the heavenly Father but never to a demon.
claims: The precise fulfillment in Christ of Messianic prophecies concerning both events and their timing (per Jacob and Daniel) cannot plausibly be explained away.
Christ's manner of working miracles — instant, by mere word, without magical apparatus, and with prayer only to the Father — is incompatible with the practices of demonically-aided sorcery.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7291.summary: Argues a malicious sorcerer would more readily and commonly work harmful miracles, as necromancers and evil spirits do, than helpful ones — especially at the crisis of his own suffering — yet Christ healed all who were ill and, at the very moment of his arrest, healed the severed ear of his own captor's servant (cut off by Peter) after rebuking Peter; asks how, if he were evil, he could have died so holily, uttering only the holiest words, and who but a truly good power could have worked all his miracles, especially the celestial signs and the resurrection of saints that occurred at his death.
claims: Christ's consistent preference for healing over harming, including healing his own captor at his arrest, and his holy death, are incompatible with malicious sorcery.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7313.summary: Argues that a sorcerer wishing to preserve and spread his sect would have taught his disciples his magical art, yet nothing in Christ's teaching contains anything but the purest worship of God, faith, hope, and charity, and prayer (the Our Father) — and his learned disciples, imitating this teaching, condemned all sorcerers and their arts as poisonous heresy, as Christian canon and civil law themselves confirm.
claims: Christ's teaching contains no trace of magical art, and his followers explicitly condemned sorcery as heretical, which is incompatible with Christ himself having been a sorcerer.
concepts: absence of magical doctrine in Christ's teaching

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7432.summary: Argues that if Christ worked miracles by sorcery, it is inexplicable that his holy disciples work similar miracles by the mere invocation of God, Christ, Mary, or other saints, without invoking demons or using any magical art at all — indeed even without ever having learned such arts, and while actively destroying sorcerers and their practices, both in life and often after death. Adds that sorcerers and necromancers among Christians work no miracles at all, only upright, blameless Christians do — and it would be implausible for demons to grant miracles gratis to their chief enemies, who devote all their strength to destroying demonic altars, idols, temples, and worship, rather than to their own worshippers, whom they would more plausibly wish to honor in order to attract followers.
claims: That miracle-working among Christians is confined to the pious, who neither know nor use magical arts and who actively oppose demonic worship, counts strongly against the theory that Christian miracles (or Christ's own) derive from demonic power.
concepts: miracle by simple invocation versus sorcery

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7471.summary: Recounts at length the legend of Cyprian, a necromancer dedicated to the Devil from childhood, who used escalating demonic aid (an ordinary demon, then a stronger one, then the prince of demons himself) over seven years to try to seduce the Christian virgin Justina of Antioch, including shape-shifting deceptions, all of which Justina overcame by the sign of the Cross; when the chief demon itself, disguised as Justina, was exposed and fled at the mere utterance of her name, Cyprian converted to Christ and was martyred alongside Justina. Cites a similar story of the Apostle James, son of Zebedee, converting the great necromancers Hermogenes and Philetus by nullifying all their magic through miracles, and concludes that if Christian faith by its power destroys demonic miracles (indeed sorceries) themselves, it is unreasonable to think Christian miracles are worked by demonic power.
claims: The legends of Cyprian/Justina and of James/Hermogenes, in which Christian faith and the sign of the Cross overpower and nullify demonic sorcery, argue against demons being the source of Christian miracles.
concepts: the sign of the Cross overpowering demons

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7409.summary: Argues that if the Devil can work some miracles, God can work still greater ones (per Suppositions 1, 3, and 7); notes that the truth of Christian miracles is shown by Christians' prayers, which in their greatest necessities are directed to God against, not toward, demons, in seeking miraculous aid — and it would be incompatible with God's supreme goodness and mercy to repel such devoted suppliants and hand them over to demons instead. Further reasons that if demons do aid praying Christians, they must do so either willingly or under compulsion; not willingly, given how much Christ and Christians work against them, so it must be under compulsion — showing the great power of Christian faith, to which even demons, though most powerful on earth, are subject and forced into unwilling service; and adds that good Christians in extreme need never use magical means but only humble prayer to God, further attesting how greatly God loves and approves the Christian faith.
claims: Christians petition God, not demons, for miraculous aid, which is incompatible with demons being the true source of Christian miracles.
If demons do assist praying Christians, it can only be under compulsion by a superior power, evidencing the supreme power of Christian faith and of God who compels them.
concepts: prayer directed to God against demons
divine goodness as incompatible with abandoning suppliants

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7452.summary: Anticipates sorcerers' objection that they themselves compel and coerce demons to act — and asks why, if so, they could not equally compel good angels of God (being of the same kind of nature) or even human wayfarers of a weaker nature. Argues philosophically and theologically that the natural free will of a rational substance cannot be compelled to its own acts by any words, charms, seals, signs, aromatics, fumigations, herbs, or celestial or terrestrial characters, nor by any creature whatsoever short of God himself, since this would violate the natural freedom of the will — so demons invoked by magicians often do not come, and when they do come freely it is only to seduce unhappy souls further or confirm them in their seduction; otherwise, being so malicious, cunning, and powerful, demons would compel especially sinful men to every wickedness.
claims: No creature, including a demon, can genuinely compel another rational creature's free will by magical means, since this would violate the natural freedom of the will — so apparent demonic 'obedience' to sorcerers is voluntary deception, not true compulsion.
concepts: critique of magical compulsion of demons

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7577.summary: Argues that if Christ's miracles were merely feigned, it is unexplained why the Jews' own true miracles ceased around the time of his preaching and Passion and have never since been renewed, as their own histories attest (dating the destruction of the Temple by the Romans to 42 years after the Passion/Ascension per Daniel's and Christ's prophecy); cites the Babylonian Talmud's list of ten miraculous signs that continuously attended Temple worship (women never miscarrying from the smell of sacrificial meat, sacrificial meat never spoiling, no flies ever seen in the slaughterhouse, no mishap ever befalling the high priest on the Day of Atonement, no corruption ever found in the sheaf or the showbread despite crowding, no serpent or scorpion ever harming anyone in Jerusalem, rain never extinguishing the wood-fire or wind scattering its smoke-column, and pottery fragments and altar/candelabrum ashes being miraculously absorbed) — all of which, per the Talmud itself, ceased forty years before the Temple's destruction, exactly as the rabbis lamented, 'we no longer see signs, there is no more a prophet, nor anyone among us who knows how long.'
claims: The Jews' own Talmudic tradition records that a specific set of miraculous signs continuously attending Temple worship ceased exactly forty years before the Temple's destruction — a fact the author reads as corroborating that Christ's ministry, Passion, and the withdrawal of divine favor from the Temple coincide.
concepts: Daniel's prophecy and the Temple's destruction

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7623.summary: Cites a further rabbinic source (a book called 'Iona') recording additional miraculous Temple signs that likewise ceased forty years before the destruction: the crimson thread hung in the Temple, which used to turn white (a sign of atonement), stopped doing so; the evening lamp, which always used to burn through the night, began sometimes to go out; the fire on the altar, once so strong it needed only two logs, thereafter varied in strength so priests had to keep adding wood all day; and the sheaf-offering and showbread, once blessed so abundantly that even a small portion satisfied a priest with leftovers, thereafter carried so little blessing that honest priests refrained from taking their share while the gluttonous endured the curse.
claims: Rabbinic sources record a cluster of Temple miracles (the whitening thread, the ever-burning lamp, the self-sufficient altar fire, the abundantly blessed offerings) that all failed simultaneously roughly forty years before the Temple's destruction.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7656.summary: Recounts the tradition that in the year Simeon the Just died, he predicted his own death that year, explaining to those who asked how he knew: on every prior day he entered the Holy of Holies, an old man clothed in white had accompanied him in and out, but on that day an old man clothed in black accompanied him in and did not come out with him; he fell ill for seven days and died, after which his priestly brothers ceased to bless in the name of the Lord.
claims: The rabbinic legend of Simeon the Just's death, marked by an ominous vision and followed by the cessation of priestly blessing, is presented as another sign of withdrawing divine favor from the Temple.
concepts: omen of the two old men

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7669.summary: Adds that the Temple gates used to open by themselves until Rabban Johanan ben Zakkai rebuked the Temple, saying 'Temple, Temple, why do you destroy yourself? I know your end will be destruction,' citing Zechariah's prophecy against it ('Open your doors, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars'); the Jerusalem Talmud is cited recounting the same signs (the sort-lot, the crimson thread, the self-opening gates) failing forty years before the Temple's fall, with Rabban Johanan repeating his lament and the same prophetic citation from Zechariah.
claims: Rabban Johanan ben Zakkai's own rebuke of the self-destructing Temple, invoking Zechariah's prophecy of its burning, is cited as further rabbinic testimony corroborating the impending, divinely-signaled destruction.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7696.summary: Notes a common rounding convention (citing round numbers and dropping small remainders, as one does with fingers/digits) to argue that although Jewish books state their miracles ceased 'forty years' before the Temple's destruction, the true figure could well be 42, 43, or 45 years — which the author holds actually corresponds to the time of Christ's baptism, preaching, miracle-working, Passion, or Ascension.
claims: The traditional rounded figure of 'forty years' for the cessation of Temple miracles before its destruction, adjusted for likely rounding, aligns with the timeframe of Christ's public ministry and death.
concepts: alignment of Temple-sign cessation with Christ's ministry

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7712.summary: Argues the Temple's miracles did not cease all at once but began to fade gradually about a hundred years earlier — as light dims before deep night, or sight dims before total blindness — citing Josephus's report that God let it be known, to those willing to see, whether he was present at sacrifice or not: the high priest's sardonyx and the twelve jeweled breastplate stones (the 'Essen'/rationale, so admired even by Greeks) used to shine with divine light signaling God's presence and foretelling victory in battle, but this splendor ceased roughly two hundred years before Josephus wrote.
claims: Josephus himself records a much earlier, gradual fading of Temple signs (the luminous high-priestly jewels ceasing about two centuries before his writing), read here as the beginning of a long decline culminating in the Temple's final desolation.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7747.summary: Explains this gradual decline as fitting, since Jacob's prophecy required the scepter and full judicial authority to be taken from Judah only gradually, through successive wars, not all at once, as the Jews' 'lamp' was similarly to be extinguished by degrees — because although they knew or should have known from their ancestors' prophecies and traditions that the Messiah's coming was near, they failed to prepare the way as prophetically commanded, and instead became his enemies, plotters, and impious opponents, as events proved and as the books of the Maccabees and Josephus's histories of the intervening years of neglect and wrongdoing attest.
claims: The gradual, decades-long decline of Judah's political and Temple authority fulfills Jacob's prophecy of the scepter's gradual departure, and reflects the Jews' failure to prepare for and their active opposition to the Messiah's coming despite ample prophetic warning.
concepts: gradual fulfillment of the Shiloh prophecy
failure to prepare for the Messiah

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7776.summary: Asks why Jewish miracles ceased precisely at the time of Christ, and answers: because the Jews corrupted, despised, denied, and killed the Author of those glorious miracles, and expelled his disciples and teaching from their territory — so it is no wonder that when the Author of miracles withdrew from them, the miracles themselves withdrew too; indeed the departure of miracles can itself argue the departure of their Author, the Lord God, who alone (per prophetic testimony) works great miracles — noting the tradition of a voice heard in the Temple around that time saying 'Let us depart from here, let us leave these dwellings' (the holy angels' voice), signifying that the Lord of Hosts and his angels migrated from the Jews to the Gentile peoples dwelling in darkness, illuminating them and becoming their Father, the Father of the age now present — which is why Christians, named after Christ as their Father, can point to his magnificent ongoing benefits, namely glorious miracles, as evidence of his continuing paternal presence among them, just as such miracles once indicated his presence among the Jews.
claims: The simultaneous cessation of Jewish Temple miracles and the rejection/killing of Christ indicates the departure of the divine Author of miracles from the Jews to the Gentiles, who became the new recipients of his miraculous, paternal presence as Christians.
concepts: departure of the divine presence from the Temple
transfer of divine favor to the Gentiles
Christians as adopted children of the Father

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7807.summary: Anticipates the Jews claiming God continually works one great miracle for them by preserving and sustaining them among their enemies, but rejects this as evidence of misery, not favor — a punishment for sin, as Moses and David prophesied (invoking heaven and earth as witnesses that God would scatter but never wholly destroy or forget them, and David speaking in the Messiah's own voice asking God not to kill but to scatter his enemies, lest his people forget), which the author reads as still applying to the Jews' continuing denial of Christ and consequent suffering, in grinding subjection, misery, toil, and sorrow, until they recognize God's universal dominion — closing with a quoted verse (from Ovid) that every land is a homeland to the brave, as the sea is to fish or the whole world's open space to a bird, mordantly applied to the Jews' condition of being at home nowhere and everywhere.
claims: The Jews' continued survival in dispersion, rather than proving divine favor, is itself the fulfillment of Mosaic and Davidic prophecy that they would be scattered, preserved, but not annihilated, as punishment continuing until their eventual recognition of God.
concepts: Mosaic/Davidic prophecy of scattering without annihilation

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7854.summary: Insists Christians are not the Jews' enemies but friends, out of love for Christ who descended from them, wishing and working for their present and future good as for themselves; explains the Jews' preservation as serving disciplinary purposes — punishing them for their sin while also serving as a warning to others, and preventing the memory of the patriarchs from being wholly extinguished — invoking again Moses' and David's promises that God would not utterly destroy or forget his covenant, and adding that the Jews' continued existence, as enemies of the Christian faith, unwittingly and faithfully attests to it through their own prophetic books, and is maintained also for the sake of Jewish converts and for 'the remnant of Israel' who will finally be converted.
claims: The Jews' preservation, rather than contradicting Christian goodwill, is explained as serving a disciplinary and providential purpose — preserving covenant memory, unwittingly attesting Christ through their own scriptures, and awaiting eventual conversion.
concepts: eventual conversion of 'the remnant of Israel'

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7879.summary: Turns to address the Saracens and their philosophers, who (per Muhammad's own tradition) admit Christ's miracles and their true cause (the true God and his power), but deny these prove Christ was God, holding instead he was a great saint, great friend of God, and great prophet, like Moses and Muhammad. Counters that since Christ, so evidently shown by God's miracles to be a great saint, friend of God, and prophet, cannot have been a lying deceiver but a truthful guide and teacher, his teaching must therefore be true — and since his teaching holds that he himself was God, Christ was truly God.
claims: The Saracens' own admission that Christ's miracles are genuinely divine, combined with their concession that he was a great and truthful prophet, entails (given that his teaching affirms his own divinity) that Christ was truly God.
concepts: argument from Christ's truthfulness to his teaching's truth
Christ's own teaching of his divinity

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7905.summary: Anticipates the Muslim reply (per the Manichaean-like move within Muhammad's own tradition) that Christ's whole teaching was true, but his uneducated disciples misunderstood and corrupted it in writing, so that Christ's divinity is not really contained in his true teaching but only in the disciples' corrupted version. Responds that the incorrupt authority and truth of the Gospels has already been sufficiently shown, and that it is far more reasonable to trust the many great disciples, apostles, and evangelists who lived continuously in Christ's presence, witnessing his life and works and hearing his teaching firsthand and wrote of it in agreement, than to trust Muhammad alone, absent, writing over six hundred years after Christ — and even granting Muhammad was a prophet, it does not follow everything he said was divinely revealed to him, so present, concordant, eyewitness testimony should be preferred to his; nor can it be claimed that Christians simply fabricated the many prophecies (Jewish and Sibylline) already shown to attest Christ's divinity.
claims: The eyewitness, contemporaneous, and mutually corroborating testimony of Christ's disciples to his divinity is more credible than Muhammad's later, solitary, absent testimony to the contrary — even granting Muhammad prophetic status in some respects.
concepts: reliability of eyewitness testimony versus later solitary testimony
not all of a prophet's statements are necessarily revealed

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7957.summary: Appeals to Avicenna's own definition of prophecy as a gift of the Holy Spirit to argue Christ's disciples possessed it abundantly, receiving the Holy Spirit visibly at Pentecost and suddenly speaking in all languages; notes Peter, Paul, and other disciples prophesied, and John in Revelation prophetically described the course of the world from Christ to the end, including (the author claims) Muhammad and the seduction of the Saracens and their assault on Christians; many other Christians likewise prophesied clearly across the centuries, and the apostles and evangelists, in writing, teaching, living, and dying (even unto martyrdom) for their testimony, had God work many glorious miracles for them both living and dead — meaning that, by the Saracens' own standard, these disciples were themselves great saints and great friends of God, indeed greater than Muhammad, for whom (as noted earlier) God worked no miracles at all.
claims: By Avicenna's own criterion that prophecy is a gift of the Holy Spirit evidenced by miracles, Christ's disciples—who received the Spirit at Pentecost, prophesied, and worked miracles—qualify as greater prophets and 'friends of God' than Muhammad, who worked no miracles.
concepts: John's Apocalypse as prophecy of Muhammad

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e7992.summary: Concludes the disciples' life and teaching were holy and true, approved and attested by God through such miracles, and that miracles have continued among Christians from Christ's time to the present among those living by his teaching — proving God's approval of that life and teaching continues: martyrs, doctors defending the faith against heretics, and confessors and virgins living by the faith have all been renowned for many miracles, attested by numerous histories. Argues it would be incredible for God to conceal the truth from every believing, God-loving Christian (for whom he works so many great miracles) while revealing it only to one unbelieving, formerly idolatrous Gentile — namely Muhammad, who was himself an idolater before receiving his supposed prophetic office, as the Saracens' own books attest.
claims: The continuous record of miracles among Christian martyrs, doctors, confessors, and virgins across history demonstrates God's ongoing approval of Christian doctrine.
It is incredible that God would withhold truth from the whole community of devoted Christians (for whom he works miracles) while revealing it uniquely to Muhammad, a former idolater.
concepts: continuity of Christian miracles across history

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8023.summary: Notes that this same pattern of revelation was given first to Christ himself (a Jew) and through him to his Jewish disciples, when he wished to expound and fulfill their law spiritually; then draws a crucial distinction in the manner of Christ's miracle-working compared to everyone else's: all others who worked or benefited from miracles prayed to God tacitly or explicitly, professing they could not work miracles by their own power and that they themselves were not God, whereas Christ, working miracles almost constantly, did so without recourse to prayer, claiming to act by his own authority, power, and will alone — precisely in order to show himself to be God and be believed as such by men.
claims: Unlike all other miracle-workers, who invoked God's aid and disclaimed personal divine power, Christ characteristically worked miracles by his own authority and will alone, a distinctive manner meant to demonstrate his divinity.
concepts: Christ's authority contrasted with other miracle-workers' dependence on prayer

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8069.summary: Develops the point: Christ, by simply expressing his will ('be it done'), caused the miracle to occur instantly, showing an infallible, omnipotent, universally efficacious will — a power no finite creature has, since only God has strictly infinite power (per Part 8); cites specific commands ('Arise,' 'See,' 'Stretch out your hand,' 'Be clean') that took immediate effect, concluding Christ was truly God, since only God could be approved this way. Notes he sometimes healed by other ministering acts, and sometimes prayed to the Father, precisely to show that in his assumed humanity alone he could not work miracles, but only by his divine power.
claims: Christ's characteristic mode of working miracles by a simple, immediately efficacious command evidences the strictly infinite, omnipotent will that belongs to God alone, proving his divinity.
Christ's occasional prayer to the Father serves to show that his human nature alone could not work miracles, only his divine power could.
concepts: two natures of Christ (human and divine)

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8114.summary: Turns astrological argument against the Saracen philosophers on their own terms (attributing earthly events to celestial causes): notes the great conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter that preceded and presignified Muhammad and his sect, but observes an even greater conjunction of the same planets, with all its circumstances, preceded Christ by a few years and signified him and his religion — a fact any astrologer of either side can calculate — concluding that by their own astrological science, Christ and Christianity must be judged more solemn, excellent, and worthy than Muhammad and Islam, and that Christian testimonies before, during, and after Christ's coming (including continuing miracles) far exceed anything comparable for Muhammad.
claims: By the Saracens' own astrological principles, the greater planetary conjunction preceding Christ (compared to the lesser one preceding Muhammad) establishes Christianity's superior cosmic significance.
concepts: astrological argument (great conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter)
argument from the interlocutors' own principles

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8143.summary: Argues that a law leading to the soul's perfection and happiness (present and future) is better and worthier than one leading merely to bodily pleasure, and that Christian law aims principally at the rational soul's happiness while Islamic law (per its own institutions and promises) aims at bodily pleasure, present and future — quoting Avicenna himself acknowledging that Muhammad's law depicts a bodily happiness and misery, while a further, intellectually and demonstratively apprehended happiness and misery of souls exists which wise theologians desired far more than bodily happiness, even disdaining the latter by comparison, promising to explain the disposition of this higher (and its contrary, lower) happiness, since the bodily kind is already set out in the [Islamic] law.
claims: A law ordered to the soul's rational happiness is superior to one ordered to bodily pleasure, and Islamic law (by Avicenna's own admission) is oriented to a merely corporeal conception of paradise, inferior to what wise philosophers/theologians truly desire.
concepts: Avicenna's critique of a corporeal paradise
hierarchy of ends in religious law

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8180.summary: Attacks the Islamic depiction of paradise as crude and irrational: Muslim authorities teach the resurrected dead will eat and drink delicacies (pastries, honey, milk, cheese, butter) and have many beautiful wives for carnal union — objecting that such an afterlife would be dishonorable, carnal, bestial, and irrational. Argues eating there must be either from necessity or for pleasure alone: if from necessity, bodies would remain subject to illness, bereavement, sorrow, and death (contrary to happiness, which all philosophers hold to be a stable, perfect good); if for pleasure alone, it amounts to unexcused gluttony and intemperance; either way, carnal eating implies carnal excretion, defiling the supposedly most blessed place with filth, stench, and disgust — and eating and drinking would be followed by sleep, another cessation of happiness.
claims: The Islamic depiction of a paradise of carnal eating, drinking, and marital pleasure is philosophically incoherent, since it entails either bodily corruptibility (incompatible with true happiness) or unrestrained gluttony, and implies degrading bodily functions unfitting for a blessed state.
concepts: critique of a corporeal Islamic paradise
happiness as stable and perfect (per philosophers)

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8211.summary: Continues the critique using the philosophical principle (shared by the interlocutors' own authorities) that act is more perfect than potency and use than habit, so true happiness must consist in actual activity, not mere capacity — citing the proverb (via Aristotle's Ethics) that the happy differ little from the miserable for half of life [i.e., while asleep]. Turns to the promised wives: asks whether they are for procreation or pleasure alone; not procreation, since there is no place, time, or need for it in an immortal afterlife with no need for heirs — and if generation continued forever it would produce an unmanageable, ever-growing population preventing the heavenly community from ever being complete, while if it ceased at some point, happiness itself would cease and eternal misery would follow; moreover children born there, never having merited beatitude (since there is no time or place to merit in the afterlife), would be as blessed as their meriting parents, which seems absurd, or else, if unable to procreate at all, would never attain blessedness and remain forever miserable — and pleasure alone is an unworthy motive for marriage, fit only for 'Epicurus's pig.'
claims: Applying the philosophers' own principle that happiness consists in actuality, sleep in the promised paradise would undermine the state's claim to be truly happy.

Marital procreation in the afterlife is philosophically incoherent whether it continues forever (producing an unbounded, ever-incomplete population) or ceases (implying an end to happiness), and either way raises insoluble problems about unmerited beatitude for children born there.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8250.summary: Presses further: the resurrected will either feel desire/appetite for sexual pleasure before the act or not; if they do, they will suffer sorrow and pain from the delay and momentary lack of the desired pleasure — citing Aristotle (Ethics III) that the intemperate person desires pleasurable things and therefore grieves at not obtaining them, since desire entails sorrow — and citing Aristotle again (Metaphysics XII) that God, always in the best state, always has maximal delight because his is an act always actually present, whereas hope for a future act and memory of a past act are not, by implication, as fully delightful as actual present possession — undermining the coherence of a paradise where anticipated pleasure would itself entail suffering.
claims: If desire precedes pleasure in the promised paradise, it entails sorrow at the pleasure's absence or delay, contradicting the state's supposed perfection — an argument drawn from Aristotle's account of desire, intemperance, and of divine delight as consisting only in fully present actuality.
concepts: divine delight as pure actuality (Aristotle, Metaphysics XII)
critique of anticipatory pleasure in paradise

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8285.summary: Concludes that without desire there can be no pleasure in the act either, making the promised paradise incoherent from the other direction too, and asks why anyone would perform an act they do not desire at all. Turns to reciprocity: if men's happiness there consists in having many wives for their full pleasure, women would equally need many husbands to be equally satisfied, or else remain perpetually unhappy; further argues the sexual act cannot be performed continuously (making its participants viler than the unclean, forbidden-to-eat pig, by their own dietary law) nor can it be performed by many wives simultaneously with one husband without adultery with other men — and if it is performed only intermittently, happiness itself is correspondingly diminished or interrupted, confirming the incoherence already shown.
claims: The logic of the promised Islamic paradise, taken to its consequences, requires either impossible continuous sexual activity or women committing adultery to achieve equal satisfaction, or else perpetually unequal and interrupted happiness — all absurd.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8312.summary: Argues from first philosophical principles (shared by Hermes, Plato, Aristotle, Avicenna, Algazel, Averroes, and philosophers of every tradition including the Saracens' own) that human happiness consists in the most perfect human operation, exercised by the most perfect human power upon its most perfect object; since the rational soul is more perfect than any bodily power, true happiness must consist in the most perfect knowledge, union, and enjoyment of God — whereas bodily, animal delight, especially sexual pleasure, actively impedes the rational soul's spiritual operation and pure delight (citing Aristotle, Ethics VII, that intense pleasures, especially sexual ones, impede prudent understanding, since one cannot understand anything in the midst of them), and so is incompatible with, not constitutive of, perfect happiness — which should instead be sought in spiritual, rational delight: more perfect, more lasting (being continuous), more honorable, purer, better, and greater, especially since the two kinds of delight cannot be had simultaneously but mutually exclude one another; and just as the soul's most perfect, tireless, honorable, holy power (the rational soul, being immaterial and incorruptible) requires a proportionate operation, so it requires a proportionate object, which can only be God.
claims: By the united testimony of pagan and Muslim philosophers alike, human happiness consists in the rational soul's perfect knowledge and enjoyment of God, not in bodily/sexual pleasure, which actively impedes rational operation and is therefore incompatible with true happiness.
concepts: happiness as perfect operation of the rational soul
incompatibility of sensual and intellectual pleasure
God as the soul's proportionate object

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8367.summary: Concludes no one may doubt that the most delightful happiness and happiest delight must be expected in the rational soul's most perfect, continuous, sincere, and holy operation concerning God, as pagan, Jewish, and Muslim philosophers alike unanimously attest; argues from the first Supposition and Parts 3 and 4 that God is supremely, most abundantly, and infinitely delightful, pleasurable, sweet, lovable, joyous, happy, and good, so there is no reason (per Parts 7 and 8) he could not show himself thus to his worshippers in future beatitude, eternally satiating them with his own sincere and unceasing delights, becoming himself their most delightful happiness — concluding with the classic teleological argument that since there is no infinite regress of ends (second Supposition), there must be an ultimate end sought for its own sake, to which all others are subordinate, and this ultimate end, humanity's true happiness, can be nothing other than God himself, on pain of contradicting Part 30's teaching that God alone is to be loved and venerated as the final end.
claims: God's own infinite delightfulness and the second Supposition's rejection of infinite regress in ends together establish that God himself, not any created good, must be the ultimate object of human happiness.
concepts: no infinite regress in ends (second Supposition)

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8404.summary: Argues from Part 3's teaching that God repays his lovers and servants abundantly, not sparingly, and this repayment must occur in future beatitude; since (per Part 30) such lovers love and serve God above every existing or even merely possible or imaginable good short of God himself, never knowingly offending him for any delight or to avoid any suffering, God will repay them with a greater good and greater delight than any such created good — namely himself and his own infinite delight, which (per the first Supposition and Parts 3, 4, and 20) is supremely holy, sincere, honorable, continuous, and abundantly infinite. Concludes that Christians, by their law and Christ's teaching, unanimously await precisely this most delightful, God-like happiness, making Christian law more reasonable, honorable, and holy than the rival law critiqued.
claims: God's promised recompense to those who love him above all things must, by the logic of Parts 3, 4, 20, and 30, consist in God's own infinite delight rather than any created (especially bodily) good — which is precisely what Christian doctrine of beatitude teaches.
concepts: beatitude as participation in God's own delight

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8433.summary: Mocks specific superstitious claims found in Islamic scripture/tradition (that the sun rises between the devil's two horns, so those who pray facing east worship the devil; that a donkey brays because it sees the devil; that a rooster crows because it sees an angel) as transparently absurd fables that no philosopher could credit. Argues it is contrary to the natural order for a subtler, more spiritual, more divine law (Christianity) to be followed and superseded by a cruder, more carnal, more bestial one (Islam), since the natural progression of things moves from crude to subtle, from carnal to spiritual, from less to more perfect — and points again to the many powerful miracles worked by God for Christians against Muslims, recorded in numerous chronicles (a few recounted earlier), as further evidence of Christianity's superiority.
claims: Certain fantastical claims in Islamic tradition are self-evidently absurd, and the natural order of development (from cruder to more spiritual/perfect) makes it implausible for a spiritually inferior law (Islam) to legitimately supersede a superior one (Christianity).
concepts: natural progression from carnal to spiritual as a criterion for superior revelation

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8455.summary: Anticipates the reply that even if Christian law is better, Islamic law is still good and sufficient for salvation — countering that if Christian law is good, it is true and right, while a law that in many respects contradicts it must, by comparison, be bad, false, and erroneous; and if Christian law truly is better, asks why Muslims persecute it so fiercely rather than adopting it, or at least tolerate those among them who wish to adopt it, rather than killing them, when Avicenna himself (the greatest of their philosophers) taught that there should be only one law, the one descended from God through a prophet whose institution is best, to be spread through the whole world, correcting dissenters first and only killing those who refuse correction.
claims: The Islamic persecution of converts to Christianity is in tension with Avicenna's own principle (that a superior divine law should be universally adopted, with correction preferred to killing), which — if Christianity is conceded to be the better law — should favor its toleration or adoption rather than violent suppression.
concepts: appeal to Avicenna against religious persecution
internal tension in the interlocutors' position

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8309.summary: Draws together the whole long dispute into a brief syllogism: whatever God has revealed and attested is true (per the first Supposition and Part 3); God has revealed and attested the Christian faith (per all the preceding argument); therefore the Christian faith is true. Anticipates skeptics quietly doubting that the preceding material really demonstrates divine revelation, and candidly concedes there is no strict mathematical demonstration here from self-evident principles — no more than there is in natural philosophy, metaphysics, or ethics — but only the kind of proof the subject matter as a moral/historical question permits, citing Aristotle (Ethics I) that it suffices to show things as clearly as the subject matter allows, since not all subjects admit equal precision, and citing Plato's Timaeus prologue on the fitting modesty of any human account of sublime matters. Invites any adherent of any other faith to bring forward the best arguments they can for their own faith, to be weighed fairly against the Christian arguments already given (or better ones), confidently predicting the rival arguments will be found wanting.
claims: The whole preceding argument reduces to: whatever God reveals is true; God has revealed the Christian faith; therefore it is true — offered not as strict demonstration but as the degree of proof appropriate to moral/historical subject matter, per Aristotelian method.
The author invites open comparison between Christian apologetic arguments and those of any rival faith, confident the comparison favors Christianity.
concepts: syllogistic summary of the whole apologetic argument
Aristotelian standard of proof proportionate to subject matter

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8364.summary: Anticipates the objection that miracles cannot prove Christian faith true, since miracles also occurred among idolaters and pagans (as noted earlier), unless their false faith could equally be 'proved' by them; responds that before and during the era of circumcision and the Law, there were some among foreign, idolatrous, and pagan nations who, by divine revelation, human teaching, or their own inquiry, truly (if dimly and partially) knew and worshipped God — some Gentiles even clearly prophesying Christ's coming, so it is fitting God worked wondrous miracles for such holy people to strengthen their knowledge and love of him and to draw others to imitate their devotion. Gives examples: righteous men and prophets before and after the Flood and before circumcision and the Law; Job, king of Edom, in the era of Abrahamic circumcision; the Queen of the South and the Ninevites in the era of the Mosaic Law (per Scripture and the Gospels); Nebuchadnezzar, great king of Babylon, after his humbling and repentance; Darius the Mede, who took the monarchy from the Chaldeans; and Alexander the Great, who took it from the Medes, attested by the respected pagan writer Cornelius [Nepos?], never Jewish or Christian — arguing that other such virtuous pagan figures should be credited similarly, even absent explicit scriptural mention.
claims: Pagan miracles do not undermine the argument from Christian miracles, since a line of genuinely God-fearing individuals outside the chosen people — Job, the Queen of Sheba, the Ninevites, Nebuchadnezzar, Darius, Alexander — attests that true knowledge and worship of God, and corresponding divine favor, were never confined to Israel or later to explicit believers alone.
concepts: universality of God's revelation outside the chosen people

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8589.summary: Supports the universality claim with two scriptural texts: God speaking through the prophet generally of his 'city and citizens' — 'I will remember Rahab and Babylon among those who know me; behold, the Philistines, and Tyre, and the people of Ethiopia — this one was born there' — and Paul's parallel realization: 'In truth I perceive that God shows no partiality, but in every nation whoever fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.'
claims: Scripture itself (the Psalms and Paul) affirms that acceptance by God is not confined to Israel but extends to the God-fearing and righteous of every nation.
concepts: Psalm on Rahab/Babylon/Tyre/Ethiopia as citizens of Zion

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8605.summary: Cites Augustine at length (Against Porphyry on the Time of the Christian Religion, and To Prosper and Hilary on the Predestination of the Saints) affirming that since the beginning of the human race, sometimes more hidden and sometimes more openly, Christ was never without prophetic witness nor believers in him — from Adam to Moses, within Israel and among other nations even before the Incarnation; that since Scripture records some who participated in this mystery without belonging to Abraham's lineage or people, one should believe others existed elsewhere unrecorded; cites Augustine (City of God 18) affirming that Jews themselves cannot deny that righteous men and prophets existed outside Israel, pointing to the celebrated case of Job, an Idumean, neither native nor proselyte of Israel, praised by divine eloquence as unmatched in justice and piety among his contemporaries, whom scriptural chronology situates as living three generations after Israel began — arguing this was providentially arranged precisely to teach that people pleasing to God, belonging to the spiritual Israel, could exist among other nations too, a status granted only to those to whom the one Mediator between God and man, Christ Jesus, was divinely revealed. Also cites Augustine (City of God 32) that the ancient righteous believed in Christ, aided by his grace, some even foretelling his coming, whether within Israel (Moses, Joshua, Samuel, David) or outside it (Job) or before it (Abraham, Noah) or others unrecorded in Scripture; and cites Augustine on Nebuchadnezzar's salutary repentance after Daniel's preaching and divine chastisement (contrasted with Pharaoh's impenitence, per canon law), with Darius's case likewise implied by the Book of Daniel, and Alexander similarly reasonably presumed virtuous given his Aristotelian education in the true first cause, first form, and final end.
claims: Augustine's authority is marshaled at length to establish that saving faith in Christ, prefigured or dimly known, was never confined to Israel but extended, through divine providence, to righteous individuals in other nations and eras — with Job as the paradigm case and Nebuchadnezzar, Darius, and (by extension) Alexander as further plausible instances.
concepts: Job as paradigm of extra-Israelite righteousness

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8694.summary: Recounts, via Josephus, the legend of Alexander the Great's approach to Jerusalem after capturing Gaza: the high priest Jaddus, warned by God in a dream after sacrifice and supplication, opened the city gates and went to meet Alexander in priestly vestments (with the people in white), trusting divine providence rather than expecting harm; contrary to the Phoenicians' and Chaldeans' expectation that Alexander would unleash his fury on the city and its high priest, Alexander instead, seeing the priest's golden headplate inscribed with the divine name, went alone to venerate God and honored the high priest first among all — to the astonishment of onlookers, who suspected his mind deranged, until Parmenio alone asked why he alone worshipped the Jewish high priest when all others worshipped him.
claims: Josephus's account of Alexander's providentially guided, reverent encounter with the Jewish high priest at Jerusalem is presented as corroborating evidence of Alexander's genuine piety toward the true God.
concepts: Alexander and the high priest Jaddus (Josephus)
providential guidance of a pagan king

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8755.summary: Offers two further explanations reconciling pagan idol-worship with true piety: some idolaters worshipped images not for their own sake but for God and divine power working through them, just as Christians honor images of Christ, the Trinity, angels, and saints (per Part 21) — so God could fittingly have heard and miraculously helped such distressed suppliants; alternatively, some idolaters truly knew and worshipped the supreme God, but under the name and idol of Jupiter (as discussed in Part 16), while also honoring other idols dedicated to angels, humans, or demons not as ultimate ends but as creatures, servants, and instruments of God carrying out his will, so that in and through them they ultimately worshipped God — just as Christians honor God, his saints, and their images ultimately for God's sake. Concludes that even where such worshippers erred in the manner of worship out of simple ignorance rather than deliberate malice, if they sincerely loved God above all (per Part 30) and diligently sought the mode of worship pleasing to him, honoring him as best their knowledge and conscience allowed, God — seeing this — could mercifully overlook their ignorant error and accept their sincere love, holy intention, and goodwill, which seems consonant with reason.
claims: Pagan worship directed, even confusedly, toward the true God through intermediary images or lesser divine agents, when motivated by sincere love of God and diligent (if mistaken) inquiry, could be mercifully accepted by God despite formal error, on analogy with Christian veneration of images and saints.
concepts: veneration of images (analogy to Christian practice)
sincere intention versus formal correctness of worship

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8803.summary: Argues God, being most just and pious, cannot require more from a person than was given them and than lies within their power, and accepts what is offered with due intention; draws an analogy from common human judgment: someone who deliberately intends to give gold but is deceived into giving counterfeit instead is still considered, and rightly regarded, as having given gold and to be generous — citing Aristotle (Ethics IV) that liberality lies in the giver's disposition, not the quantity given, and (Ethics III and VI) that what is done involuntarily through ignorance is not blameworthy, and that acting in accordance with law without the right disposition (through ignorance, unwillingness, or other motive, rather than for the sake of the acts themselves) does not make one truly just, whereas the right disposition ('cleverness,' directed by good or bad intention) determines whether an action is praiseworthy or merely cunning.
claims: By analogy with Aristotle's account of moral responsibility (liberality residing in disposition, involuntary ignorance being blameless, right action requiring right disposition), a sincerely well-intentioned but factually mistaken act of worship should be judged by its intention, not its material error.
concepts: Aristotelian ethics of intention versus material act
involuntary ignorance as excusing (Ethics III, VI)

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8846.summary: Supports the intention-over-material-act principle with Paul (Romans 2, on Gentiles who, without the Law, do by nature what the Law requires, showing the law's work written on their hearts) and Christ (on the single eye lighting the whole body), glossed at length via Augustine (On the Sermon on the Mount, and elsewhere) that the 'eye' is the intention governing all our works, so if the intention is pure and rightly directed, the works done according to it must be good; and via further Augustinine texts that a good work is made by intention, guided by faith, that one should attend not to what a person does but to what they look to in doing it, that the malicious who unknowingly do good receive not the reward of true justice but only escape the guilt of malice, that goodwill in willing benefit (even if harm accidentally results) is not blamed, that 'the disposition names the deed,' and Jerome's dictum that what matters in sacred history is not what one finds but what one seeks — concluding that a sincere will to serve God (per Part 30) is right and rationally acceptable to God even if error involuntarily creeps into the manner of service.
claims: A dense chain of scriptural and patristic authority (Paul, Christ, Augustine, Jerome, and canon law) establishes that moral and religious worth is determined by the sincerity and rectitude of intention, not by the material correctness of the act, supporting mercy toward invincibly ignorant but sincere worshippers.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8905.summary: Defends the principle with the legal/theological doctrine of 'error of person' invalidating consent, illustrated by canon law examples (a mistaken buyer who thinks he is dealing with 'Marcellus' but is really dealing with an impostor did not truly consent to that transaction; one who unknowingly buys counterfeit metal believing it gold never consented to counterfeit; a man who unknowingly sleeps with his wife's sister, believing her to be his wife, is excused by ignorance though the union remains forever without hope of marriage; the Devil disguising himself as an angel of light means someone who consents to fellowship with an apparent 'good spirit' consents to blessedness, not damnation; and one deceived into thinking a heretic is Augustine, Ambrose, or Jerome and thereby persuaded consents in truth to Catholic orthodoxy, not to heresy) — arguing by strict analogy that a person deceived by invincible ignorance about the true nature of what/whom they worship has, in the relevant moral sense, not truly consented to error but to the truth they believed they were embracing. Cites the example of Lucius Annaeus Seneca, tutor to Nero, whom Jerome's catalogue of illustrious men includes among the 'saints' on the strength of an (apocryphal) correspondence with Paul in which Seneca wished to hold among his own the place Paul held among Christians, asking rhetorically why else Seneca would be so listed.
claims: The legal doctrine of 'error of person,' whereby deceived consent attaches to the believed reality rather than the actual deceptive substitute, supports by analogy the claim that invincibly ignorant worshippers who sincerely intend the true God are not to be judged as having consented to idolatry.
Jerome's inclusion of Seneca among the 'saints,' based on the (spurious) Seneca-Paul correspondence, is cited as a precedent for crediting a virtuous pagan's sincere disposition.
concepts: canon law doctrine of 'error of person'
the Devil disguised as an angel of light
Seneca and the apocryphal Seneca-Paul correspondence

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e8977.summary: States a firm personal conviction that God, being pious and just, will at some point reveal (implicitly or explicitly) the true religion necessary for salvation — namely Christianity — to anyone who loves him above all and diligently and perseveringly seeks to worship him rightly, noting that many Jews and Gentiles clearly foresaw and prophesied Christ's coming, as attested by numerous histories and the preceding discussion; argues from God's demonstrated providence even for the lowliest inanimate things and beasts (per the first Supposition, subsequent Parts, and many philosophers) that he would not abandon a human being without providence, and from Part 27's demonstration (with supporting histories) that God graciously provides what is needed for salvation even to those not seeking or even scorning him, that he will still less deny what is needed to those who piously and perseveringly seek and worship him according to their knowledge and ability.
claims: God's universal providence, extending even to those who neglect or scorn him, guarantees a fortiori that he will not withhold the knowledge needed for salvation from those who sincerely and perseveringly seek to worship him rightly.
concepts: argument a fortiori from lesser to greater care

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9006.summary: Adds a harsher qualification: many unbelievers, in truth, exercise no or insufficient diligence in seeking the true worship of God, and even when it is gratuitously revealed to them by divine inspiration, reason, or human preaching that Christian law is better or even true (and their own erroneous), a stubborn pride hardens them, refusing to bow their proud necks, abandon their old sect, admit a better one, or accept the truth, resisting, grumbling, and contradicting instead. Illustrates with a personal anecdote: the author once urged a learned and famous Jew, in discussing his conversion, to devoutly pray to his God to illuminate his heart and show him which law was truly better and more acceptable to God; the Jew refused, saying this would amount to doubting his own law; when asked instead to let the author pray on his behalf to their common God, he again refused for the same reason, and when the author offered to pray for himself in a similar way, the Jew flatly refused, saying he knew the author would never be a good Jew, adding, 'even if you wish to doubt your law, I do not wish to doubt mine.'
claims: The Jew's stubborn refusal even to entertain prayerful openness to the possibility of Christianity's truth exemplifies the culpable, willful pride that (unlike invincible ignorance) blocks recognition of revealed truth.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9050.summary: Offers yet another line of response: distinguishing genuine miracles from illusory, deceptive, diabolical ones — the latter exemplified by Pharaoh's Egyptian magicians in Exodus, and characteristic of pagan/idolatrous 'miracles' generally, per Augustine's discussion (City of God 10). Anticipates the objection that unbelievers could say the same of Christian miracles (conceding they have), but replies that a universal denial of all Christian miracles can be refuted as before, while particular doubts about specific reported wonders among Christians (possibly mistaken for true miracles) need not always be refuted, since the two kinds can be probably distinguished by circumstantial and probable indicators — sanctity of life, manner of belief, love, prayer, and petition, and the manner of the miracle's granting — and with certainty only through divine illumination and inspiration, namely the Holy Spirit's gift Paul calls 'discernment of spirits,' available (per Part 7) especially, though not necessarily universally, to those charged with judging miracles, such as high priests and bishops, when needed — as in the canonization of a saint.
claims: Genuine (divinely-worked) miracles are distinguishable in principle from illusory/diabolical ones both by probable circumstantial signs and, with certainty, by the Spirit's gift of 'discernment of spirits' given especially to those with authority to judge such matters, such as in canonization.
