dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9092.summary: Supports the claim that God grants special revelatory gifts to those responsible for judgment by citing precedents of God revealing matters concerning their realms to various pagan rulers: Pharaoh (Genesis 41), Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar (Daniel 2, 4, 5), Alexander the Great (Josephus), Genghis Khan (per Tartar histories mentioned earlier), and Agamemnon's dream about instituting battle (per Homer, with Nestor's counsel that public matters warrant crediting a king's dream, as also discussed by Macrobius on the Dream of Scipio); and Caiaphas, the high priest of the Jews, who despite his malice, prophesied truly when touched by God's Spirit (John 11) — concluding it is all the more fitting that God grant similar spiritual gifts to the Christians' own supreme prince, the Pope.
claims: A series of precedents of divine revelation granted to pagan rulers and even the malicious high priest Caiaphas argues, a fortiori, for God granting discernment gifts to the Pope as supreme pontiff of Christians.
concepts: precedents of revelation to rulers (Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, Alexander, Genghis Khan, Agamemnon)

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9119.summary: Turns to address Gentile philosophers who might concede Christian law is the best positive law yet still maintain that natural law (natural reason/conscience, synderesis) alone suffices to regulate all human action without any revealed law. Responds first that if Christian law is good and best, it is also true, and it expressly teaches that whoever does not believe as it teaches will be damned; second, that if Christian law is the best positive law, it is more perfect than natural law alone, since it contains the whole perfection of natural law while adding to it, supplying its insufficiencies and correcting its defects — so there is no reason not to choose and hold it.
claims: Since Christian law both exceeds and perfects natural law rather than merely paralleling it, the claim that natural law alone suffices does not justify refusing the (conceded) superior and true Christian law.
concepts: natural law/synderesis versus revealed positive law
Christian law as fulfilling and perfecting natural law

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9137.summary: Asks why, if natural law alone sufficed, God (who per the first Supposition and Part 3 does nothing in vain, as the interlocutors themselves concede) would have given additional laws — old and new — each harder to know and more laborious to fulfill than natural law alone, since no wise agent multiplies means beyond what suffices unless doing so is more fitting, useful, or better (as natural reason and all philosophers agree) — implying revealed positive law, especially Christian law, must be more fitting/useful/better, so it should be accepted. Adds that pagan philosophers who thought they followed pure natural reason were frequently deceived by the thin, false, deceptive shadow-image of merely apparent reason, falling into irrational error, as shown by the plain truth and by their own frequent mutual contradictions — so such an irregular, flawed, and deceptive rule cannot suffice to direct a person in everything. Argues God, being sincere, supreme, and primary truth (per the first and second Suppositions and Part 3), loves and accepts truth over falsehood and right worship over error, especially in religion, and (per Part 30) is to be loved and worshipped above all for his own sake — so it cannot be indifferent whether such worship is given to the true God or to demons/idols through an erring, misled conscience; and even the pagan philosophers who were true philosophers themselves condemned idols and held one true God should be worshipped, yet asks to what end this matters if worshipping an idol is as good as worshipping God — pressing the further question of why philosophers labor so hard to find truth if truth and falsehood are equally valuable and fruitful for one following one's own conscience.
claims: The principle that a wise agent does not use more means than necessary implies that God's giving of additional positive laws (culminating in Christianity) beyond natural law shows positive revealed law to be more fitting and better, undermining the sufficiency of natural law alone.

Pagan philosophers' reliance on unaided natural reason, evidenced by their own frequent contradictions, shows this 'rule' is too irregular and fallible to suffice as a guide, in tension with the argument (elsewhere entertained) that sincere but mistaken conscience should be excused.
concepts: principle of parsimony applied to divine action (no more means than necessary)
tension between excusing ignorance and requiring right worship

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9213.summary: Continues the argument that natural reason alone does not suffice, and that a religious/divine law is necessary just as human political/domestic laws are necessary within their smaller domains: adds that error concerning God and divine worship is worse and graver than error concerning merely human/political matters, and since even Gentile philosophers themselves established many laws for the latter, a fortiori a law is needed for the former — citing Aristotle (Politics VII) naming care of divine matters ('priesthood') as one of the city's necessary parts, with Plato and other Gentile philosophers agreeing; and asking, if natural reason alone sufficed for everything, why philosophers themselves wrote so many books of positive human law (Plato's Laws, Aristotle's Ethics and Politics, Cicero's Republic, and others), which would be pointless on the sufficiency-of-natural-law view.
claims: Aristotle's own inclusion of priesthood/divine care among the city's necessary parts, and the sheer proliferation of positive law-books by pagan philosophers themselves, undercuts their claim that natural reason alone suffices without any positive (a fortiori, divine) law.
concepts: Aristotle's Politics on priesthood as a necessary civic function
self-undermining proliferation of philosophers' own legal writings

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9235.summary: Draws an analogy from human political authority (a ruler can grant or promise a city to someone on stipulated legal conditions) to argue God could likewise have established for the first human a law whereby perfect obedience would secure everlasting beatitude for him and his descendants, while disobedience would bring everlasting privation of beatitude and misery upon the whole line unless he, or one of his descendants, made adequate satisfaction — charging the philosophers with erring by failing to recognize humanity's shared original sin and inherited unfitness for future life, which is precisely what the argument concludes actually happened, as gathered from Christian teaching.
claims: By analogy with a ruler's conditional grant of a city, God could fittingly have instituted a law under which Adam's sin brought hereditary loss of beatitude upon all his descendants, pending adequate satisfaction — which Christian doctrine holds is exactly what occurred.
concepts: original sin as hereditary legal consequence
analogy of a conditional royal grant
philosophers' failure to grasp original sin

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9255.summary: Concludes that whatever one does by mere natural capacity, absent satisfaction for sin, accomplishes nothing toward future glory under this law; anticipates the objection that satisfying God for sin is easy, but argues true satisfaction for a sin knowingly committed against God requires rendering something equal or greater than what was owed had the sin not been committed, especially under strict justice — otherwise God's violated honor is not fully restored and the offense not fully appeased — and asks who could possibly render God so much, given (per Part 30) that no sin should ever knowingly be committed against God for any goods to be gained or evils to be avoided. Anticipates that human incapacity might excuse from incurring further new personal sin but not from the old debt/sin itself, nor restore fitness for everlasting beatitude under the stated law — illustrated by the case of a violated virgin, who however much compensation is later made, is not thereby restored to virginity — and rejects the possibility that God might simply remit sin without any satisfaction, since (even granting he could) this would contradict Part 31 and would let sin go entirely unpunished; argues philosophically that if a sinner is to become just, this requires a real change, which (per Part 6) cannot occur in God nor in anything irrelevant, but only in the sinner himself, and this change is (or requires) satisfaction for sin. Concludes, since evil/sin is a privation, not a positive thing, and a privation in a fit subject can only be fully removed by the full restoration of the possessed state it privated (with no intermediate), that only Christ, God and man together, is fully sufficient to render such satisfaction, as the first Supposition with its following Parts prove, and as the Jewish Law foretold and the Christian Law truly professes — concluding therefore all should become Christians to share in this satisfaction.
claims: True satisfaction for sin against God requires restoring an equivalent to what was owed, which finite fallen humanity cannot supply on its own, and since evil is a privation that (once incurred in a fit subject) can only be removed by full restoration of the lost good, only the God-man Christ is sufficient to make this satisfaction — the doctrine the whole treatise (and Jewish prophecy) is said to converge on.
concepts: satisfaction for sin as restoring divine honor
sin as privation (not a positive entity)

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9122.summary: States the rubric of Corollarium 33: against philosophers who deny the possibility of creation, annihilation, and re-creation.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9127.summary: Argues philosophers should reject the 'foolish harlot' doctrine (dressed up as wisdom) that creation, annihilation, and re-creation are impossible: since God (per Supposition 1 and Parts 5, 7) is supremely perfect, sufficient, powerful, and efficacious such that nothing could be more so, it is more perfect to be able to produce something from nothing by one's own power alone than to require pre-existing matter; since God's power infinitely exceeds any created efficient cause, he must be proportionally capable of a correspondingly greater mode of causing (i.e., without presupposed matter); since (per Part 8) God has a universally efficacious will, had nothing ever existed besides him, his willing something else to exist would make it exist instantly; and since (per Supposition 1 and Part 3) whatever essential and intrinsic attribute worthy of God can be held without contradiction must be held, and creative power is such an attribute defensible against all contradiction, creation must be possible — and by parallel reasoning, so must annihilation (since a finite creature cannot be more able to persist than its omnipotent maker is able to destroy it) and re-creation (once creation and annihilation are granted). Concludes by urging philosophers to weigh these reasons fairly against their own, predicting theirs will be found wanting, to humbly recognize their own fallibility (evidenced by their frequent mutual and even self-contradiction) rather than clinging to a view universally rejected by every faith and sect and supported by such strong arguments — invoking Aristotle's own principle (Ethics X) that what everyone believes must be assumed to be so, and Averroes's parallel principle that what is universally reputed among all people is necessary, wholly or in part.
claims: God's supreme, infinite power and universally efficacious will entail the possibility of creation ex nihilo, annihilation, and re-creation, and the philosophers' denial of this is refuted by their own principles (Aristotle's and Averroes's doctrine that universal human belief carries evidential weight) as well as by their notorious mutual inconsistency.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9226.summary: States the rubric of Corollarium 34: against philosophers who deny the possibility of the world's creation.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9231.summary: Argues philosophers who deny God could have created the world should be refuted, since the previous corollarium already showed God could create some thing, and the world is of finite entity and power while God is strictly infinite (per Supposition 1 and Parts 3-4); God can likewise annihilate the world (per the prior Part) and re-create it by the same reasoning, so he could equally have created it in the first place; and the chief supposed obstacle — the impossibility of creation from nothing — was already dismissed in the preceding Part, the other philosophical objections being notoriously flimsy.
claims: Since God's power to create, annihilate, and re-create something in general was already established, and the world is merely a finite entity, God's ability to have created the world specifically follows by the same reasoning.
concepts: extension of creation argument to the world specifically
finitude of the world versus God's infinity

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9470.summary: Announces a closer examination of the argument from Aristotle's Physics VIII (for the world's eternity) is needed, since he has heard that some believers, following that infidel line of reasoning, were led all the way into the abyss of unbelief; states that, even setting aside his Christian commitment and considering himself merely a lover of truth, that Aristotelian argument seems to commit a fatal error both in its matter and its form, turning on an ambiguity in how 'prior' and 'before' are understood — either according to nature or according to time.
claims: The Aristotelian argument for the world's eternity (Physics VIII) is philosophically defective in both its logical form and its material premises, turning on an equivocation between natural and temporal priority — a serious matter since it has reportedly led some believers into unbelief.
concepts: Aristotle's Physics VIII argument for eternity of the world
equivocation between priority of nature and priority of time

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9487.summary: Sets up a direct rebuttal addressed to Aristotle and Averroes: grants, for argument's sake, that the world and motion began at some first instant A, with no time, change, temporal succession, or duration (great or small) truly preceding that first motion (call it B) — just as nothing precedes the outermost heaven in local position — which Aristotle himself implies in Physics VIII.10 ('how will there be before and after, if time does not exist, or time, if there is no motion?'); but also posits that eternal God, with his eternal wisdom and will, preceded A in priority of nature, as cause precedes effect. Charges that Aristotle and Averroes, throughout their argument, illegitimately assume that the non-existence of anything made necessarily precedes its existence temporally — precisely the point they need to prove — thereby begging the question both materially and formally, since this assumption directly contradicts the position being posited (that nothing temporally precedes A).
claims: Aristotle's and Averroes's argument for the world's eternity covertly assumes, without proof, that non-being must temporally precede being — which is exactly the disputed point — making the argument formally and materially question-begging once one posits (as is coherent) that only natural, not temporal, priority separates God's eternal will from the world's temporal beginning.
concepts: priority of nature versus priority of time
charge of petitio principii against Aristotle/Averroes
God's eternal causation of a temporally finite world

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9522.summary: Applies the same diagnosis to every variant of the objection (e.g., that if God made the world at instant A, this required some new act of will, some new disposition in agent or patient, or the removal of some obstacle, or the arrival of a moment he had always intended for it, and none of these could happen without change, so an earlier change must have preceded — all of which covertly assume, without proof, that a long mutable temporal succession preceded A, exactly what was to be shown). Notes the same fallacy appears in asking 'why did God make the world at A and not earlier,' which presupposes something temporally prior to A — as absurd as asking why the sky's convex boundary is where it is and not further out. Clarifies that the supposed impossibility of a new action following immediately from an eternal will does not apply here, since God's eternal will to make the world is prior to the world only in nature, not in time (the world being neither older nor younger than that will in temporal terms, only in nature).
claims: Every version of the philosophers' objection to instantaneous creation covertly presupposes the very thing at issue (temporal priority before the world's first instant), and the supposed problem of a new temporal effect from an eternal will dissolves once the priority between God's will and the world is understood as natural, not temporal.
concepts: natural versus temporal priority applied to divine willing
eternal will producing a temporally-originated effect

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9557.summary: Anticipates a further objection: by the same reasoning used to deny God is temporally prior to the world, one might conclude either that God too began to exist (if the world began) or that the world, like God, is eternal. Responds by conceding God is not prior to the world in actual temporal antiquity, but denying that 'God began to exist' follows, since 'beginning to exist' is properly defined not as actually existing now with no actual time whatsoever having preceded, but as existing now with the thing itself not having existed in any preceding time (even if such time existed) — as with Peter's soul, which did not exist in the time before its creation, though that time existed; whereas God, had any time preceded, would necessarily have existed in it — so it is not God who was absent from time (if there had been time before A), but rather time itself was absent, not God. By the same reasoning, God is truly eternal (having no beginning or ending in the relevant sense), whereas 'eternal' in a different, stricter sense (existing through literally all actual time, as Aristotle seems to define it, citing his own citation of the ancients' definition of eternity as the encompassing limit of a thing's proper time in Physics/De Caelo) could even be conceded of the world without contradiction, if 'eternal' is redefined this way — or, adopting Aristotle's own logical principle that a verb co-signifies time, one could even grant 'God began to exist' in the sense of beginning to exist in/at time (as Lord of time and temporal things), without this implying God is new or mutable, only that time itself is what is new.
claims: Properly distinguishing 'beginning to exist' (non-existence in preceding actual time, whether or not any such time existed) from mere non-coexistence with any prior time dissolves the objection that denying God's temporal priority to the world entails either God's own temporal beginning or the world's full eternity in the strict sense — while conceding that 'eternal,' redefined per Aristotle's own citation of ancient usage, could even be predicated of the world without contradiction.
concepts: God's eternity versus the Aristotelian definition of 'eternal'

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9631.summary: Rebuts an anticipated sophistical retort that if God could have created the world beginning at a first instant, he could equally have created it together with motion and time immediately after (rather than at) a first instant, in which case the world would never have had a first instant of existing nor a first instant of not-yet-existing, and would thus be strictly eternal — replying with a physical counter-thought-experiment: since the objectors hold that surfaces terminate bodies, suppose (by God's omnipotence, or at least by their own style of conditional argument) that the sky's whole convex outer surface were destroyed while the rest of the heaven remained; the heaven would then be simply infinite, bounded neither internally nor externally by any surface. Concludes more directly that the world is not eternal but did begin — not actually preceded by any real time or instant, only 'habitually' (i.e., such that had eternal time existed, the world necessarily would have begun at some instant within it) — so its non-beginning-in-actual-time reflects the absence of any preceding time, not the world's antiquity.
claims: A hypothetical physical scenario (destroying the sky's bounding surface) is used to expose an inconsistency in the objectors' own commitments about surfaces terminating bodies.
The world's not having an actual first preceding instant is due to no time having actually preceded it at all, not to the world's beginning being eternal or infinitely early.
concepts: thought experiment on the heaven's bounding surface

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9679.summary: Anticipates a further objection that even if no true time preceded the world, at least an imaginary time did, and arguments about time apply to such fictional time as they would to real time; responds by invoking Aristotle's own principle (Metaphysics IV) that things do not follow imagination or estimation — so imagining time before the world no more entails actual prior time than imagining a place or time beyond the heavens entails their existence, quoting Aristotle himself (De Caelo I) that manifestly neither place, nor void, nor time exists outside the heaven.
claims: By Aristotle's own principle that reality does not follow mere imagination, positing an 'imaginary time' before the world's creation does not establish any actual prior temporal reality, just as imagining space beyond the heavens (which Aristotle himself denies) does not create it.
concepts: Aristotle's principle that reality does not follow imagination (Metaphysics IV)
no place, void, or time outside the heaven (De Caelo I)

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9697.summary: To confound the objectors further and lead them to truth, grants for argument's sake their 'crude imagination' that an eternal (real or fictional) temporal succession preceded the world, and argues even on that supposition God could still have voluntarily produced the world at some instant A within it, with the first new change B beginning then without any new change preceding it (aside from the eternal succession's own parts) — rejecting the inference that God must first have acquired, via some prior new change, a new disposition enabling this action, since (per Aristotle's own Metaphysics IX.10, with Averroes's own commentary agreeing) this necessity holds for irrational agents, whose active and passive powers necessarily act once duly disposed and brought together, but not for rational, voluntary agents, which can remain fully disposed to act yet freely wait through any span of time, even eternal time, before acting anew without any preceding change — a distinction the author praises Aristotle and Averroes for having themselves drawn (even if inconsistently applied elsewhere), and which he promises to also establish by reason alone.
claims: Even granting (for argument's sake) an eternal preceding temporal succession, a free rational agent — as Aristotle and Averroes themselves elsewhere teach regarding rational versus irrational powers — can remain disposed to act yet freely delay acting for any length of time, even eternally, and then act anew without requiring any preceding change to explain the timing.
concepts: rational versus irrational agency (Aristotle, Metaphysics IX.10)
free agent's ability to delay action without prior change

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9748.summary: Offers an independent philosophical proof (not resting on authority) that a free power can freely delay and then newly act without any preceding change: if this were false, no power would ever act freely and contradictorily (i.e., could equally not-act) — for if positing all the necessary and sufficient prior conditions for producing some free first act A either necessitates A's production (in which case A's occurring is not free, and the agent's power is not free at all, contrary to hypothesis) or does not necessitate it (in which case the agent, with all those conditions eternally and uniformly in place, can freely wait any span of time and then newly produce A without any preceding change affecting it, since it was already, and remains, sufficiently disposed). Preemptively rejects the common but (he says) unsound answer 'it acts then because it wills then,' since this either makes the will's own act (first free willing) precede itself, or requires another prior act of will explaining that one, launching an infinite regress; concludes that seeking a determining cause that would make free action necessary is simply seeking something that cannot be found in genuinely free active powers, and that Avicenna and Algazel likewise erred by assuming this false principle.
claims: A rigorous dilemma shows that a fully disposed free power must be able to act at any chosen moment without requiring a further, prior explanatory change, on pain of either destroying freedom altogether or triggering an infinite regress of prior determining acts of will.
Avicenna and Algazel, like Aristotle and Averroes, mistakenly assumed that free action requires such a determining prior cause.
concepts: freedom of the will and the no-infinite-regress-of-willing argument
critique of 'it acts because it wills' as circular/regressive

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9809.summary: Turns to a second Averroistic argument (attributed to Aristotle) claiming to prove universally, for any power (rational or not), that a first change must have been preceded by an earlier one: since mover and moved are correlative terms, and at one time this does not move/is not moved while later it does/is, a new relation arises that did not exist before, and every relation follows some change, so there must have been some change in the mover, the moved, or an external factor (e.g., removing an impediment) before the posited first change. Rejects this by the same rational/irrational distinction: if 'every relation follows a prior change' is meant temporally, it is false for the relation between a rational agent and patient, which need not follow (and can instead coincide instantaneously with) its first action, though it follows it in the order of nature; if meant only in the order of nature, the objection has no force at all against the author's position. Adds a further point specifically against Averroes: acting need not require any actual thought or awareness of the presence of time or 'now,' as his commentaries seem to assume, since agents often act without attending to time at all — but God, who does nothing by chance and disposes everything sweetly by infinite wisdom, always acts exactly when he eternally disposed to act, so he disposed from eternity to make the world at instant A and made it then without any preceding change (except possibly within the hypothetical eternal succession the objectors themselves posit).
claims: The Aristotelian/Averroistic argument that every new relation (like mover-moved) must be preceded by a change fails for rational agents, since their relation to their effect can coincide instantaneously (though not eternally, in the order of nature) with their first free act, rather than being temporally preceded by it.
God's action requires no temporal awareness or 'presence of an instant' to trigger it, since he eternally disposed to act at exactly the moment he acts, without change.
concepts: mover-moved relation and Aristotle's correlativity argument
critique of Averroes on temporal awareness as a precondition for action
divine eternal disposition versus temporal execution

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9870.summary: Quotes at length (as a direct block quotation) Averroes's own text (Commentary 8) objecting that the author's position is unintelligible: when a will wills to do something at some hour, some new 'concupiscence' (desire) must arise in the will at that hour which was not there before; that concupiscence is the proximate cause of acting then and not before; the cause of that concupiscence is the presence of that particular time, which not having existed before is itself necessarily a change, or follows a change; therefore the concupiscence produced by the presence of time is itself a change beyond the first posited change; so before the posited first change there is another, prior one — and Averroes insists no sound mind can escape this conclusion except by presuming on repentance (i.e., only a fool would think otherwise).
concepts: Averroes's argument from 'concupiscence' triggered by the presence of time
direct quotation of an opposing authority for rebuttal

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9896.summary: Responds sharply to Averroes's quoted argument, saying that even setting aside Christian faith and reasoning as a mere rationalist, Averroes's presumptuous sophistry and unrepentant error in both matter and form deserve the greatest penitence. Charges Averroes with erring gravely by assuming God could not do something at a set hour that he had eternally disposed to do unless he then received some new disposition enabling the action (already refuted); and with erring mortally against a necessary and immortal truth by implying (in Commentaries 8 and 15) that God's understanding or imagining of 'present time' is itself a change following a change — as if God understood a given time differently when it is future than when it is present, the opposite of which Part 6 already showed, and which Averroes himself elsewhere (and other philosophers) affirm, yet contradicts here and even in his own Metaphysics XII commentary. Similarly errs in implying God wills a given time or anything else differently when future versus present (which would make God's will mutable, against Part 6), and in supposing the mere 'presence of time' moves and produces concupiscence in the divine will (also against a prior Part); rather, God's intellect and will are unmoved and unaffected by anything posterior or by any intrinsic variation, understanding and willing a given future, then present, then past thing in exactly the same way at all times — so just as he eternally and unchangingly knew and willed to create the world at instant A, he did so through that same unchanged knowledge and will, just as he likewise now produces every immediate temporal effect. Cites Augustine (City of God 12) as a fellow Christian witness on this very topic, and finally charges Averroes with a formal fallacy: correctly noting that the 'presence of time that was not before' is itself a necessary change or consequence of change does not actually contradict the author's own position, since the author himself already posited B as the first new change, excepting only the parts of the hypothetical eternal fictional succession which he conceded only conditionally, if those really count as new changes.
claims: Averroes's argument commits a serious philosophical/theological error by implying God's knowledge and will vary with the changing status of a time from future to present to past, which contradicts the immutability of divine intellect and will already established, and Augustine is cited as concurring on divine timelessness.

Averroes's argument also formally fails to contradict the author's actual position, since the author already granted that a first new change (B) occurs, and only conditionally entertained the fictional eternal succession preceding it.
concepts: divine immutability of intellect and will (against temporal variation)
Augustine, City of God 12, on divine eternity
charge of formal fallacy against Averroes

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9959.summary: Clarifies, to avoid seeming to burden Catholic readers accustomed to saying God 'preceded the world long, eternally, or even infinitely,' that his own position (that no temporal succession or duration preceded the world) is itself the properly Catholic one: since nothing besides God existed before the world, and God (per Part 6) is wholly immutable, nothing mutable or any mutability existed before the world, hence no temporal succession or duration (which cannot be understood apart from change) existed either; since in every succession something arrives and something departs, but nothing arrives or departs in God given his total immutability, there was no succession in God before the world, nor in anything else since nothing else existed; since every such succession has greater/lesser, prior/posterior parts, but God (per Parts 10 and 26) has no such parts, no such succession existed in God or elsewhere before the world; and since if such a succession had existed, it could in principle have had distinguishable parts like hours, days, months, and years (as in present time), yet nothing existed before the world by which such measured distinctions could have been made.
claims: The properly Catholic position is that strictly no temporal succession preceded the world at all (not merely 'a very long' or 'infinite' one), since God's total immutability, partlessness, and sole prior existence rule out any real succession, arrival/departure, or measurable temporal parts before creation.
concepts: divine immutability precluding any pre-creation succession
no measurable temporal parts (hours, days, years) before the world

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e9992.summary: Forecloses various evasions: denies that mutability, arrival, departure, or measured distinction could have inhered in pure non-being, since pure non-being can contain nothing at all; every change, arrival, or departure necessarily belongs to some actually changing, arriving, or departing subject (as natural philosophy teaches throughout), and pure non-being is no such subject, nor is there any reason to locate such features in one non-being rather than another (so, having nowhere proper to be placed, they are nowhere); partibility, greater and lesser magnitude are properties of quantity, which non-being is not; by parity of reasoning such a temporal succession would equally have to exist outside the heaven (which is denied); such successive quantity is no more plausible before the world than permanent quantity, which is agreed not to have existed then; if such a temporal succession did exist before the world, God could have destroyed it before creating the world, and no one can know God's counsel well enough to assert he did not, nor can anyone prove it necessarily existed given that it need not have; if it existed, there would have been no need to create time together with the world, since the old succession would have sufficed, yet then two wholly distinct times would coexist (against Aristotle, Physics IV, explicitly); and only eternity, not any temporal succession, preceded the world, as Boethius's definition of eternity (Consolation V) — 'the whole, simultaneous, and perfect possession of unending life,' where nothing future is absent and nothing past has flowed away — and his own explicit statement (matching the author's own thesis) that God should not be considered older than creation by quantity of time, but only by the property of a simple nature, both confirm.
claims: A cascade of independent arguments (from the impossibility of change inhering in non-being, the categorial mismatch of quantity and non-being, the coexistence-of-two-times absurdity, and Boethius's classic definition of eternity) together rule out any temporal succession preceding the world, leaving only atemporal divine eternity before creation, exactly as Boethius himself states.
concepts: change cannot inhere in pure non-being
absurdity of two coexisting times (Aristotle, Physics IV)
Boethius's definition of eternity (Consolation of Philosophy V)

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10052.summary: Marshals an extended chain of Augustinian citations in support of the same thesis: on Psalm 101 ('years... in the generation of generations'), Augustine explains God's 'years' do not come and go like ordinary days/months/years (which exist only by ceasing to be), but are identical with God's own unchanging eternity/substance, in which nothing is past as no-longer or future as not-yet, only pure 'is' — this eternity called us forth, and the Word sprang from eternity, already eternity, already Word, and 'not yet time,' since time itself was made through the Word; on Genesis ('In the beginning you founded the earth'), Augustine says he knows God's eternity precedes all he made; in the Confessions, that God's 'years' are God's own single unending 'today'; elsewhere, that one thing can precede another in eternity (as God precedes all things), in time (as flower precedes fruit), in choice (as fruit is preferred to flower), or in origin (as sound precedes song); on Psalm 83 ('one day in your courts is better than a thousand'), that 'a thousand days' signifies temporal mutability while 'one day' signifies eternity's unchangeableness; and finally, from City of God 12, that the measured temporal spans (hours, days, months, years) properly called 'time' began with the motion of the heavenly bodies (as Genesis itself states, 'let them be for signs and seasons, days and years'), so that where no creature's changeable motions mark time, time simply cannot exist at all — hence angels, though always existing (in every time there has been), are not thereby co-eternal with God, since mutable time can never be co-eternal with immutable eternity; and that if God was always Lord, he always had a creature subject to his rule, yet one not begotten of himself but made by him from nothing, and not co-eternal with him.
claims: A dense sequence of Augustinian texts (on the Psalms, Genesis, the Confessions, and City of God) is marshaled to establish that God's eternity is not a very long duration of time but an utterly different, unchanging mode of being that precedes creation only 'by nature,' not 'by temporal quantity' — with time itself beginning only with the motion of created things, so that not even the always-existing angels are co-eternal with God.
concepts: Augustine on divine eternity as substance, not duration
time beginning with the motion of the heavens
angels always-existing but not co-eternal with God

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10128.summary: Anticipates the objection that Augustine (City of God 12.12) seems to say there were infinite past ages during which God 'ceased' from creating before newly creating the world, describing that eternal cessation as so incomparably vast that any finite (however immeasurably large) span of time would be as a single drop compared to the ocean beside it — one finite, however small, the other truly infinite. Also anticipates the rational objection that God could not have made the world any earlier than he did, since nothing existed before to have made it earlier in. Responds that such statements (Augustine's included) mean only that many years existed before the world potentially, not actually — just as infinite spaces and distances exist beyond the heavens potentially, since God could have made the world however much earlier, through however many years, just as he could make spaces and distances beyond the heavens surpassing any finite number — and buttresses this reading with Augustine's own explicit answer (Against the Manichees I.2-4) to the Manichean question 'what was God doing before he made heaven and earth, and why did he suddenly decide to do something he had never done through eternal ages': that God made heaven and earth 'in the beginning of time,' but also, in the Word, 'without a beginning of time,' meaning there simply was no time before time itself was made — one cannot ask what happened in a time that did not yet exist, since God is the maker of time itself, and the very question 'what suddenly pleased him' falsely presupposes that some time passed during which God did nothing. Concludes that although nothing had temporal priority before the world, there could have been such priority through God's creative choice — in which he could equally have created the world earlier — since it is precisely his creative power, not any prior time, that would ground such an earlier possibility.
claims: Augustine's rhetorical description of an 'infinite' divine cessation before creation, and the objection that God could not have made the world earlier since nothing preceded it, are both resolved by distinguishing potential from actual prior time: no time actually preceded creation, but God could have created earlier (through however many years) purely by his own power, just as he could create space beyond the heavens — a possibility grounded in his power, not in any actually preceding duration.
concepts: Augustine's Against the Manichees on 'what was God doing before creation'
God as maker of time itself

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10196.summary: Dismisses the remaining Aristotelian/Averroistic arguments for the world's eternity as too weak even to merit serious rebuttal, barely rising to the level of sophistical posturing, and turns to attack Aristotle's own authority and consistency: cites Chalcidius's remark that Aristotle characteristically dismisses whatever does not fit his own chosen doctrine; cites Aristotle against himself (De Caelo II.80) admitting that his own school habitually raises questions not to genuinely investigate the matter but to argue against an opponent, and (Topics I) explicitly classifying the eternity of the world as an undecided 'problem' with plausible arguments on both sides and no certain resolution; cites Galen (via Averroes's commentary on De Caelo) saying no one can know with certainty whether the world is eternal or new; and climactically reports that Aristotle himself, on his deathbed before his students, sincerely (not with his usual pompous rhetorical display) confessed that his eight books of Physics only teach methods and principles for arguing plausibly on any side of disputable questions, distinguishing what coheres with a position from what does not, without providing a sure path to truth — useful only as a rhetorical weapon to overpower an opponent unable to resist, 'like a scorpion in theriac' (a poison that nonetheless serves as remedy) — a deathbed confession the author cites as recorded plainly in a text on Aristotle's death.
claims: Aristotle's own writings (Topics, De Caelo) and an alleged deathbed confession undermine the authority of his arguments for the world's eternity, since he himself classified the question as undecidable and admitted his Physics teaches only rhetorical technique, not certain truth.
concepts: Aristotle's Topics classifying eternity-of-the-world as an undecidable problem

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10006.summary: States the rubric of Corollarium 35: against philosophers and heretics who deny the possibility of the Virgin's conception and childbirth, and who say Christ was not truly born of St. Mary, ever-Virgin.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10019.summary: Argues philosophers and corrupted heretics who deny the possibility of virginal conception should be refuted: God, having (per Parts 7-8) a universally efficacious will and the power to create ex nihilo, annihilate, and re-create the whole world, and to create a human being from nothing (per the immediately preceding Parts), and who works every kind of miracle (per Part 32), can surely form a child in a virgin's womb without a man's aid; notes that even in the animal kingdom, females of species that normally conceive through mating are sometimes found to conceive without a male, citing Virgil's Georgics on mares seized by desire that become pregnant merely by facing the wind (Zephyr), a claim the author insists should not be dismissed as poetic fiction since that book of the Georgics is more properly philosophical than poetic and is frequently cited as authoritative by philosophers and Catholic doctors; cites Virgil's commentator Servius explaining these Spanish mares' wind-conceived foals are shorter-lived, and corroborating natural-historical testimony from Pliny (Natural History 8, on mares near Lisbon and the Tagus conceiving from the west wind, their offspring swift but living only three years) and Solinus (repeating the same, and adding a similar report about Cappadocian mares).
claims: Since God's established omnipotence (creation, annihilation, universal miracle-working) already exceeds what virginal conception would require, and since natural history itself reports (via Virgil, Pliny, and Solinus) documented cases of female animals conceiving without a male through purely natural causes (wind), the philosophical objection to virginal conception collapses.
concepts: divine omnipotence applied to virginal conception
natural-historical precedent of wind-conceived mares (Virgil, Pliny, Solinus)

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10371.summary: Adds a further natural-historical precedent from Aristotle (History of Animals V) that female partridges standing facing the wind become pregnant by males at a distance, sometimes merely by call, or by scent when flying overhead — a threefold manner of conception without physical union (by wind, voice, and scent) — corroborated briefly by Solinus on partridges of a certain region of Europe conceiving from scent alone when the wind blows from the males. Concludes that if females of other species can, by a power of nature alone, conceive without a male, there is no reason a pure virgin of the human species could not conceive without a man by a divine power that incomparably exceeds all natural created powers — especially given the clear testimonies already cited in Corollarium 32 and much similar evidence — and reads the heavens themselves as proclaiming this, noting the celestial upheaval (an especially notable planetary conjunction) shortly before Christ's coming, and asking rhetorically why else God, who unrolls the heavens like a scroll on which nothing is written in vain (per the philosophers), would have inscribed there the image and constellation of a virgin nursing a child, if not to signify precisely this.
claims: Aristotle's and Solinus's accounts of partridges conceiving without physical mating (by wind, call, or scent) extend the natural-historical case that virginal conception in a human, effected by incomparably greater divine power, is not against reason.
The zodiacal constellation Virgo, depicted nursing a child, is read as a providentially placed celestial sign specifically pointing to the virgin birth of Christ.
concepts: Aristotle on partridges conceiving without mating
the constellation Virgo as a providential sign
argument from a fortiori natural analogy to divine power

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10411.summary: Develops the astrological sign further via Albumasar (following ancient Chaldean doctrine), who describes the decan of Virgo as depicting a beautiful, chaste maiden with long hair, holding two ears of grain, seated on an adorned throne, nursing a child called by some peoples 'Jesus,' with a man seated beside her — asking what else this could signify but a perpetually virgin woman bearing and nursing a heavenly child, since an ordinary woman conceiving after losing virginity in the normal course of nature would present nothing remarkable or sign-worthy, and would not fittingly be called 'the sign of the virgin' at all, but rather 'the sign of the woman' — appealing to Isaiah's prophecy ('the Lord himself will give you a sign: behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son... Immanuel') as making no sense as a genuine 'sign' unless it involved something beyond nature's ordinary course, and identifying the man seated beside the depicted virgin as fittingly representing her spouse, whom (per the Sibylline prophecy discussed in Corollarium 32) she took for honest reasons while remaining forever a virgin.
claims: The pagan astrological tradition's decan-image of Virgo (a perpetual virgin nursing a divine child, with a male companion) is read as corroborating, independently of Scripture, the sign Isaiah describes — since only a virginal, not an ordinary, conception would constitute a genuine 'sign' worthy of the name.
concepts: Isaiah's virgin-birth prophecy as requiring a genuine sign

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10470.summary: Finds further significance in Virgo being the sixth zodiacal sign, a 'perfect number' per Boethius (Arithmetic I), fittingly signifying that its referent would come in the sixth, perfect and full, age of the world; notes that as this age approached, a great and singularly glorious conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter occurred at the start of Aries, with a change of triplicity from watery to fiery, some six years and a few days/hours before Christ's coming (verifiable by recalculating the planetary motions, or more easily via a recently made table of such conjunctions); notes Mercury, lord of Virgo (the ascending sign at that time), governed this conjunction, all together clearly signifying the coming birth of a heavenly child from a virgin — the greatest of prophets, who would deliver a new law; adds that 'Mercury' is interpreted as 'the illuminating one who meets/encounters a sign,' fittingly his own sign of Virgo above all, given his many dignities there as astrologers attest.
claims: The astrological significance of Virgo as the sixth (perfect) sign, combined with a great Saturn-Jupiter conjunction ruled by Mercury (lord of Virgo) shortly before Christ's birth, is read as further corroborating astronomical/astrological evidence for Christ's coming as a virgin-born, law-giving prophet.
concepts: Virgo as the sixth, 'perfect number' sign (Boethius)
the great Saturn-Jupiter conjunction before Christ's birth

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10501.summary: Adds that Mercury is also interpreted as 'speech' or 'the one running in the middle,' asking what figure could be more fitting for this than the Word of God, the middle person, Mediator between God and men.
claims: Mercury's etymological association with 'speech' and 'the middle/mediating runner' is read as a fitting astrological figure for Christ as the Word and Mediator.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10508.summary: Offers the poem De Vetula (attributed to Ovid, cited either as an authority or simply for its pleasing verse) as a further witness, quoting its account (Book 3) of this same great Saturn-Jupiter conjunction, said to have occurred in the twelfth year of Augustus's reign, twenty-four years into the new order (per the poem's chronology), signifying that six years later a prophet would be born of a virgin without male union, under the strong influence of Mercury (whose house, exaltation, triplicity, and terms all fall in Virgo) — describing the same imagery of a chaste, dignified, long-haired virgin nursing a child called 'Jesus' by certain nations, drawn from ancient Indian, Chaldean, and Babylonian astrological texts, occurring at the moment of the Saturn-Jupiter conjunction near the point of Aries where the greatest such conjunctions occur, dated within the poem to a specific year of the Greek calendar.
claims: The pseudo-Ovidian poem De Vetula independently corroborates, in poetic form, the same astrological account (Saturn-Jupiter conjunction, Mercury's rulership, the Virgo decan imagery of a virgin nursing 'Jesus') already presented as signifying Christ's virgin birth.
concepts: corroboration of the Virgo/Saturn-Jupiter conjunction narrative

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10591.summary: Quotes the poem's dating (309 years and 9 months of the Greek calendar, plus nearly eighteen days) for this conjunction, calling blessed whoever could grasp its full significance, and much more on the excellence of this prophet, his sect, and his law; comments it is unsurprising that God, about to be born humanly, willed (as with any human birth, but here through certain blessed portents and glorious testimonies visible from heaven to all) to signal so great and admirable an effect, universally salutary, with a correspondingly great and admirable sign — just as a miraculous star signaled Christ's miraculous nativity, per the earlier discussion in Corollarium 32.
claims: The astrological conjunction's precise dating in the pseudo-Ovidian poem is presented as corroborating detail for the claim that God signaled Christ's coming through celestial signs, on the pattern of the Star of Bethlehem.
concepts: precise astrological dating of the sign
parallel to the Star of Bethlehem

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10607.summary: Clarifies the causal order to forestall astrological determinism: the constellation or conjunction preceding Christ was not the cause of his virgin birth or law-giving but merely a sign of it, and it was not the case that the Lord of stars and times was subject to them, but rather they to him — since (per Supposition 1, Part 8, and the philosophers themselves) all celestial bodies, together and individually, inviolably keep their divinely appointed stations and serve God's will in everything. Adds that it should not trouble anyone that the Virgo constellation is described one way by the Chaldeans (as previously recounted) and differently by the Indians and others, since celestial images are described variously by different peoples depending on which stars they include or exclude, or how they group them differently, as their own books on celestial images plainly show.
claims: The astrological sign preceding Christ was merely a sign, not a cause, of his birth — the stars serve God's will rather than determining it — and variant ethnic descriptions of the Virgo constellation do not undermine the argument, since such variation in star-grouping conventions is normal and expected.
concepts: variant cultural conventions in celestial imagery

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10630.summary: Cites Albumasar's own acknowledgment that sages of different regions differed in how they depicted these celestial images, though the Babylonians, Persians, and Egyptians agreed on the Virgo description already given, while the Indians described her somewhat differently (with a woolen cloth and old garments, standing erect among ruins, wishing to return to her ancestral home), and Ptolemy's Almagest describes her standing and winged, with proportions Ptolemy himself says differ from the earlier tradition, though the author argues this discrepancy is not so troubling given a seated, child-nursing posture is not indecorous, and reasons that the concordant testimony of the many Babylonian/Persian/Egyptian sages is more trustworthy than Ptolemy's lone dissenting account, especially since Ptolemy seems not to have known their figure at all. Announces a digression to briefly discuss the inventors, authorities, and teachers of astrology and astronomy, to make these astrological claims more credible.
claims: The concordant testimony of multiple ancient astrological traditions on the Virgo image is more credible than Ptolemy's lone, differing account, and the author will next establish the venerable pedigree of astrology's founders to bolster the credibility of these astrological arguments.
concepts: variant descriptions of Virgo across traditions (Babylonian/Persian/Egyptian vs. Indian vs. Ptolemy)
argument from concordant multiple testimony over a lone dissenter

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10682.summary: Begins the digression on astrology's venerable pedigree: the sons of Seth, along with Enoch, Noah, Abraham, and Solomon, excelled greatly in these arts, per Josephus (Jewish Antiquities I), who reports that Seth, upon reaching an age of moral discernment, pursued virtue, and being an outstanding man, left behind sons who imitated him, all of whom, being good, lived most happily in the same land without disturbance, with nothing cruel befalling them to the end of their lives.
claims: Josephus is cited as establishing Seth and his virtuous line as the founding fathers of the astrological/astronomical tradition.
concepts: Seth's line as founders of astrology (Josephus)

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10702.summary: Continues via Josephus that Seth's line first discovered the discipline and ordering of celestial matters, and to preserve this knowledge from being lost — since Adam had foretold a coming double destruction of all things, one by fire and one by a great flood of waters — they built two pillars, one of brick and one of stone, both inscribed with their findings, so that if the brick one were destroyed by the flood, the stone one would survive to preserve the writings for humanity, and (Josephus adds) the stone pillar persists in Syria to this day. Cites the Secret of Secrets (attributed to Aristotle) that God ordained means for tempering the bodily humors and preserving health and much else, and revealed these to holy prophets and chosen servants filled with the spirit of divine wisdom, from whom the philosophical traditions of the Indians, Persians, Greeks, and Latins in turn drew their principles and secrets, containing nothing false, since approved by the wise.
claims: Josephus's account of the twin inscribed pillars (surviving the prophesied flood) and the Secret of Secrets' claim of divinely revealed wisdom to ancient prophets together trace all subsequent philosophical/scientific tradition (Indian, Persian, Greek, Latin) back to a divinely sourced, holy origin.
concepts: the twin pillars of Seth's line (Josephus)
the Secret of Secrets on divinely revealed wisdom

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10737.summary: Cites the Secret of Secrets further (addressed to Alexander) on a fabled, priceless universal medicine called 'the treasure of philosophers,' whose true inventor is uncertain — some attributing it to Adam, others to Aesculapius and Hermogenes the physician, and various named Hebrew and other philosophers (eight in total) to whom the hidden secrets of the sciences were entrusted.
claims: The Secret of Secrets attributes the invention of a legendary universal medicine/'treasure of philosophers' variously to Adam or to a group of eight named ancient sages, without settling which.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10750.summary: Continues: these eight sages investigated and disputed supernatural matters (the Full, the Void, the Finite, the Infinite) and jointly compiled this medicine into eight parts; some attribute its secret to Enoch by vision, identifying Enoch with the great Hermes/Hermogenes whom the Greeks praise and credit with all secret and celestial knowledge, citing a prologue to the Hermetic book on the World and Heaven naming three ancient philosophers called Hermes: Enoch (the first Hermes), Noah (also called Hermes), and the 'triple Hermes' Mercury Trismegistus (king, philosopher, and prophet), who ruled Egypt justly after the Flood, excelled in the liberal and mechanical arts, and pioneered astronomy, writing several foundational astronomical/astrological texts. Adds Josephus (Jewish Antiquities I) on Noah and the other ancient patriarchs living extraordinarily long lives (needed to complete the 'Great Year' cycle of 600 years) as a divine reward for their piety and their continual pursuit of astrology and geometry, and a report (from a treatise on Aristotle's death) that before Noah, humanity mistakenly believed the sun, moon, and stars moved themselves and were therefore primary movers and gods, worshipping them as such via various idols.
claims: A layered tradition (the Hermetic prologue, Josephus, and a treatise on Aristotle's death) identifies Enoch and Noah as successive 'Hermes' figures and founders of astrology/astronomy, with pre-Noah humanity's idolatrous star-worship (stemming from the mistaken belief that celestial bodies moved themselves) as the backdrop against which true astronomical knowledge later corrected.
concepts: the three Hermes tradition (Enoch, Noah, Hermes Trismegistus)
the patriarchs' long lives tied to the 'Great Year'

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10805.summary: Credits Noah as the first to recognize the Creator of the spheres as the true first principle of all motion, possessing the highest degree of knowledge in these matters; cites Albumasar (Introductorium Maius V) that ancient histories record Noah as the first prophet to resettle Babylonia after the Flood and found the Babylonians/Chaldeans, all of whom became wise in astronomy and judicial astrology, drawing students from every region, with some crediting Noah's son Shem as having first taught them this science — testimony the author judges especially credible since Albumasar was himself, before becoming an astronomer, a professional chronicler/historian (per the astronomer Haly's testimony on Ptolemy's Quadripartitum), and corroborated by the pseudo-Ovidian De Vetula crediting 'the venerable prophet Noah' as having written these things first and his firstborn son Shem as having taught them.
claims: Albumasar (himself credited as a careful historian) and the corroborating De Vetula both attribute the founding of Babylonian/Chaldean astronomical science to Noah and his son Shem, strengthening the pedigree the author is constructing for astrology's divine and patriarchal origin.
concepts: Noah as first recognizer of the Creator of the spheres

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10846.summary: Continues via the treatise on Aristotle's death that after Noah came Abraham, wisest of all and attaining the highest degree of prophecy, who recognized that sun, moon, and all stars had a first mover and therefore did not follow his father's and ancestors' idolatrous ways; cites Josephus (Jewish Antiquities I) describing Abraham as exceptionally intelligent and wise, reasoning from the perceived order and behavior of earth, sea, sun, and moon to conclude and proclaim that one Creator God governs all things by his power, to which alone honor and thanksgiving are due, while other apparent goods are merely bestowed by that same providence rather than self-subsisting — and cites the Chaldean historians Berossus and Hecataeus (per Josephus), who mention (without naming) 'a certain just and great man learned in celestial matters' arising ten generations after the Flood among the Chaldeans, with Hecataeus even devoting a whole book to him, and crediting this figure with transmitting arithmetic and astrology to the Egyptians, who had been ignorant of them before Abraham's arrival, tracing the line of transmission from the Chaldeans to Egypt and then to the Greeks.
claims: Abraham is presented (via Josephus and the pagan Chaldean historians Berossus and Hecataeus) as both the first to reason his way to monotheism from celestial order and the historical conduit who transmitted astronomical/mathematical knowledge from the Chaldeans to Egypt and thence to Greece.
concepts: Berossus and Hecataeus on an unnamed wise Chaldean (identified with Abraham)
transmission of science: Chaldea to Egypt to Greece

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10898.summary: Concludes the pedigree with Solomon, divinely inspired (per 1 Kings 3 and 2 Chronicles 1) with unmatched wisdom, understanding, and knowledge exceeding all before or after him, surpassing even the proverbially wise Egyptians and easterners (per 1 Kings 3 and Josephus, Jewish Antiquities VIII), who composed 4,005 books touching on every branch of nature and philosophy. Concludes that later philosophers, informed by the most learned doctrines of these divinely illuminated patriarchs, wrote their famous scientific works by building on (and adding a few not-entirely-foreign elements to) these original, divinely-sourced fountains, exactly as Aristotle himself is said to have acknowledged — and suggests that some proud sophist philosophers may have destroyed or retitled the patriarchs' original books to steal credit for their discoveries, or that these were simply lost to time, noting that even the biblical prophecy of Enoch (seventh from Adam) is solemnly cited in Scripture (Jude) though its written text no longer survives.
claims: Solomon is the culminating figure in a chain of divinely-inspired patriarchs (Seth, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Solomon) whose lost or plagiarized original writings are claimed as the ultimate, divinely-sourced fountainhead of all subsequent pagan philosophy and science, including astrology.
concepts: loss/plagiarism of the patriarchs' original writings
Enoch's prophecy cited in Jude despite its text being lost

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10641.summary: States the rubric of Corollarium 36: against Epicureans and Sadducees who say there is no spirit and irrationally deny the immortality of the rational soul, and against Averroes's claim that all humans share a single rational soul.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10650.summary: Attacks the Epicureans and Sadducees for madly denying any incorporeal spirit and irrationally denying the rational soul's immortality, and Averroes for asserting all humans share a single rational soul; identifies these as heirs of ancient materialists who admitted only matter and sensible things, denying intellect or reducing it to a corporeal form and thus corruptible, and who accordingly placed the highest good in bodily pleasure, wallowing in it 'like a pig in mud' — noting Epicurus was nicknamed 'the pig' by philosophers and his followers 'piglets.' Explains the Sadducees (per Josephus, on the four Jewish philosophical schools: Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes, and the 'Fourth Philosophy'/Zealots) as holding that souls are mortal and perish with the body. Refutes the denial of incorporeal spirit by appeal to Parts 8 and 10 (God himself being proven an incorporeal spirit) and argues that since God, as an omnipotent spirit with a universally efficacious will (Parts 5, 8), can (per Parts 33-34) create beings like himself (disembodied spirits called angels) as well as embodied rational souls, both immortal, there is no reason to deny this — especially since it is more fitting to divine generosity and goodness, and is a matter of near-universal consensus across philosophies, faiths, and peoples, buttressed by rational arguments and countered only by the flimsiest shadow of contrary reasoning (as shown regarding Parts 3 and 33), and corroborated even by the (evil) arts of magic, which themselves presuppose the existence of spirits (as touched on in Parts 21 and 32).
claims: The Epicurean/Sadducee denial of incorporeal spirit and of the soul's immortality, and Averroes's monopsychism, are refuted by the prior demonstration of God as an incorporeal spirit and of God's power to create both angels and immortal rational souls, a conclusion further supported by near-universal human consensus and even the practice (if not the content) of magic.
concepts: Sadducee denial of the soul's immortality (Josephus)
argument from universal consensus for spirits' existence
magic as indirect evidence of spirits

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e10724.summary: Dismisses Averroes's theory of a single shared rational soul for all humans as empty, false, foolish, and fabricated, lacking any plausibility or probability, and therefore not deserving careful refutation — though offering a rebuttal so it cannot claim to have gone entirely unanswered. Argues God's evident practice of giving even lesser, imperfect species (which do not know, love, or worship him) their own individual souls/forms makes it inexplicable that he would give humanity — far nobler, and capable of knowing, loving, and worshipping him — only a single shared soul among them all; there is no reason for such an asymmetry between humans and plants, other animals, or celestial bodies. Argues further from Part 31 that God fully and abundantly rewards each of his worshippers, which manifestly does not happen equally to all in this present life, so it must happen in the future, and not equally to worshippers and despisers, nor equally among worshippers themselves (since they do not merit equally) — so individual humans must have individual souls to be rewarded or punished after death according to their own deserts. Turns this back on Averroes himself, citing his own commentary on Aristotle's Ethics I (on the truly good and wise man bearing misfortune becomingly, discussing Job — 'to whom is there salvation?'): asking why anyone would pray for the salvation of the deceased Job unless hoping that his soul, and the souls of virtuous individuals, are saved after death according to their own merits — which presupposes exactly the individual immortal souls Averroes's own theory denies.
claims: Averroes's monopsychism (a single shared intellect for all humanity) is dismissed as implausible; God's demonstrated practice of individuating lesser species and his promised individualized reward/punishment (Part 31) both require individual human souls.
Averroes's own commentary on Aristotle's Ethics (discussing prayer for Job's salvation) is turned against his own monopsychism, since such prayer presupposes individual souls meriting individually.
concepts: argument from Averroes's own commentary on Job

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e11076.summary: The paragraph argues that if a single rational soul were shared by all humans, whatever reward or punishment one person receives in the present life would necessarily be received by all others simultaneously, since it is lodged in the soul rather than the body; quotes Aristotle's Ethics on felicity as a divine gift fitting for the virtuous individually, and Averroes' own commentary praising God as giver of wisdom and felicity, to press the absurdity that all would be simultaneously blessed and wretched.
claims: If all humans share one rational soul, reward and punishment received by one would necessarily be shared by all.
This consequence contradicts the individualized felicity Aristotle and Averroes themselves describe.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e11113.summary: Drawing on the definition of nature as a principle of motion proper to its subject, the paragraph argues that since the rational soul is a form of finite power, one soul could not simultaneously move an unlimited number of human bodies with equal facility, just as no single finite celestial mover could move infinitely many heavenly bodies equally and at once.
claims: A finite soul/form has finite motive power and cannot move infinitely many bodies simultaneously.
The analogy to celestial movers moving finitely many spheres supports individual souls for individual bodies.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e11159.summary: Extends the prior argument: on Averroes' view, adding one more star to a sphere would tax its single mover, yet experience shows no such fatigue; the same reasoning is then applied to the soul's proper operations (understanding, willing, remembering, syllogizing), arguing a single finite soul cannot simultaneously and perfectly perform such varied and even contrary acts for countless individuals, since one operation impedes or expels another.
claims: A single finite soul cannot perform indefinitely many diverse and contrary intellectual operations simultaneously and perfectly.
One operation of the soul naturally impedes or displaces another, which is incompatible with a single shared intellect serving all humanity.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e11188.summary: Citing Avicenna and Algazel against the unicity thesis, the paragraph argues that if all humans shared the same soul, they would all share the same knowledge, so that nothing known by one could be unknown to another — contrary to plain experience that individuals differ in what they know, just as one cannot see a light in another's house through one's own eye unless the light is in one's own faculty.
claims: If the intellect were numerically one for all humans, all would necessarily share identical knowledge.
Ordinary experience of differing individual knowledge refutes the unicity of the intellect.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e11227.summary: Marshals further Aristotelian authority (Posterior Analytics, De Anima) on the intellect as initially in potency, without any habits actually present, like a tablet on which nothing is yet written, arguing this describes each individual's incremental acquisition of knowledge and is incompatible with Averroes' claim that the material intellect eternally and actually contains all intelligibles.
claims: Aristotle describes the intellect as beginning wholly in potency, like an unwritten tablet.
This description is incompatible with a single eternally fully-actualized shared intellect.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e11297.summary: Turning directly on Averroes, the paragraph accuses him of twisting his own earlier gloss on Aristotle's tablet analogy and of self-contradiction, likening him to a disobedient son who calls his father (Aristotle) a liar, and asks by what authority he presumes to contradict so great a philosopher when his own words convict him of inconsistency.
claims: Averroes' interpretation of the tablet analogy contradicts his own earlier exposition of the same text.
Averroes' unicity thesis is inconsistent with the deference he elsewhere shows to Aristotle's authority.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e11340.summary: Piles up further citations from Averroes' own commentaries on De Anima III in which he affirms, following Aristotle, that the possible intellect has no actual nature of its own prior to understanding and is purely receptive/potential, and presses the question why, given these admissions, Averroes elsewhere asserts the very opposite view that intelligibles are perpetually and actually inscribed in it.
claims: Averroes' own commentary repeatedly affirms the possible intellect is purely potential before act, following Aristotle.
This repeated affirmation directly conflicts with Averroes' unicity doctrine of an eternally, actually informed shared intellect.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e11475.summary: Raises a dilemma about the function of the agent intellect under Averroes' theory: if the possible intellect already eternally and actually possesses all species, the agent intellect would have nothing left to abstract or transfer from phantasm to immateriality, making its posited office of actualizing potential understanding pointless and unexplained in the individual.
claims: If the possible intellect is already fully and eternally actual, the agent intellect's abstractive function becomes superfluous.
Averroes cannot coherently explain what the agent intellect contributes to a given individual under the unicity thesis.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e11534.summary: Argues from the potential infinity of distinct thoughts, propositions, and conclusions any human intellect actually forms (e.g. concerning future eclipses) that a single shared intellect used by infinitely many humans across eternal time would have to actually contain infinitely many distinct and even contrary cognitions simultaneously — an impossibility, since actual infinite multitudes cannot exist and distinct temporally-indexed acts of assent cannot be identical.
claims: The intellect can form indefinitely many distinct particular conclusions, which cannot all be actually and simultaneously identical in a single shared subject.
Positing one eternal intellect used by all humans under an eternal world entails an impossible actual infinite of simultaneous distinct cognitions.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e11621.summary: Anticipates and rejects an Averroist reply (voiced through an imagined 'vicar' of Averroes) that the one intellect could understand many distinct particulars through the same species and the same act without real diversity, arguing instead that an agent acting through one and the same power, species, and act without any added diversity cannot distinguish and know diverse particulars distinctly, since a single undifferentiated natural cause produces a single determinate effect.
claims: A single power operating through an identical act and species cannot distinctly cognize genuinely diverse particulars.
Diversity of effects in natural (non-free) causation requires some corresponding diversity in agent or patient.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e11741.summary: Argues that contrary and mutually exclusive states — knowledge and ignorance, love and hatred, virtue and vice, supreme beatitude and supreme misery — cannot all exist actually and completely at once in one and the same indivisible soul and faculty regarding the same object, since experience and philosophical consensus hold that privative and contrary states arise successively, not simultaneously, in the same subject capable of both.
claims: Contrary and privatively opposed states cannot coexist actually and completely in the same indivisible subject with respect to the same object.
A single shared soul would have to sustain exactly such simultaneous contrarieties, which is impossible.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e11763.summary: Presses Averroes rhetorically that, on his own thesis, every error, heresy, vice, and spiritual misery of every human would exist actually and inseparably within his own single shared soul, then anticipates and rejects his likely reply that differing imaginative phantasms in different individuals explain differing knowledge — countering that this fictitious response cannot avoid the shared identity of habitual knowledge in an intellect that remains numerically one for all.
claims: On the unicity thesis, all human errors and virtues alike would inseparably belong to Averroes' own single soul.
Appeal to differing phantasms cannot rescue the unicity thesis from entailing shared habitual knowledge for all.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e11827.summary: Argues by analogy to fully-informed sense faculties — which, once perfectly impressed with the species of an object, can continue to cognize that object without further motion from it or anything else — that a comparably perfected intellect should likewise be able to operate on its retained intelligible content without further extrinsic input, citing common experience of afterimages described in Alhacen's optics.
claims: A sense faculty fully informed by a species can continue to sense without further extrinsic motion, as afterimage phenomena show.
By analogy, a fully informed intellect should be able to operate on retained intelligible content without continual extrinsic input from phantasms.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e11864.summary: Reinforces the prior analogy with a thought experiment: if God omnipotently preserved in the eye the species received from an object even after the object and every intervening species in the medium were destroyed, vision would still occur as before, since object and medium are required only to generate or conserve the species, not for the act of seeing itself; the same, it is argued, should hold for the intellect once fully informed.
claims: Object and medium are causally required only to generate or conserve a sensible species, not for the resulting act of vision itself.
By parity of reasoning, the intellect once fully actuated should not need continual extrinsic phantasms to operate.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e11890.summary: Quotes Avicenna's De Anima on how the animal (imaginative) powers assist the rational soul in the initial acquisition of intelligible principles, but once the soul has acquired them it returns to operating through itself alone, and thereafter needs the imaginative virtues only occasionally; indeed the sensitive and imaginative powers can come to hinder the soul's own perfected operation, much as a mount is later abandoned once its purpose of transport is served.
claims: The imaginative powers assist the rational soul only in the initial acquisition of intelligible principles.
Once perfected, the soul operates through itself and can even be hindered by the bodily powers that once assisted it.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e11929.summary: Presses the point rhetorically: every cognitive power knows properly through its own intrinsic, immanent act rather than through something extrinsic, so a well-disposed layman possessing the clearest actual scientific knowledge in his soul ought to be able to use and perceive it at will, just as he could perceive a light in his own house by his own bodily eye if his eye were properly proportioned to it.
