claims: Cognitive powers know through their own intrinsic acts, not through something extrinsic to them.
A soul actually possessing clear scientific knowledge should be able to access it at will, which tells against Averroes' account of why some cannot.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e11601.summary: Anticipates Averroes' fallback position, quoting his commentary at length: that the possible intellect (rational soul) is not man's essential substantial form but a separate celestial intelligence conjoined to man only through the act of understanding, mediated by imagined intentions/phantasms which serve as its quasi-material link to the individual; Averroes distinguishes senses in which a boy is 'potentially intelligent' and denies the material intellect is numbered per individual, restricting individuation instead to the imaginative forms in each person.
claims: Averroes holds the possible intellect is not the substantial form of the individual human but a separate, unified intelligence conjoined to humans via phantasms.
On this view individuation among humans belongs to the imaginative powers, not to the intellect itself.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12066.summary: Draws out an absurd consequence of Averroes' position: if man is not a rational animal until the separate material intellect is actually conjoined to him, then infants would not be human beings or rational animals prior to that conjunction, and would have to be transmuted from one species (irrational, bestial) into another (rational, human) upon conjunction — and by parity, adult humans could likewise be 'transmuted' out of rationality.
claims: On Averroes' view, infants prior to intellectual conjunction would not count as rational animals or humans.
This entails an absurd interspecific transmutation of infants into humanity, and potentially back out of it.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12083.summary: Asks by what means the separate intellect is conjoined to this particular man, noting Averroes locates it in the intellect's own operation, which would make the intellect's activity the efficient cause of, and thus naturally prior to, the conjunction — yet possessing a power is naturally prior to exercising it, as having sight precedes seeing; further presses where the separate intelligence is located (heaven, lunar sphere, or in humans) and raises difficulties about a finite immaterial substance's presence filling an unlimited number of distant human bodies.
claims: Making the intellect's own operation the cause of its conjunction with a man reverses the natural priority of power to act.
Locating a single finite separate intelligence so as to be present to indefinitely many, spatially distant humans is incoherent.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12131.summary: Argues by proportional analogy that just as the vegetative soul stands to the vegetable and the sensitive soul to the sensible thing, so the rational soul stands to the rational animal; since the former two are acknowledged substantial forms essentially actuating, constituting, and perfecting their subjects (per Aristotle's De Anima II), the rational soul must likewise be man's essential substantial form.
claims: The vegetative and sensitive souls are essential substantial forms of their respective living subjects.
By proportional analogy, the rational soul must likewise be the essential substantial form of the rational animal.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12149.summary: Cites Aristotle's universal definition of soul in De Anima II as the substantial form (species) of a natural organic body having life potentially, together with Averroes' own commentary explaining how form differs from accident, and argues this definition applies to every kind of soul universally including the rational; rejects Averroes' evasive reading of Aristotle's conditional 'si' ('if') as merely hypothetical rather than a genuine universal claim.
claims: Aristotle's definition of soul as substantial form of an organic body is stated to hold universally, including for the rational soul.
Averroes' attempt to read this universal definition as merely hypothetical misreads Aristotle's conditional usage.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12253.summary: Invoking Aristotle's Physics II definition of nature as an intrinsic principle of motion and rest, argues that what moves a man progressively (walking, speaking, eating) must be his essential form, i.e., the rational soul acting through rational will — not some other, bestial soul, since brutes are moved of necessity, not freely; notes that two people equally disposed in all bodily and sensitive powers can nonetheless differ in free rational choice, which shows the moving principle must be an individually distinct rational will/soul, not a shared external cause.
claims: Voluntary human motion must proceed from the individual's own essential form, the rational soul acting through will.
Observed differences in free choice between bodily-equal individuals prove that rational souls/wills are individually distinct, not shared.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12308.summary: Argues that the unicity thesis contradicts Aristotle's own explicit teaching that, unlike other souls, the rational soul is not educed from the potency of matter but comes from without (ab extrinseco) and does not temporally precede the individual but eternally accompanies/succeeds it; marshals passages from De Anima, De Generatione Animalium, and Metaphysics XII, plus the pseudo-Aristotelian tradition on the soul's creation by God and its individual post-mortem reward or punishment.
claims: Aristotle teaches the rational soul, unlike other souls, comes from without and is not educed from matter's potency.
Aristotelian and pseudo-Aristotelian sources affirm individual creation and individual post-mortem reward or punishment of souls, contrary to Averroes' unicity.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12365.summary: Notes that Avicenna and Algazel follow this same Aristotelian teaching, holding that rational souls are multiplied according to the multitude of human bodies, not corporeally impressed in them nor preceding them temporally but created within them, and that the soul survives the body eternally to be rewarded or punished according to merit; concludes that essentially all wise philosophers, prophets, laws, and peoples by natural instinct concur against Averroes' singular, deviant teaching.
claims: Avicenna and Algazel affirm a multiplicity of individually created rational souls corresponding to human bodies.
A broad consensus of philosophers, prophets, and peoples condemns the unicity of the intellect as an isolated aberration.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12392.summary: Returning to the chapter's founding suppositions, concludes that God, being omnipotent and most generous, both could and (more fittingly) did give individual rational souls to individual humans, just as he gave individual irrational souls or forms to individual animals and other natural things; judges this position far better attested, more fitting, and more universally favored than Averroes', which is judged widely despised and only weakly supported.
claims: It is fitting for an omnipotent, generous God to give each human an individual rational soul, as with other natural forms.
The doctrine of individual souls is overwhelmingly favored and well-supported compared to Averroes' unicity thesis.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12412.summary: Addresses what the author regards as Averroes' strongest argument — that individual rational souls would have to be created from nothing, which philosophers deny is possible — noting that Plato and the Platonists would avoid the consequence via the transmigration of souls between bodies, but affirming instead that he accepts both the argument and its consequence, namely creation ex nihilo, as already demonstrated in earlier parts of the work.
claims: Denying individual creation from nothing forces either transmigration of souls or acceptance of creation ex nihilo.
Creation of rational souls ex nihilo is accepted as already established by the work's earlier arguments.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12430.summary: Considers and rejects the objection that separated souls after death would be wholly idle since they move no body, as is argued of celestial intelligences; responds that the soul's most essential and proper activity is not moving a body but understanding, loving, and contemplating, and above all knowing and loving God and enjoying him beatifically — suggesting that intelligences with fewer external, body-directed operations are in fact more, not less, blessed, being less distracted from divine contemplation.
claims: The soul's proper and most perfect activity is intellectual and affective (understanding, loving, contemplating God), not moving a body.
Freedom from body-directed operations is compatible with, and even conducive to, greater beatitude.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12463.summary: Answers the objection that numerical plurality within a single species is impossible among intelligences and so should likewise be impossible among rational souls, by denying the parity: since God could annihilate any intelligence and create another exactly alike in species and degree, or create additional ones alongside an existing one, plurality of individuals within one species is possible for intelligences too, undercutting the objection's force against a plurality of souls.
claims: Numerical plurality within a single species is not in principle impossible even for intelligences, since God could create several alike in species.
The objection against a plurality of individual rational souls based on denying such plurality to intelligences therefore fails.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12485.summary: Dismisses a further Averroist quibble — that if the material intellect were individuated per person, it would have to be a body or a corporeally extended power, like other souls — as an inconsistent, artless, and unconvincing inference that no competent thinker should find compelling, given all that has already been shown; closes the corollarium by citing Aristotle's warning against anxiously engaging every contrary opinion, reserving serious response only for those with some semblance of reason.
claims: The objection that an individuated intellect must be corporeally extended does not follow from anything established and is unconvincing.
Not every contrary opinion merits detailed refutation, only those with some apparent rational basis.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12154.summary: Rubric announcing Corollarium 37: against philosophers who deny that the motion of the heavens and the generation of humans can cease, that the dead can rise with their bodies, that the good can ascend to the heavens and the wicked descend to hell, and that both can then live forever.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12163.summary: Sets out the target errors — Aristotle and Averroes holding celestial motion and human generation necessarily eternal, and Epicureans and others denying bodily resurrection and post-mortem reward, quoting Pliny's naturalistic limits on divine power and Augustine's remark that bodily resurrection, unlike the soul's immortality, is uniquely resisted by pagan philosophers — then argues from the prior suppositions that God, being omnipotent with a universally efficacious will, and having already halted the sun and reversed its course, can equally halt celestial motion and human generation, since neither entails any contradiction.
claims: Denying that God can stop celestial motion or human generation is inconsistent with the omnipotence and efficacious will already established.
Prior scriptural precedents of God stopping or reversing the sun show his power over celestial motion is not merely theoretical.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12620.summary: Argues briefly that since creation and re-creation of things, even of the whole world, is possible (as shown in earlier parts), and since a virgin's conceiving and bearing a son is possible, the resurrection of dead humans and bodies should likewise be demonstrable as possible by analogous reasoning.
claims: The possibility of creation, re-creation, and the virgin birth supports the possibility of bodily resurrection by parity of reasoning.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12634.summary: Argues that God, whose infinite (not merely finite) power to restore the lost, repair the destroyed, and reform the deformed has already been shown, can raise the dead; rejects the objection that matter lacks the natural potency to 'return' from privation to a prior state (since privation cannot revert to habit), replying that this measures divine power by the limited standard of created agents, whereas God can create from nothing and can even re-create what has been annihilated, and that the privation-to-habit axiom is not itself certain, since many things once lost are in fact regained.
claims: God's power to restore and repair is properly infinite, not limited to the finite powers of created agents.
The philosophical axiom that privation cannot return to habit does not bind divine power and is not even certainly true in general.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12673.summary: Opens a long array of historical and literary testimonies to bodily transformation of humans into animals — Circe's transformation of Ulysses' companions and Diomedes' companions into birds in Ovid's Metamorphoses, corroborated by Boethius, Solinus, Papias, and Pliny — arguing these cannot be dismissed as mere poetic fiction since multiple independent authors attest them as historical, and noting also natural instances of one species arising from the corruption of another (bees from rotting calf-flesh, and similar generatio ex putri examples).
claims: Multiple independent ancient authors attest human-to-animal transformations as historical fact, not mere poetic invention.
Natural philosophy already accepts analogous transformations of one corrupted species into another.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12797.summary: Continues the catalogue of testimonies with reports of men and women periodically transformed into wolves in Ireland (Ulster) and among the Neuri (per Solinus), and contemporary rumors in England and France of men who by a bodily disposition periodically become wolves and act as such before reverting; cites Augustine's own report of women in Italy reputed to turn travelers into beasts of burden via drugged cheese, while their rational minds remained intact throughout.
claims: Widely reported and geographically diverse testimonies attest periodic human-to-wolf transformation.
Even where the body is transformed, the rational mind can remain intact, per Augustine's report.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12821.summary: Adds further corroborating anecdotes — William of Malmesbury's account of a performer magically made to appear as a donkey, and Apuleius' own first-person account in the Metamorphoses (Golden Ass) of being transformed into a donkey by magic and later restored — as further evidence that such transformations, however strange, are consistently reported across independent sources.
claims: Independent medieval and classical first-person and reported accounts corroborate the reality of magical bodily transformation.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12852.summary: Extends the argument to sex transformation, citing Ovid's Tiresias and, more importantly, Pliny's Natural History reporting several documented cases of women becoming men, along with Augustine's report of a girl transformed into a boy under Emperor Constantius, arguing these need not be dismissed as poetic fiction given Pliny's historiographical seriousness.
claims: Reports of sex transformation are attested not only in poetry (Ovid) but in the historical and naturalist tradition (Pliny, Augustine).

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e1287a.summary: Recounts at length the legendary story from the History of the Britons of King Uther Pendragon being magically transformed by Merlin into the likeness of Gorlois, Duke of Cornwall, in order to gain access to Gorlois' wife Igerna at Tintagel, with his companions Ulfin and Merlin likewise disguised, resulting in the conception of Arthur — offered as a further instance of a magical transformation of bodily appearance accepted in historical narrative.
claims: The legend of Uther, Merlin, and Igerna is cited as a further historical instance of magically effected bodily transformation.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12927.summary: Adds biblical instances of miraculous transformation — Moses' rod turned into a serpent, water into blood, dust into gnats, and especially Nebuchadnezzar's transformation described in Daniel, whose heart was changed from human to bestial and who lived and ate like a beast among animals for seven periods until his reason and form were restored — corroborated by Jerome's exegesis and Josephus, as scriptural precedent for real bodily and psychological transformation reversed by divine will.
claims: Scripture itself (Exodus, Daniel) records real instances of bodily/psychological transformation and later restoration by divine power.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12953.summary: Defends having recounted all these instances as found in ancient books without personal endorsement of their truth, then draws the intended inference: if such transmutation of human bodies and other things is possible even through some created power, however small and finite, as many unbelievers and philosophers themselves concede, then reformation of dead bodies to their prior form, or transformation to a better form — that is, the resurrection of the dead — must be possible through God's infinitely infinite omnipotence, than which none greater can exist or be conceived.
claims: If finite created powers can effect bodily transformation, God's infinite omnipotence can effect the reformation of dead bodies, i.e., resurrection.
The author reports these transformation stories as found in his sources without personally vouching for their truth.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12971.summary: Turns to reports (from Avicenna, Algazel, and others) that fascination/bewitchment by certain persons' gaze or speech can weaken, wither, or kill living things, citing Virgil's Eclogues on an evil eye harming lambs, and Pliny's, Solinus', and Isigonus' reports of peoples (in Scythia, Illyria, Sardinia) whose members possess double pupils and can kill by an angry glance; argues that if such a feeble creature's gaze or word can so harm the living, and if necromancy and magic arts (attested by both technical treatises and sacred books, and by common report and frequent experience, including the sorceries of Cyprian mentioned earlier) can accomplish so much through demonic or created power, then God's infinite omnipotence must be capable of incomparably more, including truly raising the dead.
claims: Reports of the evil eye and of effective magical/necromantic arts, however feeble the underlying created power, support an a fortiori argument for God's power to truly raise the dead.
If created and even demonic powers can produce such effects, infinite divine omnipotence must be capable of raising the dead.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e13048.summary: Concludes the corollarium: if God can halt the heavens and raise the dead, he can also lift the risen to the heavens to dwell with him there (a lesser feat, demonstrable the same way), and can likewise cast the risen wicked down with their bodies to hell, and can preserve the risen in that state of life for as long as he wills — all argued as lesser or equal in difficulty to what has already been shown possible.
claims: God's power to raise the dead extends to elevating the risen to heaven or casting the wicked to hell, and to sustaining them there indefinitely.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12672.summary: Rubric announcing Corollarium 38: against philosophers and heretics who deny that temporal merit can reasonably be rewarded with an everlasting reward, or that temporal sin can justly be punished with eternal punishment.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12679.summary: Argues by analogy that just as a human lord reasonably grants land in perpetual possession to a servant and his heirs for brief temporal service, God — supremely good, rich, and infinitely generous — should all the more fittingly reward his servants' temporal service similarly or more generously; adds that if God could freely grant an everlasting good to an ever-living angel or man with no prior merit at all, he could surely reward a genuinely meritorious (if temporally limited) service with an everlasting reward, especially since God already rewards beyond strict desert.
claims: By analogy with human feudal reward, God's supreme goodness and generosity make an everlasting reward for temporal merit fitting.
God's capacity to grant an everlasting good even without prior merit supports, a fortiori, granting it for genuine merit.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e13129.summary: Rejects the objection that the goodness inseparably consequent upon a good act is itself a sufficient reward, needing no further everlasting reward, by noting that all legitimate laws nonetheless establish further rewards for merit, and that a God who rewarded no further than this would be rewarding sparingly rather than beyond due desert (as already established) — concluding that if even a good and capable human lord will reward capable servants further, God, infinitely better and more powerful than any human, will do so all the more fittingly.
claims: The intrinsic goodness of a virtuous act is not itself the sufficient reward the objection claims, since legitimate laws provide for further rewards.
Rewarding merit only with its own intrinsic consequence would make God a sparing rather than generous rewarder, contrary to what has been shown.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e13152.summary: Turns to the symmetric case of punishment: since no one should knowingly sin for any amount of good gained or evil avoided, a proportionately great — even infinite in duration — punishment can justly be imposed for any knowing sin; draws an analogy to temporal law condemning offenders to perpetual imprisonment and loss of land/fief for their heirs forever, and argues that an offense knowingly committed against a greater person deserves proportionately greater punishment, so an offense against God, the incomparably greatest person, deserves incomparably greater (i.e. eternal) punishment; also argues the sinner cannot in fact make adequate satisfaction, since true satisfaction would require never having committed the sin, and rejects the excuse that inability to satisfy excuses the sinner, since by that logic every sinner would be excused merely by being unable, at the moment, not to sin.
claims: An offense against a greater person deserves proportionately greater punishment, so sin against the infinite God deserves infinite punishment.
Inability to make satisfaction does not excuse the sinner, since accepting that principle would excuse all sin as such.
concepts: proportionality of punishment to the offended party

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e13215.summary: Argues the sinner made himself a debtor and rendered himself unable to satisfy through his own unabolished fault, so remains liable, as a thief or robber unable to restore equal or greater goods must at least suffer punishment in the meantime, since punishment restores the honor of the offended party, provides some satisfaction, chastises the sin, restrains further sinning, and preserves justice (absent gracious pardon); concludes that culpable inability to satisfy never wholly excuses one from owing what one can, so a sinner against God must render whatever satisfaction is possible and bear whatever punishment can be borne, since a well-ordered legislator's polity should not treat the knowing sinner who contemns the law the same as the one who does not sin or does satisfy.
claims: Self-incurred, culpable inability to satisfy does not excuse the debt but obliges the offender to render what he can and to bear punishment.
Justice in a well-ordered polity requires distinguishing the unpunished sinner from the innocent or the one who has made satisfaction.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e13244.summary: Closes the corollarium by noting that legitimate polities establish both rewards for merit and punishments for offenders who cannot make satisfaction, then dismantles an anticipated escape: if the sinner's inability to satisfy God led to remission of the debt, that remission would be either necessary (in which case it reflects no real grace or generosity, since nothing is given that could not but be given) or free (in which case it could equally not be granted); and if inability excused the sinner from guilt, he would have to be considered innocent throughout, including at the moment of sinning, which is absurd, so he must instead remain guilty — and guilt of any duration carries with it the punishment shown earlier (in Part 31) to be its necessary and inseparable accompaniment, which is incompatible with unpunished, eternal admission to beatitude and the company of the blessed.
claims: Remission of debt owed for sin, whether construed as necessary or free, cannot coherently follow merely from the sinner's inability to satisfy.
A sinner who is not excused from guilt remains liable to the punishment inseparably annexed to guilt, which bars unpunished eternal admission to beatitude.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12876.summary: Rubric announcing Corollarium 39: against philosophers and heretics who deny a future resurrection of the dead to differentiated eternal bliss or misery, holding instead various errors — that any afterlife occurs immediately after death or after a cyclical 'Great Year' by transmigration into new animal or human bodies for a limited earthly span; that all the dead alike rise to eternal life and none to eternal punishment; that the blessed and damned both remain on earth rather than in heaven or hell; that risen bodies are not transformed or made immortal but remain as before; and that eternal felicity consists in accustomed carnal pleasures or in something other than God.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e12911.summary: Restates, almost verbatim, the errors named in the rubric — denial of resurrection, belief in immediate or cyclical transmigration, denial of differentiated eternal reward and punishment, denial of heaven/hell as distinct places, denial of bodily transformation, and belief that eternal felicity is carnal — as a call for the philosophers holding them to rise instead to the truer position.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e13370.summary: Identifies the Epicureans and Sadducees as denying any future resurrection, holding the rational soul mortal, and quotes Pliny's Natural History at length arguing on naturalistic grounds that death ends all sensation for body and soul alike and that belief in immortality, transformation, or an afterlife is mere self-flattering vanity; cites Josephus on the Sadducees' denial of reward and punishment for souls, and Dionysius (De Divinis Nominibus) on Simon's heretical denial of bodily resurrection as contrary to nature.
claims: Epicureans and Sadducees deny the soul's immortality and hence any future resurrection.
Pliny argues on naturalistic grounds that death is the utter and final end of sensation and existence.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e13419.summary: Distinguishes among those who do admit a future resurrection: some hold it occurs immediately after death through the soul's transmigration into other animal or human bodies, denying any other post-mortem reward or punishment; quotes at length Ovid's Metamorphoses XV, where Pythagoras (via Ovid) proclaims that souls never perish but pass ceaselessly between human and animal bodies, illustrating this with his own claimed former identity as Euphorbus in the Trojan War.
claims: Some deniers of true resurrection instead hold that souls transmigrate immediately after death into other bodies.
Ovid's Pythagoras speech (Metamorphoses XV) is cited as a poetic statement of the transmigration doctrine.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e13499.summary: Traces Ovid's transmigration doctrine to Plato's Timaeus, where souls conquered by passion are degraded into inferior forms — women, or eventually beasts fitting their vice — and notes that some philosophers, per Ambrose, held that great philosophers' souls transmigrated after death into bees or fireflies as a fitting reward, and others' souls into animals corresponding to their former character (musicians into nightingales, soldiers into boars, princes into lions); adds that Plato and Ovid also allowed transmigration between human bodies of either sex, a view echoed by pseudo-poets claiming to have received Homer's spirit (mocked by Persius) and by heretics who held John the Baptist possessed Elijah's soul.
claims: Plato's Timaeus grounds Ovid's doctrine that vicious souls transmigrate into degraded forms, including animals fitting their character.
The transmigration doctrine was extended by some to claims of specific spiritual inheritance, such as pseudo-poets claiming Homer's spirit or heretics identifying John the Baptist with Elijah.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e13552.summary: Describes the position of Plato and his followers that true resurrection is the soul's return to its own original body after the span of a cosmic 'Great Year,' quoting Plato's Timaeus on the great year's completion and the Republic on vicious souls being purified through repeated cosmic cycles until fit to return to their former dignity, while victorious souls return to dwell with their companion star in a true blessed life; notes the once-common English custom of burying treasure with the dead in expectation of such a return, catalogues rival estimates of the great year's length (Varro's 440 years, Josephus' 600, followers of Ptolemy's 36,000 solar years), and concludes that Plato accordingly held the punishment of the wicked to be temporally finite rather than eternal, a view shared, it is reported, by Avicenna and Origen.
claims: Plato holds that true resurrection is the soul's eventual return to its own body after a fixed cosmic cycle (the Great Year).
On this reading Plato, like Avicenna and reportedly Origen, held that punishment of the wicked soul is temporally finite, not eternal.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e13624.summary: Notes that some who do admit a resurrection to everlasting bliss and misery nonetheless think, following certain philosophers reported by Augustine, that both states are experienced together here on earth rather than in heaven and hell respectively; observes that some Jews (per Theophylact's comment on Luke 9) similarly expected the resurrection in terms of carnal feasting and drinking, as do, it is claimed, the Saracens/Agarenes and many Tartars (per Marco Polo), the latter reportedly so absurd as to formally betroth deceased youths so they might enjoy pleasures together in the afterlife.
claims: Some hold both eternal bliss and misery are experienced together on earth rather than in distinct heaven and hell.
Reports attribute to Jews, Saracens, and Tartars a belief that resurrected life consists in carnal, earthly pleasures.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e13223.summary: Asks why philosophers deny a future bodily resurrection given that its possibility has already been demonstrated and it is attested by widespread fame, by major religious traditions (Jews, Christians, Saracens, Tartars), by many prophets and philosophers, and by specific historical accounts of persons actually rising from death; cites Plato's myth of Er (Republic) reporting a revived soldier's account of the afterlife, defends Plato's seriousness as a philosopher, and adduces further testimonies — Pliny's chapter on revivals, Heraclides' account of a woman reviving after seven days, Varro's similar reports, Democritus' concession of resurrection, Porphyry (per Augustine), and a saying attributed to the philosopher Bonellus to Pythagoras about death and rebirth through purification — concluding that no strong counter-argument has ever been offered against so widely and seriously attested a phenomenon.
claims: The possibility of bodily resurrection has already been demonstrated and is corroborated by widespread testimony across traditions and specific historical accounts of revival.
No philosopher has offered a cogent argument against resurrection proportionate to the weight of testimony favoring it.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e13728.summary: Argues from the soul's demonstrated immortality and individuality (Part 36) that each rational soul has a natural aptitude and appetite to govern and dwell in its own body and exercise its noble operations through it, as other natural forms relate to what they inform; if the soul did not naturally desire this union, it could not be joined to a body in the first place contrary to the natural order; cites Hermes Trismegistus on angels as simple beings versus humans as composites of divine and mortal nature, whose dual composition in some respects makes man even more excellent than purely immortal beings, since only he unites earthly stewardship with devotion to the divine.
claims: The rational soul has a natural aptitude and appetite for governing its own body, analogous to other natural forms and their matter.
Man's composite nature (mortal and divine) is presented by Hermes Trismegistus as making him in some respects more excellent than purely immortal beings.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e13777.summary: Argues that if the virtuous, eternal soul has a natural appetite for its body, its eternal separation from that body after death cannot itself be natural but must be violent — and no violent state can be eternal, as philosophers agree; a natural appetite cannot remain eternally frustrated and idle, so an eternally disembodied virtuous soul would be eternally hungering and thirsting rather than blessed, contrary to God's generous rewarding of the virtuous (Part 31); concludes that true final beatitude requires the soul to be reunited with its desired body, since no substitute good could fully satisfy this natural craving so long as it remains unmet.
claims: Eternal deprivation of the body the soul naturally desires would be a violent, not natural, state, and violent states cannot be eternal.
True final beatitude requires the soul's reunion with its body, since the natural appetite for the body cannot otherwise be satisfied.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e13873.summary: Argues God both can (Part 37) and, being supremely just, generous, and rewarding, would grant the soul's reunion with its body; notes every well-ordered polity establishes rewards for virtue and punishments for vice, since without them people grow lazy toward virtue and prone to vice, and God as wisest ruler of the cosmic order would not leave it without such incentives; observes that in this present life the good are often deprived and afflicted while the wicked flourish (even beasts sometimes live more comfortably than virtuous humans), so if God does not adequately reward virtue now he must do so in the future, especially since it costs him nothing; argues a virtuous person who endures suffering and even a terrible death for God's honor must receive a most delightful future life in return, else God could not fittingly inspire his 'soldiers' to face death for him; concludes the deepest human appetite, for a perfectly satisfying final good, must eventually be satisfied, and since it is not satisfied in this life it will be in the next — hence there will be a resurrection.
claims: A well-ordered cosmos requires God to establish rewards for virtue and punishments for vice, as observed in every well-run polity.
Since virtue is not adequately rewarded in the present life, it must be rewarded in a future one, fulfilling the soul's deepest natural appetite for a fully satisfying good.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e13953.summary: Argues, citing Aristotle's De Anima that it is the composite of soul and body, not the soul alone, that acts, feels, and understands, that the whole human being — not the soul in isolation — is what merits; justice therefore requires that the one who merited (the whole composite) be the one rewarded, and not eternally, since God could as easily reward the meriting person fully as partially; concludes it is most fitting that the whole man, soul and proper body together, be blessedly rewarded, which is the reasoning that led Plato, Porphyry, and many other philosophers to hold that souls separated from their bodies by death are eventually restored to them.
claims: It is the composite of soul and body, not the soul alone, that properly merits reward or punishment, per Aristotle.
Justice requires the whole meriting person, body and soul together, to receive the reward — the basis for Plato's and Porphyry's doctrine of eventual reunion.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e13988.summary: Identifies the error in the alternative view that only the soul, or the man considered as soul alone, is rewarded or punished after death — since it would make no sense for someone to labor so diligently at virtue and avoiding vice if the resulting reward or punishment accrued to something other than the composite person who acted; anticipates the Epicurean, Sadducee, and Averroist reply that man is already sufficiently rewarded in this present life alone (as touched on regarding Part 36), noting this has already been refuted by the preceding arguments.
claims: Rewarding or punishing the soul alone, apart from the composite person who acted, would make diligent moral effort pointless.
The Epicurean/Sadducee/Averroist claim that present-life reward suffices has already been refuted.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14004.summary: Reasons from the soul's demonstrated immortality and individuality (Part 36) that souls persist after death with due reward of joy or sorrow, since it would be contrary to nature and to divine goodness for such noble souls, once separated from body, to be wholly deprived of all action and passion as if asleep or dead, and indifferently so for good and bad souls alike; concludes that if souls are to be sufficiently and beatifically rewarded after death they must be restored to their bodies, and quotes Hermes Trismegistus' dialogue with Asclepius on the due reward owed to man for his faithful, pious stewardship of the world.
claims: It would be contrary to divine goodness for separated souls, good and bad alike, to be wholly inactive after death.
Sufficient and beatific post-mortem reward for the soul requires eventual restoration to its body.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14050.summary: Continues quoting Hermes Trismegistus's dialogue with Asclepius, affirming reward for the pious in contrast to the impious, who are denied return to heaven and instead undergo a foul migration into unworthy bodies, and criticizes those who, gripped by love of bodily pleasure, refuse to acknowledge the soul's divine part; distinguishes 'unnecessary' fear of death as mere bodily dissolution from a truly necessary fear concerning post-mortem judgment, in which souls are examined by a 'supreme daemon' who permits the just to remain in fitting places while casting the guilty down into perpetual aerial torment — an eternal punishment precisely because the immortal soul cannot escape it — and adds that hidden earthly sins are punished the more severely after death the more they were concealed in life.
claims: Hermes' dialogue distinguishes an unnecessary fear of mere bodily death from a properly necessary fear of post-mortem judgment.
The soul's very immortality is what makes the punishment of the guilty after death eternal, since it cannot escape through dissolution.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14114.summary: Continues the Hermes material on the reward of the just, who are protected by God from all evil and granted confidence of future immortality through purified knowledge of the divine, graded according to each one's piety and devotion; cites the deification of Asclepius, whose body remains entombed while his true self ascended to heaven, parallels this with Plato's Timaeus on victorious souls returning to their companion star for a true blessed life and with Ambrose's allegorical reading of Plato's 'garden of Jove,' and notes ancient poets and theologians who spoke of tasting nectar and manna as conferring immortality, Socrates' eagerness to join 'his gods' (the virtuous dead), and Pliny's account of the deification of great benefactors such as Vespasian as a path to eternal glory — all read here as figurative descriptions of departed souls' reward.
claims: Multiple traditions (Hermetic, Platonic, poetic, and Roman) are read as figuratively describing a real reward of departed souls through symbols of deification and ascent.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14186.summary: Continues with Hermes Trismegistus describing Egyptian veneration of deified souls (Aesculapius, Hermes, Isis) worshipped through sacred animals and idols in their cities; reiterates Plato's teaching that vice-conquered souls face due punishment while the well-instructed and virtuous prosper, contrasted with negligent souls dragged to the underworld; cites Augustine's account of Cleombrotus, who, persuaded by Plato's argument for the soul's immortality, leapt to his death seeking the better life; parallels this with the pseudo-Aristotelian Secret of Secrets on the soul's post-mortem fate depending on its perfection at separation from the body, and introduces the deathbed dialogue attributed to Aristotle in which he opens by asking his disciples whether they believe philosophical science yields truth and distinguishes humans from animals.
claims: Multiple sources (Hermetic, Platonic, pseudo-Aristotelian) are marshaled to show a cross-traditional consensus that the soul's post-mortem fate depends on its moral and intellectual state at death.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14247.summary: Continues the pseudo-Aristotelian deathbed dialogue: after the disciples affirm that philosophical science yields truth and distinguishes humans from animals, 'Aristotle' argues that the good arising from such knowledge cannot come in this present life, since many unrighteous and ignorant people end their days in worldly prosperity while many wise, God-knowing people are deprived of peace and good; concludes that death should not be feared as the soul's passage to join wise and joyful souls, but rather failure to attain 'divine degrees,' sinking instead to a bestial state, should be feared — reinforcing the work's recurring claim that virtuous people, especially studious philosophers, are not adequately rewarded in this life, since Aristotle's own Ethics affirms felicity as the best, noblest, and most delightful goal of all optimal human activity, and exhorts disciples to mortify worldly desires rather than fear death as the soul's approach to its Creator.
claims: The pseudo-Aristotelian dialogue argues that reward for virtuous, wise living cannot occur in the present life, since the wicked often prosper and the wise often suffer.
Final felicity, per Aristotle's Ethics, is the best and most delightful goal of human activity, supporting the claim that it must be attained after death rather than in this life.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14343.summary: Notes that Avicenna, Algazel, and (on this point) even Averroes concur in affirming reward and punishment of souls after death — Averroes' own gloss on Aristotle's Ethics concerning Job's hoped-for salvation after death being cited as evidence he too expects posthumous reward for virtue; adds corroborating sayings from Sixtus Pythagoricus on immortal judgment, honors, and punishments, and notes agreement among Latin/Italic philosophers (Cicero, Seneca, Macrobius, Boethius) with this same doctrine.
claims: Even Averroes' own comments imply belief in posthumous reward for virtue, despite his official denial of individual immortality.
A wide range of philosophical authorities (Avicenna, Algazel, Cicero, Seneca, Macrobius, Boethius) concur on post-mortem reward and punishment.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14376.summary: Cites Macrobius' Commentary on the Dream of Scipio promising a fixed heavenly abode of eternal blessedness for those who serve and preserve their homeland; Ptolemy's Almagest counseling one to see God's goodness both in prosperity and in adversity as purification and eternal reward; and Albumazar's astrological doctrine linking planetary houses to the soul's pilgrimage and future fortune through faith — then traces this whole line of thought back to the Pharisees (per Josephus), who held a future divine judgment rewarding each according to merit and affirmed the soul's immortality, the Essenes' stoic endurance of torture in hope of a future recompense, and broader Greek belief in a paradisal region beyond Ocean for the good and a stormy underworld of punishment for the wicked, including the Isles of the Blessed for heroes and the torments of Sisyphus, Tantalus, Ixion, and Tityus for the impious.
claims: A convergent tradition spanning Roman astrological philosophy, Jewish sects (Pharisees, Essenes), and Greek mythology affirms post-mortem reward for virtue and punishment for vice.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14457.summary: Explains the Greek notion of 'Heroes' as noble, well-deserving souls dwelling in the upper air, per Isidore's etymology, and cites Aristotle's own reference (Physics IV) to the fable of sleeping among the Heroes at Sardis, defending such fables as a legitimate rhetorical mode that conveys mystical truth under figurative narrative rather than being simple falsehood, as with Aesop's and Libyan fables (the horse and the stag, the fox and the hedgehog) used for genuine persuasive and moral instruction.
claims: Mythological 'fables,' including the Greek notion of Heroes, are defended as legitimate rhetorical vehicles for real truths, not mere falsehoods.
Aristotle himself treats such fables as containing genuine instructive and even philosophical content.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14541.summary: Continues defending mythic fables as containing physical or theological truth under figurative cover, citing Aristotle's interpretation of the Ocean fable in terms of vapor circulation, his allegorical reading of the three Fates (Clotho, Lachesis, Atropos) in De Mundo as ultimately signifying God (following Plato), and Plato's own reading of the Phaethon myth as an allegorical account of a real periodic cosmic conflagration, corroborated similarly by Aristotle's De Mundo; closes by quoting Macrobius that philosophy neither rejects all fables nor accepts all, but must discern by gradations which convey truth.
claims: Both Plato and Aristotle are cited as reading certain myths (the Fates, Phaethon) as figurative expressions of real physical or theological truths.
Macrobius is invoked for the principle that philosophy selectively accepts some fables as vehicles of truth while rejecting others.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14583.summary: Concludes that Egyptian, Hebrew, Greek, Arabic, and Latin philosophers alike concur on the post-mortem reward and punishment of souls, a consensus mirrored by Greek and Latin poets' mythology in which the good become or join the gods while the wicked are cast into the underworld and tormented in its rivers (Styx, Phlegethon, Cocytus, Acheron, Lethe), each given an allegorical meaning — Lethe ('forgetting'), for instance, plausibly signifying the river of divine mercy that frees purified souls from all sorrow before their transfer to heavenly joys.
claims: A cross-cultural philosophical and poetic consensus (Egyptian, Hebrew, Greek, Arabic, Latin) affirms post-mortem reward and punishment.
The mythological rivers of the underworld are read allegorically as figures for real processes of purification, mercy, and punishment.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14167.summary: Continues allegorizing the poetic underworld (Cerberus, Charon, the Furies, the Hydra, Ixion's wheel) as containing nothing alien to genuine mystery, then turns to refute the claim that the intrinsic goodness inseparably attending a good act is itself a sufficient reward, citing Aristotle's Ethics IX on the virtuous person's preference for a brief intense good over a long mediocre life; rejects this both on the grounds already given and because, symmetrically, it would make every evil act sufficiently punished by its own attendant vice, and asks how a just and truthful God who demands total, unconditional love and service (Part 30) could repay such love and service so meagerly, or substitute some lesser finite reward for the infinite beatifying reward he elsewhere promises to give for his own sake.
claims: The intrinsic goodness of a virtuous act cannot be its own sufficient reward, both on prior grounds and because it would symmetrically make vice self-punishing, which does not match observed injustice in this life.
A God who demands total love and service for his own sake, as established earlier, would be inconsistent in repaying it with only a finite or meager reward.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14729.summary: Briefly dismisses the further suggestion that reward might consist in Epicurean bodily pleasure ('the filth of pigs'), as already refuted in the discussion of Part 32, and notes this response can be refuted by the same reasoning as the prior one.
claims: Epicurean bodily pleasure cannot constitute the reward of virtue, as already shown in Part 32.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14740.summary: Argues that external goods of fortune likewise cannot sufficiently reward virtue, since the intrinsic goodness of a virtuous act already exceeds all external goods (per Part 31) and yet was shown insufficient as reward, and since moral virtue and virtuous action are incomparably superior to wealth, power, honor, and other external goods, as all sound philosophers agree; even honor — which Aristotle calls the greatest of external goods, whose loss is felt most gravely, and which he names as virtue's reward in the Ethics — is shown to be a disproportionate, insubstantial, and inadequate recompense for virtue, especially for the many virtuous deeds that remain secret and unrecognized; introduces, as an alternative to be examined, Averroes' view that human felicity consists in the speculative sciences acquired through study.
claims: External goods, including honor (which Aristotle calls the greatest external good), are disproportionate and inadequate rewards for virtue, especially given secret virtuous deeds that go unrecognized.
Averroes' account of felicity as consisting in acquired speculative knowledge is introduced as the next position to be examined.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14786.summary: Rejects Averroes' claim that human felicity consists in acquired speculative science, on the grounds that felicity must be the best good essentially and per se, not merely accidentally, whereas perfection in speculative science is compatible with being dishonest and morally evil, as reason, experience, and Averroes' own concession attest.
claims: Felicity must be an essentially and per se optimal good, but speculative scientific perfection is not, since one can be intellectually accomplished yet morally wicked.
Averroes himself concedes that speculative perfection is compatible with moral vice.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14798.summary: Argues that moral, heroic, or divine virtue surpasses mere speculative perfection, citing Aristotle's Ethics VII on a heroic/divine virtue exceeding ordinary humanity (exemplified by Homer's Hector) and Ethics X on felicity being directed toward virtuous operation and love of God, with God favoring those who act well and rationally rather than merely contemplate — a point Averroes' own commentary concedes; adds Aristotle's Ethics II insistence that ethical inquiry aims at becoming good, not merely knowing what virtue is, Hermes Trismegistus's definition of true philosophy as devout worship of the divine rather than sophistic cleverness, and Sixtus Pythagoricus's maxim to understand the good in order to act well, concluding that calling someone simply 'good' or 'bad' refers to moral character and conduct, not to speculative knowledge or ignorance.
claims: Moral, heroic, and divine virtue — oriented toward right action and love of God — surpasses mere speculative knowledge, per Aristotle, Hermes, and Sixtus Pythagoricus.
Even Averroes' own gloss concedes that God favors those who love and serve him through virtuous action, not mere contemplation.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14879.summary: Continues dismantling the Averroist-Aristotelian intellectualist account of felicity: no one is so knowledgeable as to be free from error, nor perfectly happy in both soul and body simultaneously in this life, since bodily and psychic flourishing perpetually conflict; asks what, on this theory, would constitute the vicious person's misery (either false belief, making the most learned but self-contradicting philosophers most miserable, or mere ignorance, equating the wicked non-learner with the innocent non-learner); objects that if speculative knowledge alone were the final good, one could rightly pursue it by any means, even sin, and that only speculative philosophers — not the morally and devoutly virtuous who lack philosophical learning but love and serve God more — could then attain felicity, which cannot be right since felicity is the common good and end of every human; dismisses the fallback that moral virtue's increase, or felicity as momentary act rather than habit (per Aristotle's remark that happy and unhappy differ little 'for half of life,' i.e. in sleep), or a combination of intellectual and moral virtue (attributed to Averroes), could rescue the theory.
claims: The intellectualist theory of felicity cannot coherently account for what constitutes vicious misery.

Restricting felicity to speculative philosophers excludes morally and devoutly virtuous non-philosophers who may love and serve God more, which is incoherent given felicity's status as the common human good.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14955.summary: Argues that since any virtuous act in the present life is free, praiseworthy, and meritorious of reward, the beatific intellectual act itself cannot be its own reward — since it is finally directed at God (Part 30) and God rewards abundantly (Part 31) — nor can its reward be some further act, on pain of infinite regress.
claims: The intellectualist felicity-act cannot be its own adequate reward, and positing a further rewarding act leads to infinite regress.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14966.summary: Presents what the author takes to be Aristotle's and Averroes' more careful position: human felicity consists in the soul's conjunction (continuatio) with the separate agent intellect in the present life, however briefly, quoting Aristotle's Metaphysics XII on the best state being attainable by us only for a short time, and Averroes' commentary explaining that human fortune as such depends on this conjunction with the agent intellect (which is both mover and final end of the soul), and his De Anima commentary describing how, as speculative knowledge becomes progressively actual in us, the agent intellect becomes progressively conjoined with us until, per Themistius, man becomes godlike, knowing all entities as God does, since entities are simply the content of divine knowledge.
claims: Aristotle and Averroes hold that human felicity is a temporary conjunction of the soul with the separate agent intellect, achieved as speculative knowledge becomes actual.
On this account, full conjunction makes the knower godlike, since for Averroes all entities are simply the content of divine knowledge.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15038.summary: Objects that even granting this momentary intellectual conjunction as felicity, its brevity (allegedly occurring only near death, in a state like ecstasy or rapture) cannot adequately compensate a lifetime of virtuous labor and suffering, drawing the analogy of an earthly prince who would be blameworthy for rewarding decades of loyal, painful military service with only a fleeting reward when he could easily give more or reward continuously — arguing God, infinitely more generous than any prince, cannot do less; further argues such momentary beatitude leaves the natural human desire for a lasting good unsatisfied, and that the 'beatified' person either knows he is about to lose this good (which should cause grief, undermining perfect happiness, contra Aristotle's own remark that even the brave grieve at losing supreme goods) or does not know it (which conflicts with the Averroist claim that the conjoined knower knows all things as God does) — concluding a momentary conjunction cannot constitute true felicity.
claims: A momentary intellectual conjunction cannot adequately reward a lifetime of virtuous suffering, especially given God's superior generosity compared to any human patron.
The momentary-felicity theory is self-undermining: the beatified person's foreknowledge or ignorance of imminent loss each independently contradicts what the theory requires.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15166.summary: Argues that if beatific reward were expected only within the present life, no young person, and no one who has not yet attained it, should rationally risk death for religion, country, family, or any cause, since one should not risk losing one's supreme good for a lesser one; and even someone who has attained the momentary felicity should avoid death, since dying would only shorten it, contrary to Aristotle's own acknowledgment that wounds and death are painful even to the brave; argues no one could then be rightly motivated to die defending faith, homeland, or friends, against the united political wisdom of Hermes, Plato, Varro, Cicero, Macrobius, and Aristotle himself (who affirms in the Ethics that the virtuous should die for friends and country), concluding that since God plainly does not sufficiently reward such sacrifice in the present life, he must do so in the future.
claims: A theory locating beatific reward only in the present life cannot rationally motivate self-sacrifice for religion, country, or friends, contrary to the unanimous judgment of major political and ethical authorities.
Since present-life reward for ultimate sacrifice is plainly insufficient, sufficient reward must come in a future life.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15250.summary: Further objects that the Averroist felicity is too diminished since it perfects the soul alone, not the body, which still fails and dies, and since it is itself a free human act (not a necessary one, since it could be otherwise), it is praiseworthy and meritorious of further reward — yet no further reward is available on this theory without either identity (already excluded) or infinite regress; notes the account implies the ecstatic person lacks free use of self, citing Averroes' own commentary that once the intellect is stripped of potency its activity becomes continuous and inseparable from it; asks what would then constitute the vicious person's final misery, since mere privation of this felicity would wrongly equate the wicked with the morally indifferent, and proposes instead that the biblical prophets — who in this life achieved the highest conjunction with the divine and thereby foresaw and worked wonders — unanimously attest a future life with reward and punishment differentiated by merit.
claims: The Averroist felicity, perfecting only the soul and not the body, and itself a further meritorious free act, cannot avoid either circularity or infinite regress regarding its own reward.
The biblical prophets, presented as the clearest historical instances of intellectual conjunction with the divine, uniformly attest a differentiated future life of reward and punishment.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15304.summary: Directly challenges Averroes' claim that the agent intellect becomes conjoined with us only once all speculative knowledge already exists actually in us, arguing this reverses the natural order of causation (requiring complete actual knowledge, itself impossible since it would demand infinite actual habits and acts, prior to and as cause of the very conjunction that is supposed to produce that knowledge); presses the question of who in all history ever actually possessed such total knowledge, noting Aristotle himself admittedly did not know the quadrature of the circle and much else, and that philosophers routinely contradicted one another to the end of their lives; suggests the only figures who plausibly match Averroes' description of complete, godlike, active knowledge of all things are the biblical prophets, who worked all manner of miracles across creation by divine knowledge.
claims: Averroes' account of the agent intellect's conjunction reverses the proper order of cause and effect and requires an impossible actual infinity of knowledge.
No philosopher, including Aristotle, ever possessed the total, godlike knowledge Averroes' theory requires; only the prophets plausibly approximate it.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15356.summary: Notes that these very prophets unanimously affirm a future life of glory and punishment, contrary to Averroes; traces Averroes' error to his mistaken doctrine of the unicity of the intellect (already refuted in Part 36), one error propagating others, and traces Aristotle's parallel error to his mistaken belief in the eternity of the world and of human generation, which led him to posit only immortal souls (not the whole body-soul composite) as beatified after death, without the Platonists' further doctrine of souls returning to bodies; dismisses Simon's objection that resurrection is 'against nature' given that God is author of all nature and, per Plato's own definition of nature as the divine will (as reported by John of Salisbury), resurrection accords with nature precisely because it accords with God's will; notes that Dionysius, Irenaeus, Hippolytus, Origen, and Epiphanius all refuted Simon on this point.
claims: Averroes' unicity-of-intellect error and Aristotle's eternity-of-the-world error respectively explain their denial of individual post-mortem beatitude and of bodily resurrection.
The objection that resurrection is 'against nature' fails once nature is properly understood as consequent on the divine will, of which God is author.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e14874.summary: Turns to condemn Plato's, Ovid's, and the Platonists' doctrine of human souls transmigrating into animal bodies as a horrible, monstrous error, arguing that natural forms only inform matter properly disposed to receive them, and that species like human and donkey differ essentially and substantially through their substantial forms/differentiae, so that a human soul cannot constitute a donkey's essence, or vice versa.
claims: Natural forms can only inform matter properly disposed for them, so a human soul cannot constitute the essence of an essentially different species like a donkey.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15411.summary: Presses that Ovid's transmigration doctrine ('all things change, nothing perishes') would absurdly entail that no human, or anyone, ever truly dies — which would also block any resurrection, contrary to what was shown in Part 37 — and shows Ovid self-contradicting by quoting his own later lines (Metamorphoses XV) that 'devouring time and envious old age destroy all things, consuming everything little by little with lingering death.'
claims: Ovid's own later verses ('time devours all things') directly contradict his stated doctrine that nothing perishes.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15434.summary: Quotes further from Ovid's Metamorphoses (on the deification of Julius Caesar's soul as a star, elevated by Venus into the heavens, and on Ovid's own hope that his 'better part' will be borne above the stars) to show that Ovid himself here affirms souls are raised to differentiated heavenly positions according to merit, rather than merely cycling through earthly bodies.
claims: Ovid's own poetic account of Julius Caesar's deification and his personal hope for astral immortality affirms merit-differentiated heavenly reward, in tension with his transmigration doctrine.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15508.summary: Draws the consequence that Ovid himself here affirms merit-differentiated placement of souls among the stars, then asks, against those positing immediate return of meritorious souls to worldly bodies, when and where such souls are sufficiently rewarded for their merit — not during their former embodied life, not at the moment of separation, and not in a second, inferior (bestial) body, since that would be a demotion, not a reward, contrary to God's overflowing generosity already established.
claims: Immediate transmigration into a new worldly body, especially an inferior one, cannot constitute sufficient reward for prior merit.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15556.summary: Notes that even virtuous souls said to reenter other human bodies immediately are not thereby fully beatified, since they return to accustomed toil, sorrow, the need to merit anew, and familiar hardship rather than to rest and reward.
claims: Immediate reentry into ordinary worldly human life, even if not bestial, still fails to constitute full beatification, since it returns the soul to accustomed suffering.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15563.summary: Argues such a recurring worldly condition cannot be a sufficient reward for prior labors, and that the soul's natural appetite is not for just any human body but specifically for its own former body, through which it performed its noble acts and which it loves more than any other — as a soldier loves his own horse and sword more than another's, illustrated by Alexander's elaborate funeral for his horse Bucephalus — concluding that fitting justice requires the very same person, in the very same soul and body that merited, to be the one rewarded.
claims: The soul's natural appetite is specifically for its own former body, not any body, by analogy to a soldier's attachment to his own instruments.
Justice requires reward of the identical person — same soul, same body — who performed the meritorious acts.
concepts: particular attachment to one's own body

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15607.summary: Supports the identity requirement with a natural-philosophical principle that an efficient cause precedes its effect in time but a formal cause never temporally precedes what it forms (per Aristotle and Averroes, Part 36), which undercuts Ovid's fiction of souls remembering distinct earlier lives (as Pythagoras claiming to have been Euphorbus); suggests a naturalistic origin for that particular legend in the historical account of Menelaus dedicating Euphorbus' shield in Juno's temple, later claimed by Pythagoras (called Panthoides), which gave rise to the story that Euphorbus' soul had entered Pythagoras.
claims: The principle that form never temporally precedes its formed subject undermines the coherence of Ovid's transmigration-memory fiction.
The Pythagoras-Euphorbus transmigration legend likely originated from a historical anecdote about a dedicated shield, not a genuine memory of a past life.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15633.summary: Considers a refined version of the theory — virtuous souls wait for the Great Year and then return to their own bodies, while only vicious souls immediately transmigrate into other, especially bestial or opposite-sex, bodies as punishment — and rejects it: God is more inclined to reward than to punish, yet this scheme lets the wicked receive swift 'reward' while the virtuous wait and remain insufficiently rewarded meanwhile; also, transforming an incontinent man into a woman, who per medical opinion and Ovid's Tiresias experiences greater sexual pleasure, would make the supposed punishment more pleasurable rather than painful, and so both fails as a deterrent and could even incentivize vice, a difficulty paralleled for transmigration into fierce beasts, reinforcing that justice requires the very person who sinned, in the very body that sinned, to be punished.
claims: A scheme rewarding vice with swift transmigration while delaying virtue's reward inverts the expected pattern of divine generosity toward the good.
Transformation into a body of allegedly greater sensory pleasure (per Tiresias/medical opinion) fails as a fitting punishment, since punishment must be contrary to pleasure, not conducive to it.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15675.summary: Notes that reward and punishment, being contraries, should by philosophical principle occur in the same kind of subject, and presses a dilemma against mixed schemes (souls alone rewarded/punished versus souls with bodies, glorious for the virtuous and wretched for the vicious); asks what becomes of souls of those who did neither good nor evil, whether reunited with bodies immediately or after delay, and what their intervening state would be; rejects the Great-Year-return-to-own-body doctrine as entailing an absurd infinite exact repetition of all events, and reiterates that full reward for virtuous humans occurs neither in present mundane life, nor in a disembodied heavenly state (soul alone being insufficient reward), nor in a second mundane life after bodily return, since none of these have been shown adequate.
claims: The Great-Year-return doctrine entails an absurd infinite exact repetition of all events.
None of the proposed timings for full reward (present life, disembodied heaven, second earthly life) is adequate, as shown by the preceding arguments.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15711.summary: Asks how it could fittingly suit God, per the prior suppositions, to give only a diminished, 'half' reward (soul alone) rather than rewarding the whole servant, or to give only some meager temporal reward during an interim embodied state, to one who wholly loved and served him without ever knowingly offending him for any good or to avoid any evil; concludes it is far more rational to hold that divine justice, generosity, and infinite goodness require that, once the faithful servant's struggle is complete, God at the fitting time abundantly repays him with full, unfading delights exceeding and outlasting any worldly pleasure, banishing all adversity, sorrow, and misery forever.
claims: It befits God's infinite justice and generosity to grant, at the fitting final time, complete and everlasting delight that exceeds and outlasts all worldly pleasure and banishes all misery.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15744.summary: Argues a soul rewarded in heaven alone, awaiting return to a body, is not perfectly blessed, since its appetite for its body remains unsatisfied and it is deprived of its proper bodily operations and former governance of its body; such a soul either wrongly believes it will remain disembodied forever, or knows it must return to bodily misery, or considers neither, each option previously shown problematic; cites Augustine's report that Porphyry corrected Plato by holding the purified soul, once returned to the Father, never returns to worldly evils, and Avicenna's and Algazel's proofs that one soul does not transfer between multiple bodies; distinguishes the Christian position that separated souls, even without their bodies in fact, possess them in certain hope, knowing they will receive them back gloriously and eternally at a divinely fitting time, and rebukes Plato for making such unauthorized, unreasoned claims as a mere philosopher rather than a prophet, unlike the Christian position grounded in prophetic authority.
claims: A disembodied soul awaiting bodily return cannot be perfectly blessed, given its unsatisfied appetite and deprived operations.

The Christian position — souls possessing their bodies 'in certain hope' pending a divinely appointed return — is presented as superior to Plato's unauthorized speculation, since it rests on prophetic authority rather than unaided philosophical conjecture.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15799.summary: Urges adoption of the Christian position on these questions as grounded in unanimous prophetic consensus and the supreme authority of Christ, demonstrated by fitting arguments (Part 32) and defended against every charge of impossibility or incongruity, and asks what truth-loving philosopher would not embrace so much more probable, reasonable, useful, and joyful a view; separately criticizes the astrological determinism implied by the Great Year doctrine, whereby human generation and all human acts would be necessarily subjected to the dispositions of the stars — an unworthy inversion of the natural order, since the rational soul is of nobler essence than any irrational thing, including the stars, and should not be necessarily ruled by them; further notes an internal contradiction in Plato and the Platonists, who hold both that the world and time had a beginning created by God (per the Timaeus, Genesis, and Ovid) and that all things recur identically at the end of each Great Year, which would require all things to be newly created from non-being again, meaning the world could not actually endure continuously to the end of the Great Year as the hypothesis requires.
claims: The Christian doctrine of resurrection rests on prophetic authority and demonstrable fittingness, making it preferable to Plato's unauthorized speculation.
The Great Year doctrine implies an objectionable astrological determinism subjecting the nobler rational soul to the rule of the stars.
Plato's affirmation of both a created world with a beginning and an identical eternal recurrence at each Great Year's end is self-contradictory.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15871.summary: Presses the contradiction further: how could the 'second gods' (angels) and immortal rational souls, declared eternal from their creation even by Plato's own Timaeus, ever return to nothingness, quoting Plato's own passage where God assures the angels that though naturally dissoluble as composites, his will guarantees they will never actually be dissolved; if all such entities were nonetheless to become non-entities again, that state of non-being would have to last some duration, yet nothing could measure or limit that duration once celestial motion itself has ceased, except the divine will — and there is no reason to assume that will chooses exactly this cyclical re-creation rather than extending existence indefinitely, as it has always been free to do; further, Plato's suggestion that only previously-corrupted things return while others persist eternally is self-contradictory, since it would still require the first human, having been created (not naturally generated) at the start, to be somehow re-produced at the cycle's end, which could happen neither by a repeated creation (contradicting the parallel-repetition hypothesis) nor by natural generation (raising insoluble questions about which parents, and an implied prior human generation that shouldn't exist under the hypothesis).
claims: Plato's own doctrine of angelic and soul immortality (Timaeus) is incompatible with a universal cyclical return to nothingness.
Only the free divine will, not any natural necessity, could determine the duration or recurrence of any cosmic cycle, undermining the necessity Plato's scheme assumes.

The requirement that even the first human be reproduced at each cycle's end cannot be coherently accommodated by either re-creation or natural generation without contradicting the cyclical-repetition hypothesis.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15960.summary: Continues that positing a newly created 'first human' at each Great Year's start is unnecessary, since ordinary natural generation by existing men and women suffices to perpetuate the species, and no natural cause — astrological or otherwise, apart perhaps from the implausible fiction of the eighth sphere's extremely slow motion, recognized as fable even by experts in celestial motions — could account for a sudden universal simultaneous death of all humans at the cycle's end; further refutes the shorter Great Year estimates (440 or 600 common years) by noting the celestial motions do not actually return to their original positions and configurations in so short a span, and by simple historical fact: figures such as Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, Nebuchadnezzar, Cyrus, Darius, Alexander, Augustus, Christ, Hermes, Plato, and Aristotle, though many such intervals have elapsed since their lifetimes, have not returned, nor been seen or heard of again.
claims: No plausible natural cause could produce a simultaneous universal death of all humans at a cycle's end.

The shorter proposed lengths of the Great Year (440 or 600 years) are refuted both astronomically and by the simple historical fact that major figures from more than that long ago have never returned.
concepts: refutation of short Great Year estimates

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e15999.summary: Adds that if all beings, not just humans, were to return identically after the proposed interval, every person should be regenerated identically — same parents, same time and place, same acts — yet histories attest that many people, along with certain cities, stones, and metals, have endured continuously well beyond such proposed cycles without any such interruption or repetition.
claims: Continuous historical endurance of people, cities, and materials beyond the proposed cycle lengths contradicts the requirement of identical periodic regeneration.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16013.summary: Turns to refute the 36,000-solar-year estimate of the Great Year (based on Ptolemaic precession): those versed in celestial motions can easily show the celestial bodies do not all return to their original positions within that span, that completion of the eighth sphere's cycle does not entail simultaneous completion of the other spheres' cycles, and that Ptolemy himself only approximately (not exactly) asserted one degree of precession per century — a figure later astronomers such as al-Battani and Thabit ibn Qurra found to be inaccurate.
claims: The 36,000-year Great Year estimate fails astronomically: celestial bodies do not synchronously return to their starting positions, and Ptolemy's precession rate was only approximate and later shown inaccurate.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16033.summary: Offers a charitable reading of Plato: if he meant that virtuous souls return not to passible, miserable bodies but to impassible, blessed ones for an everlasting (not temporal) life, occurring at the end of the world when all celestial motions complete a single all-encompassing 'great year' spanning the whole of cosmic history from beginning to end, this would not be far from the true position — noting that some theologians likewise hold that all things will be completed in a circular pattern, ending where they began.
claims: A charitably reinterpreted version of Plato's Great Year — as the single span from the world's beginning to its end, culminating in the blessed, impassible resurrection of the virtuous — is presented as compatible with, or close to, the true (Christian) position.
concepts: world history as one great year

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16051.summary: Suggests by analogy that just as God instituted angels and humans in a good but not yet optimal state so they could ascend by degrees to the best, he may similarly have ordered celestial motions to progress through stages; argues by symmetry that just as the good will rise to everlasting beatitude, the wicked should fall to everlasting misery, since eternity is the most blessed portion of beatitude and, by parity, the most miserable portion of misery, and no lesser penalty could sufficiently reform the wicked or deter potential sinners in the vast polity of the world.
claims: By parity of reasoning with eternal beatitude for the good, eternal misery for the wicked is the fitting and proportionate outcome.
No penalty less than eternal could sufficiently reform or deter sin within the world's vast moral order.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16075.summary: Rejects the suggestion that the threat of eternal punishment is a mere bluff without real substance, since God, the most truthful, faithful, and just ruler of the world, could not lie, perjure himself, or practice deception, consistent with the first Supposition; asks why, if God could deceive in his threats of punishment, he should be trusted at all in his promises of reward.
claims: God's perfect truthfulness (established earlier) rules out the threat of eternal punishment being an empty bluff.
If God could deceive regarding punishment, there would be no basis to trust his promises of reward either.
