dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16088.summary: Reiterates that temporal sin can, and absent special grace should, be justly punished with eternal punishment, and draws an analogy to human princes, who can justly establish binding legal provisions not strictly demanded by natural reason but committed to legislative discretion ('what pleases the prince has the force of law'), such as decreeing perpetual reward for loyal service and perpetual punishment for disloyalty — enforced, when the person cannot literally live forever, through consequences extending to descendants, such as disinheritance or disqualification from honors.
claims: Human legislative discretion can justly bind perpetual reward or punishment to service or disloyalty, extending to descendants where the person cannot live forever.
This provides an analogy for God's justice in decreeing eternal punishment for temporal sin.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16119.summary: Argues that if human princes can justly establish such enduring provisions reaching descendants, God — for whom souls live forever and whose resurrected humans will live forever in their own persons — can far more fittingly establish and literally enforce eternal reward and punishment on the very persons involved, as he has in fact decreed through Christ, the foremost of prophets and lawgivers, and through the unanimous witness of the holy men of the old and new law.
claims: God can and does literally enforce eternal reward and punishment on the persons themselves, since (unlike human subjects) both souls and resurrected humans live forever.
This is affirmed by Christ's authority and the unanimous testimony of scripture.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16142.summary: Cites Hermes Trismegistus, quoted approvingly in the pseudo-Aristotelian Secret of Secrets, warning against bloodshed with an elaborate image of the heavenly virtues crying out to God for vengeance whenever one creature unjustly kills another like itself, and God permitting the killer to be killed in requital, with the heavens continually representing the victim's death until vengeance is exacted upon the killer, who is destined for eternal punishment.
claims: Hermes' account (via the pseudo-Aristotelian Secret of Secrets) depicts unjust killers as destined for eternal punishment, invoked by the heavenly powers themselves.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16166.summary: Adds Avicenna's teaching that an imperfect soul separated from the body falls into a kind of eternal labor, and Algazel's explicit doctrine that some vicious souls, once separated, incur and eternally suffer punishment, and reads the four ever-flowing, never-failing infernal rivers of the poets as an apt figure for eternal infernal punishment.
claims: Avicenna and Algazel are cited as affirming eternal punishment for vicious souls after death.
The poets' ever-flowing infernal rivers are read as a figurative representation of unending punishment.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16179.summary: Argues that philosophers and heretics denying eternal punishment offer no efficacious counter-argument, merely weaving an unwarranted 'history of the future' despite lacking prophetic authority; reiterates that punishing sinners does not conflict with divine mercy (Part 31), nor does eternally punishing temporal sin conflict with divine justice (the preceding part), and clarifies that God's eternal punishment is compatible with punishing more mildly, whether by turns or continuously, than the sinner's wickedness strictly merits.
claims: Deniers of eternal punishment offer no valid argument and speak without prophetic warrant.
Eternal punishment is compatible with God punishing more mildly than strictly deserved.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16201.summary: Anticipates opponents who, unable to prove their position, instead try to weaken the author's by claiming mere privation of eternal felicity (without positive suffering) is sufficient punishment for all guilt, and rejects this because it would equate greater and lesser sinners, and even those who never did good or evil, with genuine wrongdoers; adds that no well-run polity punishes offenders merely by withholding reward or honor rather than through active penalties or death, and that beatitude and misery, being positive contraries and not merely privative opposites, must come about through positive contrary states rather than mere privation.
claims: Mere privation of felicity, without positive suffering, cannot serve as sufficient punishment, since it would equate wrongdoers of vastly different guilt.
Beatitude and misery are positive contraries requiring positive contrary states, not merely privative opposition.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16232.summary: Argues that the fitting location for the eternal reward of the risen good is heaven, God's glorious dwelling, in his presence, supporting this with the reasoning that the immaterial, immortal rational soul, not educed from elemental matter, requires a place above the material elements, since a nobler nature deserves a nobler place — citing Aristotle and Averroes on the heavens as the most divine place, traditionally assigned by all peoples, barbarian and Greek alike, to God and the angels as the sole incorruptible and eternal region.
claims: The immaterial, immortal rational soul requires a place above the material elements, befitting its nobler nature.
A cross-cultural consensus (per Aristotle and Averroes) assigns the heavens as the place of God and the angels, the sole incorruptible region.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16302.summary: Reinforces the point via the principle that natures similar to one another require similar natural places: since angelic spirits and rational souls are similar in nature (immaterial, immortal), and heaven is established as the natural place of angelic spirits, by parity heaven is also the natural place of souls.
claims: Since souls and angels share a similar immaterial, immortal nature, and heaven is the angels' natural place, it is by parity also the souls' natural place.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16314.summary: Argues that beatitude, being the noblest, most worthy, most delightful, and wholly complete good, requires a correspondingly fitting place to be perfect, and that no sub-celestial place suffices for this — only the celestial region, which Aristotle and Averroes repeatedly call the 'glorious body.'
claims: Perfect beatitude requires a fitting place, which can only be the celestial region, termed the 'glorious body' by Aristotle and Averroes.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16332.summary: Concludes from the preceding reasons that many philosophers and poets already cited concur that the virtuous, purified soul is finally rewarded in the heavens; but since man is to be beatified not in soul alone but in soul and body together (as previously shown), the whole risen man — body and soul — must be finally beatified and rewarded in heaven.
claims: Since beatification pertains to the whole person, not the soul alone, the whole risen man must be finally rewarded in heaven, not just his soul.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16345.summary: Argues this conclusion fits natural philosophy: particular natural forms, and the composites informed by them, naturally seek and come to rest in their own natural places, as philosophers attest; since the soul's natural place is heaven (as shown), the soul naturally seeks, moves toward, and rests in heaven, and so, by extension, does the whole person.
claims: By the general principle that forms and their composites naturally seek their proper place, the soul (and by extension the whole person) naturally seeks and rests in heaven.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16361.summary: Argues that since the soul is nobler and more perfect than the body, it is more fitting and natural for the soul to govern, lead, and place the body in a location suited to the soul than the reverse; hence the whole person is more naturally situated in heaven, following the soul's most natural and perfect form, than confined to earth, which pertains only to the body and its matter — concluding that in final beatitude the body will be located in heaven along with the soul, since otherwise neither the soul nor the whole person could have perfect felicity.
claims: Because the soul is nobler than the body, it is more natural for the soul to determine the body's location than vice versa, implying the whole beatified person, body included, belongs in heaven.
concepts: perfect felicity requiring bodily presence in heaven

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16381.summary: Addresses the objection of how earthly flesh could naturally ascend to and remain in heaven, replying that the omnipotent God, author of all nature, who can create and re-create bodies from nothing, raise the dead, and work any miracle, can also — perhaps in a way incomprehensible to limited human minds — miraculously refine and subtilize the grossness of flesh so that it can naturally ascend, drawing analogies to the sun refining gross elements, alchemists refining matter through fire, and a magnet drawing and holding heavy iron upward against its ordinary tendency.
claims: God's power to refine and subtilize gross matter, by analogy with solar, alchemical, and magnetic processes, addresses the objection that earthly flesh cannot naturally ascend to heaven.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16403.summary: Concludes that the omnipotent God who dwells in the heavens can likewise alter human bodies so as to raise them to the celestial realm and locate them there eternally with himself, drawing a further analogy to any well-ordered polity, in which the places of the good and wicked, of reward and punishment, of honor and dishonor, and of delight and sorrow are spatially distinguished — the virtuous honored with the best seats, the wicked expelled, imprisoned, hanged, or consigned to vile and contrary places.
claims: God can miraculously relocate transformed human bodies to the celestial realm, paralleling how any well-ordered polity spatially separates the honored from the punished.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16420.summary: Concludes that if the good are rewarded above in the heavens, it is fitting that the wicked be punished below, in or under the earth, in a horrible place called 'inferus'/'infernus' — etymologically linked by Hermes Trismegistus either to being deprived of sight or to being situated at the lowest point of the cosmic sphere — so that those who offended the God of heaven are deprived of celestial light and favor and made to inhabit, contrary to nature, a horrid and unnatural penal place, corroborated by Plato (negligent souls sent to the underworld), the pseudo-Aristotelian Secret of Secrets, numerous pagan histories and poems distinguishing gods above from gods below, and Pythagorean tradition locating Jupiter's prison (Tartarus) at the center of the world.
claims: The wicked's punishment fittingly occurs in a low, unnatural, horrid place ('inferus'/'infernus'), corroborated by Hermetic etymology, Plato, pseudo-Aristotle, and pagan mythological tradition (Tartarus).

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16468.summary: Draws the evident conclusion that the bodies of the blessed must be transformed to a better, purer, more celestial condition in the future beatitude, since otherwise they could not ascend to and naturally rest in heaven, as already shown.
claims: The blessed's bodies must undergo transformation to a purer, celestial condition, since this is required for their heavenly ascent and rest.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16477.summary: Argues that since the whole person, not the soul alone, is to be finally rewarded and beatified, and the soul is to be transformed for the better, the body too must be similarly transformed — especially since God can easily accomplish this, and a better, purer, celestial soul deserves a correspondingly fitting body; otherwise the person could not be perfectly blessed, since a body still subject to ordinary miseries would remain in conflict with the spirit — concluding the blessed will have immortal bodies, whether through natural transmutation or through the Creator's continual conserving grace.
claims: Full beatitude requires the body, not only the soul, to be transformed and rendered immortal, matching the soul's own transformation.
Without such bodily transformation, ongoing bodily misery would conflict with the soul's beatitude, preventing perfect blessedness.
concepts: correspondence of body and soul in beatitude

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16503.summary: Argues forms and bodies should naturally correspond — corruptible, temporal forms inhabiting corruptible, temporal bodies, and incorruptible, eternal forms inhabiting incorruptible, eternal bodies — a view held by ancient thinkers who held that humans could become gods (per Aristotle's Metaphysics III), though Aristotle's Topics IV and Averroes mock the notion of 'immortality' as a distinct kind of life rather than a mere attribute, perhaps from failing to grasp the metaphorical use of manna and nectar or lacking a stronger counter-argument; asks rhetorically why an omnipotent God could not remove the intrinsic corruptive causes from a human body, or perfectly balance and proportion its elements, so as to render it naturally incorruptible.
claims: Corresponding correspondence between form and body (corruptible-to-corruptible, incorruptible-to-incorruptible) supports the possibility of an incorruptible glorified body.
Aristotle's and Averroes' mockery of 'immortality' as a life-genre may stem from missing the point of ancient metaphorical language (manna, nectar) rather than from a decisive counter-argument.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16560.summary: Cites purported instances of natural incorruptibility as corroboration — Pliny's account of a boy who reportedly slept 55 years in a cave and then lived as many years again without those sleeping years counting toward his death; shrines (Paphos, a temple of Minerva in the Troad) where rain reportedly never falls or offerings never rot; and regions in England and Ireland reputed (by long report) to be places where no one dies until removed elsewhere — concluding that if such natural incorruptibility occurs, God's infinite omnipotence and efficacious will can certainly preserve glorified human bodies eternally without death, as already taught in Part 37.
claims: Reported natural instances of incorruptibility (extended sleep, non-decaying offerings, deathless regions) corroborate the possibility of divinely sustained eternal bodily incorruptibility.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16593.summary: Cites Plato's similar teaching (already quoted regarding the angels) that the created world/heavens were made immortal and indissoluble except by the maker's own will, and applies this analogously to explain how the bodies of the damned, too, must be eternally sustained (in both soul and body) in order to bear eternal misery, as otherwise they could not endure eternal punishment — comparing this to salamanders, Etna, and similar things reputedly unconsumed by fire, but appealing chiefly to God's infinite omnipotence as the real ground.
claims: The damned's bodies, like the blessed's, must be eternally sustained (through divine omnipotence) in order to bear eternal misery.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16614.summary: Concludes that future beatific felicity cannot consist in customary carnal pleasures or in anything besides God, since a body so purified and glorified as to fully serve a perfectly blessed person, without any distraction, could not harbor such base and dishonorable pleasures, which would multiply detract from the perfect beatitude that consists in perfect knowledge, love, delight, and adherence to God.
claims: A glorified body cannot harbor carnal pleasures, since these would detract from perfect beatitude, which consists in perfect knowledge, love, and adherence to God.
concepts: beatitude as knowledge and love of God

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16634.summary: Argues it is more perfect, natural, and blessed for a person to be perfected according to soul rather than body wherever the two conflict, which is why the virtuous who abstain from carnal pleasure are rightly judged more perfect than others; hence in future felicity there will be no conflict between body and soul at all, since such conflict would itself constitute a state of penalty and misery, not consummated felicity; adds that if felicity consisted in customary carnal pleasure, then Epicureans indulging every desire would already be more blessed and virtuous now — a conclusion only a shameless disciple of Epicurus would accept.
claims: Perfect felicity requires the total absence of conflict between body and soul, unlike the ordinary condition where perfection according to soul (continence) is judged superior to bodily indulgence.
If carnal pleasure constituted felicity, hedonistic Epicureans would already be the most blessed and virtuous — an absurd conclusion.
concepts: absence of body-soul conflict in beatitude

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16660.summary: Teaches that beatitude is man's final good, desired for its own sake and not for the sake of anything else, and that nothing but God is rationally desired in this ultimate way (Part 30); asks how the truthful God, who has decreed to be loved and worshipped above all else for his own sake, could then repay his lovers with anything other than himself as final reward, comparing the alternative to a father who promises gold for a day's labor but delivers dung at evening — since anything less than God himself, given to God's true lover, amounts to fraud rather than reward, being incomparably less than nothing by comparison.
claims: Since God alone is loved for his own sake as the final good, only God himself, not any lesser gift, can constitute a fitting final reward for his true lovers.
concepts: reward proportioned to what is loved

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16684.summary: Supports this with Aristotle's Ethics IX on just recompense in human exchange, where he notes disputes arise when parties receive something other than what they sought (as when a musician promised greater payment for better performance is instead offered mere pleasure rather than money) — argues that in the 'exchange' between the lover of God and God himself, where God is what is finally sought, sincerely and above all things, nothing less than God himself could constitute a fair and sufficient recompense, since no other good is comparable, equal, or even close to him.
claims: By Aristotle's own principle of just recompense in human exchange, only God himself, not a substitute good, can be a fair and sufficient reward for one who ultimately seeks God alone.
concepts: incomparability of God to any lesser good

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16713.summary: Argues that the virtuous person who does everything ultimately for God's sake (Part 30) is in continuous motion toward God as final end; since this motion is rectilinear rather than circular, it cannot naturally be infinite (any more than man is naturally, permanently imperfect), and so must terminate in God, citing Aristotle and Averroes on God as the 'beloved' first mover with whom conjunction constitutes man's true final good and 'fortune,' as elaborated in their account of the agent intellect's conjunction with us.
claims: The virtuous person's continuous movement toward God as final end, being rectilinear and thus finite, must terminate in actual union with God, not remain infinitely unresolved.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16795.summary: Argues no finite, small good can satisfy a soul or person who naturally seeks always something greater and better, since experience shows we are never fully at rest in any finite good but always press on to desire something greater; asks how such a natural, reasonable, and honest appetite, implanted by God the author of all nature (and so not implanted in vain), could remain eternally and blamelessly unsatisfied.
claims: The natural human appetite for an ever-greater good cannot remain eternally unsatisfied without frustrating the purpose of the God who implanted it.
concepts: insatiable natural desire for the good

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16811.summary: Breaks into a personal, prayer-like apostrophe to God: only God, infinitely infinite, can satisfy this hunger and desire from and through himself, and if not in the hoped-for future felicity, then where and when? Declares love and ultimate desire for God for God's own sake, asks what God will finally give if not himself — since anything less would be no gift at all, but torment rather than reward — and closes by praying that what is now taught by argument, partial knowledge, and long hope may finally be known by full experience and possession forever.
claims: Only God himself, not any created gift, can satisfy the soul's ultimate desire — expressed here as a direct, personal prayer rather than a formal argument.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16881.summary: Rejects an anticipated hedonistic objection (from 'a disciple of Epicurus, or a son of Mohammed') that since risen humans will have both souls and bodies, they will retain carnal desires and sexual acts amid a sorrow-free happiness, replying that the blessed's bodies will not remain in their prior condition but will be divinely transformed to a better, purer state (as already shown), noting that many humans already naturally lack such desire (children, the elderly, the infirm, the 'bewitched,' those of cold temperament) and that various substances or practices (castration, camphor, chaste-tree, mouse dung) can extinguish sexual appetite — concluding that an omnipotent God can certainly purify blessed bodies so thoroughly that such desire never arises in them at all, since it would be harmful and destructive of perfect beatitude, so that the whole person, soul and body together, will purely and spiritually enjoy perfect eternal beatitude.
claims: The objection that risen embodied humans must retain carnal desire is answered by the doctrine that glorified bodies are divinely purified so that such desire never arises, corroborated by natural and pharmacological analogues of suppressed sexual desire.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16283.summary: Rubric announcing Corollarium 40: against Aristotle, who asserts that the world had no temporal beginning and was not created, that human generation will never end, and that the world or its present state will never end at any time; and against Anaximander, Plato, Anaxagoras, Empedocles, and Muslim theologians who held similar or related positions on the eternity of the world.
concepts: eternity of the world (thesis to be refuted)

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16294.summary: Surveys ancient cosmological positions on the world's origin as the target of refutation: one main tradition holds the world was generated and has a temporal beginning, subdivided into creation from nothing by God versus formation from pre-existing matter, with variants attributed to Anaximander (an infinite chaos of things eternally hidden together, later separated by intellect/God into a world lasting infinite future time), Plato (things fluctuating disorderly before God's eternal ordering into an everlasting world), a view (attributed variously to Anaxagoras or Anaximander) that the world is made and will be destroyed only once, and Empedocles (world formed and destroyed cyclically, infinitely, through strife and friendship acting on the four elements); the other main tradition holds the world is unbegotten (ingenerate), subdivided between certain Muslim theologians (per Averroes) who hold it ingenerable but corruptible, and Aristotle, who holds it both ingenerable and incorruptible — the most famous position and thus the one to be addressed first, since refuting it will make refuting the others easier.
claims: Ancient cosmological positions on the world's eternity are catalogued into two main families (generated-with-beginning versus ingenerate) with multiple sub-variants, with Aristotle's fully eternal (ingenerable and incorruptible) position identified as the primary target.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17032.summary: Presents a first argument against Aristotle's eternity thesis: if the world and human generation are eternal in the past, and (per Part 31 and Aristotle's own position) individual human rational souls are eternal, multiplying without circular return (as the immediately preceding corollarium's refutation of transmigration and Aristotle's own view maintain), then an actually infinite number of separated human souls must presently exist; cites Algazel, Aristotle's follower, conceding exactly this — an actual infinity of separated souls existing together, since there is no natural causal ordering among them whose removal would make others cease to exist — and argues this consequence is so contrary to natural order that it cannot be attributed to God or nature, especially since Aristotle and all genuine philosophers typically hold an actual infinite multitude to be impossible.
claims: Aristotle's eternity-of-the-world thesis, combined with his view of the soul, entails an actually infinite number of presently existing separated human souls — a consequence Algazel explicitly concedes.
An actual infinite multitude of souls is contrary to natural order and to the very impossibility of actual infinites that Aristotle and genuine philosophers generally uphold.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17072.summary: Presses the objection further by Aristotle's own principle that positing more entities where fewer suffice is vain, asking why infinite souls specifically are needed 'for the greater perfection of the universe' rather than infinite angels, spheres, or stars, and argues a finite multitude is actually more perfect than an infinite one, since every praiseworthy kind of number recognized by arithmetic (perfect, spherical, cubic, square, and so on) is finite, while an infinite number can possess none of these praiseworthy properties, just as a finite body (with determinate shape, culminating in the perfect sphere) is more perfect than an infinite one, which has no determinate shape at all.
claims: By Aristotle's own principle of parsimony, positing an actually infinite number of souls is unjustified when a finite number would suffice.
A finite multitude or magnitude is more perfect than an infinite one, since only finite numbers and shapes can possess the determinate, praiseworthy properties arithmetic and geometry recognize.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17109.summary: Argues that order and determination are better and more beautiful than disorder and confusion, quoting Aristotle's Metaphysics rebuking Sophists who deny goodness to mathematics (since order, symmetry, and determination — the chief marks of goodness — are precisely what mathematics exhibits), his Politics on law as a kind of order requiring a city to have a moderate, bounded population, and the Pythagorean identification of limit/finitude with the good and the unlimited/infinite with evil.
claims: Aristotle's own texts (Metaphysics, Politics) affirm that goodness consists essentially in order, symmetry, and determination, which an actual infinite multitude cannot possess.
The Pythagorean tradition explicitly associates the infinite/unlimited with evil and the finite/limited with the good.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17140.summary: Argues beauty consists in order, determination, and fitting proportion, extensively quoting Alhazen's Optics on how beauty in bodies, buildings, painting, and writing arises from the ordered arrangement and proportionality of parts rather than from any single quality alone, and how even number (such as stars in the sky or candles in a house) is beautiful only through its ordered, proportionate arrangement — concluding that an infinite number, lacking any such order, would appear not beautiful but disordered, confused, and unseemly.
claims: Beauty, per Alhazen's Optics, depends essentially on the ordered proportionality of parts, which an actual infinite multitude cannot possess and so cannot be beautiful.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17210.summary: Applies this to argue it would be unfitting for the all-wise God to make his heavenly city — his own household composed of the holy souls of humans — actually infinite in number, and thus disordered, confused, and imperfect, rather than a wisely chosen, fitting, and beautifully ordered finite number, citing Aristotle's Politics on cities requiring a moderate, determinate citizenry, and asking why souls specifically, rather than angels, spheres, stars, or the world's other finite species and individuals, should uniquely be actually infinite.
claims: An actually infinite heavenly city of souls would be disordered and imperfect, contrary to God's wisdom, especially since no other class of beings (angels, spheres, stars, species) is held to be actually infinite.
concepts: singularity of the alleged infinity of souls

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17239.summary: Introduces a more rigorous, quasi-mathematical demonstration against actually infinite souls, to be developed briefly given constraints of time, leaving fuller elaboration to another occasion: supposes that, since infinitely many souls entail infinitely many corresponding bodies (each soul having its own proper body, per the preceding corollarium), those bodies can be arranged in an ordered infinite series — along a straight line extending infinitely, or along a spiral of proportional segments — purely for the sake of formalizing arguments about multitude, independent of bodily size.
claims: A formal, quasi-mathematical demonstration is introduced, modeling the infinite souls' corresponding infinite bodies as an ordered infinite series for rigorous analysis.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17281.summary: Sets up the correspondence formally: let A be the total multitude of all souls and B the total multitude of all corresponding bodies, with each soul having exactly one proper body and each body exactly one proper soul, so that the units of A and B correspond mutually and equally, one-to-one, as the prior part already established.
claims: Set A (all souls) and set B (all bodies) are stipulated to correspond one-to-one, unit for unit.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17311.summary: Constructs the core paradox: distribute souls to bodies with an increasing offset (the first soul to the first body, the second to some more distant body, the third proportionally further still, and so on); either the distribution eventually assigns every soul (implying the whole infinite multitude A corresponds only to a proper subset of B, an apparent contradiction under the axiom that a whole must exceed its part) or some souls remain unassigned after only finitely many steps (implying, absurdly, that the supposedly infinite multitude B is actually finite) — either branch yielding a contradiction of the initial hypothesis that both multitudes are actually infinite.
claims: Distributing souls to bodies with an ever-increasing offset generates a contradiction under either possible outcome, undermining the coherence of positing actually infinite, correspondingly matched multitudes.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17346.summary: Extends the paradox: if instead a thousand souls are assigned to each successive body, either the distribution eventually stops (implying the multitude of bodies, and hence of souls needed, is really finite) or it extends to all bodies (implying, absurdly, that a far smaller sub-collection of souls — such as only the souls of all past popes — would equally suffice to animate the entire infinite multitude of bodies, one-for-one, just as the whole collection of all souls does), illustrated by positing an eternal single ruling office (e.g. 'Pope') whose past-infinite succession of souls alone suffices to animate all bodies.
claims: A vastly smaller infinite sub-collection of souls (e.g., of all past popes) can be shown, by the same reasoning, to suffice for animating the entire infinite multitude of bodies — an absurdity under the whole-exceeds-the-part axiom.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17375.summary: Demonstrates the same paradox via alternating assignment (every other soul assigned to a body in sequence): the whole set of bodies gets fully animated while infinitely many souls remain left over, and this process can be repeated infinitely many times, generating ever more equal-sized collections of bodies, each fully animated, with surplus souls always remaining — showing repeatedly that a proper subset of souls suffices for the whole task.
claims: An alternating (every-other) assignment scheme can be repeated infinitely, each time fully animating an equal-sized new collection of bodies while leaving surplus souls, reinforcing the paradox of a part sufficing for the whole.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17419.summary: Concludes that the multitude A (all souls) suffices to animate B, and also double B, quadruple B, and so on without end, illustrated by further distributions across additional equal collections (C, D, E, etc.), each fully animated from A's surplus without exhausting it — extending the same demonstration that can also be made using the smaller sub-collection of 'papal' souls.
claims: The same infinite multitude of souls can, by the same reasoning, be shown sufficient to animate any multiple (double, quadruple, etc.) of the original body-collection without limit.
concepts: unbounded sufficiency of an infinite multitude

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17456.summary: Shows the same result holds for any multitude of bodies whatsoever, even the much smaller collection of 'papal' souls, which likewise suffices by the same reasoning; concludes such consequences — vast, excessive superfluity of both souls (far more than needed to animate any given number of bodies) and of bodies (far more than needed to house any given number of souls) — are absurd, unbefitting God's wisdom, contrary to nature, and detested by all philosophers.
claims: The demonstrated paradox entails an absurd, excessive superfluity of both souls and bodies beyond what any finite requirement would need, which cannot be attributed to divine wisdom or to nature.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17485.summary: Constructs a further version of the paradox: let all souls approach all bodies and each take exactly one, so that the whole infinite multitude of bodies is animated; yet this same infinite multitude could equally have been animated, one-to-one, by a much smaller infinite sub-collection (such as the souls of all past popes, or an even smaller infinite subset), with no principled reason why the larger rather than the smaller collection is the one actually used — and shows that appealing to 'these souls already animated these bodies before' does not escape the problem, nor does replacing all bodies with new ones, or restricting each soul to exactly one token (e.g., a coin) from a fixed collection.
claims: No principled reason can be given for why one infinite sub-collection of souls rather than another, smaller one, is the collection that actually animates all bodies, since any suffices equally by the same demonstration.
Attempted escapes (appealing to prior animation, or replacing bodies with new ones) fail to resolve the underlying paradox.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17538.summary: Presses the paradox with a coin analogy: if there is a surplus of souls beyond what is needed to animate a given collection of bodies, and the surplus is removed, the remaining necessary number must be either infinite (in which case surplus still remains, since even a thousand-fold ratio would still suffice, as shown) or finite (in which case it cannot suffice to animate infinitely many bodies, one soul each, contradicting the hypothesis); further notes that a surplus of souls implies an equal surplus of corresponding bodies, yet the number of actual humans cannot coherently be said to shrink or stay fixed under either removal or addition of such 'surplus' units, since removing any single soul necessarily de-souls some particular, actually existing human body.
claims: Neither an infinite nor a finite 'necessary remainder' of souls can coherently resolve the surplus paradox once a supposed excess is removed.

A surplus of souls implies a corresponding surplus of bodies, yet actual human count cannot be coherently altered by removing or adding such abstract 'surplus' units without de-souling real individuals.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17577.summary: Turns the same paradox into a wage-labor thought experiment: if each of these infinitely many men received exactly one denarius from God each evening by covenant for a day's labor, the preceding reasoning would seem to entail that they collectively possess a superfluous, indeed infinite, number of coins — yet in reality no one has more than his single coin, and neither any individual nor all of them together possess any coin in common beyond that, exposing the tension between the abstract mathematical manipulation of infinite multitudes and the fixed, determinate reality of one coin per person.
claims: The wage-labor thought experiment (one coin per worker) exposes the same contradiction between mathematically manipulated infinite quantities and the fixed, determinate reality of individual possession.
concepts: fixed reality versus abstract infinite manipulation

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17621.summary: Extends the wage-paradox to further distribution patterns (alternating, every third, every thousandth coin, and so on): whichever pattern is chosen, the workers would still end up, on the prior reasoning, with an infinite surplus beyond their just wage, and God would be equally open to the charge of injustice under any such scheme — showing the incoherence attaches to the very notion of an actually infinite just recompense, not merely to one particular counting method.
claims: The wage-paradox's incoherence persists across every possible distribution pattern, showing the problem lies in positing actually infinite recompense as such, not in any one counting scheme.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16967.summary: Shifts from arguments based on discrete quantity (counting souls) to arguments based on continuous quantity: models the infinitely many human bodies as a single continuous beam infinite in length alone ('infinite in a certain respect,' not in every dimension), then shows that by merely rearranging its existing finite unit-blocks (without adding, multiplying, or rarefying any material) one can reassemble them into a body that is infinite absolutely, in every dimension at once — an evident absurdity, since the same finite content cannot coherently constitute both a merely one-dimensionally infinite body and, through rearrangement alone, a fully infinite one.
claims: Merely rearranging the finite unit-parts of a body infinite in only one dimension can be shown to yield a body infinite in every dimension, without any addition of material — a geometric absurdity undermining the coherence of actually infinite continuous quantity.
concepts: 'infinite in a certain respect' versus 'absolutely infinite'

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17734.summary: Draws out a further 'stupendous and horribly monstrous' consequence of the continuous-quantity paradox: the same finite unit-blocks composing B, without any addition or multiplication, suffice to fill the entire infinite universal void in every direction, and moreover could be shown (by the same method) to construct two, three, or infinitely many such all-encompassing infinite bodies simultaneously, while B itself still retains exactly as many parts as before — an absurd, unbounded multiplication from a fixed finite stock of material.
claims: The same fixed, finite material can be shown, by rearrangement alone, to fill all of infinite space multiple times over while remaining undiminished — an absurd consequence used to reject actually infinite continuous quantity.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17789.summary: Applies this reasoning to refute Democritus' and Epicurus' doctrine of infinitely many worlds (recorded by Augustine, and by John of Salisbury's anecdote of Alexander lamenting, on Democritus' authority, that he had not yet conquered even one world despite there being infinitely many, and by Lactantius), arguing that even collecting the smallest conceivable particle (a speck of dust) from each of infinitely many worlds would, by the prior demonstration, already fill the entire universal space, leaving no room for the actual, much larger bodies of those worlds — especially telling given that the sphere, the most space-efficient shape by geometrical proof, is the natural shape such collected particles would take.
claims: The infinite-worlds doctrine of Democritus and Epicurus is refuted by the same continuous-quantity paradox: collecting even the smallest particle from each of infinitely many worlds would already exhaust all available space.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17834.summary: Further develops the geometric paradox by adding an equal body C to B and rearranging parts to show one 'absolutely infinite' body could be made strictly larger than another such infinite body, which should be impossible if both are truly infinite in the same respect; asks why an absolutely infinite quantity should be uniquely possible for bodies and not for other things, such as a human soul or body of infinite intensive perfection, which would subvert the whole of geometry — an evident absurdity.
claims: The paradox shows one 'absolutely infinite' body could be made strictly larger than another, which should be impossible, and extending infinite intensive perfection to souls or bodies would subvert geometry entirely.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17880.summary: Opens a third line of attack based on the collective 'power' (potentia) of the infinitely many souls, assumed individually equal: this total power A must be either absolutely infinite (yet shown augmentable by adding more souls or intensifying their power, and in any case exceeded by God's own omnipotence, so not truly maximal) or finite (which fails, since any finite multiple of the individual souls' power — double for two souls, triple for three, and so on — exceeds every finite bound), and invokes Euclid's Elements Book V on ratios and equal magnitudes to formalize the contradiction this generates.
claims: The collective active power of infinitely many souls can be shown, via Euclidean ratio theory, to be neither coherently finite nor coherently the greatest possible infinite, since it is always augmentable and exceeded by God's power.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17943.summary: Continues the Euclidean ratio-based argument, showing that a posited infinite active power C (granted hypothetically through divine power) must, by the logic of equal ratios, be equal to the total power A of all souls, yet cannot coherently be equal to it either, since a greater or differently-sized multitude D could always be constructed under the same hypothesis — demonstrating that no coherent, determinate value can be assigned to 'the total power of infinitely many souls.'
claims: No coherent, determinate value can be assigned to the total power of an actually infinite collection of souls, since Euclidean ratio reasoning forces contradictory equalities.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17985.summary: Considers a single angel of intensively infinite power posited equal to the total power of all souls, and derives further contradictions via Euclidean ratio theorems by removing finite or even infinite proper sub-collections of souls (such as all male souls, leaving only female or only 'papal' souls) — showing that the remaining sub-collection's total power would have to equal both the whole and something less than the whole, an impossibility, and thus that infinite multitudes of souls of any size or intensity would paradoxically all have to be 'equal' to one another.
claims: Removing any proper sub-collection, however defined, from an infinite collection of souls generates a contradiction under Euclidean ratio reasoning, forcing the absurd conclusion that infinite multitudes of any size are all mutually equal in power.
concepts: forced equality of all infinite multitudes

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18042.summary: Considers the alternative that not all infinite multitudes are equal, positing a hypothetical infinite multitude of angels double the souls' multitude in both number and power, and attempts to establish, via one-to-one correspondence per unit and the Euclidean axiom that things placed in correspondence without excess are equal, that the two multitudes must actually be numerically equal despite the stipulation that one is 'double' the other — generating a further contradiction that undermines any coherent notion of proportional relations ('double,' 'greater') between actually infinite multitudes ordered in series.
claims: Attempting to posit one actually infinite multitude as strictly 'double' another, while also establishing their one-to-one correspondence per the Euclidean equality axiom, generates a contradiction, showing that no coherent proportional relation between actual infinite multitudes can be maintained.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18140.summary: Argues that whatever power an infinite multitude of souls could jointly have, a single form could equally have by sheer intensity, and vice versa; sets up a single intensively infinite power B and an equal-power infinite multitude of souls C, and derives the same contradiction as before, since C (being a multitude) can always be shown augmentable and thus not truly maximal, undermining the coherence of positing it as absolutely infinite in power.
claims: An infinite multitude's total power and a single intensively infinite form's power are shown interchangeable in principle, yet the multitude case again proves incoherent since it remains augmentable.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18178.summary: Considers a soul A of infinite intensive power set against a hypothetical body B of equal resisting weight — by natural rules a mover cannot move a body whose resistance equals or exceeds its own power, so A could not move B; yet by gradually increasing a finite body's weight it must at some point become equal to A's infinite power, and by the earlier rearrangement-paradox a body's finite parts can be reassembled into one of infinite extent and weight, generating contradictory conclusions about whether A, despite being infinite, can move any such body.
claims: Positing a soul of infinite intensive motive power generates contradictions when tested against bodies of correspondingly increasing or rearranged weight, via the earlier established paradoxes of continuous infinite quantity.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18241.summary: Continues the motion-based paradox: if A can move C, A must exceed C in power, so an intermediate soul of power between the two (less than infinite A, more than C) could be posited — yet being finite, this intermediate soul could not move a body so vastly exceeding it in weight, generating a further contradiction; extends the same reasoning to show A cannot coherently move any body of finite extent but infinite intensive weight either.
claims: Positing an intermediate power between an infinite mover and its object generates further contradictions, reinforcing that no coherent account of infinite motive power succeeds.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18282.summary: Constructs a further Euclidean argument (citing Elements V.9) proving that a body of finite, uniform intensive weight but infinite extent is equal in total weight to a body of infinite intensive weight but finite extent, leading to the absurd conclusion that whole and part, double and half, would have to be equal in weight — reinforcing the earlier-established principle that comparably 'infinite-exceeding-by-infinite' magnitudes collapse into forced, absurd equalities.
claims: A Euclidean ratio argument shows that infinite-extent and infinite-intensity bodies of differing total content must be treated as equal in weight, entailing the absurdity that a whole equals its own part.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18356.summary: Proposes resolving lingering doubt with a physical balance-scale analogy — imagining souls of stipulated infinite power weighed against one another — and shows the same contradiction persists: either the supposedly infinite power is not truly maximal (since combining two such souls should, by the balance's logic, tip the scale and yield something greater), or one 'infinite' quantity must be shown proportionately double or triple another 'infinite' quantity, which is itself the same absurdity already demonstrated for comparing actual infinites.
claims: A balance-scale thought experiment applied to infinite powers reproduces the same contradiction already established for comparing actual infinite magnitudes.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e17666.summary: Introduces an argument from local motion: a body A of finite extent but infinite intensive weight, if placed above its natural place, must fall — either instantaneously (impossible, since it has some resistance, and this would hold in any medium regardless of resistance, and would require passing from one extreme to another without traversing intermediate points, an absurdity) or successively at some finite speed (which would make it fall no faster than any ordinary finite-weight body in the same medium, contradicting its supposed infinite weight); rejects Avempace's proposed escape, that heavy bodies have an inherent finite natural speed regardless of weight, since a body's weight determines its natural inclination and speed proportionally, so infinite weight should entail infinite appetite for motion and speed.
claims: A body of infinite intensive weight generates contradiction under both possible modes of falling (instantaneous or successive), refuting the coherence of infinite intensive weight in a physical body.
Avempace's proposed escape (fixed finite natural speed independent of weight) fails, since weight is shown to proportionally determine natural speed.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18435.summary: Extends the same style of argument to alteration (an infinitely hot fire A burning a finite combustible B, generating the same instantaneous-versus-successive dilemma as with motion) and to natural place (where an infinitely light and infinitely hot fire would naturally seek to be located, which would require it to seek a point infinitely distant from the earth's center — yet, per Euclid, any two points admit only a finite straight-line distance between them, since a line is by definition terminated at both endpoints, making 'infinite distance' between two locations incoherent).
claims: The same instantaneous/successive dilemma applies to alteration (infinite heat burning a finite object), and the notion of an 'infinitely distant' natural place is incoherent given Euclid's definition of a finite terminated line between any two points.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18467.summary: Argues via pure intensity that any actually infinite intensive form, if diminished by subtracting any finite part, must leave a remaining part that is finite (since two finite parts can never compose an actual infinite, as shown, and the diminished part cannot coherently be called 'infinite in a certain respect' either, since an infinitely intensive quality, however slightly diminished, immediately becomes finite, being bounded both by an intrinsic upper degree and by the absence of the quality below) — showing that positing an actually infinite intensive quality collapses into contradiction the moment any diminishment is considered.
claims: An actually infinite intensive quality cannot coherently survive even minimal diminishment without collapsing into finitude, refuting the possibility of such a quality.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18550.summary: Refines the same intensity-based argument with a specific division (D as infinite heat, E and F as its two parts), showing E cannot be infinite 'upward' since D exceeds it and a part cannot equal its whole, and that E stands in a finite ratio to any other finite heat, so that no combination of finite-seeming parts (E and F) can be shown to reconstitute something truly infinite — reinforcing the prior conclusion against actual infinite intensity.
claims: A part of a posited infinite intensive quality cannot itself be shown infinite, and no combination of its parts reconstitutes genuine infinity, reinforcing the rejection of actual infinite intensity.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18570.summary: Turns to an argument from divine omnipotence: if God could make something actually infinite in number or intensity, he could make a creature possessing, really or supereminently, all possible powers infinitely — effectively another god, or multiple gods, contradicting Part 17's proof of God's uniqueness; even granting that God cannot make a creature necessarily existent and eternal like himself, but only grants it every other possible perfection infinitely, this 'most perfect possible creature' would still be shown, by the same infinite-versus-infinite-in-a-certain-respect reasoning used throughout, to remain infinitely inferior to God — meaning God could always make something still more perfect, contradicting the premise that it was already maximally perfect.
claims: If God could create something actually infinite, he could create a rival 'god' or a supposedly maximally perfect creature that, by the argument's own logic, would still always admit of a more perfect creature, contradicting its supposed maximality — used to reject creaturely actual infinity.
concepts: impossibility of a maximally perfect creature

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18618.summary: Continues the omnipotence argument: if God could make something actually infinite, he could make an 'omnipotent' creature A, which must be either equal in power to God (impossible, since every creature depends on God as its necessary conserving and co-acting cause and cannot act at all without him) or less powerful than God, in which case God — even granting the false hypothesis that A could act independently — would still be infinitely more powerful, since God could always prevent or counteract A's actions (such as stopping a wheel A tries to move), and could do so even against any number of such creatures combined, since whatever power any creature or combination of creatures might have, God has it too, per the first Supposition.
claims: A creature cannot coherently be made equal in power to God, since creatures depend on God as necessary conserving and co-acting cause and cannot act independently of him.
Even granting a creature independent action, God remains infinitely more powerful, since he could always prevent or counteract any creature's or combination of creatures' actions.
concepts: God's power to counteract any creature

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18714.summary: Continues arguing the posited 'omnipotent' creature A cannot be equal to God, since A cannot destroy God whereas God can destroy A; if A is less powerful, a still greater power could exist and impede A, and even a merely equal hypothetical power could impede or, jointly with another, overpower A — refuting A's omnipotence; rejects the objection that no power could be made equal to an already-omnipotent creature, since that itself would deny God's own omnipotence, given God could destroy A and create an equal replacement B, or preserve both together.
claims: A creature cannot coherently be either equal to or capable of resisting God's power, and any attempt to block God from creating an equal rival would itself deny divine omnipotence.
concepts: impossibility of a rival omnipotent creature

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18749.summary: Simplifies the argument to a creature A possessing just one infinite active power (e.g., infinite local motive power), shown by the same reasoning to be either impossibly equal to God or necessarily augmentable and thus not truly infinite; introduces the key move by which opponents try to escape all these paradoxes — denying the axiom that a whole is always greater than its part, and instead claiming an infinite whole and its infinite part (or two infinite multitudes) are simply equal — and rebuts this by invoking Euclid's foundational, self-evident axiom (Elements I) that a whole always exceeds its part, affirmed by all mathematicians and natural philosophers and demonstrated syllogistically (via Alhazen) as: whatever contains another thing and more is greater than it; every whole contains its part and more; therefore every whole is greater than its part.
claims: A single-power version of the argument again forces A to be finite, not infinite.
Opponents' escape route — denying that a whole exceeds its part for infinite quantities — contradicts Euclid's foundational, self-evident axiom, defended here by an explicit syllogism.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18807.summary: Argues further that any multitude increases when units are added and decreases when subtracted, especially by an equal infinite multitude, so the whole multitude of all souls should be double the multitude of male souls alone and double female souls alone (since both are infinite) — a conclusion the opponents' 'infinites are all equal' position must deny, against evident sense; closes with an aside noting that anyone would rather flee a punishment lasting from now into eternity than one beginning after a thousand years but continuing eternally thereafter, implying real quantitative differences even among unending durations.
claims: The opponents' position that all infinite multitudes are equal contradicts the evident fact that the whole (all souls) should be double each of its infinite halves (male, female).
Even among unending durations, the moment a punishment begins matters, suggesting genuine quantitative difference persists despite eternity.
concepts: whole as double its infinite halves

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18836.summary: Shows the 'all infinites are equal' position would force calling an eternal punishment A and a punishment of half its intensity B equal, demonstrated via a proportional geometric construction of two matching infinite-in-one-dimension beams whose corresponding finite measures are shown, under the opponents' logic, to be equal despite differing in intensity.
claims: The opponents' position entails the absurd conclusion that an eternal punishment and one of only half its intensity must be counted as equal.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18860.summary: Continues the geometric demonstration by analogy to a piece of wood and its half, proving that under the 'infinites are equal' position, infinite bodies or weights of manifestly different intensity or extent would absurdly have to be counted as literally identical, invoking Euclid's proposition on proportional quantities (Elements V.16) to formalize the contradiction, and a balance-scale fairness argument to press the point further.
claims: Formal geometric proportion theory (Euclid V.16) and a balance-scale analogy both confirm that the opponents' position collapses manifestly different infinite quantities into absurd identity.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18928.summary: Extends the balance-scale demonstration to two equal infinite multitudes of souls, arguing that under the opponents' position no scale-tipping should ever occur even when a combined multitude is added to one side, which no reasonable judgment of a fair scale would accept; concludes this position entails absurdly that no creature could ever grow in power by any addition whatsoever, contrary to God's evident freedom to augment any finite creature, as the first Supposition and Part 7 establish.
claims: The opponents' position implies a creature's power could never be increased by addition, contradicting the established freedom of God to augment finite creatures.
concepts: impossibility of creaturely growth under the opposing view

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18993.summary: Applies the same 'infinite part equals the whole' logic to God's own perfections, showing it would absurdly entail that if some part of God's infinite knowledge or power (such as knowledge of geometry) were subtracted, God would remain just as knowing and powerful as before — and, worse, that some other being possessing all but one of God's perfections would then be equally perfect and powerful as God himself, a blasphemous consequence the first Supposition and following parts expressly prevent and refute.
claims: Applying the opponents' logic to God's own infinite perfections yields the blasphemous consequence that a being lacking only one of God's perfections would be equally perfect as God.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19039.summary: Cites Robert Grosseteste, Bishop of Lincoln, in his treatise on light, showing that all proportions found among finite quantities can likewise be constructed among infinite ones (e.g., all even numbers being double all multiples of four, all groups of seven being quadruple all months), granted the common assumption that such infinite multitudes actually exist; concedes that even granting this 'impossible' position for argument's sake, it still fails to answer many of the objections raised, and, pressed for time, defers further possible objections and responses to another occasion, closing the extended 'via infiniti' (argument from infinity) against Aristotle and Algazel.
claims: Robert Grosseteste's treatise on light shows proportional relations can be formally constructed among infinite multitudes, but this does not rescue the opposing position from the objections already raised.
The author explicitly closes this extended technical argument from infinity, acknowledging further objections exist but deferring them for lack of time.
concepts: closure of the via infiniti argument

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18310.summary: Shifts to a new, non-mathematical argument: asks how, on Aristotle's own philosophy, something merely possible (contingent) — as the world is shown to be in Part 17 — could be past-eternal, since Aristotle's own principles hold that whatever is merely possible does not exist sufficiently of itself but continually depends on another cause both producing and conserving it; addresses the counter-suggestion that a 'new' world could still, without formal contradiction, have been made eternal by God (as an eternal footprint from an eternal foot in co-eternal dust, or an eternal reflection from an eternal face in a co-eternal mirror), replying that if so, then neither the world's newness nor its eternity is strictly necessary or demonstrable a priori, since both depend on the free, non-necessary divine will (Parts 33–34) — and by the same logic other actually new creatures, like a given soul, could likewise have been eternal, challenging Aristotle to demonstrate with strict necessity that any particular soul is new rather than eternal, promising to reciprocate with a demonstration that the world is new rather than eternal, provided neither side smuggles in merely accidental necessity.
claims: Aristotle's own principle that the merely possible depends continually on another cause conflicts with holding the world (itself merely possible) to be past-eternal.

If a 'new' world could still coherently have existed eternally (per the footprint/mirror analogies), then neither the world's newness nor its eternity is strictly demonstrable, since both depend on the free divine will — a challenge issued reciprocally to Aristotle regarding the soul's newness.
concepts: contingency and dependence on a cause

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19123.summary: Reasserts that the possibility of the world's creation and temporal beginning has already been shown, and that all peoples (Hebrews, Greeks, Latins, and other nations), all prophets, theologians, poets, and all philosophers before Aristotle unanimously affirmed that the world had a temporal beginning, a consensus attested by every law and sect and by numerous famous histories, including Aristotle's own books.
claims: A near-universal consensus of peoples, prophets, theologians, poets, and pre-Aristotelian philosophers affirms the world's temporal beginning, against Aristotle's isolated eternity thesis.
concepts: consensus for a created, temporally-begun world

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19134.summary: Cites Hermes Trismegistus — called 'Father of Philosophers' even by Aristotle's own testimony — extensively from De Verbo Aeterno as teaching that the world and man were created by God with a real temporal beginning: that 'all things were in the creator before he created all things,' that God governs heaven, soul, and all things in the world as their effector, that the world was prepared by God as a receptacle for all forms, that man is an image of God alongside the world, and that worldly things 'were not when they were not, but already existed in him whence they were to arise'; further cites the Emerald Tablet ('all things were from one... all things were born from this one thing by adaptation') and Hermes' De Mundo et Coelo affirming that time began from eternity and returns into eternity's bosom, that the temporal world relates to eternity as a circle to its center, that the firmament's motion has continued unchanged from the hour it was divinely formed, that no one witnessed the world's actual day of origin, and that a great periodic renewal (apocatastasis) occurs roughly every three hundred years by fire or flood — noting that a great multitude of celebrated later philosophers concordantly follow their 'father' Hermes on this teaching.
claims: Hermes Trismegistus' De Verbo Aeterno is read as affirming that the world and man were really created by God with a temporal beginning, contrary to Aristotle's eternity thesis.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19217.summary: Adds that Egyptian priests, per the prologue to Plato's Timaeus and Solinus, dated the world's 'birthday' to a specific astronomical moment (the sun in Leo, in late July); that Plato's Timaeus explicitly affirms the world, worldly things, angels, and man had a temporal beginning; and that Anaxagoras, Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, Parmenides, Melissus, and, in short, all the 'fathers' of philosophy, all philosophers, prophets, theologians, and poets before Aristotle's time concordantly affirmed the world's temporal beginning, as ancient histories and even Aristotle's own natural and metaphysical books attest.
claims: Egyptian tradition, Plato's Timaeus, and essentially all pre-Aristotelian philosophers unanimously affirm the world's temporal beginning, against Aristotle's isolated position.
concepts: Egyptian dating of the world's origin

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19252.summary: Cites Aristotle's own text (De Caelo I.102), which acknowledges 'all say the heaven is generated,' and Averroes' commentary confirming that all agree heaven is generated and that no one before Aristotle ever claimed heaven is ungenerated — crediting Aristotle himself, on Averroes' testimony, as the very first Greek philosopher to make this claim — and cites Augustine (City of God VIII.12) noting that Aristotle nonetheless gathered many disciples into what Augustine calls his 'heresy' on this point.
claims: Aristotle's own text and Averroes' commentary identify Aristotle as the first philosopher ever to claim the heavens are ungenerated, against universal prior consensus, a point Augustine also notes.
concepts: Aristotle as sole originator of the eternity thesis

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19272.summary: Challenges Aristotle rhetorically: why should his solitary, rash assertion outweigh the united testimony of so many peoples, prophets, theologians, poets, and philosophers, especially since his supporting arguments are weak — barely sophistic, as already shown regarding Part 34 — and most of his objections against Plato and others (in the Physics and De Caelo) have no real rational force, obvious even to one with minimal training in logic; declines to refute them in detail as unworthy of the effort, since virtually anyone who examines them can see their weakness, whereas no one has ever found a way even faintly to undermine the position held by Hermes, the prophets, and the Christians (per Parts 33–34); asks what overwhelmingly strong, certain, and irrefutable arguments would be needed to overturn such a longstanding, near-universal, and pious conviction.
claims: Aristotle's supporting arguments for the eternity thesis are weak and barely sophistic, unlike the unassailable position shared by Hermes, the prophets, and Christian doctrine.
Overturning such a longstanding, near-universal, pious consensus would require far stronger argumentation than Aristotle provides.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19323.summary: Proposes as a general rule that, among otherwise equal opinions, the one more honoring to God, more widely held, more religious, and more favorable to humanity should always prevail; illustrates this by imagining virtually all peoples, nations, sects, prophets, poets, and philosophers, past and present, unanimously holding the world was created by God, against which Aristotle, lacking prophetic gift or evident miracle, offers only contrary arguments — concluding this would convince no one and would instead make Aristotle appear ridiculous, and notes that many later philosophers indeed mocked his arguments and refused to be called 'Peripatetics,' preferring 'Academics' or 'Platonists' instead.
claims: A general rule is proposed: among otherwise equal opinions, the one more honoring to God, more widely held, and more favorable to humanity should prevail.
Historically, many later philosophers rejected Aristotle's school affiliation, preferring identification with Plato instead, reflecting a judgment against Aristotle's position.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19358.summary: Cites Augustine (City of God VIII.12) explaining his own preference for the Platonists as the best philosophical school because of their superior teaching on the one God who made heaven and earth, and recounting that although Aristotle, Plato's student, founded the Peripatetic school and gathered many followers even during Plato's lifetime, after Plato's death his school (the Academy) passed to Speusippus and Xenocrates, becoming known as 'Academics' — yet later noble philosophers preferred to be called 'Platonists' rather than 'Peripatetics' or 'Academics,' among them the Greeks Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Porphyry, and, in both Greek and Latin, Apuleius of Africa.
claims: Augustine's testimony (City of God VIII.12) shows that later prominent philosophers preferred identification as 'Platonists' over 'Peripatetics' or 'Academics,' reflecting a historical preference against Aristotle's school.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19391.summary: Cites Calcidius's commentary on Plato's Timaeus mocking and rejecting Aristotle's criticisms of his teacher Plato, characterizing Aristotle as having selected from Plato's full and perfect teaching only what suited him while carelessly neglecting the rest, and describing later philosophers, like poor heirs squandering their father's estate, as having broken Plato's rich and complete teaching into fragmentary, diminished opinions.
claims: Calcidius's commentary on the Timaeus explicitly mocks Aristotle's treatment of Plato's teaching as selective and diminishing.
concepts: critique of Aristotle's selective use of Plato

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19407.summary: Notes that even the astronomer Ptolemy, who elsewhere cites and follows Aristotle approvingly, flatly contradicts him on this point, stating in the Almagest's second prologue that the science of the stars likens man to his Creator and pledging to add material fostering love of the eternal celestial science 'up to the limit their maker set for them' (implying the heavens have a maker), and further citing Ptolemy (Almagest III.1) remarking, in determining the length of the solar year, that investigating 'the whole time' since observations began would not stem from love of knowledge or truth, since that 'whole time' is simply the entire span elapsed since the creation of the world — asking rhetorically who would even attempt to reckon 'the whole time' if the world's duration were actually infinite.
claims: Ptolemy's Almagest explicitly refers to the heavens as having a maker and to 'the whole time' as measured from the creation of the world, implicitly rejecting an eternal past.
concepts: creation of the world in astronomical reckoning

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19438.summary: Cites the astrologer Albumasar (following Ptolemy rather than Aristotle) at length on astrological causation of the elements and seasons by the sun as ordained by the 'omnipotent Creator,' on the planets' positions 'at the beginning of their creation,' on the 'horoscope of the world' (Cancer as the ascendant sign at creation), on the naming of the days of the week beginning from the Sun/Sunday, and on a specific chronological reckoning that 2,226 years, one month, three days, and four hours elapsed from the creation to the Friday night on which the Flood occurred — presented as testimony from esteemed ancient astrological and historical tradition against Aristotle's eternity thesis.
claims: Albumasar's astrological tradition, including a precise chronology from creation to the Flood, provides further authoritative testimony against Aristotle's eternity-of-the-world thesis.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19555.summary: Argues that even Aristotle himself, compelled by truth, sometimes seems to affirm the contrary position, quoting his De Mundo calling the world 'every ordering and creation preserved by God and through God,' and the ancient, paternal teaching common to all humans that 'all things exist from God and through God'; also cites his discussion (De Mundo) of how the world, composed of contrary elements, remains incorrupt, invoking Heraclitus (whom Aristotle's own De Caelo I.102 credits with holding the world is new/created) on the harmony of opposites — convergent and divergent, consonant and dissonant, hot and cold, wet and dry, light and heavy, straight and circular — unified into one cosmic harmony.
claims: Aristotle's own De Mundo, compelled by truth, describes the world as created and preserved by God, in apparent tension with his eternity thesis elsewhere.
Aristotle's De Caelo credits Heraclitus with holding the world is new/created, invoked here via the harmony-of-opposites doctrine.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19600.summary: Continues citing the pseudo-Aristotelian Secret of Secrets at length: on natural virtues divinely implanted in plants and stones, on justice pertaining to man's relation to himself and his Creator, and on an elaborate cosmogony in which God first formed a simple spiritual substance called 'Intelligence' containing the forms of all things, from which proceeded a lesser substance called 'Soul,' and then unformed matter ('Hyle') extended in three dimensions constituting simple body, then the noblest-shaped bodies (the heavenly spheres) formed from the purest remaining matter; describes the universal Soul as a spiritual power arising after Intelligence by divine will, with intellective, sensitive, and vegetative faculties (the last governed by seven natural powers); and describes God's creation of man as noblest of animals, commanded, prohibited, punished, and rewarded, his body a 'city' ruled by intellect as 'king' — identifying the 'Adam' mentioned earlier in the work as the first man created by God at the world's beginning.
claims: The pseudo-Aristotelian Secret of Secrets presents an elaborate emanationist cosmogony (Intelligence, Soul, Hyle, spheres, man) explicitly grounded in divine creation, and names Adam as the first created man.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19646.summary: Anticipates and answers the objection that Aristotle did not actually write the Secret of Secrets, citing his ancient biography's statement that he wrote a 'Book of the Kingdom' for Alexander, and several translators' prologues (including one by 'Philip' and another by 'John') attesting that Aristotle, 'Prince of Philosophers,' composed the work at his disciple King Alexander's request, later translated from Greek through Chaldean/Syriac into Arabic; argues the text's plainer or different style does not disprove Aristotle's authorship, since he would naturally have written differently for a king, and since translation — especially sense-for-sense translation through intermediate languages, as the prologues themselves indicate — can account for stylistic differences found in several of his other works too; notes the text is not uniformly easy either, citing an obscure alchemical passage on the 'Philosophers' Stone' that resists easy explanation.
claims: The objection that Aristotle did not write the Secret of Secrets is answered by appeal to his ancient biography and multiple translators' prologues attesting his authorship, with stylistic differences explained by audience and translation history.
concepts: authenticity of the Secret of Secrets

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19692.summary: Notes that even near death, Aristotle reportedly corrected, before many wise men, his earlier proud error concerning the eternity of the world, humbly confessing his prior mistake, according to his own testimony in the pseudo-Aristotelian work on his death (already cited regarding Part 34); cites that same work at length on the soul's delights — understanding one's creator, considering the works and wisdom of the heavens, the courses and forms of the spheres, and that all things are founded in God's wisdom and knowledge — and, for those unable to grasp such great matters, contemplating instead the subtlety of one's own body, in which nothing needs adding or changing, so as to recognize the creator within oneself; reports a passage distinguishing two 'sects' of penetrating thinkers, one of which denies any beginning or end to the world, holding the earth stands forever without any sustaining cause ('deniers of the root,' i.e. of creation), against which Aristotle is shown approving the contrary, corroborating a partial retraction already discussed; defends the work's authenticity, arguing that if lesser figures' deathbed accounts are recorded, it is plausible that other philosophers, especially Peripatetics and disciples, gathered at so famous a philosopher's death and recorded what they witnessed, as public tradition attests.
claims: Aristotle reportedly recanted his eternity-of-the-world error near death, per the pseudo-Aristotelian account of his death, already cited regarding Part 34.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19753.summary: Offers to substantiate the claim about the soul's creation from Aristotle's own better-known and more famous texts, quoting De Anima ('the intellect seems to be a certain substance that exists and is not corrupted,' per Averroes' translation) and Metaphysics XII (already cited) that the intellective soul does not temporally precede the individual it belongs to but remains after it — concluding that on Aristotle's own words this soul exists in and together with the animated individual, is not educed from the potency of matter like other material forms (which would make it corruptible, contrary to his own view), and so must come to be through creation by God, especially since (per his own texts here) there is no circular return of souls.
claims: Aristotle's own De Anima and Metaphysics texts imply the rational soul is not educed from matter's potency and does not pre-exist its individual, which points to creation by God as its origin.
concepts: Aristotle's De Anima on the intellect
creation of the soul (from Aristotle's own texts)

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19777.summary: Adds that the most illustrious prophets most clearly testify that the world was created by God and had a temporal beginning, referring back to Part 32's demonstration of the prophets' authority and the credibility owed to their pronouncements.
claims: The prophets' authority, already established in Part 32, further corroborates the world's creation and temporal beginning.
