dcn2br-d1e796-d1e18982.summary: Concludes from all the preceding evidence that any sober, non-obstinate person can reasonably see the world not only had a temporal beginning but was created from nothing, since no preceding matter could account for it (whether simple or composite, eternal or new) — noting that Aristotle himself frequently and reasonably argues the world was not made from any pre-existing matter, so it follows naturally and consistently that, having conceded the world had a temporal beginning, one should likewise concede it was created from nothing.
claims: Combining the world's temporal beginning with Aristotle's own argument against pre-existing matter naturally entails creation from nothing.
concepts: consistency with Aristotle's own rejection of pre-existing matter

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19807.summary: Raises and begins addressing an objection: that the Chaldean sages, per Averroes' commentary on De Caelo, held the world to be truly eternal, without beginning or end, before Aristotle's time, and that Plato's Timaeus reports an Egyptian priest mocking Solon for recounting only one flood when infinitely many had preceded, and claiming Egyptian cities and laws existed for eight or nine thousand years — appearing to suggest the world began, if at all, far earlier than sacred scripture records, potentially undermining scripture's prophetic authority; responds that, properly considered, the ancient Chaldeans did not actually hold the world eternal, since any pre-Flood law or prophecy they might have had could not be verified (everything having perished in the Flood), and that Babylon itself was founded by Noah's sons after the Flood, from whom Noah, Shem, and Abraham later taught the Babylonians/Chaldeans the sciences — implying the Chaldeans in fact knew and taught that the world and heavens were created by God, a teaching that passed from the Chaldeans to the Egyptians and from them to the Greeks, all of whom (before Aristotle) concordantly held the world had a temporal beginning, as Aristotle himself admits regarding the ancients' consensus.
claims: The objection from Chaldean and Egyptian eternalist claims is answered by tracing the actual transmission of knowledge (Chaldean to Egyptian to Greek) back to post-Flood teachers (Noah, Shem, Abraham) who held the world was created, consistent with the universal pre-Aristotelian consensus.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19885.summary: Argues that Averroes' motivating consideration (drawn from Aristotle) — that all ancient peoples agree heaven is the incorruptible dwelling place of spirits and of the creator, and is therefore eternal — is unpersuasive, since spirits themselves began temporally yet are incorruptible, so heaven could likewise have begun temporally while being incorruptible, and since the creator needs no place at all (per the first Supposition and Part 5) but is himself needed by every place and located thing for their very existence, making every place and located thing, on Aristotle's own reasoning, incorruptible and eternal — an absurd overreach; notes further that, read strictly, the ancients' own words (that heaven is the place of the 'creator') imply they held God to be not merely a maker but a true creator.
claims: Averroes' argument from heaven being the eternal dwelling of incorruptible spirits and the creator fails, since spirits and every locatable thing would then absurdly have to be eternal too, and since the ancients' own language implies belief in a true creator, not merely an eternal cosmos.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19920.summary: Notes that Aristotle himself elsewhere testifies that all the ancients said heaven was generated, which conflicts with the eternalist reading of them; questions the Egyptian priest's claimed knowledge of infinitely many past floods, since it rests neither on direct observation, nor on reliable report (which at most proves something was said, not that it was true), nor on any credible written record, leaving no legitimate basis for such a confident, ancient historical claim.
claims: The Egyptian priest's claim of infinitely many past floods has no legitimate epistemic basis — not observation, reliable report, or credible written record.
concepts: epistemic critique of the Egyptian priest's claim

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19942.summary: Counters with the account of Noah's universal Flood, which covered even the highest mountains near Egypt by fifteen cubits and destroyed Egyptian shrines and books, as attested not only by Christian histories but also by Indian, Egyptian, and Chaldean sources; cites Josephus (Jewish Antiquities I.2), who after recounting the general Flood invokes as corroborating witnesses Berosus the Chaldean (on the surviving remains of the ark on a mountain in Armenia), Hieronymus the Egyptian, and Manasseh of Damascus (on refugees saved on Mount Baris in Armenia and the preserved wood of the ark, identified with the same event Moses recorded), and notes Albumasar, instructed by ancient records, likewise acknowledges this Flood, as do other astronomers whose astronomical eras, epochs, and tables are dated from the time of the Flood.
claims: Multiple independent non-Christian sources (Berosus the Chaldean, Hieronymus the Egyptian, Manasseh of Damascus, Albumasar, and astronomical tables) corroborate the universal Flood, undermining the Egyptian priest's claim of an uninterrupted, uncatastrophic ancient history.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e19984.summary: Notes that Solon himself, per Plato's Timaeus prologue, recounted ancient Athenian history back through the Flood associated with Pyrrha and Deucalion, tracing the lineage of the renewed human race; asks why, if Egypt were truly eternal and never devastated by flood or fire as the priest claimed, its philosophy and philosophical books were not likewise eternally preserved there, as its historical records supposedly were — noting that in fact the Egyptians received mathematical sciences from the Chaldeans and Abraham, as previously shown and corroborated by other histories.
claims: The claim of an uninterrupted, undevastated ancient Egyptian civilization is inconsistent with the historical fact that Egypt received its mathematical sciences from the Chaldeans and Abraham, implying no unbroken indigenous philosophical tradition.
concepts: inconsistency in the Egyptian priest's claim
transmission of sciences from Chaldea/Abraham to Egypt

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e20006.summary: Notes other histories record when and from whom the Egyptians first received writing, well after the general Flood, undermining the old priest's claims further, especially since other Egyptian priests themselves concordantly affirm a datable birthday of the world (as previously cited); acknowledges various historical records of localized floods but only one truly universal flood, Noah's; addresses the vast numbers of years claimed by the priest by proposing they reflect not standard solar years but shorter reckonings — since it is well known that solar, lunar, and various other year-lengths (Egyptian, Roman, Arabic lunar, Hebrew, embolismic and non-embolismic) were used historically, some far shorter than the modern solar year.
claims: The Egyptian priest's implausibly vast year-counts are explained by ancient peoples' use of much shorter year-definitions (lunar months, seasonal quarters, etc.) rather than standard solar years.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e20066.summary: Supports the calendrical reinterpretation with further examples: Ovid and other historians report early Romans (before Numa Pompilius) used ten-month years, matching the duration of human gestation, with even earlier peoples using shorter years still; Solinus reports pre-Augustan calendars varying from four months (Egypt) to three (Arcadia) to six (Caria); Pliny reports some peoples reckoned a year as one summer and another as one winter, others by four seasons (Arcadian trimestral years), and Egyptians sometimes by a single lunar month, explaining reports of individuals living many 'thousands of years' — concludes such considerations dissolve the wonder at Egypt's vast reported year-counts, and reaffirms that the world had a temporal beginning and human generation is destined to end, since an unending temporal process would otherwise yield an unfitting, ever-swelling multitude of souls and citizens of the heavenly city, a problem uniquely and inexplicably tied to humans rather than angels, stars, or spheres; notes the resurrection of all the dead together (per the prior corollarium) implies waiting for a predetermined number to be completed, since the dead plainly do not rise individually as they die, and supports this further by analogy to angels, who serve humanity as messengers ('angel' meaning messenger) by God's will.
claims: Ancient calendrical diversity (short and varied year-lengths) explains away Egypt's implausible year-counts, removing the objection to the world's temporal beginning.
The doctrine of a single, collective future resurrection implies human generation is bounded, awaiting a divinely predetermined completed number of souls.
concepts: predetermined number of souls awaiting resurrection

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e20142.summary: Cites Hermes ('Father of Philosophers') and Aristotle (his 'son,' via the pseudo-Aristotelian Secret of Secrets) as concurring: two guardian spirits accompany each person, recording their deeds for the creator, but such extrinsic occupations are incompatible with perfect angelic beatitude, since they distract from the perfection of contemplative rest in God, and the angels' beatitude will only be perfected in full once human generation ends; adds that such occupations involve a kind of change in the angels, and change is incompatible with perfect beatitude and perfect good, since motion is the act of something imperfect moving toward perfection (per Aristotle's Physics), whereas a being of simple, unchanging nature enjoys one constant, most delightful activity, as God does — citing Aristotle's Ethics VII on the variability of pleasure in composite, corruptible natures versus the constancy proper to what is simple, and the Pythagorean placement of rest among the good and motion among the class of evil.
claims: Hermes and the pseudo-Aristotelian Secret of Secrets concur that angels' perfect beatitude, being incompatible with the ongoing distraction of guardianship duties and change, will only be completed once human generation ends.
Aristotle's own principles (Physics, Ethics) support that perfect, unchanging beatitude belongs properly to simple, unchanging natures, reinforcing the case for an end to human generation.
concepts: Hermes and pseudo-Aristotle on guardian angels
incompatibility of change with perfect beatitude

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e20190.summary: Argues, per the philosophers, that nothing unnatural or violent can be eternal, especially not for beings (like the elements) that never sinned against the law or author of nature and so should not eternally bear what would amount to a punishment; notes the elements are presently in an unnatural, violent disposition regarding their forms and places, which will only be fully naturally resolved once the generation of humans and the other animals that exist for humans' sake has ended (as Part 37 shows it can, and as these arguments show it should, more persuasively than the contrary can be argued, a view the clearest prophets and virtually all laws and sects concordantly affirm); concludes the world, or its accustomed state, will therefore end, and correspondingly celestial motion should cease too, since celestial motion is ultimately ordered, through the generation and conservation of lower things, toward man, who naturally presides over and uses all these things as the more perfect over the less perfect, and as a craftsman over his instruments.
claims: The elements' current unnatural, violent disposition will only be resolved once human (and animal) generation ends, supporting the conclusion that the world's present state, and celestial motion itself, will come to an end, since both are ultimately ordered toward man.
concepts: teleological ordering of celestial motion toward man

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e20227.summary: Cites Aristotle's own Physics ('we use all things for our sake, for we are in a way an end too') against Averroes' view that celestial movers act primarily for their own perfection and only secondarily for generating and preserving lower things, arguing it cannot be certain that the first mover (identified with God) needs any motion or extrinsic thing for his own perfection (contrary to Part 5), nor that the Intelligences are perfected by something extrinsic rather than sufficiently by their own intrinsic nature, especially since they do not move by natural necessity (unlike a body) but freely, as shown when the sun was made to stand still and move backward without this constituting any obstacle to the moving Intelligence's will or any diminishment of its perfection or beatitude, which consists more in its intrinsic contemplation of God than in any such extrinsic activity.
claims: Averroes' view that celestial Intelligences move primarily for their own perfection is undermined by the fact that they move freely, not by natural necessity, and their perfection consists in intrinsic contemplation of God, not extrinsic motion.
The episode of the sun standing still shows that suspending celestial motion involves no loss of perfection or beatitude for the moving Intelligence.
concepts: critique of Averroes' teleology of celestial motion
free versus necessary motion of Intelligences

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e20258.summary: Proposes that the primary intention of any Intelligence is to please God, moving the heavens for whatever cause God wills but ultimately, and most fundamentally, for God's sake alone — this perfect contemplation, love, and conformity of angelic will with the divine constitutes the angels' principal perfection, so they are no more perfect for moving externally than for resting entirely; suggests celestial motions are principally ordered toward man rather than toward the Intelligences' own perfection or any cause besides God, citing the sun and moon's miraculous halting or reversal when human benefit required it, and ordinary continuous motion when that served humans, concluding it is not unreasonable to think celestial motion will cease once human generation ceases, an inference the argument from the angels' beatitude (above) supports.
claims: An Intelligence's primary intention is to please God, and its perfection lies wholly in contemplative conformity to the divine will, not in external motion; celestial motion is principally ordered toward man, supporting the inference that it will cease when human generation ceases.
concepts: angelic perfection as conformity to divine will

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e20295.summary: Argues that angels, like humans, are or ought to be perfectly blessed, and perfect beatitude for any rational creature consists in perfect contemplation of God (Part 23, affirmed by Aristotle and other philosophers); since any finite rational creature can contemplate, enjoy, and adhere to God more perfectly when wholly devoted to him alone than when occupied with extrinsic matters not essentially ordered to that end (such as moving external bodies), and since we experience in ourselves that external occupation diminishes our capacity for contemplation, the same must hold, a fortiori, for angels of finite power — otherwise they could take on ever more external tasks without any loss to their contemplation, which is absurd; concludes that external motion somewhat diminishes the angels' beatitude, that their perfect beatitude consists in total rest rather than motion, and notes that more perfect, higher angels moving nobler bodies do so with fewer motions and greater withdrawal from motion toward stillness, so their beatitude will not be supremely perfected until they cease moving and being externally occupied altogether.
claims: By analogy with human experience (external occupation diminishes contemplation) and the observed pattern that higher angels move with fewer motions, angelic beatitude is shown to be diminished by external motion and will only be supremely perfected once such motion ceases entirely.
concepts: diminishment of contemplation by external occupation

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e20357.summary: Concludes that the heavens will indeed eventually come to rest, and reasons this will most fittingly occur once the number of souls and blessed humans, predetermined by divine wisdom, has been completed and settled in the heavenly palace (per the preceding part), so that the heavenly city and God's most glorious household may be perfected all at once in its dwellings and citizens — angels and humans together — resting in blessed stillness around their Prince, God, in an everlasting, most delightful banquet that constitutes their full, perfect, and tranquil refreshment, beatitude, and accumulated felicity.
claims: The heavens will come to rest once the predetermined number of blessed souls is completed, so that angels and humans together may be perfected simultaneously in eternal, restful beatitude around God.
concepts: completion of the predetermined number of souls
final rest of the heavenly city

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e20377.summary: Argues that the most perfect natural body should have the most perfect bodily disposition, and rest is more perfect than motion (as already shown), so heaven, once supremely perfect, will come to rest; asks what purpose celestial motion would serve once human generation ceases, since it could not be for acquiring or preserving any perfection in an unalterable, incorruptible body; further asks when the lower elemental world could achieve its most natural disposition (spherical, evenly nested elements, and so on) except once celestial motion ceases — concluding that the whole cosmos, celestial and elemental, together with the whole company of heavenly citizens (angels and humans), will be perfected and made blessed all at once, perhaps receiving from God qualities far better than at present, the elements becoming transparent to light yet unalterable and incorruptible, like a garnet, sapphire, crystal, or emerald, just as was said earlier of the bodies of the blessed.
claims: The most perfect natural body (heaven) will come to rest once supremely perfect, and the whole cosmos — celestial and elemental — together with all its rational inhabitants will be perfected and transformed simultaneously, the elements becoming incorruptible and luminous like precious stones.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e20414.summary: Argues it is most fitting for God to perfect his own work, house, temple, and heavenly city in the most fitting way, and nothing is impossible or difficult for the omnipotent God; suggests some part of the earth (such as Tartarus) may nonetheless perpetually suffer some violence or unnaturalness as punishment for the wicked, who sinned violently and unnaturally against nature's law and author, so that both good and evil may be fittingly ordered in corresponding degrees and the blessed's glory may shine more fully by contrast; cites Ptolemy (previously quoted) affirming celestial motions will cease ('the eternal things enduring until the limit their maker set for them' in the Almagest referring precisely to celestial motions, not to the substance of the heavens, which he did not think would be corrupted), and cites Albumasar affirming the planets are incorruptible in substance yet subject to eventual cessation of their imperfect accidents and motion 'until the time God wills,' and that the effects of the planets' natural, durable motions likewise last only 'until the time God wills,' per the consensus of all ancient philosophers.
claims: Ptolemy's Almagest and Albumasar's astrological treatise both affirm that celestial motion (though not celestial substance) will eventually cease, at a time set by God's will.
The wicked's eternal punishment may involve a part of the earth (Tartarus) perpetually suffering an unnatural, violent state, contrasting with and enhancing the blessed's glory.
concepts: Ptolemy on the cessation of celestial motion

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e20456.summary: Quotes Hermes Trismegistus at length (De Verbo Aeterno) foretelling a coming cosmic old age marked by disorder and irreligion — the earth unstable, the sea unnavigable, the heavens and stars off course, divine voices silenced, the earth's fruitfulness failing — after which God, the one Lord and governor of all, observing the world's voluntary corruption, will in his goodness resist vice, undo the corruption of all errors, and cleanse away all malice (by flood, fire, or plague), restoring the world to its ancient face so that it may again be worthy of worship and wonder, and its restorer God be praised by the people then living — reads this restoration as eternal in God's mind and will even though enacted in time, and connects it to Hermes' distinction between an intelligible world in God and a sensible world in nature, a distinction followed by Plato's Timaeus (archetypal versus sensible world, the former eternal, the latter begun in time as the image of the archetype) — noting the clearest prophets and the Sibyl likewise prophesied this same teaching, as recounted regarding Part 32.
claims: Hermes Trismegistus prophesies a final cosmic corruption followed by a divine restoration of the world to its original, worthy state, paralleling Plato's distinction between an eternal archetypal world in God and a temporally-begun sensible world.
The clearest prophets and the Sibyl are said to have prophesied the same teaching of eventual cosmic restoration, as previously discussed regarding Part 32.
concepts: Hermes' prophecy of cosmic old age and restoration

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e20519.summary: Notes that all who hold the world was made from pre-existing matter rather than created from nothing are corrected by the preceding arguments, and all who hold the world must be corrupted are thereby committed to saying the same of blessed souls and humans, which the immediately preceding part also corrects; marvels at how many and how great errors this single, modest first Supposition (that God is that than which nothing better can be conceived, and has whatever is better to have) refutes and corrects, suggesting there is scarcely any possible error about God or his essential attributes that cannot be forcefully destroyed by its power, since any error about God contradicts either God's having what is better to have or his not having what is better not to have; acknowledges many errors already discussed could also be corrected by other routes not pursued here for the sake of brevity, and closes by likening this 'golden Supposition' to a cornerstone of philosophers and theologians — most powerful, precious, beautiful, proven, chosen, and perfect in every way — laid as the foundation of the whole structure of the work.
claims: The first Supposition (God as that than which nothing better can be conceived) is presented as a single, foundational principle capable of refuting virtually any possible error concerning God, and is likened to the cornerstone of the entire work's structure.
concepts: closing summation of the chapter's method

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e20554.summary: Anticipates that some will nonetheless try to disprove this 'proven stone' or at least its proof, as they will with other parts of the work, comparing them to the Sadducees who, per Josephus, gloried in contending against genuine philosophers; observes that many who have built nothing themselves are all the bolder in tearing down what others have built, risking nothing of their own, so that by appearing to destroy others' constructions — though building nothing themselves — they may seem more glorious than the actual builders, this being, as authors define it, the vice of seeking frequent, praised fame without genuine merit.
claims: The author anticipates critics who will attempt to tear down this work's arguments without having constructed anything comparable themselves, likening them to the Sadducees' vain glorying in contentious argument.

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e20579.summary: Closes the chapter with a personal prayer: that the author and his fellow disciples and servants, setting aside blinding pride, may seek with simple minds not the appearance of empty vanity but the reality of solid truth, so as to find, know, and hold it truly under God's guidance; acknowledges that God frequently frustrates, scorns, and confounds the proud and envious pursuits of the arrogant while favoring, loving, illuminating, and perfecting the simple pursuits of the humble; and, having offered these remarks as a kind of prelude, resolves to proceed confidently to the proposed cause of God with continual divine assistance.
concepts: humility versus pride in seeking truth
transition to the work's continuing argument

dcn2br-d1e796-d1e16759.summary: Argues that if man's consummated felicity consisted in anything besides God, it would consist in some finite, small good, since nothing outside God can be a greater good; asks how God — most just, most powerful, most abundant, and most generous, who has ordained that he alone be loved and worshipped by humans to such a degree that they should never knowingly offend him for any good to be gained or kept, or any evil to be avoided or removed (Part 30) — could repay such total love, worship, and service with only a paltry reward, since he ought to reward generously, not sparingly (Part 31); concludes that what he will render, once the campaign of service is complete, must be some good greater than all the goods hoped for and evils endured, especially since this is easily within his power and most fitting for both parties — and such a good, greater than every imaginable good besides himself, can only be God himself.
claims: If human felicity consisted in anything other than God, it would be a merely finite good, incompatible with the total love and service God has ordained be given to him and with his obligation to reward generously.
The only reward proportionate to total love, worship, and service of God is God himself, since nothing else could be a greater good.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e433.summary: Opens the forty-part moral corollary appended to the two suppositions, each part refuting a distinct error about God; this first part applies the preceding demonstration directly against Protagoras, who (per Lactantius) doubted the gods' existence.
claims: The moral corollary comprises 40 parts, each refuting a distinct error.
Protagoras's skepticism about the gods' existence is refuted by the prior proof of God's existence.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e462.summary: Extends the refutation to those who deny God's existence outright, calling on Diagoras and the biblical 'fool' (Psalm 14/53) to recognize God's existence in light of the demonstration.
claims: Outright denial of God's existence (Diagoras, the fool) is refuted by the prior demonstration.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e480.summary: Refutes those who doubt God really possesses every power and good, arguing from God's supreme perfection (the first Supposition) and the priority of act over potency that God's supreme actuality entails full possession of goodness with no residual potentiality.
claims: If God lacked any perfection or good, something more perfect than God would be possible, contrary to the first Supposition.
God's supreme actuality entails full possession of goodness without unrealized potentiality.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e551.summary: Refutes the claim that God's power and goodness are merely finite, arguing finite power/goodness could always be increased (contrary to supreme perfection), and illustrating, via geometrical and physical analogies, that something can be absolutely possible without being naturally possible.
claims: Finite divine power or goodness could always be increased, contrary to the first Supposition.
Something can be per se/absolutely possible without being naturally possible.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e588.summary: Refutes denial of God's full self-sufficiency, arguing sufficiency is itself a good entailed by the first Supposition, and marshaling authorities (Aristotle, the 24 Philosophers, the divine name Shaddai, Jerome) attesting that God lacks nothing.
claims: Sufficiency (needing nothing outside oneself) is a good, and so belongs to God by the first Supposition and by traditional divine names.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e630.summary: Refutes the views that God is only contingently perfect, is mutable or passible, or that 'God' names an accident rather than the essence, arguing necessary perfection is superior to contingent perfection and that God cannot change for better, worse, or an equal state.
claims: God is necessarily, not merely contingently, supremely perfect and immutable.
'God' names the divine essence, not an accident.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e701.summary: Defends God's active omnipotence together with total passive impassibility (inability to be acted upon), deriving both from the prior parts on divine plenitude, infinite power, and immutability.
claims: God is actively omnipotent.
God cannot be acted upon by anything else, since that would entail mutability.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e727.summary: Defends that God, as substance and as rational, possesses actual (not merely habitual) intellect and free will, and that God's will is universally and unfailingly efficacious, tying this to the requirement that supreme beatitude consist in having all that one justly wills.
claims: God possesses actual intellect and free will.
God's will is universally efficacious (unimpedible, unfrustrable, undefective).
Supreme beatitude requires having all that one justly wills.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e820.summary: Refutes denial of divine omniscience (attributed to some readings of philosophers and even misapplied scriptural voices), arguing God knows himself and all else — including future contingents and changeable singulars — perfectly, distinctly, and eternally rather than newly, grounding this in God's actuality, infinite power, and self-sufficiency, and in the fittingness of prayer and just recompense; addresses and dismisses Aristotelian/Averroan worries that knowledge of base or infinitely many particulars, or of mutable singulars, would compromise God's dignity or immutability.
claims: God knows himself and all things, including future contingents and changeable singulars, perfectly, distinctly, and eternally, without thereby becoming mutable.
The fittingness of prayer and of just divine recompense presupposes God's omniscience.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e1030.summary: Defends God's absolute simplicity, indivisibility, and incorporeality against any anthropomorphic or other composition, arguing that composition would entail divisibility and corruptibility, that any composing or unifying principle would be naturally prior to God (contrary to the first Supposition), and that whether God's hypothetical parts are finite or infinite, in number or intensity, composition always undermines his supreme and infinite perfection.
claims: If God were composed of parts, he could be divided, changed, or corrupted, contrary to his established perfection and immutability.
Any part or unifying form composing God would be naturally prior to God, contrary to the first Supposition.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e1119.summary: Refutes the Sabians' worship of the heavens as God, arguing (from the immediately preceding case against composition and finitude) that the heavens are finite in power, mutable, and lacking possible perfections, hence not God.
claims: The heavens are finite, mutable, and lacking possible perfections, hence not God.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e1152.summary: Extends the refutation of celestial worship to worshipers of the Sun, Moon, and planets, on the same grounds of finitude, mutability, and lack of possible perfections.
claims: Worship of the Sun, Moon, or planets is refuted for the same reasons as worship of the heavens as a whole.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e1175.summary: Refutes the deification of humans, animals, trees, and fire, cataloguing instances of such idolatry (euhemerist Roman deification of heroes, the Babylonian dragon and Egyptian Apis-bull cults linked to the golden calf, contemporary bull-worship reported by Marco Polo, the oracular Trees of the Sun and Moon), and concluding that no temporal, generable, corruptible, or irrational creature can be God, since God alone is necessary being.
claims: Ancient and contemporary deification of humans, animals, trees, or fire is attested across many sources.
No mere creature — being generable, corruptible, or irrational — can be God, since God is necessary being.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e1392.summary: Refutes polytheism positing several equal gods of one nature through multiple converging arguments: one sufficient God suffices completely; the divine nature cannot be multiplied into numerically distinct individuals without permitting an actual infinity of gods; several equal gods could not each be per se and first; and independent equal wills could obstruct one another, contrary to established divine immutability and efficacy — reinforced by the broad natural-philosophical, theological, political, and microcosmic consensus favoring a single first or ruling principle.
claims: The divine nature cannot be multiplied into several numerically distinct individuals, since that would permit an actual infinity of gods.
Broad philosophical consensus (cosmological, political, microcosmic) favors a single supreme ruling principle, supporting the necessity of one God.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e1617.summary: Refutes belief in several gods differing by species or domain (one over the East, one over crops, etc.), arguing each would lack the specific perfection proper to the others and so fail to be supremely perfect.
claims: Gods differentiated by species or domain would each lack some other's specific perfection, hence fail to be supremely perfect.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e1652.summary: Surveys and rejects ancient hierarchical pantheons (Greco-Roman gods subordinated to Jupiter, the Tartar sky-god Natagay), since none of the purported subordinate deities is supremely perfect.
claims: Various cultures' hierarchical pantheons are rejected because their subordinate deities are not supremely perfect.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e1717.summary: Defends the strict necessity, not mere possibility, of divine unicity against philosophers who held a plurality of gods possible, arguing only God is uncaused and partless, so anything else could be annihilated by God's omnipotent will and hence cannot be necessary being.
claims: Only God can be necessary being, since only God is uncaused and partless.
It is necessary that a unique necessary being exists and impossible that any other being be necessary.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e1787.summary: Traces the history of dualistic cosmogonies positing two irreducible first principles (Empedocles's Love and Strife, the Pythagorean paired principles, Manichaeism) and refutes them doubly: for positing a plurality of gods (already excluded) and for positing an evil God, impossible since everything that exists, as existing, is good.
claims: Dualist theologians err doubly, positing multiple gods and positing an evil God, both already excluded.
Every existing thing, as existing, is good; nothing is simply evil.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e1966.summary: Refutes the poetic claim that the gods envy excellent human beings, since envy is an evil incompatible with divine impassibility.
claims: Envy cannot be attributed to God, since it is an evil.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e1988.summary: Refutes attributing base and dishonorable behaviors (eating, drinking, sexual license, theatrical delight) to the gods, cataloguing pagan mythological indecencies and citing Aristotle's and Plato's own civic condemnation of such 'poetic theology'; argues by dilemma that God cannot eat (whether from necessity or pleasure) or unite sexually, since both are incompatible with his incorporeality, temperance, self-sufficiency, and unicity.
claims: Ancient religions attributed base needs and behaviors to their gods, which classical philosophers themselves condemned.
Eating and sexual union are incompatible with God's incorporeality, self-sufficiency, and unicity.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e2156.summary: Mounts the corollary's most extended sustained refutation of idol-worship in every form: idols are finite, corruptible, and composite, inferior even to natural things already shown not to be God; ritual consecration cannot confer divinity nor 'transubstantiate' an idol into God; no angel or spirit can be compelled by ritual to inhabit an idol; Hermes Trismegistus's doctrine of animated 'lesser gods' and the more sophisticated defense of one God worshiped under many names/idols (polyonymy) are both rejected as incoherent or pastorally dangerous; concludes it is more practical and secure to rely on one all-sufficient God than on a Varronian scheme of specialized patron deities.
claims: No idol, however consecrated or 'animated,' can be or contain God.
Polyonymous worship of one God through many idols is unnecessary and risks misleading the unlearned into practical polytheism.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e2672.summary: Refutes Arian subordinationism, which makes the Son and Holy Spirit temporal, unequal creatures of the Father, arguing this implies a plurality and inequality of gods and denies any divine Person the eternity and necessary existence required by the first Supposition.
claims: Arian subordinationism implies a plurality and inequality of gods, contrary to the first Supposition.
Any Person denied eternity and necessary existence thereby fails to be God.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e2706.summary: Refutes Donatist subordinationism, which holds the divine Persons of the same substance but unequal magnitude, arguing a Person of lesser magnitude could not be supremely perfect and so could not be God.
claims: A Person of lesser magnitude than the others could not be supremely perfect, hence could not be God.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e2733.summary: Refutes Sabellian modalism (identity of Person and essence in Father and Son) by dilemma — self-causation is impossible, and generation from 'another' entails either that other's being God (multiplying gods) or not being God (contradicting the first Supposition) — and rejects the fallback of successive divine roles as entailing mutability.
claims: Sabellian identity of the Persons collapses into impossible self-causation or contradicts the first Supposition.
Successive divine roles (now Father, then Son, then Spirit) would make God mutable.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e2787.summary: Distinguishes proper senses of God's 'infinite power,' denying that God is intensively infinite as a matter of degree (which would entail either diminishable power or a lesser divine nature) while affirming God is truly, if improperly, infinite in power relative to other active powers, the unique capacity for creation from nothing, and the absence of any maximal or minimal limit on action.
claims: God is neither intensifiable nor remittable, being of a simple, immutable nature.
God is truly, though improperly, infinite in power in three respects: relative to any other active power, relative to creation ex nihilo, and relative to the extrinsic measure of action.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e2897.summary: Refutes attributing accidental qualities, attributes, habits, or acts to God distinct from his essence, arguing through several dilemmas (superfluous versus necessary; finite versus infinite in number or intensity; mutability from removable accidents) that God is subject to no accidents whatsoever.
claims: God has no real accidents distinct from his essence, since any such accident, on any analysis, would compromise his supreme perfection, self-sufficiency, or immutability.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e2956.summary: Refutes despair grounded in the magnitude of one's sins (the 'Cainite' type, after Cain's own despair in Genesis 4) or their multitude (a reported contemporary Jewish view grounding a limit on repeated pardon in Amos 1's 'three...and four' formula), arguing that any finite sin or number of sins, however great, is incomparably outweighed by God's infinitely infinite mercy, and reinterpreting the true 'fourth sin' that forecloses pardon as final impenitence at death rather than a numbered relapse.
claims: No sin, however great or often repeated, can exceed the scope of God's infinite mercy.
The 'fourth sin' that truly forecloses pardon, properly understood, is final impenitence at death, not a fourth relapse into the same sin.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e3227.summary: Refutes the Cainite requirement that reconciling grace demands satisfaction proportionate to the sin committed, showing this would force any grave, repeatedly sinning person into inescapable despair, and arguing from God's supreme mercy that requiring full prior satisfaction before any remission would make it an act of justice rather than mercy.
claims: Requiring proportionate satisfaction before pardon, applied consistently, forces the grave repeat sinner into necessary despair.
Requiring full satisfaction before any remission is an act of justice, not mercy, and so is incompatible with God's supreme mercy.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e3282.summary: Refutes the Pelagian claim that God gives no benefit gratuitously but only in return for prior merit, arguing from the very meaning of gratia (grace) as definitionally gratuitous — supported by classical testimony on the Graces and on benefits owing nothing in return — and from God's infinite liberality, which entails giving beyond mere exchange for merit.
claims: A 'grace' given only in return for merit is not truly grace.
God's infinite liberality entails gratuitous giving, by analogy with human liberality.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e3343.summary: Defends, against those unversed in the 'art of loving' God, that God alone is to be loved for his own sake, with everything else loved for his sake, and that no one may ever knowingly sin against God, even minimally, for the sake of any temporal good or evil — grounded in the order of ends (nothing is more lovable than God), the impossibility of an infinite regress among objects of love (the second Supposition), and the incomparable gravity of offending the greatest possible person, and defended against a hypothetical objector by an exhaustive dilemma showing that a rightly-done, sinful, or indifferent act could never coherently justify knowing offense against God.
claims: God alone is to be loved for his own sake; all else is to be loved for God's sake and ordered to him.
No temporal good or evil ever justifies knowingly sinning against God, even minimally.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e3564.summary: Refutes the 'unrestrained' view that good and evil befall the just and the wicked equally, arguing that sin and merit each carry an immediate, intrinsic moral consequence independent of any visible outcome, that God (like any just ruler, a fortiori) differentiates treatment according to merit, and that God punishes below and rewards above strict condign measure out of mercy and superabundant liberality respectively, while divine punishment is always medicinal and corrective rather than vindictive, ordered to the good and beauty of the universe; closes with a political analogy that fear of punishment and hope of reward are both necessary for good governance.
claims: Sin and right action each carry an immediate, inseparable moral consequence regardless of external outcome.
God punishes below and rewards above condign measure, out of mercy and liberality.
Divine punishment is corrective and medicinal, not vindictive.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e3845.summary: The corollary's longest and most wide-ranging part, directed against philosophers who presume to fully comprehend God and dismiss Christian belief in matters beyond natural demonstration. It first argues that no finite mind can fully know an infinite God or even exhaust the intelligibility of a single creature, that philosophical 'certainty' is itself often only consensus-based credence, and that God's free will is not bound to produce any single 'best possible' effect — so revelation and testimony are legitimate, philosophically-precedented sources of knowledge alongside demonstration. It then mounts an extensive cumulative apologetic for Christianity's truth: assembling Old Testament, Sibylline, and other pagan prophetic testimony to Christ's birth, life, Passion, and Resurrection; defending the historicity and evidentiary force of Christ's miracles against naturalistic explanations (bodily 'complexion,' astrological conjunction, imaginative power) and against charges of demonic magic; reading the destruction of Jerusalem and the cessation of Temple signs as fulfillment of Daniel's prophecy and just punishment for the rejection of Christ; engaging Muslim philosophers on comparative astrology, the incoherence of a carnal paradise, and the superiority of a law ordered to the soul's rational happiness; affirming that virtuous pagans outside Israel (Job, Nebuchadnezzar, Alexander) could receive genuine revelation and be judged by sincere intention amid invincible ignorance; and arguing that natural law and reason alone cannot suffice, since God's giving of positive revealed law implies its necessity — culminating in the doctrine that only Christ, God and man together, can render adequate satisfaction for sin, so that all people are urged to become Christian.
claims: No finite mind, unaided, can fully comprehend God or even exhaust the intelligibility of a single creature.
God's will is free and not bound to produce any single 'best possible' effect.

Testimony, prophecy, and miracle constitute legitimate, cumulative evidence for the truth of Christian revelation, defended against Jewish and Muslim rival claims and against naturalistic or demonic explanations of Christ's miracles.
God's revelation and providence are not confined to Israel or later believers, extending to virtuous pagans judged by sincere intention amid invincible ignorance.
Positive revealed law is necessary beyond natural reason, and only Christ as God-man can render adequate satisfaction for human sin.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e9115.summary: Refutes philosophers who deny the possibility of creation from nothing, annihilation, and re-creation, arguing that God's supreme perfection, sufficiency, infinite power, and universally efficacious will entail the capacity to produce something without pre-existing matter (a greater mode of causing than any created cause exhibits), and that annihilation and re-creation follow by parallel reasoning; appeals to Aristotle's and Averroes's own principle that near-universal human consensus carries evidential weight.
claims: God's supreme, infinite power and universally efficacious will entail the possibility of creation ex nihilo, annihilation, and re-creation.
The philosophers' denial is refuted by their own principle that universal human belief carries evidential weight, and by their own notorious mutual inconsistency.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e9219.summary: Extends the case for creation from things in general to the world specifically, then mounts an extensive, technical rebuttal of Aristotle's and Averroes's argument for the world's eternity (Physics VIII): diagnoses the argument as repeatedly begging the question by covertly assuming non-being must temporally (not merely naturally) precede being; distinguishes priority of nature from priority of time in God's causation of a temporally-originated world; answers objections about imaginary prior time, the 'presence of time' triggering change in the divine will, and the coherence of a free agent's ability to act at a freely chosen moment without prior change; marshals Augustine at length on divine eternity as substance rather than duration; and closes by citing Aristotle's own admissions (and an alleged deathbed confession) that his arguments here are merely dialectical, not demonstrative, undermining their authority.
claims: Aristotle's and Averroes's argument for the world's eternity covertly and repeatedly assumes, without proof, that non-being must temporally precede being.

A free, rational agent (unlike an irrational natural power) can remain fully disposed to act yet freely delay acting for any span of time, even eternally, without requiring a prior change to explain the timing.
God's eternity precedes the world only by nature, not by any actual temporal duration, as Augustine and Boethius affirm.
Aristotle himself elsewhere classifies the eternity of the world as an undecidable dialectical problem, undermining the argument's claimed certainty.
concepts: priority of nature vs. priority of time
freedom of the will and timing of action

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e9999.summary: Defends the possibility of the Virgin Birth against philosophers and heretics who deny it, arguing first from God's already-established omnipotence (creation, annihilation, universal miracle-working) and from natural-historical precedents of non-copulatory conception in animals (wind-conceived mares, partridges conceiving by call or scent), then marshaling an extended astrological case — the zodiacal sign of Virgo (depicted across Babylonian, Persian, Egyptian, and Indian tradition as a virgin nursing a child called 'Jesus'), a great Saturn-Jupiter conjunction under Mercury shortly before Christ's birth, and the pseudo-Ovidian De Vetula — as providential signs (not causes) of the virgin birth, and closes with a genealogy tracing astrology's own origins to a line of divinely-inspired patriarchs (Seth, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Solomon).
claims: God's established omnipotence and natural-historical precedents of non-copulatory animal conception together remove any philosophical obstacle to virginal conception.

Multiple independent astrological and astronomical traditions (the Virgo decan, the Saturn-Jupiter conjunction, Mercury symbolism) are read as providential signs, not causes, of Christ's virgin birth.
Astrology and astronomy themselves trace back to a divinely-inspired patriarchal lineage (Seth, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Solomon), lending this astrological evidence additional credibility.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e10634.summary: Refutes the Epicureans and Sadducees, who deny any incorporeal spirit and the rational soul's immortality, and at much greater length refutes Averroes's doctrine that all humans share a single separate rational soul (monopsychism), marshaling a long chain of arguments: individualized divine reward and punishment presupposes individual souls; a single finite soul could not simultaneously move, know, or will diversely for countless bodies; shared knowledge would follow from a shared intellect, contrary to experience; Averroes's own commentaries on the tabula-rasa doctrine and on the possible/agent intellect are shown to be self-contradictory; the theory entails absurd consequences (infants not being rational animals, contrary states coexisting in one soul, an incoherent 'conjunction' of a separate intelligence to individuals); and the broad consensus of Aristotle (properly read), Avicenna, Algazel, and virtually all peoples and philosophers favors individually created, individually immortal rational souls, which God's omnipotence and generosity can and fittingly did bestow.
claims: Denial of incorporeal spirit and of the soul's immortality (Epicureans, Sadducees) is refuted by the prior demonstration of God as incorporeal spirit and creator of immortal souls and angels.

Averroes's monopsychism is refuted on many independent grounds: it cannot account for individualized reward and punishment, for a finite soul's inability to serve infinitely many bodies at once, for differing individual knowledge, and it is self-contradictory even within Averroes's own commentaries.

The near-universal philosophical and religious consensus (Aristotle properly read, Avicenna, Algazel) favors individually created, individually immortal rational souls, which God's omnipotence and generosity fittingly bestow on each human being.
concepts: creation ex nihilo of the soul

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e12147.summary: Refutes philosophers who deny that celestial motion and human generation can cease, that the dead can bodily rise, or that the risen good and wicked can be raised to heaven and cast to hell respectively for eternity, arguing from God's already-established omnipotence (and scriptural precedent of halting/reversing the sun) that he can halt celestial motion, and marshaling a long a fortiori case for bodily resurrection from creation, the virgin birth, God's infinite restorative power (against the axiom that privation cannot return to habit), and an extensive catalogue of reported lesser bodily transformations (Circe's metamorphoses, lycanthropy, sex change, Nebuchadnezzar's transformation, the evil eye, necromancy) — concluding that if such lesser, finite or even demonic powers can transform bodies, God's infinite omnipotence can raise the dead, elevate the risen to heaven, cast the wicked to hell, and sustain both states forever.
claims: God's demonstrated omnipotence and efficacious will, already shown to halt and reverse celestial motion, extend to halting celestial motion and human generation altogether.

A wide array of reported lesser bodily transformations (metamorphosis, lycanthropy, sex change, evil-eye magic) supports an a fortiori argument that God's infinite omnipotence can raise the dead and sustain them eternally in heaven or hell.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e12665.summary: Defends the proportionality of an everlasting reward or punishment to temporal merit or sin, arguing by analogy with human feudal grants that God's supreme generosity fittingly rewards temporal service everlastingly, rejecting the objection that a virtuous act's intrinsic goodness is itself sufficient reward, and arguing symmetrically that an offense knowingly committed against the infinitely great God deserves infinite (eternal) punishment, since the sinner's self-incurred inability to satisfy does not excuse the debt but leaves him liable to guilt and its inseparable punishment.
claims: By analogy with human generosity, God's supreme goodness fittingly rewards temporal merit with an everlasting reward.
An offense against a person of infinite dignity deserves proportionately infinite (eternal) punishment.
Self-incurred inability to satisfy for sin does not excuse the sinner, who remains liable to guilt and its inseparable punishment.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e12869.summary: The corollary's second-longest part, refuting a wide array of rival eschatologies and defending the Christian doctrine of bodily resurrection to differentiated, everlasting bliss or misery in heaven and hell. Refutes Epicurean/Sadducee denial of any afterlife; refutes Pythagorean/Platonic/Ovidian transmigration of souls into other bodies (immediate or after a cyclical 'Great Year,' whose various proposed lengths are individually refuted astronomically and historically) as incompatible with essential species-distinction, the soul's specific natural appetite for its own body, and the requirement that the very person who merited be the one rewarded; refutes Averroes's and Aristotle's intellectualist account of felicity as a momentary conjunction with the separate agent intellect, as inadequate, self-undermining, and incapable of accounting for the wicked's misery; argues at length that the whole person, body and soul together, must be beatified, that heaven is the soul's and hence the whole person's fitting natural place (with hell the fitting place for the damned), that risen bodies must be divinely transformed to an incorruptible, glorified condition; and concludes that consummate beatitude can consist in nothing other than God himself, not in any created or carnal good, since only an infinite good can satisfy the soul's naturally insatiable desire and only God befits the total love and service he has commanded.
claims: Denial of any post-mortem differentiated reward (Epicureans, Sadducees) and doctrines of transmigration (immediate or cyclical) are both refuted — the latter chiefly because justice requires that the very person, in the very body, who merited be the one rewarded.
The Averroist/Aristotelian account of felicity as momentary intellectual conjunction is inadequate: too brief, self-undermining, and unable to explain the wicked's proper misery.

The whole human person, body and soul reunited and divinely transformed to an incorruptible condition, must be beatified in heaven (its natural place) or punished in hell, and consummate beatitude can consist in nothing but God himself, since only an infinite good satisfies the soul's naturally insatiable desire.

dcn2br-d1e796-Dd1e16276.summary: The corollary's final and most technically elaborate part, refuting Aristotle's (and other ancients') doctrine that the world is eternal and uncreated and that celestial motion and human generation will never end. dcn2br-d1e796.summary: Chapter 1 of Book I of Thomas Bradwardine's De Causa Dei. It opens by proposing two suppositions — (1) God is supremely perfect and good, such that nothing better could be conceived, and (2) there is no infinite regress among beings, so there is a first in every genus — first supported by a chain of philosophical and patristic authorities (Hermes Trismegistus, Aristotle, Boethius, Anselm, Richard of St. Victor, Augustine), then established by a formal demonstration: from the bare possibility that something (A) exists, the argument moves through the priority of necessary over merely possible being to show that A must exist necessarily, per se, and uncaused — that is, that God exists as the being than which nothing more perfect can be conceived — a proof that simultaneously secures the second supposition as well. The chapter then appends a sprawling forty-part 'moral corollary,' using the two suppositions (chiefly the first) as a master key to refute forty distinct errors, moving outward from ancient skepticism and atheism (Protagoras, Diagoras), through denial of individual divine attributes (plenitude, infinity, self-sufficiency, immutability, omnipotence, intellect and will, omniscience, simplicity), celestial and idolatrous worship in all its historical and theurgic forms, the many varieties of polytheism (equal or hierarchical gods, dualism/Manichaeism), unworthy conceptions of God, the Trinitarian heresies (Arianism, Donatism, Sabellianism), despair over sin and Pelagian denial of gratuitous grace, the primacy of loving God for himself, and the proportionality of divine reward and punishment. Its longest and most wide-ranging part (Corollarium 32) mounts an extensive cumulative apologetic for the truth of Christian revelation against philosophical skepticism, Judaism, and Islam, grounded in prophecy, miracle, and testimony. The final parts take up, in turn, the possibility of creation, annihilation, and re-creation; the possibility of the world's creation against Aristotle's eternity thesis; the virgin birth; the immortality and individuation of the rational soul against Epicureans, Sadducees, and Averroistic monopsychism; the possibility and eternal, differentiated character of bodily resurrection and reward/punishment; and, in a climactic technical finale, a rigorous refutation — including a medieval mathematical 'argument from infinity' — of Aristotle's doctrine that the world and celestial motion are without beginning or end, concluding that both will cease once a predetermined number of souls has been perfected within a transformed, incorruptible cosmos. The chapter closes by presenting the whole forty-part corollary as proof of the generative power of the single 'golden' first Supposition, with a personal prayer for humility in the pursuit of truth.
claims: The chapter establishes, by both authority and formal demonstration, that God exists as supremely perfect being (nothing better conceivable) and that there is no infinite regress in being (a first in every genus).

These two suppositions, especially the first, function as a master principle from which the chapter derives refutations of forty distinct theological, philosophical, and religious errors, ranging from ancient atheism and idolatry through Trinitarian heresy to Aristotle's eternity-of-the-world thesis.

The chapter's longest sustained argument (Corollarium 32) mounts a comprehensive apologetic case for the truth of Christian revelation against philosophical skepticism, Judaism, and Islam, grounded in prophecy, miracle, and testimony.

The chapter concludes that celestial motion and human generation will cease once a divinely predetermined number of souls is completed, followed by the incorruptible transformation of the cosmos and the eternal, differentiated reward and punishment of the resurrected.
